abstract: RNA technology, most prominently messenger RNA (mRNA), has transformed vaccine development by enabling rapid, sequence-specific antigen design, scalable manufacturing, and transient protein expression. Its long-term significance, however, extends beyond prophylactic vaccination. This Perspective argues that mRNA should be conceptualised as a programmable therapeutic platform capable of integrating vaccination, immune modulation, and on-demand disease treatment. Current mRNA vaccines deliver predefined antigenic instructions, whereas emerging RNA systems, including self-amplifying RNA (saRNA), circular RNA, sequence-engineered mRNA, and targeted lipid nanoparticles (LNPs), may support more adaptable therapeutic functions. Such platforms could prime immunity, replace deficient proteins, encode antibodies, reprogramme immune cells, or induce antigen-specific tolerance. The concept of self-adaptive RNA-based therapeutics remains at an early stage and should not be overstated; most existing systems are programmable at the design stage rather than biologically autonomous after administration. Nonetheless, this conceptual position is no longer purely speculative: the first regulatory approval of a self-amplifying RNA vaccine and controlled-trial evidence of clinical benefit from a personalised neoantigen mRNA therapeutic in resected melanoma indicate that programmable RNA platforms are beginning to move from concept to clinical validation across both the prophylactic and therapeutic ends of the spectrum. Key challenges include tissue-specific delivery, expression control, innate immune activation, repeat dosing, safety assessment, regulatory classification, and equitable access. A self-adaptive RNA-based framework does not replace existing vaccines or biologics but extends them towards responsive, personalised, and temporally controlled therapy.

title: Programmable RNA therapeutics: converging vaccination and on-demand disease treatment via self-adaptive RNA platforms.

abstract: Gene therapy has emerged as a revolutionary therapeutic strategy for the treatment of inherited, acquired, and age-related diseases through the modification, replacement, or correction of defective genes. Advances in molecular biology, viral engineering, and genome-editing technologies have significantly enhanced the efficiency and safety of gene delivery systems. This review provides a comprehensive overview of gene therapy, including its classification, delivery methods, and therapeutic applications in both human and veterinary medicine. Viral vectors such as adenoviral, retroviral, lentiviral, adeno-associated viral, and poxviral vectors remain the most effective delivery platforms owing to their high transduction efficiency, whereas non-viral approaches including physical and chemical delivery systems offer improved biosafety and reduced immunogenicity. Recent developments in gene-editing technologies, particularly clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats (CRISPR)-associated protein systems, have expanded the therapeutic potential of gene therapy by enabling precise genome modifications. The review highlights the successful application of gene therapy in treating genetic disorders, cancer gene therapy, retinal diseases, neuromuscular disorders, hemophilia, and metabolic diseases in humans, as well as inherited and acquired diseases in companion and livestock animals. Despite remarkable progress, challenges related to delivery efficiency, immune responses, off-target effects, manufacturing scalability, regulatory approval, and long-term safety continue to limit widespread clinical implementation. Advances in vector design, genome-editing precision, artificial intelligence-assisted development, and regulatory frameworks are expected to address these limitations. Overall, gene therapy and CRISPRbased technologies represent promising platforms for the development of next-generation precision medicines that could transform disease management in both human and veterinary healthcare.

abstract: Targeted delivery of small interfering RNA (siRNA) to the heart remains challenging because conventional lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) predominantly accumulate in the liver following systemic administration. To improve cardiac siRNA delivery, we developed a biomimetic hybrid nanoplatform by co-extruding siRUNX1-loaded LNPs with reprogrammed macrophage-derived nanovesicles (rMNVs) obtained from sequentially LPS/TGF-β1-treated RAW264.7 macrophages, followed by surface functionalization with a cardiac-targeting peptide (CTP). The sequentially treated donor cells exhibited a phenotypic shift characterized by reduced M1-associated markers and enhanced M2-associated features. The resulting CTP-hLNPs maintained a nanoscale spherical morphology, high siRNA encapsulation efficiency, and retained donor-cell-derived membrane components, including CD206. In vitro, CTP-hLNPs showed reduced uptake by RAW264.7 macrophages while maintaining cellular internalization and siRUNX1 activity in H9c2 cardiac-derived cells. Following intravenous administration, CTP-hLNPs exhibited reduced liver-associated fluorescence and increased heart-associated fluorescence at 24 h compared with conventional CTP-LNPs. Therapeutic efficacy was subsequently evaluated in an angiotensin II (Ang II)-induced mouse model of cardiac remodeling. CTP-hLNP@siRUNX1 reduced cardiac RUNX1 mRNA expression and improved left ventricular systolic function, as indicated by increased left ventricular ejection fraction and fractional shortening. Treatment also attenuated cardiac hypertrophic remodeling, including reductions in the heart weight-to-body weight ratio and cardiomyocyte cross-sectional area. In addition, CTP-hLNP@siRUNX1 reduced myofibroblast-associated α-SMA expression, collagen deposition, and myocardial fibrotic area. Collectively, these findings support rMNV-LNP hybridization combined with CTP functionalization as a potential delivery strategy for cardiac RNA interference therapy and demonstrate its therapeutic effects in Ang II-induced cardiac remodeling.

abstract: Newcastle disease virus (NDV or AOaV-1) is an avian paramyxovirus that typically causes only mild, self-limiting disease in humans. Here, we report fatal neuroinvasive AOaV-1 infection in a patient with multiple myeloma receiving maintenance therapy with teclistamab, daratumumab, and lenalidomide following frontline teclistamab-based treatment and autologous stem cell transplantation. Following rapidly progressive brainstem-cerebellar encephalitis and negative conventional microbiological testing, unbiased metagenomic RNA sequencing of a cerebellar biopsy identified AOaV-1 at high intraparenchymal abundance. Viral genome analysis revealed striking A-to-G and U-to-C substitutions selectively concentrated in the matrix gene, consistent with ADAR-mediated RNA editing. Long-read sequencing resolved two genetically distinct, independently hypermutated CNS haplotypes. Post-mortem analysis demonstrated widespread dissemination and continued viral diversification in multiple brain regions, whereas a peripheral urine sample contained a minimally mutated putative ancestral lineage. These findings support peripheral infection followed by CNS seeding and compartmentalized within-host evolution. The selective matrix-gene hypermutation closely parallels persistent measles virus infection in subacute sclerosing panencephalitis, revealing a shared mechanism of paramyxovirus adaptation to the CNS. Profound immunotherapy-associated immune dysfunction may thus create niches enabling normally low-pathogenic zoonotic viruses to persist, evolve, and acquire severe neurovirulence.

title: Measles-like hypermutation of a Newcastle disease virus drives fatal encephalitis during BCMA × CD3 T-cell-redirecting immunotherapy.

abstract: The RIG-I pathway, a key component of the innate immune system that classically detects cytosolic viral RNA, has also been implicated in regulating tumor cell viability, radiosensitivity, and patient survival across multiple cancer types. However, these effects appear to be context-dependent and partly contradictory. Whether radiotherapy modulates tumor-intrinsic RIG-I signaling in head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC) depending on HPV status, and whether such modulation is associated with changes in the tumor immune phenotype, remains unknown. Four human HNSCC cell lines (two HPV-negative and two HPV-positive), along with siRNA-mediated RIG-I knockdown and a CRISPR/Cas9-generated RIG-I knockout derivative, were treated with radiotherapy. Tumor cells were analyzed for their immune phenotype, including RIG-I expression via Western blot and flow cytometry, IFN-β secretion via ELISA, and PD-L1 and PD-L2 expression via flow cytometry. Radiotherapy, dose- and fraction-dependent, induced the upregulation of RIG-I expression and IFN-β secretion from HPV-negative HNSCC cells. The knockdown and knockout of the RIG-I-encoding gene DDX58 in the HPV-negative cell line HSC4 minimized both IFN-β secretion and PD-L1 and PD-L2 expression. These effects could be replicated by pre-exposing HPV-negative cell lines to the RIG-I inhibitor RIG012 before irradiation. Interestingly, HPV-positive cells showed less radiotherapy-mediated modulation of RIG-I and of the tumor cell phenotype of immune-related surface markers and showed no significant reaction to the inhibitor treatment. The previously unrecognized RIG-I-IFN-β axis is a central regulator of RT-induced immune checkpoint modulation for HPV-negative HNSCC. These results provide new opportunities to reshape the immune response following RT in HNSCC.

abstract: In the pharmaceutical industry, stereopure drugs are generally preferred over isomeric mixtures to reduce the risks of side effects and to simplify pharmacodynamics (PD) and pharmacokinetics (PK) properties. This reasoning applies equally to antisense oligonucleotides (ASOs). All current ASO drugs are modified to provide appropriate PK/PD properties. Among the modifications, phosphorothioate (PS) groups provide essential nuclease resistance and advantageous biodistribution properties. However, PS groups are chiral, with Rp- and Sp-centers that are challenging to incorporate stereoselectively during solid-phase synthesis, and thus current ASO drugs are diastereoisomeric mixtures. Here, we describe the synthesis of stereodefined variants of the approved drug nusinersen (Spinraza), a 2'-O-methoxyethyl-modified oligonucleotide that redirects splicing of SMN2 during treatment for spinal muscular atrophy (SMA). We found that a single 3'-Sp linkage stabilizes nusinersen from degradation in mouse tissue homogenates. Although Rp-nusinersen has higher target-binding affinity than Sp-nusinersen, it is not more active than parent nusinersen in patient-derived cells. Finally, we show mixed results from comparing stereodefined nusinersen with parent nusinersen in a murine model of SMA. While our data do not provide definitive evidence for the superior performance of stereodefined nusinersen, we conclude that it is likely equally effective as its parent ASO, while bearing the pharmacological advantages of a single stereoisomer.

abstract: Influenza A virus (IAV) replication depends on host cells and is regulated by numerous host factors. Therefore, investigating and understanding the role of these host factors is a significant topic. In this study, we found the IAV replication was attenuated after host factor S100 calcium-binding protein A4 (S100A4) was knocked down with RNAi or knockout with CRISPR/Cas9 gene-editing technology. Conversely, IAV replication was enhanced upon the overexpression in A549 cells. The interaction between S100A4 and the IAV M2 protein was confirmed by co-immunoprecipitation. Meanwhile, confocal microscopy experiment demonstrated that the viral M2 protein co-localized with endogenous S100A4 in IAV-infected A549 cells. Truncation analysis confirmed that amino acids 45-62 of the M2 protein constitute the main interaction region with S100A4. Further study showed that viral entry was reduced after S100A4 deletion. And the polymerase activity was significantly decreased in S100A4-knockout A549 cells compared to that in wild-type A549 cells. The S100A4 overexpression resulted in the downregulation of IFN-β, while the mRNA levels of the interferon-stimulated genes ISG15 and BST2 were also significantly reduced. Therefore, the host factor S100A4 was a positive modulator of IAV replication and was involved in the viral entry, polymerase activity maintenance and innate immune regulation. Collectively, our findings shed new light on the molecular mechanisms governing IAV infection and suggest a previously underexplored avenue for antiviral therapeutic intervention.

abstract: The progression in molecular understanding of glioblastoma (GBM) enables the identification of key therapeutic targets, allowing the advances of targeted therapy in GBM. However, to date, most clinical trial results have been disappointing. The clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats (CRISPR) system is a revolutionary genome‑editing tool that has the potential to improve basic research and therapy for GBM. In the present review, the current status and challenges of targeted therapy in GBM are examined. As a potential approach to address the challenges, the development process and application scope of CRISPR are investigated. Furthermore, the application of CRISPR in the study of GBM is explored, mainly by conducting CRISPR screens and employing CRISPR to target genes associated with the malignant phenotype of GBM. Finally, delivery of CRISPR/CRISPR‑associated protein 9 (Cas9) for the treatment of GBM is briefly reviewed.

abstract: CRISPR/Cas9-based genome editing has made substantial progress in recent years and has enabled the treatment of a variety of genetic diseases, including hearing loss in congenitally deaf mice. However, successful gene editing for hereditary deafness may still induce off-target mutations in genomic DNA, which limits its clinical translation. CasRx, also known as RfxCas13d, is a compact RNA-targeting CRISPR effector that can be packaged into AAV vectors for in vivo delivery. CasRx, a recently identified member of the type VI CRISPR system, modulates target RNA expression without altering DNA sequences, thereby avoiding permanent off-target mutations and offering broad therapeutic potential. Here, we used adeno-associated virus serotype 8 (AAV8) to deliver CasRx into the cochlea and cochlear nucleus (CN) of C57BL/6J mice and evaluated its expression pattern and short-term safety. Two weeks after viral injection, the number and morphology of neurons and other cell types in the CN remained normal. Importantly, auditory brainstem response (ABR) thresholds were unchanged after viral delivery, indicating that AAV8-mediated CasRx expression did not detectably impair auditory function during the short observation period. In conclusion, this study demonstrates the feasibility and short-term safety of AAV8-mediated CasRx delivery and expression in the cochlea and cochlear nucleus, providing a delivery platform for future guide RNA-directed transcript-modulation studies in auditory disorders.

abstract: Antisense oligonucleotide gapmers degrade target RNA in a sequence-specific and RNase H-dependent manner and are emerging as a promising antiviral strategy. Locked nucleic acid-modified gapmers have shown activity against several pathogenic viruses. Tick-borne encephalitis virus is widely distributed across Eurasia, with approximately 10,000 cases reported annually, and the absence of approved therapies represents a significant public health concern. In this study, we designed 71 locked nucleic acid-modified gapmers targeting structural elements within the untranslated regions of the single-stranded positive-sense RNA genome of tick-borne encephalitis virus. The antiviral efficacy of gapmers selected via in silico analysis was evaluated using a replicon system and infectious virus assays. Gapmers targeting stem-loop structures in the 3' untranslated region effectively inhibited viral replication. Optimizing the length and composition of the lead gapmers further enhanced antiviral potency. Sequence alignment analysis revealed that the target regions of the optimized gapmers were highly conserved among the three major subtypes of tick-borne encephalitis virus. Accordingly, the optimized gapmers markedly inhibited replication of a highly pathogenic strain, suggesting broad-spectrum activity. Collectively, our findings support the development of locked nucleic acid-modified gapmers as therapeutics against tick-borne encephalitis virus and other tick-borne flaviviruses.

abstract: How phosphorothioates affect the structure and dynamics of oligonucleotide therapeutics and their complexes with target RNAs and protein machinery is not well understood, resulting in a gap in knowledge about the molecular origins of their therapeutic properties. Here we used molecular dynamics simulations to assess the structure and dynamics of Rp and Sp phosphorothioates in an antisense oligonucleotide inotersen. When bound to target mRNA, phosphorothioates shifted the helical equilibrium toward A-form as compared with the unmodified phosphodiester backbone, with Rp showing a higher preference for A-form geometry as compared with Sp. Rp phosphorothioate rigidified the base pairs and base-pair steps, providing a dynamic explanation for the experimentally observed higher thermodynamic stability of Rp over Sp mRNA duplexes. The higher population of B-form helical geometry for Sp mRNA duplexes contributed to their more favorable binding enthalpy (∼16 kcal/mol) to RNase H as compared with Rp phosphorothioate. Furthermore, phosphorothioates modulated the dynamics along the entire duplex complexed to RNase H. Pairwise energy decomposition revealed that RNase H favored Sp phosphorothioate over Rp in a majority of the duplex. Our results reveal a putative mechanism by which phosphorothioate stereochemistry impacts the structure and dynamics of biological complexes of oligonucleotide therapeutics.

abstract: Extending oligonucleotide therapeutics beyond the liver remains a central challenge for RNA medicine. Here, we describe a lipid-conjugated oligonucleotide (LiCO), a benzimidazole-enabled lipid-duplex RNA conjugate platform synthesized as a single chemical entity by standard solid-phase chemistry. Structure-activity screening identified a 5'-passenger-strand hexadecyl (C16) conjugate whose benzimidazole (SDL) linker markedly improved delivery activity relative to a linker-free analog, and studies in CD36-knockout mice established CD36-dependent uptake as the principal driver of extrahepatic tropism. A single systemic dose in mice produced >90% target knockdown in skeletal muscle, heart, aorta, and adipose tissue, with ≥50% silencing persisting for 6 months and measurable activity at 9 months, whereas hepatic silencing was transient. In cynomolgus macaques, two intravenous doses of LiCO-siMSTN achieved ∼90% myostatin mRNA knockdown, 60%-70% suppression of circulating myostatin protein through day 98, and progressive muscle hypertrophy without adverse clinical, hematological, or biochemical findings. In situ hybridization confirmed deep penetration of myofibers, myocardium, and aortic smooth muscle. LiCO also enabled potent local delivery to the synovium, retina, and bladder with minimal systemic exposure. LiCO offers a scalable, versatile platform for neuromuscular, metabolic, and localized disorders.

abstract: Oligonucleotide therapeutics have emerged as next-generation therapeutics. However, targeted delivery of oligonucleotides to extrahepatic tissues, such as skeletal and cardiac muscles and the central nervous system, at efficacious yet well-tolerated doses remain a major challenge for their clinical translation. Although antibody-oligonucleotide conjugates are promising for the treatment of genetic disorders, inadequate tissue penetration and immunogenicity have constrained their therapeutic efficacy. By combining the advantages of cell-penetrating peptides (CPPs) or cell-targeting peptides (CTPs) with those of oligonucleotides, peptide-oligonucleotide conjugates (POCs) display enhanced cellular uptake, endosomal escape, and extrahepatic delivery. The therapeutic efficacy of POC was increased through conjugation with CPPs, endosomal-escape peptides (EEPs), fusogenic peptides, nuclear localization signal peptides, or CTPs. In this perspective, innovative molecular designs such as multivalent, cyclic, and chimeric peptides, and combinations of CPPs and EEPs, were explored, highlighting key advancements in POC development and providing insights into future directions for the development of novel POCs.

abstract: This is a Phase 1, randomized, controlled, dose-ranging clinical trial to assess the safety and immunogenicity of novel influenza A Group 1 and influenza A Group 2 mRNA chimeric hemagglutinin (HA) vaccine candidates given as intramuscular injections alone and in combination. A total of 60 healthy men and non-pregnant, non-breastfeeding women aged 18 through 59 years will be enrolled in one of 6 study arms. The 6 arms will consist of: 1) Sequential influenza A Group 1 mRNA chimeric hemagglutinin: cH8/1 (25 µg) followed by cH5/1 (25 µg), 2) Sequential influenza A Group 2 mRNA chimeric hemagglutinin: cH15/3 (25 µg) followed by cH4/3 (25 µg), 3) Sequential combined influenza A Group 1 and Group 2 mRNA chimeric hemagglutinin: cH8/1 + cH15/3 (25 µg) followed by cH5/1 + cH4/3 (25 µg), 4) A single dose of combined influenza A Group 1 and Group 2 mRNA chimeric hemagglutinin: cH8/1 + cH15/3 (50 µg) followed by placebo, 5) A single dose of combined influenza A Group 1 and Group 2 mRNA chimeric hemagglutinin: cH5/1 + cH4/3 (50 µg) followed by placebo, 6) Sequential combined influenza A Group 1 and Group 2 mRNA chimeric hemagglutinin: cH8/1 + cH15/3 (50 µg) followed by cH5/1 + cH4/3 (50 µg). The primary objectives are to evaluate safety and immunogenicity: 1) To assess the safety and reactogenicity of one or two doses of monovalent or bivalent Group 1 and 2 study products and 2) To describe the Group 1 and 2 anti-HA stalk IgG antibody responses of one or two doses of monovalent or bivalent Group 1 and 2 study products by ELISA.

abstract: Halomonas bluephagenesis has emerged as a promising chassis for industrial biotechnology distinguished by its halophilic robustness and capacity for open and continuous fermentation. However, its poor transformability has substantially limited rapid, iterative, and automatable strain engineering. Here, we develop a "restriction release" strategy that increases transformation efficiency from approximately 102 to 107 cfu/μg DNA, rivaling the efficiency of standard laboratory Escherichia coli. A spontaneous IS30 insertion disrupting the type II restriction endonuclease gene notI increased plasmid transformation efficiency by about 2000-fold. Targeted deletion of notI reproduced this phenotype, confirming its role as a major barrier. Further deletion of the DNA phosphorothioation restriction locus dptFGH yielded an additional 10 to 37-fold improvement, generating the highly transformable ΔEPSΔFlgΔNotIΔPTRes chassis. Notably, the enhanced chassis further facilitated two linear-DNA-based editing strategies: direct RecET-mediated pyrF deletion using a linear donor coupled with phenotypic selection, achieving a recombination efficiency of 16.7%, and CRISPR/Cas9-assisted ribDHBA promoter replacement via co-delivery of a gRNA plasmid and a linear donor, achieving an efficiency of 11.1%. Together, these results identify endogenous restriction systems as primary barriers to genetic manipulation in H. bluephagenesis. Stepwise restriction release markedly improves plasmid transformation and enables linear DNA-mediated genome editing, providing an improved genetic platform for the iterative engineering of this industrial halophile. More broadly, this study suggests a practical strategy for overcoming the genetic inaccessibility of other non-model microorganisms and accelerating iterative strain engineering.

abstract: Genetic improvement of disease resistance against viral infections represents a longstanding and formidable challenge in animal breeding. The antiviral innate immune response is highly regulated at the RNA level, especially through RNA modifications. Adenosine-to-Inosine (A-to-I) RNA editing modifies the mRNA sequence. Growing evidence shows that this type of RNA editing plays a key role in mediating cellular responses to viral infections and disease resistance. However, the role of RNA editing in cellular response to MD remains unclear. In this study, we examined A-to-I editing in CD4+ T cells during Marek's disease virus (MDV) infection. By comparing MD-resistant and susceptible chicken lines, we identified 642 A-to-I RNA editing events in CD4+ T cells, most of which were located within repeat elements, particularly in the CR1 family. We observed differences in RNA editing levels and counts between the two chicken lines with different infection statuses, indicating distinct editing patterns across genetic backgrounds and infection states. Additionally, ADAR (adenosine deaminases acting on RNA) expression was correlated with RNA editing frequency. We identified 21 RNA editing sites (RESs) associated with gene expression and 42, 14, and 38 RESs with predicted effects on amino acid sequences, alternative splicing, and miRNA-target binding, respectively. A comparative analysis revealed 131 group-specific RESs and 21 RESs shared across groups. Functional enrichment analysis of genes associated with group-specific RESs highlighted several terms related to MD resistance, including the MHC class I protein complex in non-infected MD-resistant birds. Significantly, we identified two L63-specific candidate RNA editing sites, chr6:26,600,122 in MXI1 and chr16:1,716,632 in MHCY57, which were predicted to affect gga-miR-1759-3p binding and amino acid sequence, respectively. Our findings reveal the landscape of A-to-I RNA editing in CD4 ⁺ T cells during MDV infection and provide new insights into its potential association with immune regulation and MD resistance.

abstract: This phase II trial studies how well trametinib works in increasing tumoral iodine incorporation in patients with thyroid cancer that has come back or spread to another place in the body. Trametinib may stop the growth of tumor cells by blocking some of the enzymes needed for cell growth and may help make treatment with iodine I-131 more effective.
description:
PRIMARY OBJECTIVES:

I. To evaluate the effect of trametinib on enhancing radioiodine (RAI) activity by determining the proportion of patients alive at 6 months without disease progression by Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid Tumors version 1.1 (RECIST version \[v\]1.1) criteria following treatment with RAI in co-administration with trametinib. (Cohort A) II. To evaluate the effect of trametinib on enhancing RAI activity by determining the objective response rate (ORR) at 6 months following treatment with radioiodine (RAI) in co-administration with trametinib. (Cohort A) III. To determine the proportion of patients following trametinib therapy with increased tumoral iodine incorporation as quantified by iodine iodine-124 (I-124) positron emission tomography (PET)/computed tomography (CT) lesional dosimetry. (Cohort B)

SECONDARY OBJECTIVES:

I. To determine the proportion of patients following trametinib therapy with increased tumoral iodine incorporation as quantified with I-124 PET/CT lesional dosimetry. (Cohort A) II. To evaluate the safety/tolerability of trametinib with or without RAI. (Cohort A) III. To evaluate changes in thyroglobulin levels in patients treated with RAI. (Cohort A) IV. To explore potential correlations between genomic alterations present in the tumor and/or tumoral pharmacodynamic changes induced by trametinib to clinical outcomes. (Exploratory) (Cohort A) V. To evaluate the effect of trametinib on enhancing RAI activity by determining the ORR at 6 months following treatment with RAI in co-administration with trametinib. (Cohort B) VI. To evaluate the effect of trametinib on enhancing RAI activity by determining the proportion of patients alive at 6 months without disease progression by RECIST v 1.1 criteria following treatment with RAI in co-administration with trametinib. (Cohort B) VII. To evaluate the safety/tolerability of trametinib with or without RAI. (Cohort B) VIII. To evaluate changes in thyroglobulin levels in patients treated with RAI. (Cohort B) IX. To explore potential correlations between genomic alterations present in the tumor and/or tumoral pharmacodynamic changes induced by trametinib to clinical outcomes. (Exploratory) (Cohort B) X. Preliminary evaluation of best objective response (BOR) rate for patients treated with trametinib alone. (Exploratory) (Cohort C) XI. Preliminary evaluation of the proportion of patients following treatment with trametinib alive at 6 months without disease progression by RECIST v 1.1 criteria. (exploratory) (Cohort C) XII. To evaluate the safety/tolerability of trametinib. (Cohort C) XIII. To evaluate changes in thyroglobulin levels in patients treated with trametinib. (Cohort C) XIV. To explore potential correlations between genomic alterations present in the tumor and/or tumoral pharmacodynamic changes induced by trametinib to clinical outcomes. (Exploratory) (Cohort C) XV. To explore the impact of continued trametinib upon RAI avidity and efficacy. (Exploratory) (Cohort C)

OUTLINE: Patients with RAS gene mutations are assigned to Cohort A, while patients without BRAF/RAS gene mutations are assigned to Cohort B.

COHORT A: Patients undergo iodine I-124 PET/CT on day 5 of week 1. Beginning day 6, patients receive trametinib orally (PO) daily for 4 weeks in the absence of disease progression or unacceptable toxicity. Patients undergo second iodine I-124 PET/CT on week 5. If I-124 PET/CT shows enough iodine absorption, patients may receive iodine I-131 PO and continue receiving trametinib for another 2 days. If I-124 shows that the thyroid is not absorbing iodine, patients have the option to be assigned to Cohort C.

COHORT B: Patients undergo iodine I-124 PET/CT on day 5 of week 1. Beginning day 6, patients receive trametinib PO daily for 4 weeks in the absence of disease progression or unacceptable toxicity. Patients undergo second iodine I-124 PET/CT on week 5. If I-124 PET/CT shows enough iodine absorption, patients may receive iodine I-131 PO and continue receiving trametinib for another 2 days. If I-124 shows that the thyroid is not absorbing iodine, patients have the option to be assigned to Cohort C.

COHORT C: Patients may continue trametinib at the doctor's discretion and do not receive iodine I-131.

After completion of study treatment, patients are followed up for 30 days.

abstract: This randomized phase II trial studies the safety of and how well aspirin works in preventing Barrett's esophagus from returning after it has been successfully eliminated by radiofrequency ablation. Studying samples of tissue from patients with Barrett's esophagus for the levels of a specific protein that is linked to developing Barrett's esophagus may help doctors learn whether aspirin can prevent it from returning after it has been successfully treated.
description:
PRIMARY OBJECTIVES:

I. To conduct a randomized, double blind, placebo-controlled phase II chemoprevention trial, investigating whether supplementation with aspirin 325 mg/day for 12 months is safe and reduces the expression of CDX2 messenger ribonucleic acid (mRNA) (a biomarker which has been associated with the risk of developing Barrett's esophagus \[BE\]) in comparison to placebo after successful radiofrequency ablation (RFA).

SECONDARY OBJECTIVES:

I. To assess safety at 12 months. II. To assess differences in the expression of CDX2 at 18 months, activation status of NF-kB by assessing levels of total and phosphorylated (phospho)-p65 and cytoplasmic to nuclear translocation of phospho-p65 which is likely to be affected by aspirin.

III. To assess the prostanoid marker, prostaglandin E2, and prostaglandin synthases, which are known to respond to aspirin and to correlation with clinicopathological factors in the esophageal cancer.

IV. To assess differences in the expression of proinflammatory cytokines known to induce activation of NFkB, i.e., TNFalpha, IL-1beta, IL-6, IL-10, IL-17A, IL-23 will be measured.

OUTLINE: Patients are randomized to 1 of 2 treatment arms.

ARM A: Patients receive aspirin orally (PO) once daily (QD) for 12 months.

ARM B: Patients receive placebo PO QD for 12 months.

After completion of study treatment, patients are followed up at 1, 3, 6, 9, 12, and 18 months.

abstract: The primary purpose of the study is to evaluate the safety, tolerability, and pharmacokinetics of CMP-002 in participants with SYNGAP1-related disorder.
description: ASCEND is a global, Phase 1/2, multicenter, randomized, double-blind (Sponsor-open), controlled, multiple-ascending dose (MAD) study to assess the safety, tolerability, and pharmacokinetics, of CMP-002 in participants with SYNGAP1-related disorder (SRD). The study consists of a Baseline Period in which participants will undergo screening assessments to establish the baseline for clinical study assessments. The Baseline Period is followed by a Treatment Period consisting of 3 planned dose level cohorts wherein each participant will receive 3 doses of CMP-002 administered intrathecally (IT) or a control procedure on Days 1, 29, and 85. Each dose level cohort includes a minimum of 8 participants randomized in a 3:1 ratio (CMP-002: control). Following the completion of Dose 3, participants will be followed for an additional 24 weeks in the Follow-up Period.

abstract: This will be a Phase 1, open-label study to evaluate the safety and efficacy of BEAM-201 in patients with R/R T-ALL or T-LLy. BEAM-201 is an allogeneic anti-CD7 CART therapy.

institutions.label: Beam Therapeutics Inc.

description:
Despite favorable outcomes in newly diagnosed patients, approximately 20% of pediatric and young adult T-ALL patients and 40% of adult patients will have refractory disease or will relapse within 2 years of their initial diagnosis. Survival rates of patients with relapsed disease remain below 35%. For recurrent disease, allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplant (HSCT) is the only known potentially curative treatment. However, a prerequisite to HSCT is obtaining a complete remission, which remains a significant challenge as only 40 to 50% of patients achieve a second remission with current reinduction regimens with salvage rates even lower for patients with disease that is refractory to first-line chemotherapy.

BEAM-201 is an allogeneic anti-CD7 CAR T cell product that has shown promising early evidence of efficacy, with 3 out of 4 adult T-ALL patients infused had a CRi/CR ≥28 days after infusion. Safety of BEAM-201 has been favorable and consistent with known adverse events associated with other CAR T cell therapies.

Given the current treatment landscape of T-ALL/T-LLy, promising clinical experience with BEAM-201, and that \>98% of T-ALL cases highly and homogenously express CD7 protein on the surfaces of their lymphoblasts, the investigators think there is compelling rationale in further investigating the safety and efficacy of BEAM-201 in pediatric patients.

abstract: Cornelia de Lange syndrome (CdLS) is a rare, multi-system genetic disorder characterized by developmental and cognitive impairments with systemic manifestations. Among the genes associated with CdLS, loss-of-function variants in HDAC8 account for approximately 4% of cases (referred to as CdLS5), causing the dysregulation of the cohesin complex, a core pathogenic mechanism of the disorder. Currently, no gene-based therapeutic strategy exists to directly address CdLS resulting from HDAC8 deficiency. Here, we created a new CdLS5 mouse model by introducing a clinically reported HDAC8 p.Ile19Ser variant in the mouse Hdac8 gene using CRISPR-Cas9 technology. Comprehensive molecular, morphological, and behavioral characterization revealed that the new Hdac8I19S mouse strain exhibits a robust phenotype, including marked alterations in deacetylase activity and pronounced developmental and behavioral deficits. This model was subsequently used to evaluate a gene augmentation approach aimed at increasing HDAC8 protein levels and restoring cohesin function through delivery of human HDAC8 transgene. Two AAV vectors driving expression of human HDAC8 were assessed. Although efficient delivery and robust expression were achieved, only modest effects on Smc3 acetylation, a key HDAC8 substrate, were observed, and no significant improvement in cognitive or behavioral phenotypes was detected. Overall, these findings demonstrate that postnatal HDAC8 gene augmentation resulted in limited biochemical correction and minimal phenotypic improvement under the conditions tested. These results highlight important biological considerations, including target engagement and developmental timing, that should be considered in the development of effective therapies for cohesin-related disorders.

abstract: Transthyretin amyloid cardiomyopathy (ATTR-CM) is a progressive infiltrative cardiomyopathy increasingly recognised as a cause of heart failure. Advances in the understanding of its pathophysiology have enabled the development of targeted therapies, making ATTR-CM a paradigm of precision medicine in cardiology. Currently approved disease-modifying therapies, including two stabilisers (tafamidis and acoramidis) and one gene-silencing agent (vutrisiran), slow disease progression and reduce hospitalisations and mortality, particularly when initiated early. Because these therapies do not reverse established amyloid deposition, supportive management remains a critical component of care and presents distinct challenges. These include universal anticoagulation in AF, careful diuretic management, the benefits of sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitors and mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists, and limited tolerance to other foundational heart failure therapies. On-going intensive research is expanding the therapeutic landscape, with several Phase III trials evaluating next-generation silencers, gene-editing strategies and amyloid-removal therapies. While these advances hold promise for disease reversal and prevention, important unresolved issues arise, including optimal treatment selection, monitoring strategies and economic sustainability.

abstract: Gonadotropins regulate granulosa-cell function during ovarian follicular development, and extracellular vesicles (EVs) are potential mediators of intercellular communication within the follicle. However, the regulation of EV RNA cargo following gonadotropin stimulation remains incompletely understood. Here, we investigated human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG)-responsive EV RNA profiles using three experimental models: two Lhcgr-expressing clones of a mouse granulosa-cell tumor-derived cell line and mouse ovaries. The cell models were treated with hCG, and immature mice were primed with serotropin, followed by hCG. EVs were isolated from these cells and ovaries and characterized by transmission electron microscopy and western blot analysis. Total RNAs from these EVs were analyzed by electrophoresis, suggesting global changes in their profiles with hCG. RNA-sequencing identified thousands of potentially differentially expressed genes, including 111 commonly upregulated and 122 commonly downregulated transcripts among all three experimental models. The 111 upregulated transcripts were further narrowed down to 27 candidates based on the abundance, and five protein-coding transcripts (Ccdc200, Gm10337, Gm614, Adad2, and Spata45) were selected for further functional validation. Interestingly, EVs carrying the overexpressed Ccdc200, Gm10337, and Gm614 mRNA significantly increased the number of ovarian cells during 3-day culture. These findings indicate that hCG modulates EV RNA cargo and suggest that EV-mediated RNAs cooperatively function as a regulatory layer of hCG signaling for intercellular communication, fine-tuning granulosa-cell proliferation or survival during follicular development.

abstract: Approximately one-third of individuals with epilepsy are refractory to current anti-seizure medications, highlighting the need for new, mechanism-based therapeutic approaches. Fms-like tyrosine kinase 3 (FLT3), a receptor tyrosine kinase classically studied in hematopoiesis and leukemia, is also expressed in neurons, although its function in the brain remains largely unexplored. Our prior work identified small-molecule FLT3 inhibitors (FLT3i) as unexpected enhancers of potassium-chloride cotransporter 2 (KCC2), a neuron-specific chloride transporter essential for maintaining GABAergic inhibition. Here, we applied a functional genomics framework in mouse primary neurons and human stem cell-derived neurons to define FLT3i-induced transcriptional programs, revealing conserved gene networks governing synaptic function and ion channel regulation. A complementary CRISPR/Cas9-based screen of candidate transcription factors identified FLT3-responsive neuronal gene regulatory networks linked to epigenetic remodeling and neuroinflammatory signaling. We further demonstrate that KW-2449, an orally bioavailable FLT3 inhibitor, penetrates the blood-brain barrier, elevates KCC2 expression in vivo for up to 24 hours, and significantly reduces seizure susceptibility in a kainic acid-induced mouse model of epilepsy. Together, these findings reveal a previously unrecognized role for FLT3 in neuronal function and establish proof-of-principle for FLT3 inhibition as a mechanistically supported candidate strategy warranting further development as a next-generation anti-seizure therapy.

abstract: The worldwide emergence of antimicrobial resistance and the need for non-conventional alternatives to conventional antibiotics have been increased by multidrug-resistant ESKAPE pathogens, which cause the majority of nosocomial infections and are starting to develop resistance to even the most potent drugs. Engineered bacteriophages are promising precision antimicrobials because of their ability to selectively infect and lyse bacterial hosts, multiply at infection sites, and co-evolve with bacterial populations to overcome resistance. Advances in synthetic biology, such as tail fiber modification, depolymerase and endolysin enhancement, genome editing using the clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats (CRISPR), and computationally designed phage cocktails, have opened new possibilities for therapeutics that were hindered by the limitations of natural phages. These engineering strategies expand host range, enhance biofilm penetration, and target resistance genes. In spite of promising evidence in preclinical models, the use of engineered phages in routine clinical practice remains difficult. Specific key challenges include unclear regulations, lack of good manufacturing practice (GMP)grade production, variable pharmacokinetics and limited clinical trial data. This review critically examines engineering approaches to improve phage activity against ESKAPE pathogens, identifies the scientific and regulatory barriers limiting clinical use, and outlines the key steps needed for wider adoption.

abstract:
RATIONALE: Pulmonary ionocytes, representing approximately 1% of airway epithelial cells, exhibit high CFTR expression and unique transcriptional markers, including FOXI1, ASCL3, and V-ATPase. Their exact role in human airway physiology is incompletely understood.
OBJECTIVE: This study employs induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-derived airway epithelial models (iPSC-airways) to elucidate the role of FOXI1 in pulmonary ionocyte differentiation and function.
METHODS: CRISPR-Cas9 was used to generate FOXI1-knockout iPSCs, into which a doxycycline-inducible FOXI1-overexpression cassette was introduced. Edited and control lines were differentiated into airway epithelia to evaluate ionocyte formation, epithelial composition, and ion transport. Rescue studies assessed the effects of FOXI1 re-expression in a FOXI1-KO background, and the addition of inducible WT-CFTR ionocytes to F508del/F508del cystic fibrosis (CF) cultures on restoring chloride transport.
MEASUREMENTS AND MAIN RESULTS: FOXI1 deletion abolishes ionocyte formation and alters airway epithelial composition, with increased mucus-secreting goblet cells and decreased ciliated cells. Functional assays confirmed ionocytes as key regulators of chloride homeostasis, with FOXI1-deficient airways displaying diminished ion transport. Induction of FOXI1-overexpression restored CFTR-mediated chloride transport. Introduction of WT ionocytes into CF airway models rescued chloride transport deficits, with no rescue observed in vehicle-treated controls lacking ionocyte induction.
CONCLUSIONS: These findings highlight FOXI1's essential role in pulmonary ionocyte development, airway cell composition, and airway chloride transport. We present a fully manipulable, gene-edited iPSC-derived system that enables investigation of ionocyte biology and function within a human airway context, highlighting them as promising therapeutic targets for respiratory disorders.

abstract: Oral biofilms are spatially ordered microbial communities whose pathogenic behavior is shaped by more than taxonomic composition. Their development reflects the combined effects of adhesin-receptor recognition, interspecies coaggregation, matrix formation, metabolite exchange, local physicochemical gradients and host-derived selection. Here, we synthesize molecular and ecological evidence on the bacterial cell surface-matrix interface and consider how these interactions contribute to cariogenic, periodontal and peri-implant biofilms. Particular attention is given to glucosyltransferase-dependent polysaccharides, extracellular DNA, amyloidogenic proteins, sortase-anchored surface factors and outer membrane vesicles, together with metabolic interactions involving lactate, arginine, hydrogen peroxide and heme. We further evaluate functional-genomic and systems-level approaches (including transposon sequencing, CRISPR interference, metagenomics, metatranscriptomics, metaproteomics, metabolomics, spatial imaging, genome-scale metabolic modeling and machine learning) while distinguishing association and prediction from experimentally demonstrated mechanism. Emerging interventions are assessed according to their biological target and evidence level, including adhesion blockade, specifically targeted antimicrobials, matrix synthesis inhibition and degradation, quorum interference, probiotics, catalytic nanoparticles, antimicrobial photodynamic therapy and antibiofilm dental materials. Across these approaches, reduction in biofilm biomass is not equivalent to ecological restoration or clinical benefit. Key translational barriers include model fidelity, donor-to-donor variation, spatial heterogeneity, treatment durability, endpoint selection and the limited external validation of many computational and preclinical findings. Future precision strategies should therefore integrate microbial identity, matrix architecture, spatial metabolism and host context, with experimental perturbation used to establish causal vulnerabilities before therapeutic translation.

abstract: The transcription factor (TF) SPI1 (historically called PU.1) is a critical pioneer TF and regulator of hematopoiesis. It exerts exquisitely dose-dependent and stage-specific control over lymphoid, myeloid, and central nervous system-resident lineages. Structurally characterized by an intrinsically disordered N-terminal transactivation region and a highly conserved C-terminal DNA-binding E26 transformation-specific domain, SPI1 can operate alone as a monomer, via homodimerization, through epigenetic interactions, and in context-dependent transcriptional partnerships. While early animal models established its essentiality for leukopoiesis, modern human genomics has unveiled direct links between altered SPI1 function and disease. Heterozygous loss-of-function germline variants cause PU.1-mediated agammaglobulinemia, whereas somatic mutations and/or regulatory alterations can drive hematologic malignancies. Dysregulated SPI1 activity is also implicated in autoimmune diseases, including rheumatoid arthritis and systemic lupus erythematosus, and neurodegenerative disorders. This review reconciles foundational murine paradigms with emerging human translational data, highlights current therapeutic landscapes, and projects how single-cell multi-omics and advanced gene editing may shape future directions in the SPI1 biomedical field.

abstract: Arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy is a heritable cardiac disorder commonly linked to alterations in desmosomal proteins. While desmosomal dysfunction is a recognized pathogenic mechanism, the early molecular remodeling that precedes clinical manifestations remains unclear. Here we used a mouse model with inducible cardiomyocyte-specific knockout of Pkp2 (encoding plakophilin-2) and performed time-resolved mass spectrometry-based proteomics to map disease progression from early PKP2 loss to structural remodeling. Molecular changes preceded phenotypic abnormalities, and spatial asymmetry was evident, with earlier and more pronounced proteome remodeling in the right ventricle despite comparable PKP2 depletion in both ventricles. Downregulation of protein networks spanning desmosomes, sarcomeres and mitochondria suggests their functional coupling, with mitochondrial remodeling emerging as an early and progressively worsening feature. Intervention with honokiol attenuated changes across the major protein networks, highlighting mitochondrial pathways as promising therapeutic targets and honokiol as a potential strategy to delay arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy progression. Our findings provide critical insights into the concealed stage of disease progression and identify molecular targets for early intervention.

abstract: In this edition, we highlight several important developments across the Huntington's disease therapeutic pipeline. We discuss the launch and subsequent discontinuation of POINT-HD, the first-in-human phase I study of RG6496 (Hoffmann-La Roche), an allele-selective antisense oligonucleotide designed to selectively lower mutant huntingtin while largely preserving wild-type huntingtin expression. We also discuss the launch of two phase III efficacy trials: INVEST-HD, evaluating votoplam (Novartis Pharmaceuticals), and PRECISE-HD, evaluating pridopidine (Prilenia). In addition, we summarise recent advances across the field, including preclinical updates for LQT-23 (LoQus23), SRP-1005 (Sarepta Therapeutics) and HRN001 (Harness Therapeutics); interim 12-month clinical results from SKY-0515 (Skyhawk Therapeutics); the announcement by uniQure that 3-year data from the phase I/II AMT-130 study may support a Biologics License Application seeking accelerated approval and Roche's discontinuation of the phase II GENERATION HD2 study of tominersen. Finally, we provide an updated listing of registered and ongoing clinical trials in Huntington's disease.

abstract:
BACKGROUND: Hypertension remains a leading cause of global morbidity and mortality, yet current therapeutic strategies lack sustained efficacy and long-term stability. Our study aimed to construct a humanized rodent model for drugs development especially currently prevalent small interfering RNA medication.
METHODS: A humanized hypertensive mouse model was generated by subcutaneous injection of neonatal mice with adeno-associated viruses encoding hAGT (human angiotensinogen) and hRENIN (human renin). Blood pressure was monitored weekly via tail-cuff plethysmography. Expression of hAGT and hRENIN was assessed by ELISA, Western blot, and reverse transcription quantitative polymerase chain reaction. Cardiac function was evaluated by echocardiography at 4 and 6 months postinjection. Hypertension-associated comorbidities were examined through histological analysis and ELISA. A modified N-acetylgalactosamine-conjugated small interfering RNA targeting human hepatic AGT (GalNAc-siAGT) was screened and subcutaneously administered to humanized hypertensive mice, either alone or in combination with valsartan, to evaluate therapeutic efficacy.
RESULTS: The dual adeno-associated virus-induced humanized hypertensive model exhibited a sustained hypertension for 6 months and manifested prevalent comorbidities, including heart failure and kidney disease. This modified GalNAc-siAGT demonstrated significant activity in knocking down hAGT both in vitro and in vivo. Only a single subcutaneous injection of GalNAc-siAGT in humanized hypertensive mice led to a sustained reduction in blood pressure lasting for 2 months, accompanied by cardio- and renoprotective effects. Moreover, combining GalNAc-siAGT with the renin-angiotensin system blocker, valsartan, significantly enhanced therapeutic efficacy.
CONCLUSIONS: Our study validated the antihypertensive therapeutic effect of GalNAc-siAGT in a humanized hypertensive murine model while highlighting the translational potential of this model for clinical drug development.

abstract: CRISPR-Cas genome editing represents one of the most transformative advances in modern molecular biology, enabling programmable site-specific genetic modification that has revolutionized functional genomics and precision therapeutic development. Beyond canonical Cas9 nucleases, the CRISPR toolkit has diversified into precision base editors, prime editors, CRISPR-associated transposases, and Cas12/Cas13 RNA-targeting effectors, each with distinct mechanistic properties. Clinically, ex vivo CRISPR therapies for hemoglobinopathies have secured regulatory approval, while base editing, prime editing, and in vivo Chimeric Antigen Receptor (CAR)-T candidates are advancing through trials for a broad spectrum of hematologic, oncologic, and rare genetic disorders. However, existing reviews largely address technical innovation or clinical translation in isolation, lacking a holistic, up-to-date synthesis of the full bench-to-bedside trajectory of CRISPR technology. This review systematically dissects the molecular mechanisms, advantages, and limitations of core CRISPR editing platforms; summarizes pivotal clinical data across hemoglobinopathies, CAR-T immunotherapy, muscular dystrophy, cystic fibrosis, cardiometabolic diseases and rare monogenic diseases; evaluates delivery systems including lipid nanoparticles and viral vectors; and discusses key translational barriers such as off-target genotoxicity and immunogenicity alongside emerging optimization strategies. This work provides a holistic bench-to-bedside framework for CRISPR research, offering critical insights to advance next-generation precision genetic medicine.

abstract:
UNLABELLED: Impaired fracture healing remains a significant clinical challenge. Bone marrow mesenchymal stem cells (BMSCs) and the exosomes (BMSC-Exos) play a pivotal role in bone regeneration, partly by transferring functional microRNAs (miRNAs). A-to-I RNA editing can profoundly alter miRNA function, but its role in fracture healing, particularly for miRNA-99a-5p, is underexplored. We first profiled differentially edited miRNAs in serum from 50 fracture patients and healthy controls. A murine fracture model was established and treated with BMSC-Exos, where either the edited or wild-type form of miRNA-99a-5p was knocked down. In vitro studies involved transfecting BMSCs with ADAR expression vectors to investigate editing mechanisms, and overexpressing/inhibiting edited/wild-type miRNA-99a-5p in MC3T3-E1C osteoblasts to elucidate its direct functional impacts on osteogenic differentiation, apoptosis, proliferation, and migration. Validation of target genes were performed by dual-luciferase reporter assays, qPCR, and Western blot. Key readouts included alkaline phosphatase (ALP) activity, Alizarin Red S (ARS) staining, flow cytometry, Transwell migration, CCK-8 proliferation assays and HE staining. Clinical analysis revealed significantly lower A-to-I edited miRNA-99a-5p levels in fracture patients, correlating with delayed union. In mice, BMSC-Exos promoted fracture healing, an effect attenuated by edited miRNA-99a-5p knockdown. In vitro, edited miRNA-99a-5p enhanced osteogenesis and inhibited apoptosis, while the wild-type form had opposing effects. ADAR2 mediated this editing. Edited miRNA-99a-5p directly targeted and suppressed Growth Differentiation Factor 11 (GDF11) expression. Importantly, GDF11 overexpression reversed the pro-osteogenic effects of edited miRNA-99a-5p, in both direct and exosome-mediated contexts. Reduced A-to-I editing of miRNA-99a-5p is associated with impaired fracture healing. BMSC-Exos facilitate bone repair by delivering ADAR2-edited miRNA-99a-5p, which promotes osteogenic differentiation and bone formation through the specific targeting and downregulation of GDF11. This study uncovers a novel exosome-mediated RNA editing pathway critical for fracture healing and highlights edited miRNA-99a-5p and GDF11 as potential therapeutic targets for bone repair.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION: The online version contains supplementary material available at https://doi.org/10.1007/s10616-026-01080-x.

abstract: Frailty, an age-related state of increased vulnerability, is associated with greater susceptibility to infection and impaired vaccine response. In this Review, we examine how frailty-associated immunosenescence, including altered haematopoiesis, chronic inflammation, and dysfunction of innate and adaptive immune responses, can affect the immunogenicity, efficacy, and safety of lipid nanoparticle mRNA vaccines. Evidence from COVID-19 lipid nanoparticle mRNA vaccines and other vaccines suggests that people living with frailty can mount weaker or less durable responses than non-frail peers, although findings remain heterogeneous and frailty-specific evidence is scarce. The high customisability of lipid nanoparticle mRNA platforms creates opportunities for frailty-tailored vaccination. We discuss optimisation of lipid nanoparticle composition, targeting and dosing, mRNA cargo and combination-vaccine approaches, alongside host-directed measures addressing comorbidities, nutrition, and immune dysfunction. Integrating frailty into vaccine design, evaluation, and deployment could support safer, more effective, and more individualised vaccination strategies for older adults.

abstract: Advanced therapeutics, including programmable nucleic acid-based therapies (NATs), such as small interfering RNAs (siRNAs), antisense oligonucleotides (ASOs), CRISPR-Cas 9 editing systems, modified in vitro transcribed messenger RNAs (mRNAs) and Adeno-associated viruses (AAVs), have the potential to transform healthcare. However, while there have been considerable successes, there have also been notable clinical failures in early-stage human trials, which slowed down the progression of these therapeutic platforms. Multiple trials of NATs have been halted or discontinued, or approved products carry black box warnings as unforeseen or underestimated toxicities and poor efficacy have been observed in humans. There are a variety of reasons for failure of NATs, one of which is that many preclinical studies lack disease modelling in a human-relevant manner and, therefore, do not capture disease-specific effects on therapy tolerability and efficacy. This Perspective provides a short overview of why better human disease modelling is required to understand the potential therapeutic liabilities of NATs across modalities.

abstract: Gynecological cancers, including ovarian, cervical, and endometrial cancers, remain major contributors to female morbidity and mortality worldwide. Conventional treatments-surgery, chemotherapy, and radiotherapy-have improved outcomes, but advanced or recurrent disease is still associated with poor prognosis, chemoresistance, and tumor heterogeneity. Immunotherapy has emerged as a transformative strategy because of its specificity and potential for durable responses. However, the immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment and inefficient delivery of immunotherapeutic agents limit clinical benefit. Nanocarriers, including organic, inorganic, and biomimetic platforms, can improve targeted delivery, sustained release, biocompatibility, and tumor microenvironment remodeling, thereby enhancing immunotherapy. This review summarizes major immunotherapeutic modalities for gynecological cancers-immune checkpoint blockade, CAR-T cell therapy, tumor vaccines, and oncolytic viruses-and the classification and characteristics of commonly used nanocarriers. We focus on nanocarrier-mediated immunotherapeutic mechanisms in ovarian, cervical, and endometrial cancers, and further highlight emerging lipid nanoparticle/mRNA and programmable RNA delivery strategies. Finally, we analyze challenges in clinical translation and provide perspectives for future development, aiming to support fundamental research and clinical application of nano-immunotherapy in gynecological malignancies.

abstract: Mitochondrial dysfunction is increasingly recognized as a shared mechanism across neurological disease. Specifically, impaired oxidative phosphorylation, oxidative stress, and mitochondrial DNA damage are factors in primary mitochondrial disorders and major neurodegenerative diseases such as Parkinson, Alzheimer, and Huntington diseases, and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis. This review surveys the mechanisms driving mitochondrial dysfunction and evaluates the current landscape of gene-editing technologies developed to address them. We examine mitochondria-targeted editors and nuclear-targeted editors, examining the editing capability, delivery constraints, and off-target risk of each. Heteroplasmy-shifting nucleases currently offer the strongest in vivo evidence for mtDNA-directed therapy, while base editors extend correction to homoplasmic mutations at the cost of a narrower editing scope and off-target editing. Nuclear editing platforms avoid the mitochondrial gRNA import barrier entirely, allowing current technologies to achieve the most progress toward functional, behavioral rescue in animal models. Across all platforms, delivery efficiency, off-target specificity, and translation from rodent to primate models remain unresolved barriers to clinical application. Gene editing for mitochondrial dysfunction is highly creditable as a precision therapy for genetically defined disease subsets, including primary mitochondrial disease and other neurodegenerative disorders with a known nuclear driver, rather than as a universal strategy for sporadic neurodegeneration, where mitochondrial dysfunction arises from multifactorial and poorly localized causes.

title: Genome Editing of Mitochondrial Dysfunction in Neurological Disease: Progress and Translational Barriers.

abstract: Choroidal melanoma is the most common primary intraocular malignancy, and effective gene therapy remains limited by ocular barriers, tumor heterogeneity, and inefficient nucleic acid delivery. This review critically analyses the molecular rationale, engineering principles, emerging nanoarchitectures, biological validation, and translational prospects of dual-vector nanoengineered mRNA-CRISPR delivery systems for precision gene therapy in choroidal melanoma. The manuscript also highlights key challenges and future strategies for clinical implementation. Current evidence indicates that dual-vector platforms enable independent optimization of mRNA and CRISPR cargos while maintaining coordinated spatiotemporal therapeutic activity. We conducted a literature search in PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science for relevant studies published from January 2015 to September 2026. Functional cargo partitioning, vector modularity, programmable intracellular trafficking, and ocular-targeted nanoengineering improve delivery precision and reduce biological compromise associated with co-encapsulation. Lipid, polymeric, hybrid, biomimetic, and viral-nonviral architectures each provide distinct engineering advantages depending on therapeutic objectives. Preclinical studies support enhanced genome editing, transient protein restoration, improved tumor suppression, and reduced off-target effects. Nevertheless, manufacturing scalability, regulatory standardization, long-term safety, and clinical validation remain major barriers to translation. Dual-vector nanoengineered mRNA-CRISPR systems represent a promising next-generation platform for precision gene therapy in choroidal melanoma by enabling coordinated and programmable therapeutic delivery. Continued advances in modular nanoengineering, personalized cargo selection, and clinically scalable manufacturing will be essential for successful translation into precision ocular oncology.

title: Dual-vector nanoengineered mRNA-CRISPR delivery systems for precision gene therapy in choroidal melanoma.

abstract: Viral diseases remain a major global health challenge despite substantial advances in vaccination, antiviral therapeutics, and public-health interventions. However, current antiviral strategies are still constrained by important gaps, including rapid viral evolution, limited broad-spectrum efficacy, immune escape, antiviral resistance, incomplete durability of protection, and inequitable global access to prevention and treatment. This review provides a comprehensive and integrated overview of contemporary antiviral prevention and therapeutic strategies, spanning vaccines, monoclonal antibodies, direct-acting antivirals, host-targeted therapies, immunomodulators, RNA-based therapeutics, gene-editing technologies, and cellular immunotherapies. We discuss the mechanistic foundations, clinical applications, pharmacologic considerations, and translational challenges associated with each modality across major human viral pathogens, including HIV, HBV, HCV, influenza, SARS-CoV-2, RSV, Ebola virus, arboviruses, and herpesviruses. Particular emphasis is placed on emerging innovations such as long-acting prophylaxis, Fc-engineered monoclonal antibodies, nanoparticle and mucosal vaccine platforms, CRISPR-based antiviral systems, and broadly protective host-directed approaches designed to overcome resistance and enhance pandemic preparedness. In addition, we highlight the growing importance of real-time genomic surveillance and equitable global deployment strategies in shaping future antiviral responses, collectively underscoring that the next generation of antiviral medicine will depend on the convergence of universal immunization strategies, durable therapeutics, precision immune modulation, and rapidly deployable platform technologies capable of addressing both endemic and emerging viral threats.

title: Therapeutic and Prophylactic Agents for Viral Diseases: Current Status, Challenges, and Future Prospects.

abstract:
BACKGROUND: Metabolic adaptation is a crucial driver of melanoma progression and therapy resistance. The pseudokinase Tribbles homolog 2 (TRIB2) is highly expressed in melanoma and is associated with poor outcomes and treatment resistance. However, its specific role in the metabolic profile of melanoma cells remained unexplored. This study aimed to investigate the impact of TRIB2 on cellular metabolism, and its role in metabolic adaptation in melanoma.
MATERIALS AND METHODS: The study used UACC-62 human melanoma cells with high endogenous TRIB2 expression and isogenic TRIB2-knockout (KO) clones generated via CRISPR-Cas9. Cell proliferation was assessed using trypan blue exclusion assays under treatment with metabolic drugs including 2-deoxyglucose (2-DG), and dichloroacetate (DCA). Metabolic phenotypes were evaluated by measuring glucose consumption, lactate production, and real-time analysis of glycolytic flux (ECAR) and mitochondrial respiration (OCR) using a Seahorse bioanalyzer. Reactive oxygen species (ROS) levels were measured by dihydroethidium (DHE) fluorescence. Gene expression was analyzed by qPCR, and protein levels were determined by western blot. Citrate synthase activity was measured enzymatically.
RESULTS: TRIB2-KO cells exhibited significantly reduced basal proliferation compared with wild-type (WT) cells. KO cells were also more sensitive to the glycolytic inhibitor 2-DG. Conversely, WT cells were more susceptible to DCA treatment. Metabolic analyses confirmed that TRIB2-KO cells had lower glucose consumption, lactate production, and glycolytic capacity than WT cells. Mitochondrial respiratory function and the protein levels of key respiratory complexes were unchanged. Despite the reduction in glycolytic activity, TRIB2 depletion did not increase mitochondrial respiratory capacity and was associated with elevated basal intracellular superoxide levels. Among the molecular alterations identified, PDK4 was consistently reduced at both the mRNA and protein levels, whereas citrate synthase activity was significantly decreased despite preserved protein abundance, indicating selective alterations in mitochondrial carbon metabolism.
CONCLUSIONS: TRIB2 expression promotes a glycolytic phenotype and contributes to metabolic adaptation in melanoma. Loss of TRIB2 does not induce a metabolic shift towards oxidative phosphorylation but instead results in broader metabolic rewiring characterized by reduced glycolysis together with selective alterations in mitochondrial carbon metabolism. These findings identify the TRIB2-PDK4 axis as a previously unrecognized component of metabolic regulation in melanoma and provide a rationale for further investigating its therapeutic potential.

title: TRIB2 supports a high glycolytic phenotype in melanoma cells.

abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) is an aggressive breast cancer subtype characterized by high metastatic potential and limited targeted therapeutic options. Lipocalin-2 (LCN2) has been implicated in tumor progression and metastatic dissemination, but its functional role in TNBC remains incompletely understood. This study investigated the role of LCN2 in the human TNBC cell line MDA-MB-231.
METHODS: Stable LCN2-deficient (LCN2KO) cells were generated using CRISPR/Cas9 genome editing, followed by isolation of single-cell-derived clones. RNA sequencing was performed to characterize transcriptomic changes, with selected findings validated by reverse transcription quantitative PCR (RT-qPCR). Western blotting was used to assess protein-level changes. Transwell migration and invasion assays and adhesion assays were performed to evaluate functional effects.
RESULTS: LCN2KO cells largely retained the mesenchymal phenotype of parental cells. RNA sequencing revealed changes associated with inflammatory signaling, iron homeostasis, oxidative stress, ferroptosis-related processes, and cellular metabolism. Functional assays demonstrated reduced migration, invasion, and adhesion, accompanied by altered adhesion to extracellular matrix components.
DISCUSSION: LCN2 deficiency is associated with transcriptional and functional changes in MDA-MB-231 cells, particularly affecting migratory and invasive behavior and cell-matrix interactions, while largely preserving the mesenchymal phenotype. These findings provide further insight into the role of LCN2 in cellular processes relevant to TNBC progression and metastatic behavior.

title: Comprehensive characterization of the cellular and molecular consequences of LCN2 loss in MDA-MB-231 triple-negative breast cancer cells.

abstract: Cancer remains a leading cause of mortality worldwide. Conventional modalities, namely surgery, radiotherapy, chemotherapy, and immunotherapy, continue to face substantial limitations. The advent of gene therapy, particularly CRISPR-based genome editing, offers new opportunities to overcome these barriers. Nuclease systems such as CRISPR/Cas9 enable precise excision of mutant alleles and targeted insertion of exogenous sequences by harnessing endogenous DNA-repair pathways, achieving durable and accurate genomic modification; derivative tools including CRISPRi, base editing, and prime editing enable diverse forms of gene regulation or precise genome modification through transcriptional repression, base conversion, or related editing mechanisms. To enhance the efficiency, specificity, and spatiotemporal control of CRISPR editing in vivo, sophisticated delivery platforms have been engineered to respond to endogenous tumor-microenvironment cues (e.g., pH, redox potential, hypoxia, ATP, enzymes and microRNAs) or exogenous triggers (e.g., light, ultrasound and magnetic fields). Distinct from material-centric classification schemes, this review organizes these stimuli-responsive systems according to their pathological relevance to the tumor microenvironment (TME), establishing a conceptual framework that links specific TME aberrations with corresponding delivery paradigms. These stimuli-responsive systems represent a major innovation and markedly expand the therapeutic potential of genome editing in oncology. In this review, we summarize the mechanistic basis of CRISPR-based editing, delineate design principles and engineering strategies for stimuli-responsive delivery, and highlight recent advances, outstanding challenges, and future directions toward clinical translation. We aim to provide a concise reference to guide the rational design of gene-editing cancer therapeutics.

title: Stimuli-responsive CRISPR-based genome editing delivery system for cancer treatment: A review of fundamentals and applications.

abstract: Breast cancer progression is driven by molecular heterogeneity, drug resistance (DR), and interactions within the tumour microenvironment (TME), creating an urgent need for therapies that can selectively suppress disease-associated genes. Small interfering RNA (siRNA) can silence targets involved in tumour growth, treatment resistance, and immune evasion. Its therapeutic potential, however, depends on overcoming rapid degradation and clearance, limited tumour accumulation, poor cellular uptake, and endosomal entrapment. Lipid-based and polymer-mediated delivery systems (DS) protect siRNA and facilitate its transport, while chemical modifications, molecular conjugates, and physical delivery methods offer additional ways to improve stability or access to target cells. In BC models, these strategies have been investigated for targeted therapy, reversal of DR, and modulation of the TME to support antitumor immunity. Despite encouraging preclinical findings, effective tumour delivery, sustained gene silencing, off-target effects, and immune activation remain significant barriers to clinical translation. This review brings together advances in siRNA delivery and their applications against BC progression, DR, and immune evasion, while defining the barriers that must be overcome to translate effective gene silencing into meaningful clinical benefit.

title: Advances in siRNA delivery for breast cancer therapy: from molecular design to therapeutic application.

abstract: Messenger RNA (mRNA)-based therapeutics have transformed cancer treatment strategies, especially after the success of lipid nanoparticle (LNP)-enabled mRNA vaccines. LNPs are effective non-viral delivery vehicles that protect mRNA, enhance intracellular delivery, and improve therapeutic safety. This review discusses recent advancements in LNP-mediated mRNA therapies, including mRNA vaccines, cytokine delivery, immune modulation, and CAR-based strategies. Innovations in lipid formulations and high-throughput technologies have enhanced delivery efficiency. We also discussed how LNP-mRNA formulations elicit immune responses and improve tumor microenvironments. We highlight promising personalized mRNA vaccines and therapies. However, challenges such as tissue specificity, immunogenicity, and manufacturing remain. Emerging strategies in lipid engineering and personalized medicine aim to address these issues, making LNP-mediated mRNA therapeutics a pivotal approach in precision oncology. This report provides a comprehensive review of recent developments in LNP-mRNA therapeutics for cancer treatment. This report also highlights recent innovations and clinical trials. We further highlight the limitations and challenges associated with LNP-mRNA therapeutics in clinical translation. Finally, we outlined the prospects of LNP-based mRNA therapeutics for personalized cancer treatment.
