title: CRISPR-based pipeline for generating and validating multi-kb deletions and indels in iPSCs.

abstract: RNA aptamers are short, single-stranded RNA molecules that fold into specific three-dimensional structures and selectively bind molecular targets. Despite applications in therapeutics, diagnostics, and biosensing, tools for aptamer validation remain scarce compared to well-established pipelines for other biomolecular binders such as antibodies. Here, we introduce SecAntiGami─a secondary-antibody-inspired RNA origami─as a modular tool for signal enhancement and aptamer characterization. SecAntiGami binds aptamers of interest through programmable kissing-loop interactions and carries a fluorescent aptamer for visualization. It amplifies aptamer-dependent size increases in dynamic light scattering assays and enables fluorescence-based aptamer localization. We rationally design three different variants of a biotin-binding aptamer and use SecAntiGami to demonstrate that all of them retain their functionality, enabling efficient integration of aptamers into RNA origami structures. SecAntiGami serves as a versatile tool for qualitative aptamer validation for synthetic biology, structural RNA nanotechnology, RNA therapeutics, and diagnostics.

abstract: Filamentous fungi are important microbial cell factories for producing antibiotics, organic acids, enzymes, and other valuable products, with broad applications in food, agriculture, and medicine. However, inefficient and imprecise genome editing remains a major bottleneck limiting rational strain engineering. This review summarizes major genome-editing tools in filamentous fungi, including Cre-loxP, TALENs, and CRISPR-Cas systems, with emphasis on their mechanisms, advantages, and limitations. We highlight CRISPR-Cas9 as the predominant platform and discuss optimization strategies involving sgRNA design, engineered Cas9 variants, promoter engineering, AMA1-based replicative plasmids, and ribonucleoprotein delivery. Emerging technologies, including base editing, prime editing, Cas12a, and Mad7, are also discussed for their potential to broaden editing capabilities. Finally, we outline future perspectives focusing on extending the application of existing genome-editing systems in filamentous fungi and discovering novel genome-editing tools from large-scale omics data sets. This review will accelerate the development of filamentous fungi as versatile platforms for biomanufacturing.

abstract:
MOTIVATION: Post-translational modifications (PTMs) are critical to protein activity, yet the biological role of most known modification sites remains uncharacterized. CRISPR-mediated phenotypic screens using base editors offer a powerful approach to dissecting PTM function at scale. However, existing single-guide RNA (sgRNA) design tools for base editing applications are DNA-centric and lack the throughput required to integrate seamlessly with mass-spectrometry-based proteomics experimental outputs.
RESULTS: We introduce protein editing in R, PrEditR, an open-source, protein-centric tool for high-throughput sgRNA design for custom base editor screens. PrEditR enables users to designate specific amino acid residues in proteins and design protospacer sequences that target the corresponding gene and annotate every resulting amino acid change (missense, nonsense, or silent), including bystander edits.
AVAILABILITY AND IMPLEMENTATION: PrEditR is available on GitHub and Docker Hub.

abstract: Interface integration failure after implanting bone repair material is a core challenge in treating bone defects. This study aimed to investigate the molecular mechanism by which endothelial cell-derived small extracellular vesicles (EC-sEVs) deliver lncRNA DLX1 (lncDLX1) to regulate the osteogenic differentiation of BMSCs through both in vitro and in vivo experiments. The results showed that lncDLX1 expression was significantly downregulated in an inflammatory microenvironment and that overexpression of lncDLX1 promoted BMSC osteogenic differentiation while inhibiting inflammatory responses. Mechanistic studies revealed that lncDLX1 binds to RBMX, which then transcriptionally activates β-catenin expression and enhances its mRNA stability by binding to the CTNNB1 promoter region, thereby activating the Wnt/β-catenin pathway. Functional experiments confirmed that EC-sEVscould be effectively taken up by BMSCs and functionally deliver lncDLX1, and GW4869 treatment attenuated this regulatory effect, supporting the involvement of sEVs. In vivo experiments showed that hydroxyapatite materials loaded with lncDLX1-overexpressing BMSCs significantly promoted bone repair in a rat femoral defect model. In summary, this study reveals the central role of the EC-sEVs/lncDLX1/RBMX/Wnt/β-catenin signaling axis in bone repair, providing a new theoretical basis for the development of sEV-based lncRNA bone repair strategies.

abstract: Acute myeloid leukemia (AML) is a heterogeneous and aggressive hematologic malignancy associated with poor survival despite recent therapeutic advances. To identify novel anti-leukemic agents, we performed a high-throughput viability screen of 10,000 small molecules across 56 genetically diverse primary AML samples. Compounds with similar activity profiles were grouped into Compound Correlation Clusters (CCCs), leading to the identification of CCC163, which includes AML874, as a potent and selective hit. Integrated pharmacological and CRISPR-Cas9 approaches identified the Mediator complex as the molecular target of AML874. We demonstrated that AML874 acts as a selective CDK8/CDK19 inhibitor, disrupting Mediator-dependent transcription. FLT3-mutated AML showed increased sensitivity to AML874, suggesting a subtype-specific vulnerability. Notably, CDK8 inhibition synergized with venetoclax in AML cell lines and patient-derived xenograft models, resulting in enhanced anti-leukemic activity in vivo. Collectively, these findings establish CDK8/CDK19 inhibition as a therapeutically relevant strategy in AML.

title: Mediator kinase inhibition exposes a transcriptional vulnerability and synergizes with venetoclax in AML.

abstract: Activating mutations in PIK3CA (encoding the p110α kinase) are among the most frequent oncogenic drivers in human tumors. The two major hotspot mutations, E545K (helical domain) and H1047R (kinase domain), both hyperactivate PI3K-AKT signaling, yet they exhibit distinct functional behaviors and differential drug sensitivities. The mutation-specific protein-protein interaction (PPI) networks underlying the differences, however, remain largely unexplored. In this study, we established experimental approaches to identify proteins in proximity to oncogenic PI3K using biotin ligase-based proximity labeling. Our data revealed that the PIK3CA H1047R and E545K mutants fused to BioID2 formed structurally distinct complexes, each associating with unique proximal proteins identified by liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry. Further integration of the PPI networks with CRISPR dependency screens and multiomic profiling mapped the divergent functional interactomes of p110α hotspot mutants. H1047R exhibited a synthetic lethal dependency on the adaptor protein TAB2, which is associated with aggressive clinical phenotypes in breast cancer. Distinctly, E545K interacted with core subunits of the SWI/SNF chromatin remodeling complex, corresponding to a globally repressive chromatin state at distal enhancers. This SWI/SNF association also revealed a mutation-specific epigenetic vulnerability, with E545K-mutant cells displaying increased sensitivity to EZH2 inhibitors. Collectively, these findings demonstrate that the molecular network complexity of oncogenic PI3K can be interrogated through proximity labeling and that distinct PIK3CA point mutations rewire non-overlapping PPI networks, revealing domain-specific dependencies. Our study provides a framework for mapping mutation-specific interactomes and offers molecular insights and potential therapeutic strategies for PIK3CA-mutant tumors.

title: Integrative proximity labeling and multiomic profiling uncover domain-specific interactomes and molecular vulnerabilities of oncogenic PI3K.

abstract: Accurate detection of gene mutations is crucial for acute myeloid leukaemia (AML) diagnosis and treatment. Although CRISPR/Cas systems enable sensitive mutation detection, their adaptability is constrained by dependence on restriction endonucleases. Herein, we propose a two-step strategy, termed Fpg-RCA-CRISPR/Cas12a for ultrasensitive detection of the p53 R175H, which integrates formamidopyrimidine DNA glycosylase (Fpg)-mediated recognition with rolling circle amplification (RCA)-coupled CRISPR/Cas12a technology. Validation confirmed that Fpg exhibits minimal activity when adenine (A) is opposite the damaged site. Based on this finding, we designed a padlock probe with a site-specific 8-oxoguanine (8-oxoG) modification. This modification enables selective recognition of G > A mutations. For the target TP53 c.524G > A (p53 R175H), the G > A substitution opposite the 8-oxoG site blocks Fpg cleavage, facilitating probe circularization and subsequent RCA. The resulting RCA products then activate the trans-cleavage activity of Cas12a, enabling cascade signal amplification and generating a strong fluorescence output. For wild-type p53, Fpg-mediated cleavage prevents circularization and amplification, yielding weak fluorescence. Taking advantage of the high specificity of the Fpg enzyme and the cascade amplification effect of the RCA-CRISPR/Cas12a system, this method achieves a limit of detection (LOD) of 0.29 fM and covers a linear range from 0.8 fM to 800 pM, along with high reproducibility, excellent selectivity, and negligible background interference. Notably, the assay can detect mutation frequencies as low as 0.1% in excess wild-type p53. Crucially, its clinical feasibility was confirmed by analyzing human serum samples, yielding results consistent with standard assays and thus demonstrating its practical reliability and translational potential.

title: A Two-Step Strategy Based on Fpg Recognition and RCA-CRISPR/Cas12a for Ultrasensitive Detection of Gene Mutation.

abstract: Cell-surface proteins are important biomarkers for cell phenotyping, disease diagnosis, therapeutic evaluation, and drug screening. However, their quantitative analysis on intact living cells remains challenging because conventional methods often require cell lysis, fixation, repeated washing, extensive sample processing, or bulky instrumentation. Herein, we developed a modular and reconfigurable cell-surface-to-solution CRISPR-Cas12a platform for wash-free quantitative analysis of cell-surface proteins on intact living cells. Aptamer recognition of extracellularly accessible targets deblocks a DNA activator, thereby activating Cas12a trans-cleavage in solution and converting localized cell-surface recognition into amplified fluorescence while maintaining a low background in the absence of targets. Using EpCAM as a model target, we engineered a split dual-aptamer architecture that enabled cooperative target recognition, efficient activator deblocking, and low-background signal amplification. The platform achieved sensitive EpCAM detection with a limit of detection of 32 fM and enabled live-cell analysis down to 2 cells/μL. It distinguished cell populations with different surface EpCAM levels and quantitatively monitored epithelial-mesenchymal transition-associated changes in cell-surface EpCAM abundance. Coordinated redesign of the target-responsive nucleic acid components extended the platform to PTK7 detection and the analysis of drug-induced cell-surface PTK7 remodeling. Coupling the system to a lateral flow readout enabled portable visual detection. This work establishes a modular and reconfigurable CRISPR-Cas12a sensing strategy for wash-free amplified quantification of cell-surface proteins on living cells, providing a convenient tool for investigating their dynamic remodeling during physiological and pathological processes and therapeutic responses, as well as for drug screening.

title: Modular Cell-Surface-to-Solution CRISPR-Cas12a Platform for Wash-Free Quantification of Cell-Surface Proteins on Living Cells.

abstract: Immunoglobulin A (IgA) is the most abundant antibody isotype produced by mammals, and has a specialized role in mucosal homeostasis1. IgA is constantly secreted into the intestinal lumen and binds to commensal microorganisms to regulate their colonization and function2,3, with unclear implications for health. IgA deficiency is common in humans, but difficult to study, because of its complex aetiology and comorbidities4-8. Here we use genetically and environmentally controlled mice to show that various models of IgA deficiency result in increased susceptibility to several models of endogenous colorectal cancer. Cellular and molecular analyses revealed that, in the absence of IgA, colonic epithelial cells induce antibacterial factors and accelerate cell cycling in response to the microbiota. Oral treatment with IgA was sufficient to reduce steady-state proliferation and protect mice from tumours; however, this function was due to the structure of the antibody rather than to binding specificity. In a reductionist culture system, IgA directly suppressed epithelial growth. Co-immunoprecipitation mass spectrometry and targeted CRISPR screening identified DMBT1 as an IgA-binding epithelial surface protein that is required for IgA-mediated suppression of proliferation. Together, IgA and DMBT1 tune the normal cycling of absorptive colonocyte progenitors. In IgA-knockout mice, deleting the transmembrane and cytoplasmic signalling portions of DMBT1 was sufficient to reverse both the increased epithelial cell proliferation and the increased tumour susceptibility seen in these mice. These experiments establish a homeostatic function for IgA in tempering physiological epithelial responses to the microbiota to maintain mucosal health.

title: Suppression of epithelial proliferation and tumorigenesis by IgA.

abstract:
AIMS: Type 1 diabetes results from autoimmune destruction of insulin-producing pancreatic β-cells. Although exogenous insulin remains the standard treatment, it does not restore physiological glucose regulation. Differentiation of human pluripotent stem cells into β-cells offers a scalable alternative to cadaveric islet transplantation and has progressed rapidly over the past decade, resulting in nine clinical trials at various stages of completion. Despite this progress, durable graft function remains constrained by two major challenges: the absence of key islet microenvironment components, such as vasculature, extracellular matrix and supporting cell types and continued vulnerability to autoimmune and alloimmune rejection.
METHODS & RESULTS: This review considers emerging technological approaches to overcome these barriers. Bioengineered niches, including multilineage organoids, functionalized hydrogels, decellularized matrices and bioprinting, aim to recreate the native islet microenvironment, while synthetic biology approaches, such as hypoimmune gene editing, CRISPR-based transcriptional control and stimulus-responsive survival circuits, seek to enhance grafts' resilience. Computational and single-cell approaches, including gene regulatory network analysis and digital twin frameworks, are beginning to provide predictive tools for benchmarking differentiation quality and forecasting graft outcomes.
CONCLUSION: Together, these complementary strategies, potentially tailored to individual patients, represent a realistic path towards safer, more effective and durable β-cell replacement therapies for type 1 diabetes.

title: The road ahead for stem cell therapies in type 1 diabetes.

abstract: Pyroptosis is a form of programmed cell death characterized by activation of inflammasome complexes and caspase signaling cascades, ultimately leading to the cleavage and activation of pore‑forming executioners such as gasdermin D (GSDMD), ‑E and ‑B. Accumulating evidence indicates that pyroptosis induction in cancer cells exerts potent antitumor effects. As a result, recent therapeutic strategies such as cancer nanotherapy have increasingly focused on harnessing pyroptotic cell death to improve cancer treatment outcomes. This review aimed to explore recent advances in nanotechnology‑based approaches designed to induce pyroptosis in cancer cells, with an emphasis on their potential to enhance antitumor immunity and overcome treatment resistance. It explored four distinct nanoplatforms: i) Chemo‑photodynamic systems that trigger GSDME‑mediated death by generating reactive oxygen species; ii) magneto‑plasmonic nanoparticles that use GSDME activation to modulate the tumor microenvironment, turning 'cold' tumors 'hot'; iii) bioorthogonal chemical delivery tools leveraging click chemistry for site‑specific gasdermin release; and iv) nano‑CRISPR activation scaffolds designed to boost GSDME expression and work alongside cisplatin. Beyond these platforms, the present review highlights how immune cell‑derived granzymes and interferon‑γ drive vital downstream pyroptotic pathways via GSDME and GSDMB activation. Lastly, the review weighs clinical risks, such as chronic systemic inflammation and tumor‑promoting environments, providing a realistic perspective on how to safely progress these preclinical nanotherapies into selective, effective clinical immunotherapies.

title: Pyroptosis in cancer nanotherapy: Molecular mechanisms and advanced nanosystems (Review).

abstract: Bovine mastitis is a complex inflammatory disease. Somatic cell count and bacteriological culture are central to bovine mastitis diagnosis. Complementary molecular measurements could clarify processes underlying persistent mammary injury. Circular RNAs (circRNAs) are relatively stable, back-spliced transcripts with context-dependent expression and potential regulatory functions, making them relevant candidates for investigating post-transcriptional control in the bovine mammary gland. This review critically evaluates circRNA evidence in bovine mastitis, with particular emphasis on Staphylococcus aureus and Escherichia coli. It integrates findings from mammary epithelial-cell models, mammary tissue and animal studies, peripheral blood, milk extracellular vesicles and N⁶-methyladenosine-associated circRNA profiling. Available studies report changes in circRNA abundance and modification patterns under mastitis-associated conditions. Candidate circRNAs are associated with inflammatory signalling, epithelial organization, vesicle and phagosome biology, and apoptosis. One functional study also implicates a circRNA in ferroptosis. However, most reported circRNAs are supported only by differential expression, expression validation, host-gene enrichment or predicted circRNA-microRNA-mRNA networks. These findings identify candidate mechanisms but do not establish direct regulation. Functional evidence remains limited, although circPRIM2 and circ_HOMER3 demonstrate that individual circRNAs can modify inflammatory, secretory, apoptotic and ferroptotic phenotypes in bovine mammary epithelial-cell models. Milk extracellular vesicle circRNAs are analytically detectable and infection responsive, but diagnostic sensitivity, pathogen discrimination and added value beyond established tests remain unproven. Progress now depends on coordinate-based nomenclature, full-length isoform resolution, direct interaction and rescue experiments, pathogen-defined animal studies and independent longitudinal cohorts. The immediate priority is therefore to move beyond circRNA catalogues and identify a smaller set of reproducible candidates with validated mechanisms and measurable translational value.

abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD) is characterized by the progressive loss of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra pars compacta. Genetic and epidemiological studies have suggested that mitochondrial dysfunction is implicated in the development of PD. PRKN/Parkin is known to play an essential role in mitochondrial quality control and mitophagy. Indeed, mutations and inactivation of this gene are associated with hereditary and idiopathic forms of PD. Despite extensive studies on PRKN-dependent mitophagy, the molecular regulators of PRKN-independent mitophagy in dopaminergic neurons remain incompletely understood. We generated a PRKN knockout iPSC-derived dopaminergic neuronal line expressing the fluorescent mitophagy biosensor mito-SRAI, which reports the delivery of mitochondria to lysosomes as an increase in the TOLLES/YPet fluorescence ratio. We used this cell line to conduct a genome-wide CRISPR knockout screen to reveal genetic regulators involved in PRKN-independent mitophagy. Dozens of genes were identified whose knockout increased the TOLLES/YPet ratio in an uncoupler-dependent manner. Of these, several genes emerged as candidates with potential therapeutic implications, one of which was Cathepsin F (CTSF). CCCP treatment increased the TOLLES/YPet ratio in neurons with siRNA-mediated CTSF knockdown, and CTSF knockdown partially preserved the proportion of tyrosine hydroxylase-positive dopaminergic neurons after paraquat exposure. These results suggest that CTSF is a candidate regulator of PRKN-independent mitophagy and that this lysosomal enzyme may represent a potentially druggable candidate target for PD.

abstract:
BACKGROUND: Multiple myeloma (MM) is a clonal plasma cell malignancy in which disease relapse and treatment resistance remain major clinical challenges. Identifying molecular dependencies that support myeloma cell fitness may reveal therapeutic vulnerabilities beyond recurrent genomic alterations. Mesencephalic astrocyte-derived neurotrophic factor (MANF) is an endoplasmic reticulum-resident, stress-responsive protein, but its clinical and biological significance in MM remains poorly defined.
METHODS: Publicly available DepMap CRISPR dependency data were analyzed to identify candidate MM-preferential dependencies. MANF expression and prognostic associations were examined in the MMRF CoMMpass cohort. Single-cell RNA sequencing and in silico perturbation analyses characterized its cellular distribution and predicted functional associations. MANF knockdown and genetic rescue using an siRNA-resistant MANF construct were performed in RPMI-8226 and OPM-2 cells to assess proliferation, cell-cycle distribution, and bortezomib sensitivity. Transcriptomic profiling characterized gene expression changes following MANF knockdown, while measurements at multiple time points assessed the temporal patterns of IRE1α-XBP1s-associated readouts.
RESULTS: MANF was identified as a candidate MM-preferential dependency. Higher MANF expression was associated with advanced ISS stage and inferior overall survival, with the survival association retained after adjustment for established clinical and cytogenetic risk factors. Single-cell analysis localized MANF expression predominantly to plasma cells, while virtual knockout predicted changes involving ER protein processing, proteasome function, and metabolism. MANF knockdown inhibited proliferation, increased G0/G1 accumulation, and reduced MYC/E2F-associated transcriptional programs and cell-cycle regulatory proteins. Time-course analyses revealed early enhancement followed by later attenuation in selected IRE1α-XBP1s-associated readouts. MANF knockdown also increased bortezomib-induced apoptosis and reduced its IC₅₀. MANF re-expression partially reversed proliferation and cell-cycle phenotypes, restored IRE1α-XBP1s-associated protein abundance, and attenuated bortezomib sensitization.
CONCLUSION: These findings identify MANF as a previously underexplored candidate myeloma-associated dependency that supports proliferative fitness and modulates bortezomib sensitivity in the tested MM models. MANF depletion is associated with dynamic changes in IRE1α-XBP1s-related readouts. These results support further investigation of MANF as a candidate therapeutic vulnerability in MM.

abstract:
INTRODUCTION: TB (tuberculosis) due to Mycobacterium tuberculosis continues to be a significant worldwide health issue. Timely and reliable diagnostic tests will improve treatment outcomes and reduce the spread of disease. Traditional TB diagnostics currently available, such as smear microscopy and culture, have significant limitations with regard to sensitivity and turnaround times, especially for smear-negative cases and for tuberculosis in extrapulmonary locations.
OBJECTIVES: The purpose of this review is to analyze the evolution of TB diagnostics from traditional microbiology to new molecular diagnostic methods (including CRISPR, biosensor technology, and microfluidic methods), including an assessment of their diagnostic testing performance, feasibility, and potential for the future.
METHODS: The systematic narrative review aimed to systematically assess literature published from 2020 to 2025 retrieved from PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, IEEE Xplore, ScienceDirect, and Google Scholar. The review was carried out according to the PRISMA guidelines and included 89 studies after screening and assessing for eligibility. The data were analysed qualitatively (i.e., through thematic analysis) by comparing data from conventional, molecular, and next-generation diagnostic methods.
RESULTS: Molecular tests (e.g., GeneXpert, Line Probe Assays, PCR, and Whole Genome Sequencing) provide greater sensitivity and specificity than traditional methods and allow for faster diagnosis. Additionally, newer CRISPR-based tests, biosensors, and microfluidic devices hold promise for rapid, portable, point-of-care diagnosis of tuberculosis.
DISCUSSION: The findings indicate that molecular diagnostics improve rapid detection and drug-resistance profiling, while CRISPR and biosensor platforms offer potential for rapid point-of-care testing. However, affordability, infrastructure, clinical validation, and scalability remain important barriers.
CONCLUSION: The use of molecular diagnostic testing, CRISPR technology, biosensors, artificial intelligence, and portable platforms will dramatically enhance existing TB surveillance systems and strategies for controlling the disease globally.

title: Next-Generation Mycobacterium tuberculosis Diagnostics: A Systematic Review of Molecular, CRISPR, and Biosensor Technologies.

abstract: The management of allergic and immunologic diseases has long centered on symptom management rather than disease modification. Conventional pharmacotherapy controls manifestations of the immune dysregulation but does little to treat the underlying cause. Newer monoclonal and small molecule therapies target downstream effectors of the type 2 inflammatory cascade, and allergen immunotherapy, while disease-modifying, requires years of administration for effect. Nucleic acid therapies represent a different approach that intervenes at the level of genetic information itself, at the DNA, RNA, or protein-production step. This includes mRNA treatments that direct cells to produce therapeutic proteins or modify allergen-specific immune responses; antisense oligonucleotides and small interfering RNAs that selectively silence disease genes; adeno-associated viral vectors for sustained gene delivery; and CRISPR-based systems that permanently edit the genome. Several technologies have advanced to clinical proof of concept including a CRISPR gene-editing therapy (lonvoguran ziclumeran) that reduced hereditary angioedema attacks by 87% compared with placebo in a randomized controlled trial. An inhaled DNAzyme targeting the intracellular transcription factor GATA3 attenuated allergen-induced late asthmatic responses by 34% in humans, and CD19 CAR-T cell therapy induced drug-free remission in severe autoimmune disease. As of 2025, 24 oligonucleotide therapeutics have received FDA approval, including donidalorsen, the first RNA-targeted prophylactic therapy approved for hereditary angioedema. This review examines each therapeutic technology, its mechanism and delivery strategy, and the evidence relevant to allergic and immunologic disease. Persistent challenges, including delivery beyond the liver, immune responses to viral vectors, and the need for long-term safety data, are addressed alongside a proposed integration with existing treatment paradigms.

description:
For dose 1 and 2, the currently available mRNA vaccines (Pfizer-BioNTech BNT162b2 and Moderna mRNA-1273) are two dose vaccines which were studied in schedules of either 0 and 21 days or 0 and 28 days, respectively. The ChAdOx1 nCOV-19 (Astra-Zeneca) adenovirus-vectored vaccine is authorized to be given in two doses one month to 12 weeks apart. We will compare the interval 0, 28 days to a 0, 112 days (16 weeks) schedule, and assess the immunogenicity of both heterogeneous and heterologous second doses using the Canadian schedule.

For dose 3, the currently available mRNA vaccines (Pfizer-BioNTech BNT162b2 and Moderna mRNA-1273) and plant-based virus-like particle (Medicago Covifenz) are anticipated to be administered 6 months apart. We will assess the immunogenicity of both heterogeneous and heterologous third doses using the Canadian schedule.

For dose 4, the currently available mRNA vaccines (Pfizer-BioNTech BNT162b2 and Moderna mRNA-1273) and plant-based virus-like particle (Medicago Covifenz) are anticipated to be administered 3 months apart. We will assess the immunogenicity of both heterogeneous and heterologous third doses using the Canadian schedule.

abstract: Human norovirus is a leading cause of acute gastroenteritis worldwide across all age groups, yet no licensed vaccine is available. The major capsid protein, VP1, self-assembles into highly immunogenic virus-like particles (VLPs) that have shown promise in clinical studies. Recently, mRNA has emerged as a compelling platform for norovirus vaccination. However, whether VP1-encoding mRNA can drive authentic VLP formation in human cells relevant to the vaccination environment has remained unknown. In this study, we used multiple human cell lines, including THP-1-derived macrophage-like cells, to model the post-vaccination environment. Transfection with norovirus GII.4 VP1 mRNA or lipid nanoparticle-formulated VP1 mRNA induced both intracellular and extracellular VP1 expression. Sucrose gradient purification and electron microscopy confirmed VLP assembly. These particles retained key antigenic and functional properties, including recognition by norovirus-specific antibodies in human serum and binding to histo-blood group antigens. Collectively, our findings provide direct evidence that VP1-encoding mRNA can generate structurally and functionally relevant norovirus VLPs in physiologically relevant human cell systems. These results strengthen the mechanistic rationale for mRNA-based norovirus vaccines and support their continued development.

abstract:
INTRODUCTION: mRNA-lipid nanoparticle (mRNA-LNP) therapeutics represent a transformative pharmacological paradigm in which the delivery vehicle, genetic payload, and expressed protein form a tightly coupled system. This multicomponent structure introduces nonlinear, multiscale dynamics that challenge traditional pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic frameworks, making quantitative modeling essential.
AREAS COVERED: This review provides a structured biological framework for mRNA-LNP therapeutics, detailing the key processes governing delivery, endosomal escape, mRNA stability, and translation, and highlighting their associated temporal and spatial scales, providing the key aspects to consider for modeling. Building on this foundation, we summarize mathematical modeling approaches, including pharmacokinetic (PK), pharmacodynamic (PD), physiologically based pharmacokinetic (PBPK), and quantitative systems pharmacology (QSP) models, used to represent these mechanisms. The literature was surveyed to identify representative preclinical and translational studies, focusing on model structure, assumptions, and their use in human projection and dose optimization.
EXPERT OPINION: Mathematical models are increasingly critical to interpret and predict mRNA therapeutic behavior, yet challenges remain in parameter identifiability, data availability, and model standardization. Future advances will depend on biologically grounded modeling frameworks, improved integration of mechanistic insight with quantitative approaches, and tighter coupling between experimental design and model development. These developments will support more efficient translation and enable precision medicine applications.

abstract:
Ovarian, fallopian tube, or primary peritoneal cancer, collectively referred to as ovarian cancer, remains the deadliest type of gynaecological cancer. The most common and aggressive form is called high-grade serous ovarian cancer.

The main purpose of this study is to understand whether an experimental study vaccine, CryptiVax-1001, is safe when administered to patients with high-grade serous ovarian cancer (HGSOC). The study vaccine is a cancer vaccine, which aims to delay or possibly prevent the cancer from coming back. However, as this is the first study of the vaccine in patients, the primary purpose of this study is to assess the safety of the study vaccine.

Following surgery and platinum-based chemotherapy participants may enter the trial and receive CryptiVax-1001 as an explorative maintenance therapy.

The main purposes of this study are therefore to:

* assess how well the study vaccine is tolerated and identify any side effects.
* analyse the study vaccine's capacity to activate your immune system

The study will test escalating dose levels of CryptiVax-1001 based on the safety evaluations to estimate appropriate future dose levels for CryptiVax-1001.
description:
The OVACT study is the First in Human clinical evaluation of Cryptivax-1001 in patients with advanced high-grade serous or predominantly serous ovarian, fallopian tube, or primary peritoneal cancer, following optimal debulking surgery (R0 or R1 after either IDS or PDS), and no recurrence or progression after completion of platinum-based chemotherapy. This phase I/Ib dose escalation and expansion study will assess safety, tolerability, and immunogenicity in a population where there is a high unmet need and no clearly effective maintenance therapy options. By focusing on the BRCAwt/HRP subgroup, the study addresses the majority of patients who currently lack access to biologically-matched maintenance strategies.

The study consist of 2 parts - a dose escalation part and an optional dose expansion part

abstract: RNA modifications are being investigated as contributors to multiple myeloma (MM) biology alongside genomic lesions and bone marrow interactions. This narrative review examines N⁶-methyladenosine (m⁶A), 5-methylcytosine (m⁵C), adenosine-to-inosine editing, and pseudouridylation, with emphasis on the distinction between MM-specific findings and mechanisms proposed from other systems. Functional studies in MM cells and animal models link METTL3, WTAP, FTO, ALKBH5, and YTHDF2 to selected growth, metabolic, and treatment-response programs. Adenosine deaminase acting on RNA 1 (ADAR1) has been implicated in GLI1 editing and regulation of double-stranded RNA sensing during lenalidomide exposure. Patient expression and outcome associations support clinical relevance but do not establish that these regulators determine disease behavior. Evidence for m⁵C is more limited, including an NSUN2-exosomal MALAT1 mechanism in myeloma bone disease, while the pseudouridylation studies discussed here largely concern non-myeloma cancers. Stage-specific regulatory changes across precursor disease and relapse remain hypotheses requiring longitudinal testing. Therapeutic approaches include enzyme inhibition, targeted protein degradation, and RNA-directed strategies; most remain preclinical, and several have been evaluated mainly outside MM. Plasma cell-free RNA studies provide early diagnostic observations, but modification-aware liquid biopsy has not been clinically validated for MM risk stratification, treatment selection, or relapse prediction. Progress will depend on disease-specific target validation, selective delivery, assessment of normal hematopoietic effects, and prospective clinical studies. Epitranscriptomic regulation therefore offers a useful research framework for understanding and potentially targeting MM, without displacing the established contribution of genomic and clinical risk factors.

title: Epitranscriptomic regulation contributes to multiple myeloma biology and offers potential therapeutic targets.

abstract: Cancer remains a leading global mortality cause, driven by complex interactions within the tumor microenvironment (TME) that facilitate progression, immune evasion, and therapeutic resistance. Cytokines form the central regulatory network governing TME intercellular communication, exerting highly context-dependent pro- and anti-tumorigenic effects. Dysregulated cytokine signaling drives chronic inflammation and immunosuppression, limiting durable therapeutic responses. While cytokine-based immunotherapies show clinical potential, their widespread use is hindered by poor stability, rapid clearance, limited specificity, and dose-limiting toxicities. Advances in nanomedicine offer innovative solutions by improving cytokine pharmacokinetics, tumor-selective delivery, and spatiotemporally controlled release. Beyond passive delivery, engineered nanoplatforms act as active modulators of the tumor immune ecosystem, remodeling cytokine networks to restore antitumor immunity. Nanotechnology interventions effectively regulate key signaling pathways- including JAK/STAT, TGF-β/SMAD, NF-κB, MAPK/ERK, and PI3K/AKT- disrupting pathological feedback mechanisms and crosstalk. Furthermore, localized cytokine delivery, gene silencing, mRNA therapeutics, and CRISPR-enabled genome engineering are expanding precision immunotherapy. Despite significant translational challenges such as tumor heterogeneity, biological barriers, immunogenicity, and manufacturing complexity emerging biomimetic and personalized nanoplatforms offer promising avenues for precise immune modulation and biomarker-guided patient stratification. Literature searches were conducted across PubMed, Web of Science, Scopus, and ScienceDirect (with Google Scholar for citation tracking) covering peer-reviewed publications from 2003 to 2026.

title: Cytokine networks in the tumor microenvironment: nanotherapeutic modulation of immune-cell communication and signaling networks.

abstract: RNA-binding proteins (RBPs) are emerging as critical post-transcriptional regulators that control multiple stages of RNA life cycle, thereby linking post-transcriptional programs to cellular function. Increasing evidence implicates dysregulated RBP-RNA interactions in key pathological mechanisms underlying interstitial lung diseases (ILDs), including epithelial injury, fibroblast activation, immune dysregulation and impaired tissue repair. In idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF), cytoplasmic retention of the RBP Fused in Sarcoma (FUS) in patient derived fibroblasts is associated with preferential binding to profibrotic transcripts, while antisense oligonucleotide mediated suppression of FUS attenuates fibrotic signaling and enhances epithelial regenerative programs in cellular, ex vivo and 3D models. Emerging findings across ILD subtypes suggest that RBP dysregulation may represent a broader post-transcriptional phenomenon. Here, we review the principles governing RBP-RNA interactions, approaches for identifying and measuring these interactions and the links between RBPs, aging and lung pathology. We further discuss the emerging role of RBPs as post-transcriptional orchestrators of ILD pathogenesis and consider their potential as therapeutic targets.

title: RNA-binding proteins as emerging regulators in interstitial lung diseases.

abstract: Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) and osteoarthritis (OA) are debilitating joint disorders with distinct etiologies but share common pathological features of chronic inflammation and progressive cartilage damage. Current therapeutic options are largely palliative and yet fail to achieve desired effect. In this study, we developed a combinatorial mRNA therapy using a rationally engineered lipid nanoparticle (LNP) containing a novel ionizable lipid for enhanced cartilage penetration upon intra-articular administration. This LNP co-delivers mRNAs encoding two complementary therapeutic proteins: interleukin-1 receptor antagonist (IL-1Ra) for inflammation attenuation and a C-terminal truncated derivative of angiopoietin-like 3 (ANL3) for cartilage degeneration prevention. In pre-clinical models including collagen-induced arthritis mice, TNF-transgenic mice with spontaneous RA and destabilization of medial meniscus (DMM) surgical OA model, this dual therapy significantly ameliorated disease severity, reduced synovitis and bone erosion, and potently repaired cartilage damage. Mechanistically, transcriptomic profiling of joint specimens revealed that the combinatorial therapy concurrently suppressed inflammatory pathways and extracellular matrix degradation pathways, meanwhile upregulating anabolic genes facilitating chondrogenesis. Collectively, our study establishes a versatile and synergistic mRNA therapy that offers a potent disease-modifying immunomodulatory strategy capable of addressing the long-standing unmet needs in arthritis treatment.

title: A Combinatorial mRNA Therapy for Treating Rheumatoid Arthritis and Osteoarthritis by Inhibiting Inflammation and Preventing Cartilage Degeneration.

abstract: This pilot study evaluates the safety and feasibility of paclitaxel carried in cholesterol-rich lipid nanoparticles (LDE-paclitaxel) in heart transplant recipients with cardiac allograft vasculopathy (CAV). Changes in coronary atherosclerosis measured by intravascular ultrasound (IVUS) are assessed as secondary outcomes.

companies.label: University of Sao Paulo General Hospital
matched_phrases: University of Sao Paulo General Hospital

companies: University of Sao Paulo General Hospital
description:
Cardiac allograft vasculopathy (CAV) is a leading cause of late graft failure and death after heart transplantation and has no effective pharmacological treatment. LDE is a cholesterol-rich lipid nanoemulsion that binds to LDL receptors and concentrates in tissues with high receptor expression. In a rabbit heterotopic heart transplant model, LDE-paclitaxel reduced coronary stenosis and macrophage infiltration of the graft without observable toxicity. LDE-paclitaxel (175 mg/m²) was previously well tolerated in patients with breast and ovarian cancer and in patients with aortic atherosclerosis.

In this single-center, randomized (1:1), quadruple-blind, placebo-controlled pilot study, adult heart transplant recipients more than 1 year after transplantation with angiographically documented CAV receive six intravenous infusions, every 3 weeks, of LDE-paclitaxel (paclitaxel 175 mg/m² body surface area) or LDE without paclitaxel (placebo), each infused over 2 hours without premedication. Coronary angiography and IVUS of up to three epicardial vessels are performed at baseline and approximately 1 month after the sixth infusion, and IVUS analyses are performed in matched segments by an analyst blinded to treatment allocation. Laboratory safety tests are performed before each infusion, and participants are followed clinically for 12 months after the follow-up angiography.

The protocol planned 24 participants (20 plus 20% anticipated losses); 22 were enrolled.

abstract: Artemisinin-based combination therapies are the frontline treatment for Plasmodium falciparum malaria, but their efficacy is threatened by Artemisinin partial resistance (ART R ). ART R in Plasmodium falciparum is mediated by Pfkelch13 ( k13 ) mutations but remains rare in West Africa. A critical question is whether short-term drug survival intrinsically predicts long-term evolutionary persistence. Here, using CRISPR-Cas9 editing, and nanopore-assisted allele tracking in a contemporary Senegalese isolate, we evaluated ART R receptivity using the ring-stage survival assay (RSA), a proxy for clinical resistance. We demonstrate that ART R survival and drug-free persistence are biologically separable traits. While the WHO-validated Asian I543T mutation conferred the RSA phenotype, it was rapidly counter-selected during drug-free growth. In contrast, emerging African alleles (R561H, M579I) and a regional novel variant (C473S) establish stable resistance without a competitive penalty. These findings reveal that a parasite's genetic background acts as a strict evolutionary filter, uncoupling short-term tolerance from long-term persistence and establishing that genomic context determines allele-specific resistance trajectories.

abstract:
An open-label, controlled, multi-site, interventional, 2-arm, Phase II/III trial of BNT113 in combination with pembrolizumab vs pembrolizumab monotherapy as first line treatment in patients with unresectable recurrent or metastatic HPV16+ HNSCC expressing programmed cell death ligand-1 (PD-L1) with combined positive score (CPS) ≥1.

This trial has two parts.

Part A, is an initial non-randomized Safety Run-In Phase to confirm the safety and tolerability at the selected dose range level of BNT113 in combination with pembrolizumab.

Part B, is a randomized part to generate pivotal efficacy and safety data of BNT113 in combination with pembrolizumab versus pembrolizumab monotherapy in the first line setting in patients with unresectable recurrent or metastatic HPV16+ HNSCC expressing PD-L1 with CPS ≥1. Patients included in the Safety Run-In Phase of the trial (Part A) will not be randomized to Part B and will continue on-trial treatment (BNT113 plus pembrolizumab) within Part A.

For Part B, an optional pre-screening phase is available for all patients where patients' tumor samples may be submitted for central HPV16 DNA and central PD-L1 expression testing prior to screening into the main trial.

Patients will be treated with BNT113 in combination with pembrolizumab or with pembrolizumab monotherapy for approximately up to 24 months.

abstract: Genome editing has emerged as a promising tool to complement selective breeding programmes and accelerate genetic gain in aquaculture. Although CRISPR-based genome editing has been successfully applied in several economically important fish species, its application at an industry-relevant scale remains challenging due to limitations of current delivery methods, which primarily rely on manual embryo microinjection. This approach is labour-intensive, technically demanding, and frequently results in high levels of mosaicism in founder individuals, necessitating additional generations of breeding to establish stable genotypes. In this mini review, we discuss the potential of combining germline stem cell (GSC) culture and transplantation approaches as an alternative platform for further improved genome editing in fish. By enabling genetic changes to be introduced, validated, and expanded in vitro prior to germline transmission, this approach has the potential to improve scalability, reduce mosaicism, and shorten breeding timelines. Although several technical challenges remain, continued progress in GSC culture and transplantation methodologies could facilitate the practical implementation of tailored genome editing for improved genetic gain, fish health, and welfare in aquaculture.

abstract: Huntington's disease (HD) is traditionally regarded as a progressive neurodegenerative disorder caused by an expanded CAG repeat in the HTT gene, resulting in selective striatal neuronal degeneration and progressive motor, cognitive, and psychiatric impairment. However, accumulating evidence indicates that HD is a systemic disorder involving profound metabolic, mitochondrial, and immune dysfunction in peripheral organs, particularly the liver. Emerging studies suggest that hepatic mitochondrial dysfunction induced by mutant huntingtin remodels the hepatic secretome through altered secretion of hepatokines, extracellular vesicles, complement proteins, inflammatory cytokines, and metabolic mediators. These circulating factors may disrupt blood-brain barrier integrity, promote microglial immunometabolic reprogramming, enhance complement-mediated synaptic pruning, and amplify chronic neuroinflammation, thereby accelerating neurodegeneration. This review summarizes current evidence supporting the liver-brain axis in HD and discusses how hepatic metabolic dysfunction contributes to central nervous system pathology. Furthermore, we highlight therapeutic strategies aimed at restoring hepatic mitochondrial homeostasis, modulating hepatokines, extracellular vesicles, exosomal microRNAs, and complement signaling to interrupt pathological liver-to-brain communication. Finally, we discuss emerging translational approaches, including multi-omics technologies, engineered extracellular vesicles, gene-editing platforms, and precision medicine, that may facilitate the development of disease-modifying therapies. By integrating peripheral metabolic regulation with central neuroimmune mechanisms, this review presents the hepatic secretome microglia axis as a potential conceptual framework for understanding HD pathogenesis and identifies liver targeted interventions as promising therapeutic opportunities beyond conventional neuron centric strategies.

abstract: Insect-pests remain a major constraint to global agriculture, causing yield losses through direct feeding and transmission of phytopathogens. Chemical pesticides and transgenic crops expressing Bacillus thuringiensis toxins have shown initial success; however, their use is increasingly constrained by resistance, non-target effects, environmental contamination and regulatory restrictions. Although RNA interference (RNAi) presents a targeted and eco-friendly alternative, it is limited by species variability, rapid double-stranded RNA (dsRNA) degradation, inconsistent silencing and off-target effects. Nuclease-active Clustered Regularly Interspaced Short Palindromic Repeats/CRISPR-associated protein 9 (CRISPR/Cas9) enables genetic editing, but its irreversible genome modifications raise ethical, ecological and regulatory concerns. CRISPR interference (CRISPRi) offers a programmable approach for sequence-specific, reversible transcriptional suppression without inducing double-strand DNA breaks. Using catalytically inactive Cas9 (dead Cas9 or dCas9) -guided by single-guide RNA (sgRNA), CRISPRi inhibits transcription initiation or elongation while maintaining genomic integrity. Experimental studies in insect models, including disease-vector mosquitoes, have demonstrated effective suppression of coding and non-coding genes, supporting CRISPRi as a functional genomics tool. This review discusses CRISPRi mechanisms, applications, advantages and limitations in insects, comparing it with RNAi and CRISPR/Cas9. Overall, current evidences indicate that CRISPRi is a precise and non-mutagenic platform for insect-pest management, particularly where controlled, reversible and species-specific gene regulation is desirable. However, its application in agricultural pest management remains an extrapolation from functional-genomics studies and requires validation in pest species under whole-organism and field-relevant conditions.

abstract: Plant mitochondrial genomes retain conserved coding content but evolve rapidly in structure. We assembled mitogenomes of four Hippophae taxa from long reads and compared them with four published mitogenomes. Gene content and codon usage were largely conserved, whereas the assemblies of closely related taxa differed by up to four inversions and two translocations. Long reads spanning repeats of 1.3-9.6 kb supported both assembled and recombinant arrangements, and allowing for repeat-mediated isomers removed all inversions among the seven records compared. RNA-seq identified 80-262 candidate editing sites per taxon, and mitogenome-plastome homologous fragments made up 12.54-12.77% of each assembly. A 31-gene phylogeny supported Hippophae monophyly but weakly resolved relationships within the genus (16 parsimony-informative sites). Only nad4 showed a Hippophae-specific increase in ω; its fixed C-to-T substitutions and intron loss point to retroprocessing rather than positive selection. Most structural differences among Hippophae mitogenomes can be explained by repeat-mediated isomerization.

abstract: Long non-coding RNAs (lncRNAs) regulate human dental pulp stem cell (hDPSC) differentiation and stress responses, offering potential targets for dentin-pulp regeneration. This narrative review critically evaluates their roles in self-renewal and osteogenic/odontogenic commitment, distinguishing direct hDPSC evidence from findings in other cell populations. Key mechanisms include miRNA-associated networks, chromatin regulation, RNA-protein interactions, and mRNA stabilization, with effects shaped by inflammatory and hypoxic conditions. Emerging evidence links R-loop accumulation to cGAS-STING activation, increased inflammation, and impaired odontogenic differentiation; however, a causal lncRNA-R-loop pathway remains unestablished in hDPSCs. Extracellular vesicle-mediated lncRNA transfer provides an additional avenue for regenerative investigation. Current evidence remains predominantly preclinical, limited by two-dimensional models, cellular heterogeneity, and incomplete mechanistic validation. Future priorities include single-cell and spatial multi-omics, rigorous interaction and rescue experiments, standardized extracellular-vesicle studies, and organotypic and in vivo validation. Delivery specificity, RNA stability, and safety also require careful evaluation. LncRNAs thus represent promising mechanistic regulators and candidate regenerative targets, but their clinical utility requires stronger causal and translational evidence.

abstract:
This phase II trial studies how well autologous tumor infiltrating lymphocytes LN-145 (LN-145) or LN-145-S1 works in treating patients with ovarian cancer, triple negative breast cancer (TNBC), anaplastic thyroid cancer, osteosarcoma, or other bone and soft tissue sarcomas that do not respond to treatment (refractory) or that has come back (relapsed).

LN-145 is made by collecting and growing specialized white blood cells (called T-cells) that are collected from the patient's tumor. LN-145-S1 is made using a modified process that chooses a specific portion of the T-cells. The T cells may specifically recognize, target, and kill the tumor cells.

description:
PRIMARY OBJECTIVE:

I. To evaluate efficacy using objective response rate (ORR) using Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid Tumors (RECIST) version (v)1.1 in each cohort.

SECONDARY OBJECTIVES:

I. Determine the disease control rate (DCR) within and across cohorts. II. Determine the duration of response (DOR). III. Determine progression-free survival (PFS) and overall survival (OS). IV. Further characterize the safety profile of adoptive cell therapy with tumor infiltrating lymphocytes (TIL) across multiple tumor types.

EXPLORATORY OBJECTIVES:

I. Establish duration of tumor-infiltrating lymphocyte (TIL) persistence. II. Compare the molecular and immunological features of tumors before and after TIL therapy.

III. Prospectively evaluate the existing immunotherapy response criteria (immune-related \[ir\]RECIST) as the best response assessment tool for TIL therapy among a diverse group of solid tumors.

IV. To investigate TIL attributes (CD8 percentage \[%\], CD27 and CD28 expression) and correlation with response to therapy.

V. Assess tumor marker (CA-125) response in patients who produce this tumor marker.

VI. To assess Health-Related Quality of Life (HRQOL).

OUTLINE: Patients are assigned to 1 of 2 cohorts.

THYROID CANCER COHORT: Patients receive cyclophosphamide intravenously (IV) over 2 hours on days -7 and -6, fludarabine IV over 15-30 minutes daily on days -5 to -1, autologous tumor infiltrating lymphocytes LN-145 IV over 45 minutes on day 0 and aldesleukin IV over 30 minutes on days 1-4 for up to 6 doses.

ICI OVARIAN CANCER, OSTEOSARCOMA, Triple Negative Breast Cancer, or OTHER BONE AND SOFT TISSUE SARCOMAS COHORT: Within 2-4 weeks prior to surgery, patients receive a single dose of nivolumab IV over 30 minutes, followed by a single dose of ipilimumab IV over 30 minutes Patients receive cyclophosphamide IV over 2 hours on days -7 and -6, fludarabine IV over 15-30 minutes daily on days -5 to -1, LN-145-S1 IV over 45 minutes on day 0 and aldesleukin IV over 30 minutes on days 1-4 for up to 6 doses. Within 12 weeks after receiving LN-145-S1, patients receive nivolumab IV over 30 minutes every 4 weeks in the absence of disease progression or unacceptable toxicity.

For cohorts treated without immune checkpoint inhibitors, completion of treatment is defined as having received any volume of LN-145/LN-145-S1 infusion followed by at least 1 dose of adjuvant IL-2. For cohorts treated with TIL + ICI, completion of treatment will correspond to the last dose of nivolumab or IL2 (if the subject is deemed unsuitable to receive adjuvant nivolumab). Patients are followed up at 18 weeks, 6, 9, 12, 18 and 24 months, then every 3 months for at least 3 years.

abstract: To evaluate efficacy and safety of Neoadjuvant of Sintilimab Combined Weekly Metronomic Chemotherapy (POLF) in resectable locally advanced gastric cancer.
description:
This is a single-arm clinical study to enroll 50 patients with gastric cancer (cTNM diagnosis of cT3-4aN1-3M0). Each enrolled patient will be assigned a case number. Both this case number and the patient's initials will be entered on each page of the case report form.

Enrolled patients receive a neoadjuvant regimen of POLF in combination with sindilizumab: preoperatively, they receive a POLF regimen (paclitaxel 60 mg/m2, oxaliplatin 50 mg/m2, and 5-fluorouracil 425 mg/m2) administered once weekly for a total of 6 doses, and in combination with sindilizumab 200 mg intravenously once every 3 weeks for a total of 2 doses. Upon completion of the evaluation, patients whose tumors were judged to be resectable underwent radical surgery and received six postoperative doses of the POLF regimen and two doses of Sindilizumab as adjuvant therapy.

Postoperative imaging evaluations will be performed every three months until disease recurrence. Survival follow-up was performed every three months after disease recurrence. Patients will receive neoadjuvant therapy for 6 weeks preoperatively and adjuvant therapy for 6 weeks postoperatively unless intolerable toxicity occurs, the patient refuses to continue treatment, or treatment is delayed beyond 3 weeks. Patients will be under study observation during treatment and 30 days after treatment termination, and will receive long-term follow-up for 5 years postoperatively. Ultimately, pCR and MPR will be the primary study endpoints, and ORR, DCR, 2-year PFS rate, 3-year OS rate and safety will be the secondary study endpoints to evaluate the efficacy and safety of the neoadjuvant regimen of POLF combined with sindilizumab, as well as to explore the immune activation effect and mechanism of the regimen using peripheral blood and tumor tissue samples.

abstract:
The goal of this clinical trial is to learn if AIC263029 is safe and well tolerated in adult kidney transplant recipients with BK virus (BKV) in the blood (viremia). The study will also examine how the body processes AIC263029 and whether it lowers BKV levels in the blood.

Researchers will compare AIC263029 to a placebo (a look-alike injection with no active drug). Participants will be assigned by chance to receive AIC263029 or placebo and will receive weekly injections under the skin for 4 weeks. Participants will have clinic visits and blood tests during treatment and follow-up to monitor safety and measure BKV levels, and will be followed for up to about 24 weeks after treatment.
description:
This study is Part A (Phase 2a) of a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled clinical trial evaluating AIC263029 in adult kidney transplant recipients with BK virus (BKV) viremia. Part A is designed to assess safety and tolerability of multiple dose levels, characterize pharmacokinetics (PK), and explore antiviral activity based on changes in plasma BKV DNA.

In Part A, participants are enrolled into sequential dose cohorts. Within each cohort, participants are randomized in a 3:1 ratio to receive AIC263029 or matching placebo. Three dose levels are planned (100 mg, 200 mg, and 330 mg). Study drug is administered as subcutaneous injections once weekly, for a total of five injections over a 4-week treatment period. Up to three additional optional cohorts may be added based on emerging safety, PK, and antiviral activity data.

Participants undergo screening (up to approximately 30 days), followed by the 4-week treatment period and a follow-up period of up to approximately 24 weeks after the end of treatment. Safety evaluations include monitoring of treatment-emergent adverse events, adverse events of special interest (including injection site reactions and kidney transplant outcomes such as graft loss and acute/chronic rejection), and clinically significant changes in laboratory parameters, vital signs, and electrocardiograms. PK sampling is performed to estimate standard PK parameters. Antiviral activity is assessed by quantitative plasma BKV DNA measurements over time, including assessment of change from baseline and time to clinically meaningful reductions. Viral genotyping/resistance monitoring may be performed to assess baseline polymorphisms and potential treatment-emergent resistance.

abstract: Amyloidosis comprises a group of systemic disorders caused by extracellular deposition of misfolded precursor proteins, leading to progressive organ dysfunction. Cardiac amyloidosis, particularly transthyretin-related amyloid cardiomyopathy (ATTR-CM) has transitioned from a rare and underdiagnosed condition to a treatable disease, driven by major advances in diagnostic imaging, increased disease awareness, and the approval of disease-modifying therapies. These therapies target transthyretin (TTR) stabilization and amyloid production or deposition and have led to an evolving therapeutic landscape. As therapeutic efficacy is greatest in earlier disease stages, timely recognition is crucial. Effective management of ATTR-CM requires structured screening of high-risk populations, multidisciplinary collaboration, and longitudinal follow-up. This review provides a practical, clinician-focused framework that addresses clinical presentation and "red flags" to facilitate early detection. It offers a comprehensive overview of the diagnostic pathway, including (AI-enabled) electrocardiography analysis, (non-)invasive imaging modalities, biomarkers, and genetic testing. Additionally, emerging therapeutic strategies are discussed, encompassing supportive heart failure management, amyloid-specific treatments such as TTR stabilizers and gene silencers, and novel approaches including fibril depletion and gene-editing therapies. As the therapeutic paradigm shifts from disease stabilization toward potential reversal, early diagnosis and personalized treatment strategies are essential to improve prognosis and quality of life in patients with cardiac amyloidosis.

title: Transforming cardiac amyloidosis care: navigating the evolving diagnostic and therapeutic landscape.

abstract: Progressive supranuclear palsy (PSP) is a neurodegenerative disorder characterised by a combination of motor, ocular, cognitive, and behavioural impairment, but has a heterogeneous clinical presentation. It is a devastating and rapidly progressive atypical parkinsonian disorder with no current disease-modifying treatments. PSP is classified as a primary tauopathy characterised by abnormal accumulation of tau within neurons and glial cells, primarily in the brain stem, culminating in cell death. While genome wide association studies have been instrumental in identifying multiple risk loci, recent multi-omics studies combining brain gene expression and other omics measures have revealed a plethora of perturbed transcripts and molecular pathways that may play pivotal roles in PSP. This includes genes such as MAPT, STOM, KANK2, DDR2, LRRK2, and STX6, but their precise roles remain elusive. These genes are differentially expressed and may regulate processes including neuroinflammation, glymphatic clearance of tau, cytoskeletal maintenance, and synaptic function. In this review, we summarise current treatment strategies attempted in PSP, compile disease-modifying therapies in development, and explore potential disease mechanisms suggested by multi-omics studies. By targeting several underlying disease processes at once, combination strategies have the potential to improve both motor and cognitive function, slow neurodegeneration, and ultimately alter disease progression.

abstract: Gene therapy holds considerable promise for treating a wide range of intractable diseases through the modification of specific genes. However, gene therapeutics such as plasmid DNA, messenger RNA, and CRISPR-based systems are susceptible to degradation, face challenges in crossing cellular barriers, and may induce immune-related adverse effects, thereby limiting their clinical translation. Microneedles create microchannels that penetrate tissue barriers and, when combined with various carrier materials, enhance nucleic acid stability and intracellular delivery efficiency. This review summarizes the compatibility of different microneedle configurations with gene-delivery vectors, compares the effects of various fabrication processes on the activity of therapeutic agents, and elucidates the mechanisms underlying barrier penetration and delivery by microneedles. Recent advances in the application of microneedle-based gene therapy in dermatology, oncology, and nucleic acid vaccination are also discussed. Finally, current challenges, including drug loading, mass production, and safety evaluation, are analyzed, and the prospects for smart, responsive, and integrated diagnostic and therapeutic microneedles are highlighted.

abstract: The field of plant genetic engineering has advanced considerably since the development of the first transgenic crop plants, and even though transgenic varieties of various crops are now commercially available, consumer reluctance and environmental concerns over transgene escape pose limits on their expansion. Gene editing offers the opportunity to selectively and precisely alter DNA sequences without reliance on stably integrated transgenes, assuaging both concerns. Considerable progress has been made with the advent of programmable nucleases such as Cas9 and its derivatives. The transgenes encoding the gene editing components can be expressed transiently without integration in the plant's genome or removed from the genome via outcrossing or haploid induction to result in gene-edited plants that are no longer considered transgenic. Nonetheless, gene editing systems remain challenging to implement in some plant species, notably those that have long generation times or are vegetatively propagated, precluding the removal of editing tools through crosses. In these cases, a transgene-free method for introduction of all components needed to enable gene editing will bring the promise of modern breeding tools within reach. Transgene-free genome editing can be accomplished through the delivery of editing components as DNA, RNA, or ribonucleoproteins with delivery via Agrobacterium, microprojectiles, nanocarriers, DNA and RNA viruses, and grafting. Between technical constraints and scientific goals, it can be challenging to determine an appropriate transgene-free genome editing method. Following a review of the literature, a decision tree is provided to help select an appropriate method for a given plant species and to show how emerging tools, including smaller editors, can advance the field.

abstract:
This study tests an investigational cancer vaccine called ITI-5000 in people who have completed standard treatment for early-stage triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC).

ITI-5000 is a self-amplifying RNA (saRNA) vaccine that instructs the immune system to recognize and attack cancer cells expressing two proteins found on TNBC cells-HERV-K and CT83-fused with a molecule called LAMP-1 that helps the immune system respond more strongly. The vaccine is delivered inside lipid nanoparticles (LNPs), similar to other approved mRNA vaccines.

The study has two parts:

* Part A: Participants receive ITI-5000 alone at one of two dose levels (1 µg or 10 µg), given as an injection into the upper arm muscle every 28 days for 3 doses total. The goal is to find the safest dose.
* Part B: Participants receive ITI-5000 at the best dose identified in Part A, combined with the following approved immunotherapy drugs pembrolizumab (Keytruda) and either olaparib or capecitabine.
description:
This will be a phase 1, FIH, multicenter, open-label, two-part, ascending dose study to evaluate the safety, tolerability, and immune response of the ITI-5000 vaccine in adult participants with TNBC (stage 2-3). The study will be divided into 2 parts: in Part A, participants will receive the ITI-5000 vaccine as a single agent in the post-adjuvant setting, and in Part B, participants will receive the ITI-5000 vaccine in combination with standard of care adjuvant therapy.

Part A will be divided into 2 dose level cohorts - Cohort 1A conducted at the dose of 1 μg (low dose) per vaccination and Cohort 2A conducted at the dose of 10 μg (high dose) per vaccination. In Part A, three vaccinations of ITI-5000 will be administered with a 28-day interval.

The first 3-6 participants will be enrolled sequentially, with the first participant designated as a sentinel participant who will be monitored for 28 days after receiving the first ITI-5000 vaccination before subsequent participants are enrolled. If 0/3 participants experience a DLT, Cohort 2A may proceed. If 1/3 of the participants experience a DLT, the cohort will expand to include 3 additional participants (total of 6). If ≥2/6 participants experience a DLT, the dose will be considered not tolerable, and the cohort will be stopped.

At the conclusion of each cohort, the safety review committee (SRC) will review safety signals and determine a rationale for dose escalation, de-escalation, or potential intermediate doses to be evaluated. The SRC will also determine the dose to be evaluated in Cohort 3A and Part B.

The MTD will be evaluated in Cohort 3A which will enroll up to 15 participants who did not achieve pathological complete response (pCR) following neoadjuvant therapy. This expansion will allow further assessment of safety and immunogenicity in a participant population that is at high risk of disease recurrence.

Part B will evaluate the MTD of ITI-5000 in combination with standard of care (SOC) adjuvant therapy among participants who did not achieve a pathological complete response (pCR) following neoadjuvant therapy.

A safety lead-in group comprising 3 participants will be enrolled at the beginning of Cohort 1B and 2B to assess the safety of the combination treatment. Unlike Part A, no sentinel participant will be required, as the safety of ITI-5000 alone will already have been established in Part A. The safety lead-in will provide an early evaluation of the tolerability of the combination regimen before enrolling additional participants.

Cohort 1B will enroll up to 20 participants with BRCA1/2 mutation who did not achieve pathological complete response (pCR) following neoadjuvant therapy. Three doses of ITI-5000 will be administered in the adjuvant setting with a 21-day interval in combination with standard of care (pembrolizumab 200 mg Q3 weeks or 400 mg Q6 weeks and olaparib as per FDA approved label and currently accepted guidelines).

Cohort 2B will enroll up to 20 participants with wild-type BRCA1/2 who did not achieve pCR following neoadjuvant therapy. Three doses of ITI-5000 will be administered in the adjuvant setting with a 21-day interval in combination with standard of care (pembrolizumab 200 mg Q3 weeks or 400 mg Q6 weeks and capecitabine as per FDA approved label and currently accepted guidelines).

Following SRC review of the safety lead-in participants, an expansion cohort of up to 17 additional participants will be enrolled in both Cohorts 1B and 2B, bringing Part B to a total of up to 40 participants (up to 20 participants per cohort).

After all Part B participants have completed the Follow-up #1 visit, the SRC will meet to guide further clinical development of ITI-5000. The final analysis will take place after the end of the study.

In both Part A and Part B, participants will undergo 3 main study periods: a screening period, a treatment period (also named study vaccination period) with 3 study visits during which each participant will receive a total of 3 ITI-5000 vaccinations: 28 days

abstract: Double-stranded RNA (dsRNA) can activate potent anti-tumor immunity, but its clinical translation remains challenging. We sought to identify clinically applicable strategies to induce endogenous dsRNA and enhance anti-tumor immune responses. Here, we integrated genome-wide CRISPR-Cas9 screening data with the Therapeutic Target Database (TTD) and identified Topoisomerase I (TOP1) as a potential inducer of dsRNA. Mechanistically, we found that TOP1 was associated with suppression of endogenous retroviruses (ERVs) in an enzyme activity-dependent manner, and this was accompanied by "viral mimicry" through the induction of dsRNA. Pharmacological inhibition of TOP1 using Irinotecan (CPT-11) triggered dsRNA accumulation across cancer models, including patient-derived organoids (PDOs), activating the RIG-I/MDA5-MAVS pathway and antiviral interferon responses (Type I/III IFNs, ISGs). scRNA-seq revealed that CPT-11 remodeled the tumor microenvironment, promoting infiltration of dendritic cells (DCs), macrophages, and T cells. Combining CPT-11 with PD-1 blockade in "cold" tumors dramatically improved survival. CPT-11 also generated a potent in situ vaccine effect, establishing immunological memory that prevented tumor rechallenge. Moreover, tumor cells pretreated with CPT-11 in vitro were also able to exert a vaccine-like effect, inhibiting the growth of subsequently inoculated tumors. Collectively, our findings support the repurposing of TOP1 inhibitors such as CPT-11 to harness dsRNA-mediated immune activation for more effective cancer therapy.

title: Title: Topoisomerase I Inhibition Serves as a Tumor Vaccine by Inducing the ERVs-dsRNA-Interferon Pathway.

abstract: Myc is an evolutionarily conserved transcription factor that is necessary for the restoration of tissues in multiple regenerative species. The adult mammalian heart lacks regenerative capacity and cardiomyocytes fail to divide following damage-induced signaling. Transgenic expression of Myc and cyclin T1 can drive substantial adult cardiomyocyte proliferation to replace lost cardiomyocytes. Here, using transgenic models and a prototypical mRNA therapeutic, we show that Myc and cyclin T1 require transient induction for cardiomyocyte proliferation that leads to myocardial repair and functional recovery after myocardial infarction in mice. This research provides a strategy to translate Myc-cyclin T1 coexpression for cardiac regeneration to address serious unmet needs in the treatment of cardiovascular disease.

title: A transient modified mRNA encoding Myc and cyclin T1 improves cardiac function after myocardial injury.

abstract:
BACKGROUND: Pelacarsen, an antisense oligonucleotide, reduces serum levels of lipoprotein(a). However, the effect of pelacarsen on cardiovascular outcomes remains uncertain.
METHODS: We conducted an international, randomized, placebo-controlled trial involving patients with preexisting cardiovascular disease and a lipoprotein(a) level of at least 70 mg per deciliter. Patients were randomly assigned in a 1:1 ratio to receive subcutaneous pelacarsen (80 mg) administered monthly or matching placebo. The primary end point was a major adverse cardiovascular event, defined as a composite of death from cardiovascular causes, nonfatal myocardial infarction, nonfatal stroke, or urgent coronary revascularization.
RESULTS: A total of 8350 patients underwent randomization, with 8322 included in the efficacy analysis; 4157 patients were assigned to receive pelacarsen, and 4165 to receive placebo. The mean age of the patients was 59.7 years, and 27.0% were women. The median lipoprotein(a) level at baseline was 236 nmol per liter. At 12 months, the lipoprotein(a) level was 64.4 nmol per liter in the pelacarsen group and 233.4 nmol per liter in the placebo group. The median follow-up was 4.7 years. A primary end-point event occurred in 511 patients (12.3%) in the pelacarsen group and in 503 (12.1%) in the placebo group (hazard ratio, 1.02, 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.90 to 1.15, P = 0.76). Among patients with a baseline lipoprotein(a) level of at least 90 mg per deciliter, a primary end-point event occurred in 402 of 3266 patients (12.3%) in the pelacarsen group and in 403 of 3274 (12.3%) in the placebo group (hazard ratio, 1.00; 95% CI, 0.87 to 1.15; P = 0.99). Serious adverse events occurred in 1553 of 4166 patients (37.3%) who received pelacarsen and in 1709 of 4154 (41.1%) who received placebo.
CONCLUSIONS: Pelacarsen did not result in a lower risk of major adverse cardiovascular events than placebo at a median follow-up of 4.7 years. (Funded by Novartis; Lp[a]HORIZON ClinicalTrials.gov number, NCT04023552.)See also in NEJM Evidence: Extended Analyses of Pelacarsen and Cardiovascular Outcomes in Patients with High Lipoprotein(a).
