title: Pelacarsen and Cardiovascular Outcomes in Patients with High Lipoprotein(a).

abstract: Glioma, particularly glioblastoma, remains difficult to treat because of limited drug penetration across the blood-brain barrier, profound immune suppression, and insufficient intracranial exposure of systemic immunotherapies. Intranasal nano-immunotherapy is being explored as a potential strategy that may integrate noninvasive nose-to-brain delivery with nanocarrier-mediated immune reprogramming. Intranasal administration may partially bypass conventional vascular barriers through olfactory, trigeminal, mucosal, cerebrospinal-fluid, and perivascular transport routes, while nanoparticles are designed to protect immune-active payloads, support brain tumor targeting, and enable controlled release. Current evidence spans three distinct levels: direct intranasal glioma nano-immunotherapy, intranasal glioma nanodelivery without demonstrated immune reprogramming, and non-intranasal glioma nano-immunotherapy that provides mechanistic support for future intranasal adaptation. Across these evidence levels, investigated platforms include peptide-guided nanomicelles, lipid nanoparticles, biomimetic nanoparticles, ferritin-based nanovectors, spherical nucleic acids, extracellular vesicles, bacterial outer membrane vesicles, and stimuli-responsive systems. These platforms can deliver immune-activating cargos, such as STING or TLR agonists; gene-regulatory cargos, such as siRNA and CRISPR-Cas9 components; and microenvironment-modulating cargos, such as chemokine-axis inhibitors, checkpoint-modulating agents, and combination payloads. Through these payloads, intranasal nanoplatforms may activate innate immune sensing, reverse myeloid-mediated suppression, enhance T-cell infiltration, and induce immunogenic cell death. However, translation remains limited by dosing uncertainty, species differences in nasal anatomy, mucosal and neurological safety concerns, manufacturing complexity, and incomplete immune pharmacodynamic validation. This review summarizes recent advances in intranasal and brain-targeted glioma nano-immunotherapy, highlights key immune mechanisms, and proposes a preclinical validation framework for evaluating whether experimental efficacy can be advanced toward clinically testable treatment designs.

title: Intranasal nano-immunotherapy for glioma: bypassing the blood-brain barrier, reprogramming the immune microenvironment, and bridging preclinical validation.

abstract: Lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) are a leading platform for mRNA delivery, yet improving their performance often requires complex chemical modification or reformulation of core components. Here, we report a modular peptide-coating strategy for post-formulation engineering of LNP interfaces through physical assembly. A modular multifunctional peptide (MFP) library was developed to systematically investigate how peptide composition, secondary structure, chirality, and concentration regulate coating assembly and delivery performance. In vitro, MFP coatings enhanced cellular uptake, endosomal escape, and mRNA translation. In vivo, optimized coatings improved mRNA delivery across multiple LNP formulations and promoted receptor-mediated tumor-specific accumulation and expression. In an IL-12 mRNA immunotherapy model, MFP-coated LNPs elicited potent antitumor immune responses and inhibited tumor growth without observable systemic toxicity. This work establishes a modular peptide surface engineering strategy for regulating LNP biological performance and provides an expandable framework for developing a tissue- and disease-specific nanomedicine platform through the tailoring of peptide functional modules.

abstract: Accurate and dynamic visualization of nucleic acids at the single-molecule level is essential for elucidating cellular processes, defining disease-associated molecular mechanisms, and advancing molecular diagnostics. Conventional imaging methods often lack the sensitivity, specificity, or spatiotemporal resolution required in complex biological systems. Engineered clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats (CRISPR) technologies, leveraging the high programmability of Cas proteins and guide RNAs, have expanded nucleic acid imaging from repetitive and non-repetitive genomic loci to sequence-variant discrimination and individual RNA imaging. This review summarizes major engineering strategies, including Cas protein labeling, guide RNA scaffold modification, and nanomaterial- or protein-assisted signal amplification platforms. We further discuss biomedical applications in live-cell tracking, spatial nucleic acid analysis, and real-time monitoring of cellular dynamics. By examining the biochemical and engineering principles underlying these platforms, we provide a framework for the rational design of CRISPR-based nucleic acid imaging strategies and identify key considerations for overcoming persistent limitations in complex biological environments. Collectively, these advances position engineered CRISPR imaging as a programmable platform for spatially resolved nucleic acid analysis; however, broader application to clinically relevant specimens will require rigorous validation of quantitative robustness and specimen compatibility, together with standardized imaging workflows.

abstract:
BACKGROUND: Triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) is an aggressive breast cancer subtype with limited targeted therapeutic options. Mucin-type O-GalNAc glycosylation mediated by N-acetylgalactosaminyltransferase (GALNT) family enzymes contributes to tumor progression, while GALNT14's functional substrates and mechanisms in TNBC remain largely unknown.
MATERIALS AND METHODS: Expression profiling was performed using clinical tissue microarray and TCGA dataset. Cellular loss-of-function, gain-of-function and rescue experiments were conducted in TNBC cell lines. In vivo tumor growth and lung metastasis were evaluated in nude mice. Co-IP-LC-MS/MS, VVA-lectin pulldown and cycloheximide-chase assays were applied to identify interacting partners, characterize O-GalNAc glycosylation and assess protein stability.
RESULTS: GALNT14 was markedly upregulated in TNBC tissues (P < 0.05). GALNT14 knockdown inhibited TNBC cell proliferation, migration and invasion in vitro (P < 0.001), and suppressed xenograft growth and lung metastasis in vivo (tumor weight: P < 0.001; metastatic nodules: P < 0.01). α-Enolase 1 (ENO1) was identified as a novel substrate of GALNT14. GALNT14 catalyzed O-GalNAc glycosylation of ENO1 at Ser63. This modification did not change ENO1 mRNA level, yet enhanced ENO1 protein stability (P < 0.001). Under GALNT14-proficient background, glycosylation-deficient ENO1-S63A displayed attenuated oncogenic capacity compared with ENO1-WT (P < 0.05). Both ENO1-WT and ENO1-S63A rescued malignant phenotypes upon GALNT14 silencing (P < 0.001).
CONCLUSION: A GALNT14-ENO1 Ser63 O-GalNAc glycosylation axis drives TNBC progression, providing new mechanistic insight and candidate therapeutic targets for TNBC.

abstract:
This study will test a Regeneron study drug called ALN-CIDEB to find out whether it may help treat a liver disease called MASH.

In this study, researchers are looking at the effect of ALN-CIDEB on reducing liver fat, liver injury, and liver scarring. The study will compare ALN-CIDEB with placebo to understand how well ALN-CIDEB works to lower the amount of fat in the liver.

The study is looking at:

* What side effects ALN-CIDEB might cause
* How well ALN-CIDEB works to change liver fat, liver injury, and liver scarring
* How the body and the liver change after having ALN-CIDEB, which can help researchers understand why ALN-CIDEB works better for some people than others

abstract: This study will evaluate 2 dose levels of mRNA-1283 in participants ≥6 months to \<12 years to determine the optimal dose level per age group.
description:
mRNA-1283 will be administered at 2 different dose levels (Dose Level 1 and Dose Level 2), with mRNA-1273 serving as the active comparator. Dose Level 1 will be the lower dose, and Dose Level 2 will be the higher dose.

The study will consist of 2 cohorts. In Cohort 1, mRNA-1283 will be administered as a single dose to participants aged ≥2 to \<12 years, regardless of prior coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) vaccination status, with mRNA-1273 included as a comparator. In Cohort 2, mRNA-1283 will be administered as a 2-dose series to participants aged ≥6 months to \<2 years who are previously unvaccinated for COVID-19, with mRNA-1273 included as a comparator.

abstract:
Background:

CGD is caused by a gene mutation. For people with CGD, their cells cannot kill germs well, so they can get frequent or life-threatening infections. Researchers want to see if a new procedure can help a person s cells kill germs for a short time. It uses messenger RNA (mRNA) to deliver correct instructions for the gene mutation to the cells.

Objective:

To test a procedure in which mRNA is added to a person s blood cells.

Eligibility:

Males aged 18-75 with CGD with a mutation in the gene that makes the protein gp91phox.

Design:

Participants will be screened with:

Medical history

Physical exam

Blood and urine tests

Swab to test for strep throat

Some screening tests will be repeated during the study.

Participants will be admitted to the NIH Clinical Center hospital for at least 7 days. They will have apheresis. For this, a medicine is injected under their skin to prepare their white blood cells for collection. An IV line is placed into an arm vein. Blood goes through the IV line into a machine that divides whole blood into red blood cells, plasma, and white blood cells. The white blood cells are removed, and the rest of the blood is returned to the participant through an IV line in their other arm. The next day, they will get their mRNA-corrected cells via IV. They will be monitored for 3 more days.

After discharge, participants will keep a symptom diary. They will be contacted weekly for one month, and then once a month. They will have a follow-up visit 3 months after the infusion.

description:
Study Design:

This is a phase 1, open-label, dose-escalation trial to assess the safety and feasibility of administering CGD-Grans to adult patients with X-linked CGD and to identify the maximum tolerated dose (MTD). Subjects will undergo granulocyte-enriched apheresis to provide cell product for mRNA-correction and then receive 1 administration of study agent. The first subjects enrolled will receive the study agent at the lowest dose, and when a level has been determined to be safe, the dose level will be increased to a second and then third dose level for subsequent subjects.Subjects will be hospitalized for at least 3 days after study agent administration and will return for a final study visit about 3 months after administration. Blood will be collected regularly for safety and research evaluations. The study hypothesis is that it is safe and feasible to administer mRNA-transfected autologous granulocyte-enriched apheresis product to restore protein expression and phagocyte nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide phosphate (NADPH) oxidase function in patients with CGD.

Study Agent Description:

The study agent is one administration of autologous CGD mRNA transfected granulocyte-enriched cells, referred to as CGD-Grans. The study agent is derived from apheresis product enriched for granulocytes, which are then transfected with CGD mRNA and administered as an intravenous (IV) infusion. CGD-Grans will be evaluated using the 3+3 modified Fibonacci model at the following 3 escalating dosages:

Dose K: 1 x 10\^6 granulocyte-enriched cells/kg body mass

Dose K+1: 1 x 10\^7 granulocyte-enriched cells/kg body mass

Dose K+2: 1-5 x 10\^8 granulocyte-enriched cells/kg body mass

Each dose will be evaluated in at least 3 subjects. Dose escalation will be managed by a predetermined algorithm depending on the occurrence of drug-related toxicity (DRT). There will be at least 1 week between study agent administration to each subject.

Primary Objectives:

1. Determine the safety and feasibility of CGD-Grans infusion.
2. Determine an MTD for administration.

Secondary Objectives:

1. Assess efficacy of CGD-Grans at restoring NADPH oxidase.
2. Determine the kinetics of CGD-Grans.

Exploratory Objectives:

1. Assess for inflammatory responses to CGD-Grans infusion.
2. Assess for immune responses to protein expressed by the transfected mRNA.
3. Evaluate in vitro bactericidal activity of CGD-Grans.

Primary Endpoints:

1. Determine safety and feasibility by:

   Safety: Frequency of grade 3 or greater adverse events (AEs) or serious adverse events (SAEs) related to the study agent.

   Feasibility: Recruitment, implementation, and manufacturing of CGD-Grans for infusions.
2. MTD determination based on the rate of AEs. MTD is defined as the highest dose level that does not cause the same grade 3 or 4 AEs in 3 or more patients.

Secondary Endpoints:

1. Determine percent of circulating dihydrorhodamine (DHR) positive granulocytes following study agent infusion.
2. Serial measurement of circulating DHR+ granulocytes from peripheral blood until day 3 following study agent infusion or disappearance of DHR+ granulocytes.

Exploratory Endpoint:

1. Assess for increased expression of inflammation-related genes after study agent infusion.
2. Evaluate for development of antibodies against mRNA-expressed CGDphox.
3. Perform in vitro bactericidal activity of CGD-Grans.

abstract: This Phase 1, multi-center, open-label, first-in-human study evaluates multiple ascending daily oral doses of STC-15 in Q3W treatment cycles in a 3+3 cohort design with dose levels determined by a modified Fibonacci algorithm. The study is designed to systematically assess safety and tolerability, pharmacokinetics, pharmacodynamics and clinical activity of STC-15 in adult subjects with advanced malignancies. Dose levels for further evaluation in expansion cohorts will be selected based on all available PK, pharmacodynamic, target engagement, efficacy, safety, and tolerability data including long-term safety data beyond dose limiting toxicities (DLTs). The study may be amended to evaluate STC-15 in combination with a Food and Drug Administration-approved standard of care treatment regimen, which could encompass targeted/chemotherapy, radiation therapy and/or immunotherapy with immune checkpoint blockers.

abstract: Ornithodoros moubata and Ornithodoros erraticus are important vectors of African swine fever virus and relapsing fever Borrelia spp., highlighting the need for effective and sustainable control strategies. In this study, six previously identified O. moubata vaccine candidates, including salivary and/or midgut antigens cyclophilin (OmCPH), peroxiredoxin (OmPXR), hypothetical protein 275 (OmH275), aquaporin 23 (OmAQP23), subolesin (OmSUB) and Om85, were evaluated as messenger RNA-lipid nanoparticle (mRNA-LNP) vaccines. Rabbits received three intradermal immunisations with individual mRNA-LNP formulations, and humoral, cellular, and protective immune responses were assessed. All mRNA-LNP constructs induced antigen-specific IgM and IgG responses and generated antibodies capable of recognising native proteins in tick salivary glands and/or midgut tissues. Antigen stimulation of peripheral blood mononuclear cells revealed antigen-specific cellular responses characterised by increased expression of IFN-γ, TNF-α, IL-8, CXCL10, IL-2, and IL-4, although the extent of these responses varied among antigens. OmCPH induced the strongest IL-8 response, OmSUB markedly increased CXCL10, IL-2 and IL-4 expression, and OmH275 elicited consistent IFN-γ and TNF-α responses. Vaccination adversely affected tick feeding, reproduction, development, and survival, with the most pronounced effects observed on female oviposition and fertility. Vaccine efficacies against O. moubata reached 19.8% (OmCPH), 3.7% (OmPXR), 25.6% (OmH275), 10.1% (OmAQP23), 25.2% (OmSUB), and 38.5% (Om85), while efficacies against O. erraticus reached 0%, 26.5%, 6.2%, 11.7%, 10.6%, and 18.5%, respectively. These findings demonstrate that mRNA-LNP vaccination induces both humoral and cellular immune responses against Ornithodoros antigens and provides measurable protection against tick infestations, supporting the application of mRNA technology for the development of multivalent anti-tick vaccines.

abstract: Multiple myeloma (MM) orchestrates immune evasion by subverting natural killer (NK) cell function. CD48, one of the most abundant NK ligands on MM cells, paradoxically enhances NK cell activation yet is associated with high-risk cytogenetics and poor patient survival. We integrated multiomics (bulk and single-cell RNA-seq, assay for transposase-accessible chromatin using sequencing [ATAC-seq], chromatin immunoprecipitation sequencing [ChIP-seq]), genome-wide CRISPR knockout/activation screens, and machine learning to dissect CD48 regulation and function. In human MM and Vκ*MYC mouse scRNA-seq datasets, NK cells exhibit stepwise increases in inflammatory and exhaustion signatures and loss of cytotoxic potential as disease progresses. In vitro coculture assays show that CD48 overexpression on MM enhances NK cell cytokine secretion, whereas chronic exposure leads to ex vivo NK dysfunction. In vivo, CD48-overexpressing Vκ*MYC tumors progress more slowly and extend host survival, while NK cell depletion accelerates disease. These findings support a context-dependent role for CD48, potentiating acute NK responses while coexisting with chronic NK exhaustion, and suggest strategies to modulate CD48 for therapeutic benefit.

abstract:
BACKGROUND: Among molecular subtypes of glioblastoma (GBM), the mesenchymal subtype (MES) exhibits the most aggressive clinical course, marked by heightened invasiveness and therapeutic resistance. To overcome the challenge of intrinsic drug resistance in MES GBM, we performed a high-throughput screen of Food and Drug Administration (FDA)-approved compounds on NF1-silenced human GBM cells.
METHODS: We performed a high-throughput screen of 2,697 FDA-approved compounds on NF1-silenced human GBM cells, engineered via CRISPR/Cas9.
RESULTS: This screen nominated poly(ADP-ribose) polymerase 1 (PARP1) inhibitors as top candidates, demonstrating selective cytotoxicity against NF1-deficient cells. Integrated analyses of The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) data, immunofluorescence, and immunoblotting revealed significant PARP1 upregulation in GBM tissues, establishing its role as a proto-oncogene that drives tumor cell proliferation and migration. Using orthotopic xenograft models, we confirmed that NF1 knockdown (KD) profoundly sensitized GBM tumors to the anti-tumor and pro-apoptotic effects of PARP1 inhibition in vivo. Mechanistically, co-immunoprecipitation (co-IP) assays identified a physical interaction between the NF1 gene product neurofibromin and PARP1, suggesting a direct regulatory nexus.
CONCLUSIONS: This study breaks through the traditional limitation of PARP inhibitors being used only for DNA repair defects, and for the first time reveals a novel selective killing mechanism of PARP1 inhibitors in NF1-deficient GBM. Collectively, our findings delineate NF1-mutant, MES GBM as a distinct clinical subset poised to derive therapeutic benefit from PARP1-targeted therapy.

title: Inhibition of malignant progression in mesenchymal glioblastoma by PARP1 inhibitors.

abstract: Neurodevelopmental disorders (NDDs) represent a heterogeneous class of early-onset conditions marked by impairments in cognition, reduced social function, hyperactivity and repetitive-stereotyped behaviour. Traditionally classified as discrete clinical entities, NDDs such as autism spectrum disorder (ASD), attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), and intellectual disability (ID) are now increasingly understood as overlapping, multifactorial conditions shaped by converging genetic, epigenetic, immune, and environmental influences. This review synthesizes current evidence challenging categorical diagnostic boundaries and instead proposes a transdiagnostic and mechanistic framework that integrates shared disruptions in neural circuits, excitatory/inhibitory balance, synaptic architecture, and immune-metabolic signalling. We explore how genes and environment interact during early development, how epigenetics influences long-term outcomes, and how these insights are driving a shift toward precision medicine guided by biomarkers and patient-derived models. Emerging therapies include neuromodulation, immune and microbiota-based interventions, and gene editing, supported by insights from animal and iPSC models. A time-sensitive and biologically grounded approach is needed, moving beyond symptom-based classifications to allow for earlier diagnosis, personalized treatment, and the development of innovative interventions. This paradigm shift aligns with precision approaches already transforming other biomedical domains and holds the potential to more effectively address the complex and lifelong challenges posed by NDDs.

title: Beyond diagnostic categories: A narrative review of transdiagnostic mechanisms in neurodevelopmental disorders.

abstract:
PURPOSE OF REVIEW: Inherited cardiomyopathies are increasingly recognized among patients with advanced heart failure, yet genetic testing remains substantially underutilized. This review examines the evolving clinical utility of genetic testing across advanced heart failure and transplantation and highlights opportunities to integrate genetics into routine advanced heart failure care.
RECENT FINDINGS: Pathogenic or likely pathogenic cardiomyopathy variants are identified in approximately one-third of heart transplant recipients and in up to 44% of explanted hearts from patients with idiopathic cardiomyopathy. Recent studies have linked genotype to heart failure progression, ventricular arrhythmias, and outcomes after advanced therapies, including a higher risk of right ventricular failure following left ventricular assist device implantation. Genetic diagnoses can also uncover multisystem disease relevant to transplant evaluation and posttransplant management. At the same time, the emergence of gene replacement, gene editing, and RNA-based therapies is creating new therapeutic implications for establishing a molecular diagnosis before end-stage disease.
SUMMARY: Genetic testing is becoming an increasingly actionable component of advanced heart failure care. Integrating genetics into advanced heart failure programs may improve recognition of inherited disease, individualize management, and better position patients and their families for emerging precision therapies.

title: The role of genetic testing in heart transplant candidates.

abstract: The circulating tumoral biomarkers in the blood are the object of numerous researches for several decades. The potential clinical interests of these circulating biomarkers are diagnostic, prognostic, predictive of the efficiency of targeted therapies (according to the mutational profile of the cancer), and could allow the study of the mechanisms of resistance under process. In the multiplicity of these blood potential biomarkers joins a permanent evolution of the technological means used to detect them/to quantify, as well as to estimate their clinical utility.

description:
The new major challenge in the research concerns the circulating biomarkers, which aim at replacing the molecular analyses on tumour tissue obtained by biopsy (for example the search for somatic mutations of cancer) by a simple blood test (liquid biopsy). The other current important challenge is to have an idea of the interest to analyse the kinetics of blood markers, in particular in answer to a clinical "event", either through the chemotherapy, a biopsy and / or surgery. There is almost no data in the literature on this aspect. It is very likely that the liberation in the blood of the blood tumoral markers is strongly dependent on medical interventions on the tumour.

The study ALCINA 2 rests exactly on the principle of small cohorts, which correspond each to a clinical situation and/or a technique of different implemented detection, so as to generate data of feasibility and proof of concept. In case of success, statistical hypotheses will be necessary for the implementation of wider studies (being then the object of a specific approval by competent authorities).

abstract: Irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) is a chronic disorder of gut-brain interaction that causes abdominal pain and altered bowel habits. Many people with IBS also experience symptoms outside the bowel, such as headaches, widespread pain, poor sleep, anxiety, and depression; these symptoms are especially common in females. This study focuses on stress reactivity (SR), a persistent pattern of stress-system activity that may be linked to autonomic nervous system function, immune activity, the gut microbiome, and brain processing. The investigators will enroll adults with at least moderate IBS symptoms and randomly assign them to 8 weeks of non-invasive vagal nerve stimulation (nVNS) or Usual Care. Participants assigned to nVNS will use a handheld device on the left side of the neck at home twice daily. The investigators will compare changes in IBS severity and other physical symptoms and examine whether baseline or treatment-related changes in blood, stool, heart-rate variability, sex hormones, and brain imaging measures are associated with response. The study will also explore whether treatment effects and predictors differ by sex.

outcomes.description: The IBS-SSS questionnaire is a validated measure of IBS symptom severity and has been shown to be responsive to treatment. The IBS-SSS assesses the severity of abdominal pain, frequency of abdominal pain, severity of abdominal distention, dissatisfaction with bowel habits, and interference of IBS with daily life over a 10-day period. Each of the five categories will receive a score from 0-100, and the total IBSSSS is calculated by taking the sum of these categories (range 0-500, 0 - no symptoms, 500 - very severe symptoms).
outcomes.measure: Change in IBS Severity Scoring System (IBS-SSS)
outcomes.time_frame: 8 weeks, from baseline to end of intervention

outcomes.description: The PHQ-15 is a widely used measure of widespread somatic symptoms over 1 month that is sensitive to treatment effects. The PHQ-15 assess 15 different somatic symptoms (back pain, stomach pain, headaches, chest pain, trouble sleeping, etc.) rated by 0 - not bothered at all to 3 - bothered a lot. The scale is scored as follows: 0-4: Minimal somatic symptom severity, 5-9: Low somatic symptom severity, 10-14: Medium somatic symptom severity, 15-30: High somatic symptom severity.
outcomes.measure: Change in Patient Health Questionnaire-15 (PHQ-15)
outcomes.time_frame: 8 weeks, from baseline to end of intervention

outcomes.description: SR-related brain phenotypes will be derived from prespecified MRI measures of brain structure, functional connectivity, and brain activity. MRI data will be collected at baseline and Week 8. The primary imaging analysis will compare baseline-to-Week-8 change in prespecified SR-related brain phenotypes between nVNS and Usual Care.
outcomes.measure: Change in stress reactivity (SR)-related brain phenotypes.
outcomes.time_frame: 8 weeks, from baseline to end of intervention

outcomes.description: The proportion of participants with IBS who experience a ≥50-point reduction in IBS-SSS score from baseline will be compared between treatment groups. A reduction of at least 50 points represents a clinically meaningful improvement in IBS symptoms. The IBS-SSS questionnaire is a validated measure of IBS symptom severity and has been shown to be responsive to treatment. The IBS-SSS assesses the severity of abdominal pain, frequency of abdominal pain, severity of abdominal distention, dissatisfaction with bowel habits, and interference of IBS with daily life over a 10-day period. Each of the five categories will receive a score from 0-100, and the total IBSSSS is calculated by taking the sum of these categories (range 0-500, 0 - no symptoms, 500 - very severe symptoms).
outcomes.measure: IBS Severity Scoring System (IBS-SSS) responder rate
outcomes.time_frame: 8 weeks, from baseline to end of intervention

outcomes.description: Changes in the sympathetic nervous system (SNS)-immune gene expression profile will be evaluated as a peripheral biologic measure of stress reactivity. Whole-blood SNS-immune gene expression will be measured using mRNA-targeted sequencing. Total RNA will be isolated from whole blood, converted to cDNA using Lexogen QuantSeq 3' FWD, sequenced using Illumina sequencing, mapped to the GRCh38 reference human transcriptome using STAR, and quantified as gene-specific reads per million mapped reads. Baseline-to-Week-8 changes will be compared between nVNS and Usual Care and examined in relation to clinical symptom change. Moderator analyses will also test whether baseline SNS-immune gene expression modifies the treatment response using an SNS-immune measure-by-treatment-by-time interaction.
outcomes.measure: Biologic measures of Stress Reactivity - SNS-Immune gene expression profile
outcomes.time_frame: 8 weeks, from baseline to end of intervention

outcomes.description: HRV will be evaluated as a peripheral autonomic measure of stress reactivity and compared over the treatment period. HRV will be derived from physiologic data collected using a Fitbit equipped with photoplethysmography sensors that estimate heart rate and intervals between successive beats. Participants will wear the device from baseline through the post-intervention assessment, including during sleep, to characterize longitudinal and circadian HRV. Changes in HRV will be compared between nVNS and Usual Care and correlated with symptom change. Moderator analyses will additionally test whether baseline HRV modifies treatment response through an HRV-by-treatment-by-time interaction.
outcomes.measure: Biologic measures of Stress Reactivity - heart rate variability (HRV)
outcomes.time_frame: 8 weeks, from baseline to end of intervention

outcomes.description: Changes in the fecal microbial stress index will be evaluated as a peripheral biologic measure of stress reactivity. The fecal microbial stress index will be derived from stool samples collected at baseline and Week 8 using shotgun metagenomic sequencing. Microbial sequencing data will undergo species-level taxonomic and functional characterization. Baseline-to-Week-8 changes in the microbial stress index will be compared between nVNS and Usual Care and correlated with clinical symptom change.
outcomes.measure: Biologic measures of Stress Reactivity - fecal microbial stress index
outcomes.time_frame: 8 weeks, from baseline to end of intervention

outcomes.description: Changes in the fecal metabolite stress index will be evaluated as a peripheral biologic measure of stress reactivity. The fecal metabolite stress index will be derived from stool metabolomic data obtained using LC-MS/MS-based profiling. Baseline-to-Week-8 changes in the metabolite stress index will be compared between nVNS and Usual Care and correlated with clinical symptom change. Moderator analyses will additionally test whether the baseline metabolite stress index modifies treatment response through a metabolite stress index-by-treatment-by-time interaction.
outcomes.measure: Biologic measures of Stress Reactivity - fecal metabolite stress index
outcomes.time_frame: 8 weeks, from baseline to end of intervention

outcomes.description: Examine associations between changes in scores on the SR-related brain phenotype signatures and changes in IBS severity, comorbid symptom scores, and peripheral biologic measures of SR. General linear models will examine associations between baseline-to-Week-8 changes in SR-related brain phenotype signature scores and corresponding changes in IBS-SSS, PHQ-15, HRV, SNS-immune gene expression, and microbial and metabolite stress indices, with adjustment for relevant covariates. Alternative approaches may be used to examine multivariate associations between changes in symptom severity, stress reactivity, comorbidity, and brain connectivity.
outcomes.measure: Brain changes associated with IBS severity, comorbid symptom scores, and peripheral biologic measures of SR
outcomes.time_frame: 8 weeks, from baseline to end of intervention

outcomes.description: Predict response (Pre-Post change in extraintestinal symptoms) in nVNS compared to Usual Care. General linear model-based moderator analyses will evaluate whether baseline SR-related brain phenotype scores predict pre- to post-treatment change in extraintestinal symptom severity differently in participants assigned to nVNS versus Usual Care. Models will include baseline SR brain phenotype score, treatment group, the brain phenotype-by-treatment interaction, and prespecified covariates. A significant interaction will indicate differential prediction of treatment response.
outcomes.measure: Change in extraintestinal symptoms in nVNS compared to Usual Care
outcomes.time_frame: 8 weeks, from baseline to end of intervention

outcomes.description: Examine whether females with IBS with higher comorbid symptom scores will present with greater changes in SR-related brain signatures following the nVNS intervention compared to male IBS. Exploratory models will examine whether females with IBS with greater baseline comorbid symptom burden demonstrate greater baseline-to-Week-8 changes in SR-related brain signatures following nVNS compared with males with IBS. The moderator analysis includes the comorbid symptom score-by-group interaction, with adjustment for age, BMI, and diet.
outcomes.measure: Exploratory outcome - Sex differences
outcomes.time_frame: 8 weeks, from baseline to end of intervention

abstract: Chromosome loss events are common across tumor types but rarely occur in normal tissue, raising the possibility that these alterations could be exploited as cancer-specific therapeutic vulnerabilities. Here, we integrate genome-scale CRISPR screening data with chromosome-level copy number profiles from 1,150 cancer cell lines and identify 389 dependencies that are selectively associated with individual chromosome loss events. The most significant vulnerabilities uncovered by our analysis are paralogous gene pairs, in which the loss of a paralog on an aneuploid chromosome establishes a unique dependency on its redundant paralog encoded elsewhere in the genome. We experimentally validate two paralog dependencies: loss of chromosome 8p, which encodes the phosphatase PPP2CB , creates a specific dependency on its paralog PPP2CA , while loss of the Y chromosome, which encodes the helicase DDX3Y , creates a specific dependency on its paralog DDX3X . Systematic benchmarking of CRISPR screening data indicates that the selective dependency on DDX3X in loss-of-Y cells exceeds other published aneuploidy-associated vulnerabilities and matches or exceeds most clinically-validated biomarker-target relationships. Furthermore, we found that the acute degradation of DDX3X was sufficient to trigger apoptosis in vitro and tumor regressions in mice. Collectively, these findings establish chromosome loss as a recurrent source of biomarker-defined therapeutic targets, identify paralog insufficiency as a general vulnerability in aneuploid cells, and provide in vivo proof-of-concept for targeting DDX3X in cancers with Y chromosome loss.

title: Systematic analysis of genetic vulnerabilities caused by chromosome loss events in cancer.

abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) represents a critical global health threat, surpassing the pace of discovery and clinical development of new antimicrobial agents. Therefore, innovative therapeutic strategies are urgently needed to enhance antibiotic efficacy, overcome multidrug-resistant infections, and limit resistance development. Smart liposomal nanoplatforms have emerged as promising tools capable of improving antimicrobial therapy through targeted delivery, enhanced bacterial uptake, biofilm penetration, protection against enzymatic degradation, and controlled drug release.
AREAS COVERED: This review examines recent advances in the rational design of evolved liposomes, including stimuli-responsive and programmable systems, for combating resistant bacterial infections. It discusses their ability to improve pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic profiles, overcome biological barriers, and enable precision antimicrobial delivery. Current translational challenges, including large-scale manufacturing, physicochemical characterization, regulatory requirements, and clinically relevant preclinical models, are critically evaluated. Emerging strategies, such as artificial intelligence-driven formulation optimization, continuous microfluidic manufacturing, multifunctional therapeutic platforms incorporating gene editing, and next-generation antibiotic-adjuvant combination strategies, are also explored.
EXPERT OPINION: Liposomal drug-delivery systems may improve the exposure, distribution, and intracellular or local delivery of antimicrobial agents, but improved delivery should not be equated with reversal of bacterial resistance. Successful clinical translation will depend on formulation- and infection-specific evidence, clinically relevant preclinical models, controlled and scalable manufacturing, and appropriate regulatory frameworks, while artificial intelligence, digital-twin, and precision-medicine approaches are best viewed as decision-support tools that complement experimental and clinical validation.

title: Engineering smart liposomes to combat antimicrobial resistance: from mechanistic design to clinical translation.

abstract: Plant-based expression systems have emerged as low-cost, scalable, and safe alternatives for producing therapeutic recombinant proteins. Among them, Nicotiana benthamiana stands out as a versatile chassis due to its rapid growth, high biomass, efficient transient expression, and weak RNA silencing. In this review, we systematically summarize the key technical procedures and recent advances in the expression of therapeutic recombinant proteins in N. benthamiana, covering gene design and subcellular targeting, expression vector engineering and delivery, host engineering for enhanced yield, and cultivation optimization. We discuss strategies to address major bottlenecks, including codon optimization, endoplasmic reticulum retention, protease knockout, glycoengineering to eliminate immunogenic plant-specific glycans, and the use of viral-based transient expression systems such as magnICON, pEAQ-HT, and geminiviral replicons. Additionally, we highlight emerging approaches such as CRISPR-based multiplexed chassis engineering, artificial intelligence-assisted vector design, and hydroponic cultivation for scalable production. Despite significant progress, challenges remain in achieving coordinated high-level expression of multiple proteins and reducing downstream processing costs. This review provides a comprehensive framework for understanding the current state and future directions of plant molecular farming in N. benthamiana, emphasizing its irreplaceable value for rapid emergency response, personalized vaccines, and safe biopharmaceutical manufacturing.

title: Plant molecular farming: from gene design to scalable expression of therapeutic recombinant proteins.

abstract: Antisense oligonucleotides are small synthetic DNA or RNA molecules that can be used to modulate gene expression, particularly to block the production of unwanted proteins. This makes them potentially powerful drugs to contrast cancer growth. Drug development is a long process that includes preclinical and clinical studies. Preclinical animal studies are designed to assess drug kinetics and safety before progressing to clinical trials, as they may predict the therapeutic dose to be used in the "first in human" (FIH) studies. This is usually achieved by applying allometric scaling methods that allow predicting the human pharmacokinetic (PK) parameters from those estimated in animals. Selecting the appropriate scaling formula reduces the risk of translational uncertainty and supports the design of FIH studies. The aim of this study is to compare the accuracy of different allometric scaling methods in predicting human PK of the antisense oligonucleotide LNA-i-miR-221, a powerful inhibitor of microRNA miR-221, which was found to be deregulated in several malignancies, favoring cancer progression. To do that, we exploited the availability of PK data of the drug in both Sprague Dawley rats and humans and we found that the best scaling method for both clearance and distribution volume is the simple allometry, with predictions laying within the 2-fold and 4-fold error interval, respectively. This study contributes to identifying the most accurate scaling methods among the evaluated single-species approaches to extrapolate human pharmacokinetic for LNA-i-miR-221, possibly offering a starting point for future studies involving antisense oligonucleotides.

title: Assessment of Allometric Scaling Methods for the Prediction of Human Pharmacokinetic of LNA-i-miR-221.

abstract:
AIMS: Vascular endothelial growth factors (VEGFs) and their endothelial tyrosine kinase receptors are crucial mediators of vasculogenesis and angiogenesis, with FLT1 (VEGFR1) acting as a decoy receptor for VEGFs. Alternative polyadenylation (APA) of Flt1 transcripts produces a truncated mRNA transcript encoding soluble (s) FLT1, which contains only the extracellular ligand-binding domain. The relative roles of full-length (fl) FLT1 and sFLT1 in angiogenesis are incompletely understood. Alternative polyadenylation is an important post-transcriptional mechanism of gene regulation that is increasingly recognized to affect the expression of many genes related to cardiovascular diseases. However, there are no in vivo models available to target APA and to examine the physiological roles of gene isoforms.
METHODS AND RESULTS: We here generated mice by introducing silent mutations into the Flt1 exon 13/intron 13 5' splice site through homology-directed repair with CRISPR/Cas9 gene editing. Embryonic development, postnatal retinal vascular development, and reparative angiogenesis were evaluated in models of hindlimb ischaemia and myocardial infarction, complemented by assessments of cardiac functional recovery and cell phenotypes through snRNAseq, as well as in vitro assays examining endothelial cell phenotype and function. The introduction of specific splice site mutations within Flt1 to activate APA led to a complete loss of flFLT1 and an increase in sFLT1 expression. Using this mouse model, we demonstrate that sFLT1 alone is sufficient for developmental vasculogenesis, whereas the specific loss of flFLT1 enhances reparative revascularization and angiogenesis and improves cardiac recovery after myocardial infarction.
CONCLUSION: Our findings show that APA can be effectively targeted to modulate FLT1 isoform expression in vivo. Our mouse model may help to understand diseases driven by an imbalance in FLT1 isoform expression. Given the widespread presence of APA signals, our approach could furthermore serve as a model for studying the function of other truncated gene isoforms.

title: Redirecting full-length FLT1 expression towards its soluble isoform by targeting alternative polyadenylation promotes postischaemic angiogenesis.

abstract:
BACKGROUND: Our knowledge about mitochondrial genome evolution in plants is lacking far behind our knowledge of plastome evolution. In heterotrophic plants, it is well-known that plastome degradation and reduced or lost photosynthesis go hand in hand, and there is little if any difference between plastome evolution in mycoheterotrophic and haustorial parasites. The mitochondrial genome appears less affected by a heterotrophic lifestyle, although exceptions occur. In contrast to plastome evolution, mitochondrial evolution may differ between mycoheterotrophic and haustorial parasites, in particular with regards to the occurrence of horizontal gene transfer. However, data from mycoheterotrophs are scarce, and complete mitogenomes are only known from three of ten clades.
RESULTS: Here we present data from the complete plastome and mitogenome from Thismia angustimitra, representing a fourth clade of mycoheterotrophs. The 18,215 bp plastome is much reduced and includes only few genes. The mitogenome has a multicircular structure consisting of 22 chromosomes with a total length of 422,400 bp. The gene content and the pattern of RNA editing are normal. The mitogenome includes only few repeats and recombinational activity is limited. A search for foreign DNA did not reveal any fungal sequences, the content of plastid DNA is low, but a large proportion of intergenic DNA shows similarity to distantly related angiosperms. Just a few plastid inserts appear to have originated through intracellular transfer, whereas others most likely stem from horizontal gene transfer. Synteny patterns of the intergenic sequences suggest that horizontal transfer may happen in either direction.
CONCLUSION: The highly reduced plastome of T. angustimitra fits completely the general picture of plastome degradation in heterotrophic plants. Whereas the mitogenome in many aspects appears unaffected by the lifestyle, the recombinational activity is unusually low. Surprisingly, we find evidence suggesting horizontal gene transfer, indicating that this phenomenon may be more common among mycoheterotrophic plants than previously thought.

title: Characterization of the organelle genomes of mycoheterotrophic Thismia angustimitra and evidence suggesting horizontal gene transfer.

abstract: Local tumor therapies rarely induce systemic immunity capable of controlling metastatic disease. Here, we engineer an mRNA lipid nanoparticle (LNP) platform to coordinate innate immune sensing and T cell activation in situ through co-delivery of an autoactivated cyclic GMP-AMP synthase mutant (cGAS R241E ) and membrane-tethered IL-12 (IL-12TM). cGAS R241E mRNA LNPs autonomously generated cyclic GMP-AMP in vivo , activating host STING signaling and initiating antitumor responses. Co-administration with IL-12TM mRNA LNPs promoted localized cytokine production, reduced regulatory T cells, and restored effector function in tumor-infiltrating T cells. This combination elicited systemic antitumor immunity and suppressed distal tumors across multiple mouse models. The therapeutic efficacy required CD8 + T cells and IFN-γ signaling in host, supporting a model in which innate DNA sensing is coupled to IL-12-mediated T cell functional reinforcement. In addition, the combination enhanced responsiveness to PD-L1 blockade. Together, these findings establish a clinically translatable strategy to integrate cGAS-STING activation with cytokine-driven T cell programming to drive systemic tumor control.

abstract:
BACKGROUND: Despite substantial advances in therapeutic strategies, non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) remains the leading cause of cancer-related death worldwide. The poor prognosis of NSCLC is largely due to the limited efficacy of existing clinical treatments and the lack of reliable and effective molecular therapeutic targets. Studies have shown that small nucleolar RNAs (snoRNAs) play pivotal regulatory roles in multiple pathological processes involved in tumor formation and malignant progression. However, the specific biological functions and underlying molecular mechanisms of individual snoRNAs in the occurrence and development of NSCLC remain largely unclear, highlighting the need for systematic exploration.
METHODS: A reanalysis of genome-scale clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats (CRISPR)-Cas9 knockout screening data covering all annotated snoRNAs in NSCLC cell lines was performed. Colony formation assays confirmed the functional role of SNORD42A in NSCLC cells. A combined bioinformatic analysis of our internal sequencing data and public datasets further identified the molecular locus of SNORD42A in the pathogenesis of NSCLC.
RESULTS: Genome-wide screening identified SNORD42A as a key candidate snoRNA regulating NSCLC cell proliferation. Both the in-house snoRNA sequencing data and bioinformatics analysis of The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) cohort demonstrated that SNORD42A was significantly overexpressed in clinical NSCLC tissues compared with paired adjacent normal lung tissues, indicating its potential oncogenic role in NSCLC. Functional validation experiments further demonstrated that SNORD42A knockdown markedly inhibited the clonogenic capacity of NSCLC cells. Moreover, an integrative bioinformatics analysis of TCGA data revealed that SNORD42A expression was closely correlated with cell cycle regulation and cellular senescence signaling pathways, and its expression level was significantly associated with the clinical prognosis of patients with NSCLC.
CONCLUSIONS: SNORD42A functions as a pro-tumorigenic factor that promotes NSCLC progression, with its effects potentially linked to alterations in cellular protein synthesis. This study revealed the functional importance of SNORD42A in NSCLC malignancy, suggesting that SNORD42A may serve as a novel prognostic biomarker and a promising therapeutic target for the treatment of NSCLC.

abstract: Pyroptosis is a lytic form of cell death executed by gasdermin pores. Through a CRISPR screen to uncover macrophage genes required for gasdermin D (GSDMD) pore activity, we identify the endosome adaptor Rabgef1 as a positive regulator of pore formation. Rabgef1 deficiency preserves NT-GSDMD membrane binding but prevents NT-GSDMD oligomerization and lytic death. Mechanistic analyses revealed that Rabgef1 deficiency is associated with an overabundance of cholesterol in the plasma membrane. Cholesterol depletion or redistribution through multiple approaches restores GSDMD oligomerization and pyroptosis. The Rabgef1-mediated control of membrane cholesterol and pore formation was found to be a general regulator of the gasdermin family. In cancer cells, organoids, and tumors, cholesterol reduction sensitizes resistant cells to GSDME pyroptosis driven by synthetic mRNAs, chemogenetic induction, and chemotherapy treatment. These results establish membrane cholesterol content as an endogenous checkpoint for gasdermin-mediated pyroptotic cell death during the execution phase, with implications for metabolic disease and cancer immunotherapy.

abstract: Prion diseases are fatal, transmissible neurodegenerative disorders characterized by the conformational conversion of the cellular prion protein (PrP C) into its pathogenic isoform PrP Sc . Propagation of prions depends on the fragmentation of PrP Sc aggregates to generate new seeds. However, the factors regulating this process remain incompletely understood. For yeast prions, Hsp104 that has no mammalian homologue, is firmly established as a disaggregase. Hsp110 has emerged as a potential mediator of protein disaggregation and aggregate remodeling in mammalian cells. Although Hsp110 proteins have been implicated in several protein misfolding disorders, their individual contributions to mammalian prion propagation have not been characterized. In this study, we examined the roles of the three Hsp110 proteins-Apg-1, Apg-2, and Hsp105-in cellular prion infection. CRISPR-generated knockout cell lines were established for each Hsp110 and evaluated for their effect on de novo prion infection. PrP Sc accumulation was assessed by immunoblot across serial passages and up to 40 days, and prion seeding activity was quantified using real-time quaking-induced conversion (RT-QuIC). Loss of individual Hsp110's produced distinct effects on prion propagation. Apg-1-deficient cells exhibited strongly reduced levels of PrP Sc over all passages analyzed, suggesting a role for Apg-1 in establishing persistent prion infection. Interestingly, prion seeding activity was detectable in later passages. Hsp105-deficient cells displayed reduced PrP Sc levels during the early stages, indicating that Hsp105 contributes to early prion replication. In contrast, Apg-2 knockout resulted in high prion seeding activity over all passages analyzed and only slightly reduced PrP Sc levels in early passages. Collectively, these findings demonstrate that Hsp110 family members perform distinct functions during early phases of prion infection and establishment of persistent infection. This work provides new insight into the role of molecular chaperones in prion biology and identifies Hsp110 proteins as potential modulators of prion replication and potentially therapeutic targets for protein misfolding diseases.

abstract: Lipoprotein(a) [Lp(a)] is a genetically determined causal risk factor for atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease and calcific aortic valve stenosis. Pelacarsen, a hepatocyte-directed antisense oligonucleotide targeting apolipoprotein(a), was evaluated in Lp(a)HORIZON, the first large phase 3 cardiovascular outcomes trial specifically designed to test whether pharmacological Lp(a) lowering reduces cardiovascular events. Topline results announced in September 2026 indicated that pelacarsen lowered Lp(a) but did not reduce the primary composite cardiovascular endpoint in patients with established cardiovascular disease. Full trial data are awaited, and the mechanisms underlying this neutral result remain uncertain. We discuss potential explanations, including treatment after prolonged cumulative Lp(a) exposure, advanced vascular disease, intensive background prevention, the magnitude and duration of Lp(a) suppression, patient selection, baseline cardiovascular risk, and biological heterogeneity. We also examine implications for emerging therapies, including olpasiran, zerlasiran, lepodisiran, and muvalaplin, and for the design of ongoing cardiovascular outcome trials.

abstract:
BACKGROUND: Low-density lipoprotein receptor-related protein 1 (LRP1) in smooth muscle cells (SMCs) is essential for maintaining aortic wall integrity. This study investigated whether deletion of LRP1 in SMCs induces region-specific aortic pathology and evaluated a potential therapeutic strategy.
METHODS: Lrp1 -floxed mice were bred with Sm22-Cre +/0 mice to generate mice with SMC-LRP1 deletion (SMC-LRP1-/-) and wild-type littermates (SMC-LRP1+/+). Micro-computed tomography (micro-CT) was used to visualize the aorta, and aortic tissue sections were characterized histologically. To evaluate a potential therapeutic strategy, antisense oligonucleotides (ASOs) targeting hepatocyte-derived angiotensinogen (AGT) were administered to inhibit AGT synthesis.
RESULTS: Immunostaining and Western blotting confirmed LRP1 deletion in aortic SMCs. At 40 weeks of age, micro-CT revealed marked increases in aortic width and volume. Although dilatation occurred throughout the aorta, the infrarenal region exhibited the greatest expansion in both male and female SMC-LRP1-/-mice compared with SMC-LRP1+/+ littermates; subsequent analyses therefore focused on this region. LRP1 deletion in SMCs caused pronounced SMC loss and increased collagen deposition in the infrarenal aorta. Inhibition of hepatocyte-derived AGT with ASO attenuated infrarenal aortic dilatation and preserved aortic wall integrity in both male and female mice.
CONCLUSIONS: Deletion of LRP1 in SMCs causes progressive aortic dilatation that includes the infrarenal aorta. Pharmacologic inhibition of hepatocyte-derived AGT attenuates infrarenal aortic dilatation.
WHAT ARE THE CLINICAL IMPLICATIONS?: Deletion of low-density lipoprotein receptor-related protein 1 (LRP1) in smooth muscle cells (SMCs) causes diffuse aortic dilatation, with spontaneous aneurysm formation most prominent in the infrarenal abdominal aorta-the most common site of abdominal aortic aneurysms (AAAs) in humans. Given the strong association between LRP1 variants and human AAAs, these findings identify SMC-derived LRP1 as a critical contributor to aortic wall integrity and provide a valuable tool for investigating disease mechanisms. Importantly, pharmacological inhibition of hepatocyte-derived angiotensinogen with an antisense oligonucleotide significantly attenuated infrarenal aortic dilatation, highlighting a promising therapeutic strategy for AAAs.

abstract:
BACKGROUND: Pelacarsen is an antisense oligonucleotide that reduces serum levels of lipoprotein(a). In a randomized placebo-controlled trial in patients with established cardiovascular disease, pelacarsen did not reduce the risk of major adverse cardiovascular events compared to placebo. We further investigated the association of pelacarsen treatment with cardiovascular outcomes.
METHODS: We report the association of pelacarsen treatment with a primary composite end point of death from cardiovascular causes, nonfatal myocardial infarction, nonfatal stroke, or urgent coronary revascularization. Analyses included on-treatment, uninterrupted treatment, total primary end point events (first and recurrent events), landmark analyses classified by changes in and achieved lipoprotein(a) at 3 months, and key subgroups including baseline lipoprotein(a), low-density lipoprotein (LDL) cholesterol, high-sensitivity C-reactive protein (CRP), and time from qualifying event to enrollment.
RESULTS: For participants on treatment, a primary end point occurred in 434 participants (10.4%) randomly assigned to placebo and 380 participants (9.1%) assigned to pelacarsen (hazard ratio, 0.98; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.85 to 1.12). When evaluating participants with uninterrupted treatment, a primary end point event occurred in 167 participants (11.0%) in the pelacarsen group and 204 participants (10.1%) in the placebo group (hazard ratio, 1.09; 95% CI, 0.89 to 1.34). When evaluating total primary end point events, there were 644 events in the pelacarsen group and 646 events in the placebo group (rate ratio, 1.00; 95% CI, 0.87 to 1.14). In landmark analyses evaluating participants alive and free of the composite end point at 3 months, when compared to placebo there was no association between pelacarsen treatment and the primary end point either in participants with reduction in lipoprotein(a) greater than or equal to the median (170 nmol/l) (hazard ratio, 1.09; 95% CI, 0.92 to 1.29) or in participants who achieved lipoprotein(a) lower than or equal to the median (69.5 nmol/l) (hazard ratio, 1.10; 95% CI, 0.93 to 1.29). There was also no association between pelacarsen treatment and the primary end point in any of the evaluated key subgroups including classification by median baseline lipoprotein(a), LDL cholesterol, high-sensitivity CRP, or time from qualifying cardiovascular disease to enrollment.
CONCLUSIONS: Pelacarsen was not associated with a reduction in major adverse cardiovascular events when evaluated by treatment exposure, changes in or achieved lipoprotein(a) levels at 3 months, considering total events, or within subgroups of baseline lipoprotein(a), LDL cholesterol, or high-sensitivity CRP levels.

abstract: Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF) is a fatal interstitial lung disease with limited treatment options. Here, we investigated MR3, a macrophage-targeted polysaccharide-peptide delivery system, for the pulmonary delivery of siRNA against growth arrest-specific protein 6 (GAS6). MR3 facilitated effective siRNA endosomal escape, while intratracheal administration ensured sustained lung retention with targeted uptake by macrophages. Functionally, siGAS6@MR3 selectively downregulated macrophage GAS6 expression to inhibit profibrotic M2 polarization, thereby improving survival, restoring lung function, and reversing histological and molecular indices of fibrosis in IPF models. Furthermore, MR3 conferred intrinsic antioxidant protection that enhanced macrophage survival under oxidative stress. siGAS6@MR3 was well tolerated in long-term repeat-dose studies, with no evidence of systemic toxicity. These findings identify GAS6 as a promising antifibrotic target and establish MR3 as a versatile, macrophage-selective siRNA platform for fibrotic and other macrophage-driven diseases.

abstract: Tolerogenic dendritic cells (TolDCs) contribute to immune tolerance and have demonstrated therapeutic potential in early clinical studies of autoimmune diseases. However, the key molecular pathways driving their differentiation and tolerogenic phenotype remain elusive. Here, we investigated the molecular mechanisms underlying the functional status of TolDCs in response to different tolerizing agents and identified CD86 as a consistent and robust marker downregulated in tolerogenic state. CD86 is functionally required for TolDC-mediated suppression of T cell proliferation and cytokine secretion, supporting its use as a surrogate marker of tolerogenic potential. Leveraging CD86 expression as a readout, we performed a genome-wide CRISPR-Cas9 knockout screen and characterized genes associated with TolDC phenotypes. This approach positions UBE2L6 as a regulator of CD86 expression through modulation of an ISG15-USP18-associated pathway, implicating its involvement in tolerogenic functions. These findings describe therapeutically targetable pathways to promote immune tolerance.

abstract: This study developed a pH/ROS dual-responsive SmartGel platform for local CRISPR-Cas9 RNP delivery and TRPV4 inhibition in intervertebral disc degeneration (IVDD). The GelMA/PBA-based SmartGel responded to acidic and oxidative microenvironmental cues and released Cas9/sgRNA under disease-mimicking conditions. In nucleus pulposus (NP) cells, SmartGel-Cas9/TRPV4 lowered ROS accumulation, restored mitochondrial membrane potential (ΔΨm), and coordinated apoptosis, senescence, Ca2+ homeostasis, CaMKKβ-dependent AMPK-mTOR signaling, and autophagic flux. CaMKKβ knockdown weakened AMPK activation and mTOR inhibition and autophagic-flux restoration, supporting CaMKKβ as a required link in this mechanism. In the rat IVDD model, the system preserved disc architecture, improved hydration status, reinforced extracellular matrix (ECM) homeostasis, and restrained downstream pathological signaling. Exploratory scRNA-seq and proteomic analyses further indicated treatment-associated shifts in Ca2+/autophagy/MAPK/Wnt-related programs. Overall, SmartGel-Cas9/TRPV4 may attenuate IVDD by restoring CaMKKβ-associated autophagic degradation and ECM balance while limiting aberrant signaling activation.

abstract: CRISPR-Cas9 genome editing has transformed biomedical research and is advancing toward clinical translation. The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) offers improved precision in guide RNA design, off-target prediction, and delivery optimization. This review synthesizes recent advances in CRISPR-Cas9 for medical applications, covering core mechanisms, engineered variants, base and prime editors, and therapeutic applications including CAR T-cell and CAR-NK engineering, genetic disorders, infectious diseases, and regenerative medicine. Delivery strategies are evaluated with emphasis on AI-driven optimization. AI applications are highlighted across deep learning architectures for guide RNA design, AI-designed nucleases such as OpenCRISPR-1, structure-guided and AI-assisted design of compact high-fidelity SaCas9 variants, reinforcement learning for pipeline optimization, and roles in CAR T-cell therapy and safety assessment. Safety challenges are examined, including off-target effects, chromosomal rearrangements, immunogenicity, and regulatory concerns. Future directions emphasize multi-scale modeling, explainable AI, clinical validation, and integration with synthetic biology, single-cell sequencing, organoids, and nanomaterials. The convergence of AI and CRISPR-Cas9 holds substantial potential for personalized medicine.

abstract: Noncoding RNAs have recently emerged as promising targets for therapeutic drugs. However, their high conformational flexibility presents significant challenges in structure-based rational drug discovery. Therefore, it is essential to gain detailed mechanistic insights into the millisecond-time scale ligand recognition process coupled to RNA conformational dynamics. Enhanced sampling simulations can help investigate these intricate dynamical processes by effectively exploring the rugged conformational landscapes of RNA-ligand complexes. In this study, we applied the on-the-fly probability enhanced sampling algorithm and its flooding variant to compute the free energy surface, kinetics, and binding mechanism for three different natural and synthetic ligands to a prototypical RNA aptamer. Our simulations revealed the dynamic coupling between ligand recognition and the base-flipping transition. In addition to reproducing the relative trends of binding affinities and residence times, our results uncovered a competing effect between the conformational selection and the induced fit mechanisms. The preference for one mechanism over the other is influenced by the binding affinity. By integrating these mechanistic insights with the binding affinity and kinetics derived from our simulations, we provide an atomistically detailed understanding of the RNA-ligand recognition process.

abstract: Identifying genes associated with the mechanism of action (MOA) of anticancer therapies is essential for understanding drug response. Functional genomics approaches, including genome-wide CRISPR knock out screens, enable systematic gene prioritization following treatment; however, findings from individual datasets are typically interpreted after identifying overlapping genes across datasets to confirm biological hypotheses. Integrating such heterogeneous datasets remains challenging due to variability across experimental conditions. Existing approaches can miss biologically relevant genes due to dataset-specific noise, can fail to capture genes exhibiting consistent but moderate effects across studies. Here, we present ConcuRx, a statistical framework for cross-study integration and gene prioritization across heterogeneous CRISPR drug-response screens. This approach produces more stable gene rankings than single-dataset analyses, improving prioritization of known MOA-associated genes and recovering biologically relevant genes that are overlooked by average- and overlap-based approaches. Applied to CRISPR drug-response screens for the synergistic drug pair of ATR and PARP inhibitors, ConcuRx strengthened support for 15 experimentally validated hypotheses collected from published studies, including mechanisms supported by independent studies not included in the ConcuRx analysis. These findings demonstrate that modelling between-study variability improves identification and prioritization of MOA-associated genes and provides a robust strategy for integrating heterogeneous functional genomics data in precision oncology.

abstract:
BACKGROUND: Loss of function mutations in the lipid transporter ABCA7 have been linked to increased risk for late onset Alzheimer's disease (AD). Although rare and common variants in ABCA7 associated with AD alter the coding sequence and are predicted to impair protein function, the precise cell-type consequences of ABCA7 deficiency remain incompletely defined.
METHODS: We used CRISPR/Cas9 gene editing to generate induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) that were deficient for ABCA7 (ABCA7-KO) and their wild-type (ABCA7-WT) isogenic counterparts and subsequently performed unbiased proteomics on differentiated astrocytes (iAs), neurons (iNs) and microglia (iMGs). ABCA7 deficiency in iMGs produced the largest proteomic changes, so we therefore conducted additional functional analyses to define its effects on microglial lysosomal activity, phagocytosis, and lipid metabolism. In addition, we leveraged CRISPR/Cas9 to correct the ABCA7 rs3752246 AD risk variant in patient-derived iPSCs and compared proteomic and functional phenotypes between corrected iMGs and isogenic mutant carriers. Finally, we examined the functional consequence of ABCA7-deficient microglia on neurons.
RESULTS: ABCA7-KO iMGs were deficient for proteins involved in lysosome function, measured by down-regulated lysosomal proteomic signatures, as well as reduced DQ-BSA activity and reduced LAMP1+ area. Additionally, ABCA7-KO iMGs displayed impaired phagocytic capacity and increased inflammatory markers, including MHC proteins CD1A and CD1E, and IL-18,. Multi-omic integration of lipidomic and proteomic profiles nominated a dysregulated metabolic network characterized by altered phospholipid steady-state metabolism and increased lipid peroxidation in ABCA7-KO iMGs. This was complemented by an accumulation of polyunsaturated triacylglycerols and lipid droplets, suggesting that ABCA7 deficiency disrupts intracellular lipid dynamics. This was supported by the alleviation of lysosomal and lipid droplet phenotypes through the inhibiting the synthesis of triacylglycerols. Concordantly, proteomic and functional analyses revealed lysosomal dysfunction in rs3752246-mutant iMGs, suggesting a shared ABCA7-dependent mechanism underlying AD risk. Tri-cultures of iNs, iAs and iMGs revealed that ABCA7 deficiency in iMGs worsened AD-relevant neuronal measures such as tau phosphorylation and synapse number.
CONCLUSIONS: This work supplies evidence for the important role of ABCA7 in microglia and provides unique insights into the molecular and functional consequences of reduced ABCA7 function in lysosomal and lipid regulation, paving a path forward to a more comprehensive understanding of AD molecular subtypes and personalized therapeutics.

title: The Alzheimer's disease risk gene ABCA7 regulates microglial lysosomal and lipid homeostasis and promotes phagocytosis to maintain neuronal health.

abstract: Developing broadly protective influenza vaccines remains a major challenge for global public health. Influenza B viruses cause about one-third of all annual influenza virus infections and current vaccines only show moderate effectiveness against matched virus strains, therefore, development of more effective and broadly protective vaccines against them is important. Chimeric and mosaic hemagglutinin (cHA and mHA) immunogens are under investigation as broadly protective influenza B vaccine candidates. The lipid nanoparticle (LNP)-encapsulated nucleoside-modified mRNA technology has recently revolutionized vaccination and gained widespread interest due to its successful use in the coronavirus disease 2019 pandemic. Here, we evaluated influenza B cHA and mHA mRNA-LNP vaccines in non-human primates and compared their immunogenicity to a quadrivalent seasonal influenza virus vaccine. mHA mRNA-LNPs induced high binding antibody titers against antigenically distant influenza B virus strains, with significant hemagglutination inhibition and antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity activity and provided protection in mice in a serum transfer challenge experiment. This approach shows great promise for developing broadly protective influenza B vaccines.

title: Mosaic Hemagglutinin-Based Influenza B mRNA-LNP Vaccine Induces Strong Humoral Immune Response in Non-Human Primates.

abstract: Adenosine-to-inosine (A-to-I) RNA editing is one of the most abundant RNA modifications and is involved in multiple critical biological processes; however, the precise localization of inosine and the mechanisms governing their selective editing remain incompletely understood. Integrating high-accuracy detection technologies with deep learning models can accelerate our understanding of the selective positioning and functional implications of A-to-I editing. To address these challenges, this study simultaneously developed RNA inosine sequencing by endonuclease V (EndoV) and XRN-1 (REX-seq), a highly sensitive and accurate detection method for inosine sites, and Inosine Deep Residual Enhanced Attention Model (InoDREAM), a predictive deep learning framework. REX-seq combines EndoV cleavage specificity with XRN-1 exonuclease activity to enable comprehensive A-to-I editome profiling while maintaining accurate gene expression quantification. Using this method, we identified 590,249 high-confidence inosine sites in HEK293T cells, including 84,645 novel sites. Leveraging the high-confidence A-to-I editing sites identified by REX-seq, we developed InoDREAM, which successfully predicted multiple regulatory proteins that exhibit specific binding affinity to A-to-I edited transcripts while simultaneously identifying disease-associated mutation sites and relevant cis-regulatory elements that are functionally linked to RNA editing events. These findings provide novel mechanistic insights into both the molecular regulation of RNA editing and its pathophysiological implications in disease development.

title: Deciphering the regulatory code of RNA inosine through enzymatic precision mapping and an explainable deep learning model.

abstract: C9ORF72 is involved in multiple neuronal functions and a major factor in Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis, a fatal neurodegenerative disease. Pathogenicity is implemented through an intronic repeat expansion in the gene's mRNA leader that produces long, repetitive RNA and dipeptides when translated through repeat associated non-canonical translation. The expanded repeat also suppresses transcription of the major transcript variant (Variant 2) which comprises 90% of the C9ORF72 levels in healthy cells, leading to an additional loss-of-function effect. Examining the sequence, structure, and ribosome occupancy of Variant 2's mRNA leader in detail, we found that translation of C9ORF72 is tightly regulated through a multi-layered system. To deconvolute this system, we conducted a mutant screen and developed a method to evaluate the results quantitatively. We found that near-cognate start codons in all three frames, a start-stop element in frame 2, a uTranslon in frame 1, and secondary structures cooperate to keep baseline C9ORF72 translation low. Further, initiation at upstream near-cognate start codons reduces the impact of both the start-stop and the uTranslon, effectively buffering their repressive function and creating a feedforward loop. A strong secondary structure in the Variant 2-specific sequence further modulates initiation at all the elements. We hypothesize that this buffered repressor system has evolved to ensure reliable, noise-insensitive expression of this critical regulator of neuronal function. Finally, we used ADAR-based RNA editing of specific sites in Variant 2's mRNA leader, increasing translation of the gene and providing a novel avenue to rescue the loss-of-function phenotype in disease.

title: Multi-level repression ensures tight translation control of C9ORF72.

abstract: Following the successes of the messenger RNA (mRNA) lipid nanoparticle (LNP) vaccines against COVID-19, mRNA-LNPs are being explored for varied multidose applications including cancer immunotherapies and protein replacement therapies. LNPs rely on poly(ethylene glycol)-lipid (PEG-lipid) coatings for stability, but increasing anti-PEG antibody prevalence threatens repeat-dose efficacy and increases pseudoallergic risk, creating an urgent need for alternatives. Here, we introduce poly(acrylamido) lipids (PAM-lipids), a family of polymer lipids that effectively replace PEG-lipids in mRNA-LNP formulations. Systematic variation of monomer chemistry, molar mass, and end group reveals critical structure-activity relationships determining LNP size, polydispersity, and transfection efficiency. Varying PAM monomer chemistry allows minimization of antipolymer antibody cross-reactivity, with multiple PAM-lipids demonstrating no anti-PEG antibody binding. Several PAM-LNPs exhibit superior mRNA transfection efficacy to PEGylated clinical benchmarks in vitro and in vivo across multiple cell types, organs, routes of administration, and mRNA cargos. In particular, lead PAM-LNPs enhance mRNA delivery to dendritic cells (up to 120-fold in vitro and 3-fold in vivo) and macrophages (4-fold in vivo), with 2.5-fold superior lymph node expression, driven in part by increased cellular association and lymphoid targeting. Crucially, PAM-LNPs evade circulating anti-PEG antibodies to rescue lost mRNA efficacy after repeated dosing, resulting in 300% mRNA expression relative to that of PEG-LNPs. These findings demonstrate PAM-lipids as a chemically varied, immunologically compatible family of PEG alternatives for mRNA-LNP therapeutics.

title: Poly(acrylamido) PEG-Alternative Lipids Rescue mRNA Efficacy during Repeated Dosing and Enhance Immune Cell Delivery.

abstract: Lactobacillus johnsonii N6.2-derived extracellular vesicles (EVs) provide protection against murine norovirus (MNV-1) both in vitro and in vivo. Within the proteins enriched in EVs, the SH3b2 domain of Sdp was shown to be sufficient to recapitulate the antiviral effects shown by EVs. In this report, we compared the effects of six SH3b domains of Sdp and identified amino acids expected to be important for interactions with host proteins. We found that SH3b2 showed the highest activity in inducing NF-ĸB/AP-1 and IRF pathways in RAW macrophage reporter cell lines. Structure-guided site-directed mutagenesis of SH3b2 revealed residues in SH3b2 potentially responsible for interactions with host proteins. SH3b2-G501D had significantly lower stimulation of NF-ĸB/AP-1 and IRF pathways. In addition, SH3b2-G501D showed reduced IL10 and Oas1 mRNA levels, resulting in an impaired MNV-1 antiviral response in RAW 264.7 cells. mCherry fusions to SH3b2-G501D confirmed that the effects observed were not related to reduced uptake into macrophages, as quantified by confocal microscopy. Additionally, the role of the C-terminal linker sequence in Sh3b2, which is absent in SH3b6, in uptake or signaling in macrophages was evaluated. It was found that deletion of the C-terminal linker (SH3b2ΔC2 treatment) resulted in reduced promoter activity, while SH3b6::C2 partially regained function through restoration of uptake in macrophages. These results indicate that the C-terminal linker plays an important role in internalization by macrophages. We propose that once internalized, SH3b2 mimics eukaryotic SH3 domains involved in signal transduction to activate the cellular innate immune response in macrophages.
