title: Advances in therapeutic oligonucleotide conjugates.

abstract: The traditional "one gene, one protein" paradigm is insufficient to capture the vast phenotypic and physiological complexity of eukaryotes. This review aims to comprehensively elucidate the molecular mechanisms of transcriptomic diversification, namely, alternative splicing, alternative usage of promoter, and alternative polyadenylation, and their profound impacts on cellular homeostasis and human disease. By synthesizing recent breakthroughs in targeted long-read RNA sequencing, single-cell isoform-specific multiomics, and AI-driven 3D structural modeling, we systematically examine how transcript variants are generated and functionally annotated. Our analysis highlights that multiple transcript variants originating from a single genetic locus are not merely redundant copies; rather, subtle sequence alterations dynamically rewire protein-protein interaction networks and dictate precise subcellular localization. The exquisite spatiotemporal regulation of these variants controls critical cell fate decisions and organ development. Consequently, the pathological dysregulation of these processes, frequently termed spliceopathies, acts as a primary driver in severe pathologies, including cancer multidrug resistance, metabolic reprogramming, and neurodegenerative disorders. In conclusion, understanding the eukaryotic proteome requires a fundamental shift from conventional gene-level to isoform-level perspectives. Decoding the complex regulatory syntax of transcript variants paves the way for next-generation precision medicine, highlighting the therapeutic potential of RNA-targeted interventions, such as antisense oligonucleotides and CRISPR-based RNA editing, to correct pathogenic isoforms.

abstract:
PURPOSE OF REVIEW: Apolipoprotein C-III (apoC-III) has emerged as a validated target for lowering triglycerides, triglyceride-rich lipoproteins, and remnant cholesterol. This review summarizes the biology of apoC-III, the genetic and clinical trial evidence supporting its inhibition, and remaining questions.
RECENT FINDINGS: Loss-of-function variants in APOC3 are associated with lower levels of triglycerides and reduced cardiovascular risk. Pharmacologic inhibition of apoC-III with RNA-based agents has led to substantial reductions in apoC-III and triglycerides across familial chylomicronemia syndrome (FCS), severe hypertriglyceridemia (sHTG), and moderate hypertriglyceridemia (mHTG). In FCS, agents volanesorsen, olezarsen, and plozasiran have demonstrated reductions in triglycerides and acute pancreatitis. In sHTG, olezarsen has extended this benefit to a larger, multifactorial population. In mHTG, olezarsen and plozasiran lower triglycerides, remnant cholesterol, non-HDL-cholesterol, and apolipoprotein B, but an imaging study with olezarsen demonstrated neutral findings on coronary plaque composition, and cardiovascular event reduction has not been demonstrated. ApoC-III inhibition provides a potent strategy for lowering triglycerides and triglyceride-rich lipoproteins. Its most immediate clinical role is in FCS and sHTG, where prevention of acute pancreatitis is the main objective. Its future as a cardiovascular therapy will depend on whether reductions in remnant cholesterol and apolipoprotein B translate into fewer atherosclerotic events in a dedicated cardiovascular outcomes trial.

abstract: Mixed-species biofilm infections are important causes of persistent and difficult-to-treat infections. Compared with monospecies biofilms, mixed-species communities contain microorganisms with different physiological and genetic characteristics that interact through metabolic cooperation, chemical signaling, competition, and modification of the local environment. These interactions, together with the EPS matrix, physiological heterogeneity, and HGT, can increase antimicrobial tolerance, contributing to treatment failure and infection recurrence. Polymicrobial biofilms are associated with chronic wounds, respiratory infections, catheter- and device-associated infections, and other persistent infections. However, treatment of polymicrobial biofilms remains challenging because their complex structure and interspecies interactions can reduce antimicrobial efficacy. This review summarizes the clinical significance, formation, and persistence of mixed-species biofilms and discusses recent therapeutic strategies for their control. We also discuss recent approaches for controlling polymicrobial biofilms, including natural compounds, QS inhibition, CRISPR-Cas-based approaches, biofilm matrix targeting, metabolic and nutrient disruption, nanotechnology, and phage therapy. Recent studies show that these approaches can inhibit biofilm formation, disrupt established biofilms, enhance antimicrobial activity, and selectively target specific microbial populations. However, their effectiveness varies with microbial composition, biofilm maturity, matrix characteristics, and treatment conditions. Overall, current evidence supports the development of targeted and combination-based strategies for mixed-species biofilms. Further studies using clinically relevant models are needed to exactly define treatment efficacy and support the translation of these approaches into clinical practice.

title: A comprehensive review of mixed-species biofilm infections and innovative therapeutic strategies.

abstract: The underlying mechanisms of Moyamoya disease (MMD), a rare, progressive cerebrovascular disorder marked by distal internal carotid artery stenosis or occlusion and the formation of fragile collaterals, remain poorly understood, in part because conventional models fail to capture the genetic, vascular, and neurovascular complexity of human MMD. Driven by recent advances in disease modeling, MMD research has moved beyond early endothelial progenitor cell studies toward patient-derived induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-based platforms. Here, we summarize the generation and validation of MMD-specific iPSCs and their differentiation into endothelial cells (ECs), vascular smooth muscle cells (VSMCs), and related vascular lineages, and we discuss how two-dimensional (2D) iPSC-based models have provided insights into impaired angiogenesis, endothelial dysfunction, abnormal VSMC behavior, and disrupted vascular cell interactions. We then highlight the emerging use of three-dimensional vascular and neurovascular organoids, which reproduce cellular heterogeneity, vessel-like organization, and neurovascular unit interactions more closely than conventional 2D cultures. These models may provide a more integrated platform for investigating the complex vascular pathophysiology of MMD. Finally, we discuss future directions for MMD modeling, including the integration of multi-omics profiling and CRISPR-mediated genome editing with patient-derived iPSC and organoid platforms. These approaches may help clarify genotype-phenotype relationships, RNF213-dependent and RNF213-independent mechanisms, and disease-relevant molecular pathways. With further standardization and validation, iPSC- and organoid-based models could support mechanistic studies, therapeutic screening, and personalized disease modeling. Our review underscores the emerging role of patient-derived stem cell and organoid technologies in advancing MMD research and in informing future translational efforts.

abstract: Antisense oligonucleotides (ASOs) are versatile disease-modifying therapies for genetic diseases. An accelerated US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) pathway enables ASO treatment trial initiation in an individual within a year. However, this rapid N-of-1 pathway lacks extensibility to broad use necessary for sustainability. Individualized ASOs bind pre-mRNAs encompassing an entire locus. Thus, ASOs targeting common heterozygous polymorphisms (SNPs) are potentially haplospecific in many individuals with dominant disorders. We developed haplospecific ASOs for two probands with SCN2A-complex neurodevelopmental disorder (CND) and gain-of-function (GOF) or mixed gain-loss dysfunction (GLD) variants. The ASOs targeted reference SCN2A intronic sequences containing SNPs. The probands each had SCN2A haplotypes with reference SNP alleles in cis with causal variants and alternate SNP alleles in cis with normal mRNA. Following N-of-1 demonstration of safety and efficacy, we evaluated their applicability to 21 SCN2A-CND probands using whole-genome sequencing (WGS) with haplotyping by read proximity. Ten (48%) probands had ASO-eligible diplotypes. Haplotype analysis of unrelated 1000 Genomes Project (1kGP) participants revealed 18 additional SCN2A haplotypes present in >20% of subjects, tagged by 156 SNPs. In silico assessment of specificity and potency identified additional haplospecific ASOs for validation in reprogrammed 1kGP cells heterozygous for the tagging SNPs. A combination of four haplospecific ASOs provided coverage for 76.2% of 1kGP subjects, potentially allowing scaling of N-of-1 FDA applications in future individuals with SCN2A-CND and GOF/GLD variants. Thus, population resources have potential to prepare haplospecific ASO therapies a priori for many persons and genetic diseases, with individual ASO selection by diagnostic WGS with haplotyping.

abstract: Endogenous retrotransposable elements (ERE) can modulate immune responses. We explored ERE transcription in relation to response to immune checkpoint inhibition in advanced solid tumors. ERE expression was measured in pre- and on-treatment samples from patients treated in a clinical trial with pembrolizumab. We evaluated immune cell infiltration and correlated ERE expression with interferon (IFN)-stimulated gene profiles and cytolytic activity. Two independent datasets were retrospectively analyzed as external validation. ERE transcription, notably Alu repetitive elements followed by long interspersed nuclear elements (LINE), is upregulated in immunotherapy responders, and higher ERE expression correlates with durable clinical benefit and improved long-term outcomes. In responders, this dynamic increase correlates with CD8+ T-cell infiltration and cytolytic activity, particularly during treatment. A trend toward increased A-to-I RNA editing was observed in responders. External validation in melanoma and non-small cell lung cancer cohorts confirmed a consistent pattern in ERE transcription. Therefore, ERE transcription is emerging as a potential biomarker for personalized immunotherapy in solid tumors.

abstract:
BACKGROUND: Robust non-clinical safety models are crucial to the development and evaluation of messenger ribonucleic acid (mRNA)-based drugs and vaccines. In this study, we leveraged cross-study data to explore whether the Göttingen minipig could serve as an alternative to the rabbit, a commonly used species in vaccine safety assessment.
METHODS: Results from two independent toxicity studies of lipid nanoparticle-encapsulated mRNA encoding the hemagglutinin H3 antigen, administered at equivalent dose levels, were qualitatively compared. Clinical observations, local reactions, body weight, food consumption, body temperature, clinical pathology, immunogenicity, inflammatory biomarkers, and anatomical pathology endpoints were evaluated.
RESULTS: Both species exhibited expected vaccine responses, with minor differences in local reactogenicity and body temperature. The vaccine candidate was well tolerated at the injection site in both species. However, mild and transient vaccine-related effects (i.e., injection site induration and increased body temperature) were observed only in minipigs. Transient increases in neutrophil, fibrinogen, and C-reactive protein levels were observed in both species following vaccination, consistent with an inflammatory response. Microscopic findings (i.e., inflammation at the injection site and increased germinal center cellularity in the draining lymph nodes) were comparable between species and aligned with expected immune activation following vaccination.
CONCLUSIONS: This qualitative comparison provides preliminary, supportive evidence for the potential use of the minipig as an alternative to the rabbit in non-clinical safety evaluation of mRNA vaccines, with the added benefit of larger blood volume for sampling and availability of validated key inflammatory markers.

abstract: Group A Streptococcus (GAS), or Streptococcus pyogenes, causes a connected spectrum of pharyngeal, cutaneous, invasive and immune-mediated diseases. Although beta-lactams remain active, treatment alone has not controlled transmission, recurrent infection, rapid invasive progression or acute rheumatic fever and rheumatic heart disease. Control is further weakened by increased macrolide and clindamycin resistance, heterogeneous diagnostic access, asymptomatic carriage, crowded living conditions and unreliable continuity of secondary prophylaxis. These limitations have shifted the field from a predominantly treatment-centered approach toward the development of vaccines as a prevention strategy. Target selection is guided by virulence functions that are required for colonization, immune evasion and tissue injury. These include the M protein, group A carbohydrate (GAC), streptolysin O, Streptococcus pyogenes cell envelope protease (SpyCEP), Streptococcus pyogenes adhesion and division protein (SpyAD), C5a peptidase and other conserved surface or secreted antigens. Current strategies include multivalent type-specific M-protein vaccines, conserved M-protein peptide vaccines, glycoconjugates, multicomponent non-M-protein formulations and mRNA-lipid nanoparticle platforms. The clinical pipeline has recently broadened. Phase I studies have been completed for StreptAnova and MJ8VAX, whereas the J8-K4S2 and p*17-K4S2 clinical trial studies have been completed, with peer-reviewed results pending. The GSK four-component vaccine initiated phase I evaluation in 2025 and remained under clinical evaluation in 2026, whereas the VAX-A1 formulation entered a first-in-human phase I study in 2026. However, no licensed GAS vaccine is available. Progress remains constrained by uncertain correlates of protection, autoimmune safety requirements, geographical emm diversity, endpoint selection and the need for trials in high-burden populations. This narrative review therefore focuses on the disease problem, targetable virulence mechanisms, limits of antimicrobial control, current vaccine pipeline and interventions required to complement future vaccine use.

abstract:
PURPOSE: MEDI1191 is a lipid nanoparticle-formulated messenger RNA (mRNA) designed to induce local interleukin (IL) 12 production and intensify antitumor T-cell responses. We report dose-escalation results from a first-in-human, open-label, phase I study of intratumoral MEDI1191 plus intravenous durvalumab (NCT03946800).
PATIENTS AND METHODS: Patients were ≥18 years with advanced/metastatic solid tumors and had progressed on ≥1 line of prior therapy (immunotherapy permitted). Cutaneous/subcutaneous (parts 1A and 1B) or deep-seated lesions (part 1D) were injected; patients had ≥1 noninjected lesion measurable per Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid Tumors (RECIST v1.1). Target lesions were noninjected. MEDI1191 and durvalumab were given sequentially (part 1A) or concurrently (parts 1B and 1D). Primary objectives were safety and determination of maximum tolerated dose (MTD). Secondary objectives included efficacy.
RESULTS: As of February 27, 2023, 61 patients were treated. Patients had a median of four prior regimens (range, 1-17); 39 (63.9%) received prior anti-programmed cell death protein 1/programmed cell death ligand 1 [PD-(L)1] immunotherapy. Treatment-emergent adverse events (TEAE) occurred in 96.7% of patients, and 41.0% experienced grade 3/4 TEAEs. There were no dose-limiting toxicities. The MTD was not reached. The objective response rate was 9.8%, including 1 confirmed complete response and 5 confirmed partial responses (PR). The duration of response was 2.7 to 22.3 months; the median was not reached. Responses occurred in injected lesions, local noninjected lesions, and distant lesions. Three of the 39 patients with prior anti-PD-(L)1 therapy had PRs.
CONCLUSIONS: MEDI1191 and durvalumab were tolerated. Preliminary antitumor activity was encouraging in these heavily pretreated patients, including patients previously treated with immune checkpoint inhibitors.

abstract: Limitations in the druggability of challenging protein targets, coupled with recognition of the diverse roles of noncoding RNAs in cellular regulation and disease have spurred interest in RNA as a druggable macromolecule. The rapidly emerging field of RNA-targeted small-molecule therapeutics is now exploring induced proximity mechanisms in the form of RNA-targeting chimeras that recruit effector proteins to catalyze RNA decay. Inspired by "molecular glue" natural products such as rapamycin and cyclosporin A, which induce protein-protein interactions to sterically modulate protein function, we propose the new application of immunophilin recruitment to alter RNA function. Here in, we report the design and characterization of heterobifunctional molecules that induce highly cooperative RNA-FKBP12 ternary complexes and describe efforts to assess their impact on RNA metabolism. We also evaluate applications and report off-target liabilities associated with the chosen RNA ligand for our heterobifunctional series. Finally, we discuss the challenges faced and highlight opportunities for future success in the RNA space.

abstract: The clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats (CRISPR)/CRISPRassociated protein 9 (Cas9) system has revolutionized genome editing through its precision, simplicity, and programmability. The clinical translation of CRISPR/Cas9 Ribonucleoproteins (RNPs) remains constrained by major delivery challenges, including large molecular size, instability in biological fluids, and limited cellular penetration. Nanoparticle-mediated, non-viral delivery systems have emerged as a compelling strategy to overcome these barriers by providing targeted, transient, and biocompatible transport of Cas9 RNPs into cells. This review systematically evaluates recent advances in lipid-based, polymeric, peptide, and exosome-derived nanocarriers, focusing on their design principles, mechanisms of uptake, and endosomal escape strategies. Particular attention is given to receptor-mediated targeting, intracellular trafficking, and the emerging translation of lipid nanoparticle systems such as NTLA-2001, which exemplify clinical progress in genome editing. Despite these advancements, several challenges persist. Nanoparticle systems exhibit trade-offs between efficiency, biocompatibility, and scalability. For example, lipid nanoparticles may trigger anti- PEG immune reactions, exosome production faces manufacturing constraints, and polymeric systems risk cytotoxicity or limited degradability. Pre-existing immunity to Cas9 proteins and unpredictable immune responses to nanoparticle components remain significant translational hurdles. By integrating current preclinical and early clinical evidence, this review highlights both the promise and the limitations of nanoparticle-mediated CRISPR/Cas9 RNP delivery. Understanding these biological, immunological, and engineering challenges will be crucial for developing safe, efficient, and clinically scalable genome editing platforms.

abstract: The clinical validation of mRNA-based COVID-19 vaccines in 2020-2021 accelerated the development of synthetic messenger RNA as a precision therapeutic platform beyond infectious disease prevention. Unlike gene therapy approaches that permanently modify genomic DNA, synthetic mRNA enables transient protein expression through programmable molecular engineering. This narrative review examines therapeutic applications of engineered mRNA, emphasizing its epigenomic potential. It discusses key engineering strategies, including nucleoside modifications, codon optimization, untranslated region engineering, cap chemistry, and advances in lipid nanoparticle and alternative delivery systems. Six therapeutic domains are explored: cancer immunotherapy, cardiac regeneration, monogenic diseases, genome and epigenome editing, autoimmune disease, and somatic cell reprogramming. Particular attention is given to mRNA-mediated replacement of chromatin regulators, dCas9-based epigenome editing, epigenetically derived tumor antigens, and transcription-factor-driven cellular reprogramming. The review distinguishes chemical nucleoside modifications from endogenous epitranscriptomic regulation and examines the differences between transient protein expression, heritable but reversible chromatin changes, and permanent genomic modifications. Clinical evidence, discontinued programs, and preclinical developments are critically evaluated. Despite promising advances, major challenges remain regarding delivery specificity, durability, safety, and clinical translation. Overall, synthetic mRNA represents an emerging platform for molecular and epigenetic therapeutic reprogramming beyond vaccination.

abstract: CRISPR-dCas9 epigenome editing represents a paradigm shift from static DNA sequence editing to dynamic reprogramming of gene expression, offering a powerful and precise toolbox with the potential to develop stable and climate-resilient crops without altering DNA sequences. The escalating challenges of global food security, driven by climate change and population growth, necessitate innovative crop improvement strategies that extend beyond conventional breeding. Although CRISPR-Cas9 has revolutionized plant biotechnology through direct genome editing, CRISPR-based epigenome editing has emerged as a new frontier. By repurposing nuclease-dead Cas9 as a programmable targeting platform fused to epigenetic effector domains, researchers can precisely modulate gene expression without altering the DNA sequence. This approach has already yielded compelling successes, such as the engineering of durable resistance to cassava bacterial blight through targeted epigenetic silencing of a susceptibility gene. This review focuses primarily on the current state of CRISPR-based epigenome editing systems, including acetyltransferases, demethylases, DNA methyltransferases, and deacetylases, and their applications in crop improvement research. We critically evaluate their mechanisms in rewriting epigenetic regulatory information, their demonstrated efficacy in enhancing yield components, disease resistance, and abiotic stress tolerance, and their potential to create stable meiotically heritable epialleles, although most demonstrations remain at the proof-of-concept stage in model plants, with field validation in major crops still limited. This review provides a balanced analysis of key challenges, including editing specificity, context-dependency, delivery limitations, and regulatory considerations. Finally, we outline future directions focusing on technological refinement, multi-omics integration, and field validation. Epigenome editing shows promise as a conceptually distinct and transformative approach in crop biotechnology, through targeted modulation of a plant's epigenetic landscape. However, its full potential hinges on overcoming challenges related to stability, predictability, and field-scale validation.

abstract: Coleoid cephalopods exhibit the highest levels of adenosine deaminases acting on RNA (ADAR)-mediated RNA editing of any known taxon, yet the functional consequences of most recoding events remain unclear. Here, we integrated proteomics with biochemical and cellular assays to characterize recoding across the Doryteuthis pealeii proteome. This confirmed the translation of 7,997 recoded sites at the protein level and revealed how recoding reshapes the proteome by altering protein stability, subcellular localization, post-translational modifications, and enzymatic activity. We find that recoding also creates or ablates post-translational modification sites, with direct effects on protein function and protein-protein interactions. Recoding the E3 ligase MARCHF5 drives widespread changes in substrate ubiquitylation and perturbs mitochondrial homeostasis, illustrating how RNA editing can influence organelle function. Together, these data give a proteome-scale view of how extensive RNA recoding diversifies protein function in coleoid cephalopods and offer a framework for understanding how RNA-level plasticity shapes protein function and cellular physiology.

abstract: Genome-targeting strategies to address NaV1.7-mediated signaling in nociceptive afferents are of great clinical interest given its high selectivity and persistent analgesic outcomes. In the present work, we analyze concentration-dependent effects of suppressing primary afferent NaV1.7 using the intrathecal delivery of an antisense oligonucleotide (ASO) on pain behaviors and demonstrate that NaV1.7 ASOs are likely to modulate pain traffic by blocking afferent signaling at the dorsal root ganglion (DRG) level. Intrathecal NaV1.7 ASOs induced a concentration-dependent gradient of knockdown in DRGs (lumbar to cervical) of Scn9a mRNA and ATTO488-ProTx-II binding in small DRG neurons, and a suppression of pain behaviors initiated by mechanical compression, inflammation, and the NaV1.7 agonist OD-1. The rostro-caudal reduction in mRNA correlated with ASO distribution, with implications for dose-related analgesic profiles. Marked reduction in DRG NaV1.7 binding was seen after intrathecal delivery of an ASO optimal dose, with high selectivity for small DRG neurons. Changes in sciatic nerve NaV1.7 binding were not detected, indicating a pain traffic modulation likely happening due to a block of afferent signaling at the DRG level.

abstract:
Background:

Chronic granulomatous disease (CGD) is a rare immune disorder caused by a mutation in the CYBB gene. People with CGD have white blood cells that do not work properly and are at greater risk of getting infections. Researchers want to know if gene therapy using the patient's own base-edited stem cells can improve the white cells' functioning and result in fewer CGD-related infections.

Objective:

To learn if base-edited stem cells will correct the white blood cells in people with CGD.

Eligibility:

Males aged 18 years and older with X-linked CGD.

Design:

This is a non-randomized study. Participants with the specific mutation under study will be screened during the initial phase.

During the development phase, participants will undergo apheresis to collect stem cells for base-editing correction of the mutation.

During the treatment phase, participants will first receive Campath (alemtuzumab) to reduce the risk of an immune response to the new protein expressed by the base-edited cells. This will be followed by conditioning chemotherapy with busulfan and subsequent infusion of the base-edited stem cells. Participants will be maintained on sirolimus to further reduce the risk of an immune response to the new protein expressed by the base-edited cells.

Follow-up visits will continue for 15 years.

description:
Study Description:

Open-label, phase 1/2 trial to determine the safety, and efficacy of a single infusion of base-edited (BE) autologous hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells (HSPCs) for treatment of X-linked chronic granulomatous disease (X-CGD). Base editing is performed to repair CYBB missense gene mutations (eg, CYBB c.676C\>T). The study hypotheses are that 1) base editing can efficiently repair gene mutations in HSPCs; and 2) BE HSPCs can engraft and differentiate into functional phagocytes with restored nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide phosphate (NADPH) oxidase activity.

During the initial development phase each study participant will undergo apheresis for CD34+ HSPC collection for the development and validation of a mutation-specific BE system.

During the treatment phase, participants will receive a one-time infusion of the BE autologous HSPC (study product) after the administration of Campath (alemtuzumab) and of busulfan conditioning (total 12 mg/kg with a targeted total AUC of 65,000 ng/mL x hr). Sirolimus will be initiated on Day -1 and may be given for approximately 3-6 months.

Participants will have follow-up evaluations at months 3, 6, 12, 18, and 24, and yearly thereafter until 5 years after treatment. Key study assessments include adverse event (AE) assessment, blood laboratory evaluations of functional protein made from the target gene (CYBB, encodes for gp91\^phox), and deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) sequencing to identify rates of gene repair and off-target mutation.

The final study follow-up under this protocol will be at 5 years, but long-term follow-up under a separate NIH protocol will continue annually to 15 years after treatment.

Objectives:

Primary Objectives:

* To evaluate the safety of BE autologous CD34+ cells.
* To evaluate the efficacy of BE autologous CD34+ cells.

Secondary Objectives:

-To evaluate:

* Efficiency of base editing (percentages of target nucleotide conversion).
* Engraftment capability of BE HSPCs.
* Efficiency in restoring gp91\^phox expression
* Efficiency in restoring NADPH oxidase function.
* Clinical efficacy.
* Stability of gene correction.

Exploratory Objectives:

-To evaluate:

* Specificity of base editing by assessing rates of off-target edits at top predicted sites.
* Random off-target edits by whole genome sequencing (WGS).

Endpoints:

Primary Endpoints:

* Safety of gene therapy using BE autologous HSPCs as measured by study product-related AEs and serious AEs (SAEs) through 2 years after treatment.
* Efficacy of gene therapy determined as percentages of subjects who have \>= 10% oxidase-positive granulocytes at 12 months after infusion.

Secondary Endpoints:

* Determine frequency of converted target nucleotide alleles.
* Assess the frequency of gene-modified alleles compared to infusion product in peripheral blood at 12 months.
* Evaluate efficacy of restoring gp91\^phox expression.
* Evaluate efficacy of NADPH oxidase functional restoration as measured by the dihydrorhodamine (DHR) flow cytometry oxidase assay at 12 months after treatment (\>=10% oxidase-positive neutrophils), or by quantitative measurement of reactive oxygen species (ROS) using the ferricytochrome C assay on peripheral blood granulocytes.
* Evaluate clinical benefit by improvement of baseline clinical problems such as recurrent infections, growth failure, malnutrition, inflammatory bowel disease, or antibiotic usage.
* Assess stability of gene correction by serial measurement of percent of nucleotide-converted alleles.

Exploratory Endpoints:

* Evaluate specificity by assessing for off-target edits at predicted sites with high-throughput sequencing of the 5 most common candidate off-target loci identified by a comprehensive in vitro screen, Circularization for High-throughput Analysis of Nuclease Genome-wide Effects by sequencing (CHANGE-seq-BE), in peripheral blood cells.
* Determine rate of random off-target edits WGS.

The goal of this clinical trial is to assess the safety, reactogenicity and immunogenicity of an mRNA-based vaccine, JCXH-108, the prevention of Respiratory Syncytial Virus (RSV) infection and diseases.

Participants will be randomized to receive either JCXH-108 or placebo.

description:
This Phase 1 study plans to enroll a total of 75 participants.

Three cohorts with two different dose levels will be explored and each cohort will enroll 25 participants. Participants in each cohort will be randomized (4:1) to receive either JCXH-108 (n=20) or placebo (normal saline, n=5). A low dose of JCXH-108 will be explored vs placebo in the 18-45 years of age group first. A high dose will be explored vs placebo in the 18-45 years and ≥ 60 years of age groups once safety data is reviewed for the Sentinel subjects in the low dose cohort. The dose level of JCXH-108 will depend on the time the participant joins the study. Each participant will receive a single dose of JCXH-108 administered intramuscularly (IM) on day 1.

abstract: Chimeric antigen receptor T cell (CAR-T) therapy has emerged as a prominent cancer treatment modality, demonstrating significant clinical success. To date, several CAR-T products have been approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) for the management of hematological malignancies. Despite these advances, several challenges continue to limit the broader application of CAR-T therapy. These challenges include complex and costly manufacturing processes, safety concerns associated with integrating viral vectors, individualized production requirements, therapy-related adverse effects, and limited efficacy against solid tumors. Recent progress in ribonucleic acid (RNA)-based technologies has introduced promising strategies to improve the safety, adaptability, and therapeutic performance of CAR-T cells. This review provides a comprehensive translational perspective on the integration of RNA technologies with CAR-T therapy. Specifically, it categorizes current approaches into four key areas: RNA-driven non-viral CAR-T cell manufacturing, RNA vaccine-mediated enhancement of CAR-T activity, RNA interference (RNAi)-based modulation, and in vivo CAR-T cell generation. Among the reviewed approaches, ex vivo messenger RNA (mRNA)-based CAR-T engineering currently has the greatest clinical maturity, whereas RNA vaccine-mediated boosting shows particular promise for enhancing CAR-T expansion and persistence, especially in solid tumors. In vivo RNA-mediated CAR-T generation remains at an early stage of development, with evidence still predominantly derived from preclinical studies, but may ultimately represent the most transformative approach by simplifying manufacturing and improving accessibility.Trial registration number: Not applicable.

title: Integrating RNA technologies with CAR-T cell therapy: strategies to overcome current limitations and expand clinical applications.

abstract: Curative therapies for genetic diseases caused by pathogenic mutations demand precise and safe genome editing technologies. Prime editing (PE), a CRISPR-Cas9-derived technology that enables precise base conversions without double-strand breaks (DSBs), has emerged as a transformative tool with the ability to correct 89% of human pathogenic mutations. However, transitioning PE from preclinical models to clinical applications faces critical challenges, particularly in the development of in vivo delivery systems and scalable manufacturing. This review systematically summarizes advances of in vivo PE therapeutics, focusing on the therapeutic outcomes across some retinal, metabolic, and hematologic genetic diseases. We further dissect barriers to clinical translation, including in the immunogenicity of viral vectors, off-target risks in nondividing cells, and large-scale production bottlenecks. By highlighting the unique advantages of in vivo PE and proposing actionable solutions for scalable manufacturing, the work provides a roadmap for accelerating in vivo PE-based therapies toward clinical reality.

title: Research progress of gene correction for genetic diseases via in vivo prime editing.

abstract: Human embryonic stem cells (hESCs) exhibit pluripotency, self-renewal, and broad therapeutic potential in diverse disease contexts. Meanwhile, allogeneic grafts derived from hESCs are confronted with the formidable challenge of immune rejection. Specific human leukocyte antigens (HLAs) are critically involved in mediating transplant rejection, thus establishing HLA-deficient stem cells can be an important step toward achieving immune evasion. However, there is currently no consensus on which gene editing strategy can reduce hESC immunogenicity to a level suitable for broad clinical applications. This study performed HLA-A/-B gene hetero/homozygous knockout in an HLA double-knockout hESC line using a CRISPR/Cas9 system, established HLA-DRA-/-/-DQA1-/-/-A+/-/-B-/- knockout monoclonal cell lines, and revealed the multi-omics profiles, along with preserved pluripotency and trends to reduced immunogenicity of the hESC lines, through multi-omics analyses, in vitro assessment of pluripotency-related gene expression, in vivo teratoma formation assays and xenotransplantation experiments in mouse models. This study presents two novel monoclonal HLA genes homo/heterozygous knockout hESC lines, along with their multi-omics landscapes, pluripotency and immunogenicity. The findings exhibit crucial application potential and reference value in the development of hypoimmunogenic hESCs for their universal clinical use.

title: Quadruple HLA-I/II gene homo/heterozygous knockout hESC line: generation, multi-omics profiling, pluripotency, and immunogenicity.

abstract:
UNLABELLED: Alveolar rhabdomyosarcoma (aRMS) is a fusion-driven pediatric cancer with poor survival and limited therapeutic options. To uncover novel vulnerabilities, we used complex-Map functional genomic data, identifying CDK8 as a dependency in aRMS. Both CDK8 knockout and pharmacologic inhibition impaired tumor cell growth and induced myogenic differentiation in vitro and in vivo. Compared with genetic loss, CDK8 pharmacologic inhibition induced more dynamic transcriptional changes. With a genome-scale CRISPR-Cas9 drug modifier screen, we determined that the maximal antitumor activity of the CDK8 inhibitor requires the presence of the Mediator kinase module, including CDK8, and transcriptional cooperation with the SAGA complex. We further identified SIX4 as a key transcription factor mediating CDK8 inhibitor-induced transcriptional activation of myogenic differentiation genes and impaired tumor proliferation. These findings suggest a distinct gain-of-function mechanism of the CDK8 inhibitor and establish a strong rationale for CDK8 inhibition as a differentiation-inducing therapeutic strategy in aRMS.
SIGNIFICANCE: We provide a framework for uncovering therapeutic targets by network-based analysis of functional genomic screens. We identify CDK8 as a druggable target in aRMS and determine that CDK8 inhibition drives myogenic differentiation and impairs tumor progression via a collaborative mechanism involving the Mediator kinase module, SAGA complex, and SIX4. See related commentary by Stevens and Hatley, p. 2210.

title: CDK8 Inhibition Releases the Muscle Differentiation Block in Fusion-Driven Alveolar Rhabdomyosarcoma.

abstract: T-cell exhaustion limits durable antitumor responses and remains a barrier to adoptive cell therapies (ACT) in solid tumors. To identify regulators of T-cell persistence, we performed genome-wide CRISPR knockout screens in primary human CD8⁺ T cells expressing an NY-ESO-1-specific T-cell receptor and subjected them to repeated tumor cell rechallenge. These screens revealed enrichment of single-guide RNAs targeting components of Cullin-RING E3 ligases, particularly Cullin-5 (CRL5) assemblies comprising CUL5, RNF7, and ARIH2. Disruption of CRL5 genes in T cells preserved cytotoxic activity and enhanced cytokine production while sustaining effector-associated transcriptional programs and suppressing exhaustion-related signatures. Pharmacologic inhibition of cullin neddylation with the NEDD8-activating enzyme inhibitor MLN4924 recapitulated CRL5 loss and enhanced T-cell effector function in vitro. In a human melanoma xenograft model, ACT with CRL5-deficient T cells improved tumor control. Together, these findings identify CRL5 as a negative regulator of T-cell fitness and a potential therapeutic target to enhance ACT durability in solid tumors.

title: Cullin-5 RING E3 ligase limits CD8⁺ T-cell persistence and effector responses during chronic antigen stimulation.

abstract: mRNA-lipid nanoparticles (LNP) have emerged as a versatile modality, enabling diverse applications by changing encoded mRNA sequences. However, the conventional mRNA-LNP preparation process poses significant barriers to non-specialists because it requires specialized equipment and technical expertise. In this study, we aimed to report a simple post-encapsulation approach where mRNA is mixed with preformed empty LNP in solution to form mRNA-LNP for effective in vitro and in vivo delivery. Process optimization revealed that heating mRNA and empty LNP at 75°C and pH 4.0 achieved approximately 90% mRNA encapsulation while maintaining an LNP size of approximately 100 nm. The resulting post-encapsulated LNP were comprehensively compared with conventional LNP prepared via microfluidic mixing. Both LNP formulations exhibited over 90% cellular uptake and comparable concentration-dependent expression in vitro. The intravenous administration of post-encapsulated LNP in mice resulted in robust luciferase expression in the liver and spleen at 0.01 mg/kg, with no notable changes in serum chemistry at 1 and 3 mg/kg. However, the activity of the post-encapsulated LNP was slightly reduced compared with that of the conventional LNP. Sucrose density gradient centrifugation indicated that post-encapsulated mRNA-LNP formed heterogeneous populations with varying mRNA/lipid ratios, in contrast to conventional mRNA-LNP. These findings support a working hypothesis that this heterogeneity could contribute to the reduced in vivo activity. Our simple post-encapsulation method potentially could lower entry barriers for non-specialists in this field and accelerate RNA-LNP research through its compatibility with 96-well-format preparation.

abstract:
OBJECTIVE: Rare de novo variants in GNAO1 cause a severe neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by a heterogenous display of early onset epilepsy, movement abnormalities, and global developmental delay. More than 100 pathogenic variants in GNAO1 have been identified and categorized into four groups according to their protein features. Most pathogenic variants affect both GNAO1 isoforms, whereas approximately 20% of patients have a GNAO1A-specific variant. Response to therapy is notoriously variable, even among patients harboring the same variant. Here, we set out to model GNAO1A-related encephalopathy using human induced pluripotent stem cells (hiPSCs) from monozygotic twins carrying the Gαo1 K278del variant and uncovered-while taking advantage of the identical genomic setting-phenotypic features that further our understanding of the defects underlying the disorder.
METHODS: We generated hiPSCs expressing the c.832_834delAAG; p.K278del variant in GNAO1A obtained from monozygotic twins who both developed seizures 2 days after birth. For either twin, Gαo1 K278del and CRISPR-Cas9-repaired isogenic control hiPSC lines were differentiated into neural progenitor cells (NPCs) and subsequently into cortical neurons. Variant-specific transcriptomic, morphological, and electrophysiological characteristics were analyzed.
RESULTS: Gαo1 K278del mutated hiPSC-derived NPCs showed disorganized neural rosette structures and revealed an altered transcriptome. In cortical neurons, the Gαo1 K278del variant caused a reduction in the size and complexity of dendrites that was accompanied by an increase in pre- and postsynaptic puncta. Multielectrode array (MEA) recordings revealed an abnormal cortical neuron bursting activity pattern with fewer bursts and more spikes per burst. The antiepileptic drug levetiracetam reduced the spike frequency and the number of spikes per burst in cortical neurons from both patients.
SIGNIFICANCE: The developed GNAO1A hiPSC-derived in vitro model uncovered key structural and functional features of GNAO1-related encephalopathy. The comparable in vitro phenotypes in neurons from both twins underscore the utility of hiPSC-derived models to investigate molecular mechanisms underlying GNAO1-related encephalopathy as well as effects of therapeutic intervention.

title: Human induced pluripotent stem cell-derived cortical neurons from monozygotic twins with the Gαo1 K278del mutation reveal disease mechanisms relevant to GNAO1-related encephalopathy.

abstract: Systemic nucleic acid delivery to hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells (HSPCs) remains a major barrier to in vivo gene therapy due to hepatic sequestration of lipid nanoparticles (LNPs). Here, we report a scalable, ligand-free HSPC-tropic LNP enabling efficient mRNA delivery to human HSPCs in vivo without conditioning. In humanized NBSGW mice, the LNP preferentially delivered mRNA to human HSPCs and early myeloid progenitors, with limited delivery to lymphoid and non-hematopoietic cells. Single-cell transcriptomic and multiomic analyses revealed no broad transcriptional perturbation associated with delivery. Compared with the SM-102 LNP, the HSPC-tropic LNP achieved greater mRNA delivery to human HSPCs, while exhibiting substantially reduced hepatic delivery. The LNP also enabled functional delivery of Cas9 mRNA and β2M-targeting sgRNA to human CD34+ HSPCs, resulting in efficient gene editing and reduced β2M expression. These findings establish a ligand-free platform for functional RNA delivery and genome engineering in human HSPCs.

abstract: Alternative lengthening of telomeres (ALT) is a telomerase-independent telomere maintenance mechanism that supports the growth of approximately 5-10% of human tumors and represents an attractive but insufficiently explored therapeutic target. CRISPR-based functional genomics has emerged as a powerful approach to systematically interrogate ALT biology and identify genetic dependencies associated with the ALT state. In this Review, we discuss the CRISPR-based strategies applied to ALT, including hypothesis-driven targeted loss-of-function screens, phenotype-driven optical screens, in silico mining of large-scale dependency datasets, and genome-wide screens in ALT-adjacent states. Across these approaches, recurrent dependencies converge on pathways mediating replication stress buffering, DNA repair, and telomere maintenance, including FANCM, SMARCAL1, and SUB1. Collectively, these findings support a model in which ALT-positive cells rely not on a unique ALT-specific factor, but rather on stress-buffering mechanisms that prevent chronic telomeric dysfunction from triggering replication catastrophe and cell death, highlighting these pathways as promising candidates for further therapeutic investigation.

title: CRISPR-based interrogation of alternative lengthening of telomeres: mapping dependencies, stress-buffering pathways, and therapeutic vulnerabilities.

abstract: Recent breakthroughs in pig-to-human xenotransplantation have successfully prevented hyperacute rejection of kidney, heart, liver and lung xenografts, marking a milestone long considered a critical barrier. However, these major advances also brought new challenges into focus, as immune-mediated graft injuries including antibody-mediated rejection, T cell-mediated rejection and innate immune activation have been observed in most xenotransplantation procedures to date. Detection and management of these injuries remain a critical bottleneck, as conventional histopathology and standard clinical monitoring lack the sensitivity required to identify subclinical injury early enough to guide timely intervention. This diagnostic gap underscores an urgent need for the development of advanced, multimodal precision diagnostic frameworks to enhance immune surveillance, which will be essential for standardizing clinical protocols and enabling pathogenesis-driven therapeutic intervention. This approach will inform both immunosuppressive regimens and future gene editing strategies aimed at engineering rejection-resistant porcine organs, ultimately prolonging graft survival. Broad adoption of such an integrative strategy will be essential to transition xenotransplantation from an experimental intervention into a safe, scalable and patient-centred clinical therapy. In this Review, we synthesize recent progress in xenotransplantation and position multimodal precision diagnostics as a pivotal strategy to address the remaining immunological and clinical barriers to widespread clinical implementation.

abstract: This review examines the expanding role of PARP inhibitors in cancer therapy, moving beyond the traditional model of single-strand break repair inhibition and BRCA-dependent synthetic lethality. We highlight emerging evidence that PARP inhibitors induce cytotoxicity through replication-associated DNA damage, including defects in Okazaki fragment maturation and replication gap accumulation. By integrating recent mechanistic insights with findings from CRISPR-based screens, we outline how disruptions in DNA replication and repair pathways define a broader BRCAness phenotype. We further emphasize the clinical implications of these discoveries, including novel combination strategies that extend the therapeutic applicability of PARP inhibitors beyond prevailing treatment regimens.

title: Widening the BRCAness therapeutic window for its synthetic lethality effects with PARP inhibitors.

abstract: Like many other immune cell types, natural killer (NK) cells exhibit impaired functionality in people with HIV (PWH), limiting their ability to efficiently target and eliminate HIV-infected cells and contributing to the persistence of the HIV reservoir. Recently, adoptive NK cell therapy using activated or engineered NK cells has emerged as a promising immunotherapeutic strategy for cancer; however, its application to HIV remains in the early stages of development. NK cells primarily rely on interleukin-15 (IL-15) signaling for their development, survival, and maintenance, and dysregulated IL-15 signaling has been reported in PWH. We hypothesized that simultaneous enhancement of IL-15 and IL-15 receptor alpha (IL-15Rα) expression would improve NK cell effector function and promote clearance of HIV reservoir. Utilizing dCas9-VPR-mediated multiplex CRISPR activation (CRISPRa), we successfully upregulated both IL-15 and IL-15Rα expression in the same primary NK cells without altering the genomic sequence. CRISPRa-treated NK cells displayed increased IL-15 and IL-15Rα transcript levels, as measured by RT-qPCR and significantly elevated surface expression of IL-15Rα, as determined by flow cytometry. Enhanced IL-15/IL-15Rα expression increased NK cell metabolic activity and cytotoxicity against target K562 cells, a chronic myelogenous leukemia cell line, indicating improved effector function. Furthermore, in co-culture experiments using an HIV-positive T-cell line, IL-15/IL-15Rα-CRISPRa-treated NK cells demonstrated enhanced target cell elimination and increased secretion of IFN-γ. Together, these findings provide a proof of concept that multiplex CRISPRa can be used to enhance NK cell function, representing a novel strategy to improve persistence and therapeutic efficacy in HIV and other disease settings.

abstract: Deciphering cancer metabolic reprogramming mechanisms can identify new targets to potentiate EZH2 inhibitor efficacy. Using an in vivo genome-wide CRISPR loss-of-function screen in a CRC mouse model, we pinpointed IDO1 as a key mediator of EZH2 inhibitor resistance. EZH2 blockade remodeled CRC cell metabolism by upregulating IDO1 protein and hyperactivating the tryptophan-kynurenine pathway. Both genetic and pharmacological inhibition of IDO1 suppressed tumor growth and rescued EZH2 inhibitor resistance in vitro and in vivo. Mechanistically, EZH2 directly binds and methylates IDO1. Methylation of IDO1 facilitates IDO1 ubiquitination and subsequent degradation. Accordingly, EZH2 inhibition stabilizes IDO1, augments tryptophan-kynurenine metabolic flux, and ultimately confers therapeutic resistance. In summary, our study identifies IDO1 as a non-histone substrate of EZH2 methyltransferase activity and validates that disrupting IDO1-mediated tryptophan metabolism is a viable strategy to overcome EZH2 targeted therapy resistance in cancers.

abstract: Myeloid cells regulate immune exclusion, T-cell dysfunction, angiogenesis, stromal remodeling, and resistance to immune checkpoint blockade in solid tumors. Pharmacological development has moved from nonspecific depletion toward recruitment or survival blockade, intracellular state reprogramming, restoration of antigen presentation, and tumor-selective phagocytosis. Clinical experience nevertheless shows a recurrent gap between biological activity and attributable therapeutic immune conversion. We introduce the Myeloid Immune Conversion Audit Trail (MICAT), a fixed four-level extension of the pharmacological audit trail that grades intratumoral target engagement, conversion of the intended myeloid state, propagation through the immune ecosystem, and randomized clinical attribution. Each level is scored as not demonstrated, partial, or demonstrated. Applying MICAT across representative trials shows that most programs stop at systemic pharmacodynamics or partial lineage effects; few establish ecosystem propagation, and none yet completes the entire causal chain for an immunological switch in a solid-tumor carcinoma. The analysis identifies compensation and redundancy as the central biological obstacle: CCR2 blockade can recruit CXCR2-positive neutrophils, CSF1R inhibition can spare resistant SPP1-high macrophages, and CD40 or PI3Kγ activation can induce interferon-linked PD-L1 feedback. We therefore prioritize lineage-resolved paired tissue, preservation of cDC1 and cDC2 function, absolute cell quantification, orthogonal functional and spatial readouts, and randomized component-controlled trials. Disease context is decisive: tenosynovial giant-cell tumor establishes CSF1R dependence without proving immune conversion; macrophage-rich triple-negative breast cancer is a rational PI3Kγ test-bed; pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma permits sequence-aware CD40 and stromal studies; and microsatellite-stable colorectal cancer is a stringent failure benchmark. CAR-macrophages, in vivo mRNA/lipid-nanoparticle reprogramming, myeloid engagers, and artificial-intelligence-assisted spatial scoring are mapped to the same evidence requirements. MICAT is intended as a reproducible tool for pharmacological go/no-go decisions rather than a claim that target modulation alone constitutes therapeutic immune conversion.

abstract: Although poly(ADP-ribose) polymerase inhibitors (PARPi) show promise for treating homologous recombination-deficient cancers, the observed PARPi hypersensitivity in additional genetic contexts expands their potential use in precision oncology. Yet, the DNA lesions driving PARPi-induced cytotoxicity remain poorly defined. Here we uncover distinct replication-fork lesions in specific genomic regions as key determinants of PARPi cytotoxicity. Using CRISPR screens, we identify that loss of replication-coupled cohesin acetyltransferase ESCO2 confers PARPi hypersensitivity independently of homologous recombination deficiency. Quantitative single-molecule imaging reveals that ESCO2 loss promotes accumulation of G-quadruplex (G4) DNA structures at a subset of replication-associated sites, associated with PARP1 activation and engagement of fork protection factor TIMELESS to mitigate G4-induced stress. Notably, these G4 lesions localize to fragile pericentromeric regions and engage the G4 helicase DDX11. PARP inhibition disrupts this protective G4-processing response by preventing PARP1-dependent engagement of TIMELESS and DDX11, leading to G4 accumulation, DNA damage and chromosomal instability. Together, our findings define the G4-PARP1-TIMELESS-DDX11 axis as a critical safeguard of replication fork stability at hard-to-replicate loci and reveal ESCO2 as a therapeutic target for promoting synthetic lethality in PARPi-treated cancers.

abstract: Lung cancer is the leading cause of cancer-related deaths worldwide, and radiotherapy, a commonly used treatment for lung cancer, is associated with a variety of complications while treating cancer, among which radiotherapy-induced pneumonia is a common complication whose underlying mechanism remains unclear and requires further investigation. To address this, cell lines with ATMLP overexpression and knockdown were created using gene editing techniques, and Western blot, immunofluorescence and trans-well co-culture were used to explore the role of mitochondria-derived vesicles (MDVs) in mediating radiotherapy-induced inflammation, as well as the effects of ATMLP, DRP-1 and PGAM5 on MDVs. Ionizing radiation promoted the expression of ATMLP and the release of ATMLP-mediated MDVs. Up-regulation of ATMLP expression led to increased levels of PGAM5 and activation of phosphorylation at the Ser616 site of DRP-1. The increased number of MDVs further promoted macrophage polarization toward the M1 phenotype. Overall, ionizing radiation induces ATMLP expression, which enhances MDVs release through the PGAM5/DRP-1 axis. This process leads to macrophage polarization toward the M1 phenotype, contributing to the inflammatory response.

abstract: PhrS (Pseudomonas Hfq-binding RNA S) is a dual-function small RNA of Pseudomonas aeruginosa. The base-pairing small regulatory RNA PhrS-R positively regulates pyocyanin biosynthesis. PhrS-R stimulates the production of the Pseudomonas quinolone signal (PQS) by indirectly activating the translation of pqsR mRNA, encoding the quorum sensing regulator PqsR (MvfR), and by inhibiting the synthesis of the anthranilate degradation regulator AntR. Furthermore, PhrS-R was shown to promote biofilm formation, swarming motility and CRISPR-Cas immunity. In addition, PhrS encodes a 37 amino acid long and conserved small protein (PhrS-P), the function of which remained unknown. Here, we provide evidence that PhrS-P is an inner membrane protein which does not contribute to the known physiological roles of its RNA counterpart. RNA-Seq-based transcriptome analyses revealed that multiple aminoglycoside resistance genes, including those of the AmgR regulon, are differentially expressed depending on PhrS-P. AmgR is the response regulator of the AmgRS two-component system (TCS), which affects aminoglycoside and zinc resistance in P. aeruginosa. A PhrS-P-deficient mutant strain exhibited reduced fitness when exposed to sub-inhibitory concentrations of the aminoglycosides tobramycin and amikacin as well as zinc. Based on our findings, we present a working model wherein PhrS-P positively regulates the AmgRS TCS activity through an unknown mechanism, leading to increased bacterial fitness in the presence of aminoglycosides.

abstract: In this editorial, I summarize recent progress on phage-encoded anti-defence against bacterial anti-phage systems (APS). Computational approaches based on structural predictions of co-folding bacterial and phage proteins identified many new PAD sponge proteins. New anti-CRISPR-Cas systems were characterized that destroy cas12a mRNA, inactivate Cas12a by acetylation, engage the seed region of the crRNA, or prevent Cas3 from cleaving DNA. The phage defence protein Gad1 forms an octamer web that wraps around the complex of the Gabija APS. Tad1 and 2 are phage sponge proteins that sequester signalling nucleotides of the Thoeris APS. Tad3 to 7 interact directly with the ThsB sensor and Tad8 with the ThsA effector of the Thoeris APS. Phage sponge proteins were also described inactivating the CBASS and Pycsar APS. Still other phages use phosphodiesterases that cleave cyclic nucleotide signals to inactivate APS. Many bacterial APS effectors are NADase, destroying the essential metabolite NAD+. Phages evolved enzymes that resynthesize NAD+ from its cleavage products or proteins directly inactivating the NADase. Many phages degrade the bacterial genome which creates signals activating the Metis or the Kongming APS. Phages counteracted these APS by suppressing pathways leading to the creation of particular mononucleotides degradation products detected by these APS. Several APS cleave specific tRNA, phages responded by mutating cleavage sites in tRNA (anti-PARIS) or increasing tRNA expression to compensate for their destruction (anti-Septu). Phages counteract toxin-antitoxin APS by evolving their own antitoxin or by blocking the toxin protein. Researchers described cases where phages escaped detection by mutating phage proteins detected by bacterial sensors. Against the stringent response phages responded by destroying alarmones or inactivating enzymes producing these stress signals. The arms race between bacteria and phages can involve complicated layers of defence and anti-defences and both bacteria and phages encode multiple defence systems.

abstract: In an extended series of studies, we have shown that Heat shock protein 90 (Hsp90) has a novel role in regulating opioid signal transduction and antinociception in both the brain and spinal cord. Inhibition in the spinal cord enhances opioid antinociception, which led to the finding that an isoform-selective Hsp90 inhibitor could improve opioid therapy, both enhancing pain relief and reducing side effects. However, the signaling mechanisms for this activity are still not fully understood. We thus identified Dual Specificity Phosphatase 15 (DUSP15) from an earlier proteomic study as a protein enhanced in the spinal cord after Hsp90 inhibition. Using male and female CD-1 mice, we confirmed that DUSP15 is upregulated in the dorsal horn of the spinal cord after Hsp90 inhibitor (17-AAG) treatment. Using CRISPR and siRNA-mediated knockdown, we showed that DUSP15 was necessary for the enhanced morphine antinociception after Hsp90 inhibitor treatment in both the tail flick and post-surgical paw incision pain models. Using immunohistochemistry (IHC) and behavioral tools, we placed DUSP15 upstream of both ERK MAPK and AMPK in the opioid signaling cascade. We then used IHC to demonstrate that DUSP15 upregulation occurs at least in part in CGRP neurons, and using cell-selective CRISPR, showed that DUSP15 in CGRP neurons is necessary for the enhanced antinociception observed with spinal Hsp90 inhibitor treatment. Together these studies further expand the known mechanisms by which Hsp90 regulates opioid signal transduction and pain relief and provide basic science insight into a potential strategy to improve opioid therapy using Hsp90 inhibitors.

abstract: Cellular and gene-based therapies are being investigated as potential strategies to address current treatment limitations in breast cancer. Adoptive cell therapies, such as CAR-T, TCR-T, TILs and NK cell-based therapies, are currently under investigation for their ability to selectively target tumor-associated antigens. Also, CRISPR/Cas9-mediated genome editing is being investigated as a strategy to enhance T cell persistence, improve tumor infiltration, and increase resistance to immunosuppressive signaling. Although cellular and gene-based therapies have transformed the treatment of hematologic malignancies, their application in breast cancer remains limited by antigen heterogeneity, immune exclusion, and the immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment. Among current approaches, TIL-based therapies have provided some of the clearest evidence of clinical activity selected patients, whereas the clinical efficacy of CAR-T and gene-editing strategies as standalone interventions remains uncertain. Future progress may depend on biomarker-guided, combinatorial approaches rather than single-modality therapies. This review examines the current applications, clinical evidence, and limitations of these approaches in breast cancer.

abstract:
BACKGROUND: Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD) is an X-linked recessive disorder characterized by progressive muscle weakness and muscle wasting. Exon skipping therapies have been approved as part of the therapeutic arsenal for DMD, however, there is contrasting evidence regarding their clinical benefits. The aim of this study was to determine the efficacy and safety of exon skipping therapies for DMD.
METHOD: ology: A systematic review was conducted in three databases including PubMed, ClinicalTrials.gov, and Cochrane-Ovid, based on the following question using PICO strategy: What is the efficacy of exon skipping therapies for DMD? Search was limited to randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and Open Label RCTs with reported results, published between January 2016 and December 2024, involving patients with DMD treated with any of the existing exon-skipping therapies, reporting efficacy measured by primary clinical and secondary molecular outcomes. Secondary safety outcomes were also registered. Eligible studies were assessed for risk of bias. A descriptive analysis was performed in subgroups according to variants amenable to exon 45, 51, or 53 skipping.
RESULTS: A total of nine studies were left after the final filters were applied. Studies were conducted across centers in seven different countries. Four studies used viltolarsen (exon 53), three eteplirsen (exon 51), and two golodirsen (exon 53). Trial length was heterogeneous with an average length of 119.6 weeks (±78.5). Overall, studies with exon skipping medications reported improvement in the clinical outcomes including the 6-minute walking test, time to stand and the North Star Ambulatory Assessment. Biological measurements showed an increase in dystrophin expression and exon skipping percentage. Long term follow up evidenced stabilization of both clinical and molecular outcomes in DMD patients, compared to age and treatment-matched controls.
CONCLUSION: Exon skipping therapies have evidenced improved clinical and molecular outcomes. Longer follow-up extension studies are needed to further elucidate their effect in comparison to age-matched controls.

abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Hereditary angioedema (HAE) is a rare disorder with a prevalence of approximately 1 in 50,000. Management of HAE brings challenges, including the frequency of delivery of the medication, routes of medication delivery, cost of treatment and a significant impact on quality of life for patients with HAE. Donidalorsen is the newest FDA-approved long-term prophylaxis medication for HAE that offers substantial benefits over its competitors.
AREAS COVERED: A search of the current literature on donidalorsen was conducted using the PubMed and Cochrane libraries. In this review, we discuss the mechanism and clinical efficacy of donidalorsen. We also explore the comparison between donidalorsen and other agents on the market for the long-term prophylaxis of HAE. The safety profile of donidalorsen as well as a discussion on the economic impact of donidalorsen is also reviewed.
EXPERT OPINION: Donidalorsen offers a promising option for treatment of HAE, with substantial attack reduction, infrequent dosing, and improved quality of life. Continued long-term safety data are needed, but donidalorsen may become a leading prophylactic option for HAE worldwide.

abstract: Ovarian cancer remains one of the most lethal gynecological malignancies, largely due to late diagnosis and the frequent development of resistance to platinum-based chemotherapy and taxanes. Increasing evidence implicates microRNAs as key regulators of drug response through their control of DNA damage response and repair, apoptosis, epithelial-mesenchymal transition, and therapy-induced cellular senescence. Senescence is a double-edged process characterized by irreversible cell-cycle arrest and the secretion of pro-inflammatory factors collectively known as the senescence-associated secretory phenotype, which may suppress tumor growth but also promote chemoresistance and disease recurrence. This review summarizes current evidence on microRNA (miRNA)-mediated regulation of therapy-induced cellular senescence and its role in drug resistance in ovarian cancer. We integrate data from mechanistic studies, preclinical models, and clinical observations, focusing on senescence-associated miRNAs and their regulatory networks. miRNAs including miR-34a, miR-21, miR-146a, miR-200c, miR-506, and miR-433 regulate key senescence pathways, notably p53/p21 and p16-RB signaling, and modulate the senescence-associated secretory phenotype by controlling inflammatory mediators, extracellular matrix remodeling, and angiogenic factors. Several of these miRNAs are also associated with resistance to platinum-based chemotherapy, taxanes, poly ADP-ribose polymerase (PARP) inhibitors, and immunotherapies through effects on PI3K/AKT and Hippo signaling pathways, as well as DNA repair mechanisms. Emerging therapeutic strategies aim to modulate or eliminate senescent cells using miRNA mimics, inhibitors, or gene-editing approaches, including nanoparticle-based delivery systems. Although preclinical studies suggest that these approaches may restore chemosensitivity, clinical translation remains limited by delivery challenges, off-target effects, and the context-dependent role of senescence. Targeting miRNA-senescence regulatory axes may represent a strategy for addressing drug resistance in ovarian cancer and warrants further investigation as part of combination treatment strategies.

abstract: Nonalcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) is globally the leading cause of liver disease and frequently progresses to cirrhosis and liver cancer. The identification of effective drugs is the main unmet clinical need. Changes in liver histones methylation accompanies the development and progression of NAFLD. Our preliminary data demonstrate that inactivation of the methyltransferases SUV420H1/2 in hepatocytes protects mice against NAFLD. In this project we propose to examine the relevance of these findings by evaluating the impact of genetic deletion of hepatic SUV420H1/2 in mice fed a steatogenic diet. To further evaluate the potential for clinical translation of these results, we will next 1) evaluate the expression of SUV420H1/2 in human liver transcriptomic data and 2) analyze the impact of genetic variations on disease outcomes in population-based cohorts; 3) test an innovative therapeutic approach based on hepatocyte-targeted antisense oligonucleotides downregulating SUV420H1/2 in human liver organoids/assembloids.

description:
Nonalcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD), the leading cause of liver damage worldwide, is characterized by liver fat accumulation and association with insulin resistance, and frequently progresses to steatohepatitis (NASH), ultimately leading to cirrhosis and liver cancer.

NAFLD/NASH is becoming globally a leading cause of liver-related morbidity and mortality and by altering liver function contributes more widely to the burden of cardiometabolic, renal and neoplastic diseases. In the presence of concomitant hepatotoxic factors such as in particular atrisk alcohol intake and some medications (defined in this case as metabolic dysfunction associated fatty liver disease or MAFLD) synergizes with them representing a major driver of liver disease progression. However, for those with advanced disease or who cannot successfully change their diet and lifestyle, no effective treatment is yet available to prevent or treat this condition, which is therefore projected to become a major public health threat in the next decade. Although understanding the mechanisms of NAFLD development and progression is essential for its prevention/treatment, molecular players involved in its progression are poorly defined. Recently, an epigenetic component is recognized in this disorder and the histone methyltransferases SUV420H1/2 are promising candidates for this function. Multiple evidences connect lipid and iron metabolism in the hepatocyte: 1) Genome Wide Association Studies (GWAS) in human populations showed an overlap of loci affecting iron and lipid metabolism, and excess iron in hepatocytes favors dyslipidemia and NAFLD; 2) upregulation of the liver hormone hepcidin, under the control by the BMP-SMAD pathway, is protective against NAFLD-NASH. Interestingly, a GWAS performed in mouse strains kept on high-iron diet identified a shared association between liver iron and triglyceride levels at a region of chromosome 7 encompassing the histone methyltransferase Suv420h2. Our preliminary data show that mice with Suv420h inactivation in adipose tissue are resistant to diet-induced liver steatosis due to increased PPAR signaling. Since mice with liver BMP-SMAD pathway upregulation showed Suv420h downregulation, we hypothesize that the protective effect of increased hepatocyte BMP-SMAD signaling on NAFLD development is due to Suv420h. In agreement, Suv420h inactivation in hepatocytes counteracts diet-induced NAFLD, as highlighted by our preliminary results.

The present study is part of the RF project (Ricerca Finalizzata) - Project code: RF-2021-12373889 funded by the grant call of the Ministery of Health (2020-2021). In the attached project we proposed 3 different aims:

* To characterize the disease progression in Suv420h1/2-liver conditional KO mice and to identify
* To examine the impact of SUV420H1/2 genetic, epigenetic and transcriptional variability on clinical outcomes for the identification of novel biomarkers of NAFLD-NASH.
* To propose and test an innovative therapeutic approach based on hepatocyte-targeted antisense oligonucleotides (ASOs) against Suv420h1/2 in preclinical models in mice and in human liver organoids and assembloids. The present clinical study protocol will focus on the clinical aspects and procedures that will regard an intervention on data and sample of clinical cohorts. Further details about the analyses conducted in animal models, for which a specific Authorization has been requested, can be found in the attached project.

outcomes.description:
The primary aim is the identification of biological pathways differentially ex- pressed in NAFLD individuals.

Considering the large number of individuals with severe liver disease in the NAFLD PERSPECTIVE and MAFALDA cohorts (n= 500) and the large size of UKBB population-based cohort (n=350,000 for common variants and n=200,000 for rare variants), for variants with a minor allele frequency (MAF) \>0.01, we estimated that the study has a power \>80% to detect six-fold difference in the risk of severe NAFLD in the PERSPECTIVE/MAFALDA, a 1.8% difference in the NAFLD prevalence (UK Biobank), and 4.4% difference in the liver fat content as measured by PDFF (UK Biobank) between carriers and non-carriers (Aim A and B).

outcomes.description:
The identification of a correlation between genotype influencing the SUV420H1/2 pathway and NAFLD phenotype.

Reduction of intracellular fat accumulation, collagen accumulation and inflammation in terms of TNFalpha mRNA expression levels.

abstract:
BACKGROUND: mRNA-based vaccines are emerging as a promising platform for cancer immunotherapy, including in hematologic malignancies. Current vaccine development has largely focused on antigen selection, mRNA engineering, lipid nanoparticle (LNP) formulation, and combination with established immunotherapies. However, increasing evidence indicates that the cellular and tissue distribution of antigen expression may critically influence the quality and durability of the immune response. In this context, the term "cellular pharmacology" refers to the principle that the pharmacodynamic effect of an mRNA vaccine is shaped not only by the encoded antigen and formulation but also by the cell types in which antigen expression occurs.
OBJECTIVES: Here, we propose a cellular pharmacology framework for mRNA vaccines in hematologic malignancies, moving beyond the traditional dendritic-cell-centric model and considering antigen expression as a determinant of immune activation, tolerance, and T-cell exhaustion.
DISCUSSION: Three functionally distinct compartments can be considered: professional antigen-presenting cells, immunogenic non-immune cells at the injection site, and tolerogenic tissues, particularly hepatocytes. This tripartite model is intended as a simplified functional framework rather than a complete anatomical or cellular classification. While antigen expression in dendritic cells and other antigen-presenting cells supports effective T-cell priming, antigen production by skeletal myocytes and stromal cells may provide a sustained source of antigen for uptake and cross-presentation. Importantly, myocytes should not be regarded as professional antigen-presenting cells, but rather as potential antigen-producing cells whose antigens can be presented by professional APCs. Conversely, hepatic antigen expression may promote peripheral tolerance and impair antitumor CD8+ T-cell responses. Recent preclinical evidence indicates that microRNA-guided hepatocyte detargeting may enhance vaccine-induced immunity and tumor control in experimental models, although its clinical relevance in hematologic malignancies remains to be established. This concept may be particularly relevant in hematologic malignancies, characterized by disseminated disease, chronic antigen exposure, immune dysfunction, and frequent treatment-related organ vulnerability. We discuss how cellular targeting could be incorporated into mRNA vaccine strategies for lymphomas, acute leukemias, chronic lymphocytic leukemia, and multiple myeloma, as well as into combination approaches with CAR-T cells, bispecific antibodies, and immune checkpoint inhibitors.
CONCLUSIONS: The therapeutic potential of mRNA vaccines in hematologic malignancies may depend not only on the antigen encoded but also on the cellular compartment in which it is expressed. Incorporating tissue biodistribution and cell-type specificity into vaccine design could represent a new strategy to improve immunogenicity while limiting tolerogenic signals and potentially reducing unwanted tissue exposure. At present, however, hepatocyte detargeting should be considered a promising and testable translational strategy rather than a clinically validated approach. Prospective clinical studies integrating biodistribution, immune correlates, and tissue-specific antigen expression will be essential to translate this cellular pharmacology concept into clinical practice.

abstract: Delivering mRNA to the lungs promises treatment of genetic, infectious and non-communicable lung diseases. Yet, conventional lipid nanoparticle formulations lack the stability needed to endure the harsh mechanical stress during nebulization. Additionally, once deposited in the respiratory tract, gene delivery systems may first have to overcome the mucus barrier, before actually transfecting the target cells. To overcome these challenges, we utilize lipid-polymer hybrid nanoparticles (LPH), merging the stability of pharmaceutical polymers with the transfection efficiency of cationic and ionizable lipids. LPH are produced in a robust microfluidic process, accomplish near-complete encapsulation efficiency, even after nebulization, and confer high transfection efficiency in A549 cells. To provide colloidal stability after aerosolization, we developed a coating strategy with hyaluronic acid (HA) and poly(vinyl alcohol) (PVA), ensuring ideal nebulization stability by steric shielding. This formulation showed good transfection efficiency of air-liquid interface grown Calu-3 cells, producing and covered by mucus. The potential of LPH to deliver mRNA to mammalian cells was first shown in primary human lung fibroblasts in vitro and could also be confirmed after intratracheal administration to mice in vivo. Together, these findings validate LPH as a versatile and aerosolizable mRNA delivery platform, overcoming the key technological and biological barriers in pulmonary gene delivery.
