title: Overcoming technological and biological barriers to pulmonary mRNA delivery with lipid-polymer hybrid nanoparticles.

abstract: Genome editing has been revolutionized by Clustered Regularly Interspaced Short Palindromic Repeats (CRISPR)-associated protein 9 (Cas9) technology. However, efficient intracellular delivery of Cas9 ribonucleoprotein (RNP) remains a major challenge, particularly in cells that are refractory to conventional transfection methods. Integrating viral vectors carry a risk of insertional mutagenesis, whereas physical methods such as electroporation are not well suited for in vivo or clinically relevant applications. Cell-penetrating peptides (CPPs) offer a promising alternative for direct RNP delivery, although their efficiency is often limited by endosomal entrapment and limited cytosolic release. In this study, we developed two recombinant CPP-fused Cas9 proteins, polyglutamate (PE)-trans-activator of transcription (TAT)-nuclear localization signal (NLS)-Cas9 (PETATCas9) and TAT-NLS-Cas9 (TATCas9), designed to improve solubility, membrane penetration, RNP complex formation, and nuclear targeting. PE tag in PETATCas9 was introduced to optimize charge balance and reduce nonspecific electrostatic interactions between TAT and guide RNA (gRNA), thereby enhancing RNP stability and delivery performance. Both recombinant proteins were expressed, purified, and assembled with gRNA into functional RNP complexes for delivery into SH-SY5Y neuroblastoma cells. The optimized CPP-Cas9 RNP system enabled efficient intracellular delivery and glucosylceramidase beta 1 (GBA1) gene editing in SH-SY5Y cells. These findings establish PETATCas9 as a scalable, transient, nonviral, and self-delivering RNP platform for CRISPR-based genome editing in cells that are refractory to conventional transfection methods.

abstract: Messenger RNA (mRNA)-based therapeutics hold great promise in preventing and treating various diseases. However, the instability and high immunogenicity of raw mRNA molecules, along with the inefficient delivery vectors, strictly limited the proteins translation and therapeutic applications. In this work, we successfully engineered a folded structural mRNA for enhancing its stability by leveraging a magnesium ion (Mg2+)-mediated charge neutralization and structural compression strategy. Further, a functionalized highly branched poly(β-amino ester)s (HPAEs) was utilized to efficiently deliver the folded mRNA, achieving specifically targeting to the spleen. Notably, compared with polyplexes containing non-folded mRNA, the optimal folded mRNA-based polyplexes exhibited stronger mRNA encapsulation, smaller size, and a more homogeneous morphology; ultimately, demonstrated higher mRNA transfection efficiency up to 85.4% across five different cell types, maintaining high cell viability. Mechanistic studies demonstrated that Mg2+-mediated mRNA folding strategy dramatically enhanced the folded mRNA-formulated polyplexes cellular uptake and endosomal escape. Encouragingly, when administered systemically, the representative folded mRNA-based polyplexes demonstrated robust protein expression, yielding 3-fold enhancement in spleen, compared to the unfolded mRNA-based nanoparticles, showing superior biosafety in vivo. Collectively, the work establishes a new class of the folded structure mRNA polymer delivery system, and provides a foundation for the next generation of RNA-based therapeutic drugs for spleen-related diseases.

abstract:
This study is researching an experimental drug called ALN-CIDEB, also referred to as "study drug". The study is focused on participants with metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) (Part A) and metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH) (Part B). MASLD and MASH are long-lasting liver conditions caused by having too much fat in the liver.

The aim of the study is to see how safe and tolerable the study drug is.

The study is looking at several other research questions, including:

* What side effects may happen from taking the study drug
* How the study drug works to change liver fat content
* How much study drug and study drug metabolites (byproducts of the body breaking down the study drug) are in the blood at different times

abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Peripheral artery disease (PAD) reduces tissue perfusion and causes ischemia, conditions in which hypoxia-responsive pathways have an important adaptive role. Hypoxia- inducible factor 1-alpha (HIF-1α), a central regulator of this response, is tightly controlled by prolyl hydroxylase domain protein 2 (PHD2), encoded by EGLN1. Here, we used an RNA-targeting CRISPR-Cas13d system to downregulate EGLN1 in human umbilical vein endothelial cells (HUVECs) under normoxia and hypoxia.
METHODS: A PHD2-knockdown (PHD2-KD) HUVEC line was generated by lentiviral delivery of an EGLN1-targeting RNA guide, alongside non-transduced (CTRL) and non-targeting gRNA (NTG) control lines. Molecular and functional assays assessed hypoxia-related signaling, metabolic activity, migration, and sprouting responses under normoxia and hypoxia.
RESULTS: Western blotting confirmed a marked reduction in PHD2 protein abundance in PHD2-KD cells relative to both CTRL and NTG cells. PHD2-KD HUVECs exhibited increased VEGFA transcript levels (6.5-fold under normoxia and 5.3-fold under hypoxia) and secreted VEGF concentrations (6.6-fold and 9.4-fold, respectively), together with early increases in HIF1A transcript and HIF-1α protein levels and lower TNF-α concentrations. Functional assays showed higher metabolic activity, faster wound closure (2.0-fold under normoxia and 2.2-fold under hypoxia), and enhanced sprouting, with up to 7.2-fold more sprouts per bead and sprouts up to 2.7-fold longer than those formed by CTRL.
DISCUSSION: CRISPR-Cas13d-mediated EGLN1 targeting reduced PHD2 protein abundance and was associated with higher endothelial metabolic activity, faster wound closure, enhanced sprouting behavior, and lower TNF-α secretion.
CONCLUSION: CRISPR-Cas13d-mediated downregulation of EGLN1/PHD2 was associated with increased pro-angiogenic signaling and improved angiogenesis-related endothelial responses in vitro, supporting RNA-targeting strategies to modulate hypoxia-responsive pathways.

abstract: Chimeric antigen receptor (CAR)-T cell therapy has transformed the treatment of haematological malignancies, but its efficacy remains limited by multiple negative regulatory mechanisms intrinsic to T cells1-4. Here we perform a high-throughput in vivo CAR-T double-knockout (DKO) CRISPR screen, and identify multiple DKO gene pairs that are both effective and synergistic. The top pair, NR4A1-SOCS3 DKO, has multiple favourable immunological features. Whole-transcriptome profiling and in vivo single-cell RNA sequencing reveal that NR4A1-SOCS3 DKO specifically upregulates metabolic pathways in CAR-T cells, which show significantly higher metabolic fitness and mitochondrial activity. NR4A1-SOCS3 DKO CAR-T cells and T cells exhibit exceptionally potent antitumour efficacy and long-term tumour control across different tumour models without compromising safety features. NR4A1-SOCS3 DKO outperforms several benchmark single-gene and dual-gene modifications in T cells and CAR-T cells5-9. These data demonstrate high-throughput in vivo CAR-T DKO screening for rapid discovery of combination targets, and establish NR4A1-SOCS3 as a promising pair of intracellular checkpoints to engineer high-performance CAR-T therapies against cancer.

title: In vivo CAR-T double knockout screen maps synergistic antitumour gene pairs.

abstract: The rising global burden of depression necessitates novel mechanistic insights and therapeutic targets. Voltage-gated sodium channel β2-subunit (Navβ2, coded by SCN2B) has been implicated in neuropsychiatric disorders, yet its role in depression remains unexplored. Here, we identify SCN2B as a previously unrecognized driver of depression-like pathophysiology. Using SCN2B-overexpressing (SCN2B-OV) mice across different ages (1, 12, and 20 months) and CRISPR- engineered Navβ2V173A,V175K mice with selective reduction of the Navβ2 intracellular domain (NICD), we combined behavioral phenotyping, electrophysiology, neurotransmitter profiling, and molecular analyses, with chronic unpredictable mild stress (CUMS) as an environmental challenge. SCN2B-OV mice exhibited accelerated depression-like phenotypes, including anhedonia (sucrose preference 52.42% reduction, P<0.05), behavioral despair (forced swim test immobility 67.42% increase, P<0.05), and cognitive deficits (Y-maze alternation 50.90% reduction, P<0.05), independent of natural aging. Electrophysiologically, SCN2B overexpression induced a striking prefrontal-hippocampal imbalance: prefrontal cortex (PFC) became hyperexcitable (glutamate release increased by 64.7%; sEPSC amplitude increased 2.05-fold, P<0.05), whereas the hippocampus showed synaptic suppression (GABA release reduced by 32.65%; sIPSC frequency reduced by 66.67%, P<0.05). Mechanistically, SCN2B overexpression suppressed BDNF/TrkB/PI3K/AKT signaling axis (BDNF reduced by 53.17%; p-TrkB reduced by 63.62%, P<0.05), accompanied by decreased synaptic proteins (PSD95 43.45%, synapsin I 40.31%, P<0.05). Remarkably, NICD-reduced Navβ2V173A,V175K mice were fully resistant to CUMS-induced behavioral and neurotransmitter deficits, establishing NICD as a critical mediator of stress vulnerability. Collectively, these findings unravel a causal pathway in which SCN2B overexpression drives NICD-dependent suppression of BDNF signaling, leading to region-specific excitatory/inhibitory imbalance, synaptic disintegration, and depression-like phenotypes. Targeting Navβ2 proteolysis to block NICD generation may thus represent a novel therapeutic strategy for mood disorders.

title: SCN2B Drives Depression-like Phenotypes in Mice by Suppressing BDNF Signaling via Its Intracellular Domain NICD.

abstract: Rubella virus (RuV) causes rubella and, when acquired during pregnancy, congenital rubella syndrome1. Despite its clinical significance, the cellular entry mechanism of RuV remains poorly characterized, owing to limited identification of host receptors2, which hinders pathogenesis research and therapeutic development. Here, using proximity biotin labelling-based proteomics coupled with CRISPR-Cas9 validation, we identify nectin-4 as a functional RuV entry receptor. Ectopic expression of nectin-4 conferred susceptibility to RuV in non-permissive cells, whereas blocking or genetic ablation of nectin-4 reduced infection, results that demonstrate that nectin-4 is a major entry factor. Mechanistically, nectin-4 directly interacts with the RuV envelope glycoprotein heterodimer and facilitates receptor-mediated endocytosis following initial calcium-dependent viral attachment to cellular lipids. In polarized airway epithelial models, nectin-4 mediates basolateral entry of RuV and supports apical progeny release, a finding that provides a molecular mechanism for respiratory transmission. In placental models, nectin-4 is highly expressed on syncytiotrophoblasts and facilitates infection at the maternal-fetal interface, although additional nectin-4-independent pathways contribute to infection of other trophoblast populations. Together, these data establish nectin-4 as a key factor for respiratory transmission and early placental infection of RuV and highlight it as a promising therapeutic target for the prevention of rubella and related diseases.

title: Nectin-4 mediates rubella virus entry in airway and placental cells.

abstract: Effective delivery of RNA therapeutics to the brain remains challenging due to the multiple barriers of the central nervous system (CNS). To probe molecular scaffolds that could help overcome these barriers, we analysed the pharmaceutical profiles of over 100 CNS-active drugs and identified hydroxyzine (HX) as a promising scaffold for designing ionizable lipids with improved brain-targeting properties. Specifically, HX1 liquid nanoparticles (LNPs) achieved robust mRNA delivery to the brain through multiple trafficking pathways across CNS barriers. HX1 LNPs also enabled efficient gene editing in mouse brains via co-delivery of CRISPR mRNA and guide RNA and effectively delivered luciferase mRNA to the brain of a non-human primate. Moreover, HX1 LNPs carrying Il10 mRNA mitigated radiation-induced brain injury in mice, highlighting their potential for preventive treatment in the presence of intact CNS barriers. These findings establish HX1 LNPs as a promising translational platform for delivering therapeutic mRNAs and genome-editing components to the brain.

title: Rational design of lipid nanoparticles for brain delivery of RNA therapeutics.

abstract: We have previously proposed a combined therapy for spinal muscular atrophy based on the upregulation of exon 7 (E7) inclusion into SMN2 mRNA by the antisense oligonucleotide nusinersen (ASO1) together with histone deacetylase inhibitors (HDACi). Using a CRISPR-deadCas-based strategy in a human cell line, we show here that targeting histone acetylation at the SMN2 E7 region duplicates the HDACi effect, which overcomes pleiotropic effects. Most noticeably, targeted acetylation at the E7 region causes acetylation and activation of the 30-kbp-distant promoter. Since the nusinersen target site maps near the SMN2 gene 3' end, this crosstalk between the two ends of the gene prompted us to use chromosome conformation analysis (3C) to find that ASO1 promotes gene looping. This unpredicted property of ASOs in modulating chromatin 3D configuration depends on cohesin, CTCF, cleavage/polyadenylation factors, and a canonical poly(A) signal and causes promoter activation at a long distance, which expands the therapeutic potential of splicing-correcting ASOs.

title: An SMN2 splicing-correcting antisense oligonucleotide promotes gene looping and transcription activation.

abstract:
BACKGROUND: CRISPR/Cas9-mediated gene editing targeting the BCL11A erythroid enhancer has transformed therapeutic approaches for transfusion-dependent β-thalassemia (β-thal) and sickle cell disease (SCD). Even though clinical efficacy is well demonstrated, translating these therapies to global patient populations requires a strong evidence-based framework to address critical concerns regarding long-term genotoxic safety and long-lasting engraftment dynamics.
METHODS: Following the 2020 PRISMA guidelines, we conducted a systematic review of 21 key clinical and preclinical studies (published during 2014-2026) to evaluate CRISPR/Cas9-mediated gene editing in β-thal and SCD. The inclusion criteria focused on studies reporting foetal haemoglobin (HbF) induction, transfusion independence (TI) and safety outcomes.
RESULTS: Clinical data indicate high efficacy, with exagamglogene autotemcel (exa-cel) achieving TI in 91% of β-thal patients and a vaso-occlusive crisis (VOC)-free status in 97% of SCD patients. Safety profiling confirmed that severe adverse events, including febrile neutropenia and stomatitis, are primarily associated with busulfan-based myeloablation rather than gene editing. Gene-editing safety and conditioning toxicity are interlinked because conditioning is part of the process, and edited clones might interact with stress pathways during long-term repopulation. Preclinical benchmarks substantiate molecular reliability, with negligible off-target activity reported in most validated platforms. However, rare instances of complex structural rearrangements and intergenic off-target indels highlight the necessity for in-depth, unbiased long-term genomic surveillance.
CONCLUSION: CRISPR/Cas9 therapeutics for β-thal and SCD treatment constitute a treatment option within current clinical frameworks. These therapies need continuous surveillance. Rather than establishing a perfect plan, this systematic review highlights that while current platforms are thought to have short-term molecular precision, the use of Multilayer Safety Risks Screening and Surveillance for pretransplant conditioning is critical. This approach helps address long-term genotoxic concerns and ensures the safety and scalability of gene-editing therapies for global β-thal and SCD patient care.

title: Genotoxic safety and long-term engraftment dynamics of efficient translational CRISPR/Cas9 therapeutics for β-haemoglobinopathies from bench to clinical trials.

abstract: Osteoarthritis (OA) progression involves cartilage matrix loss and persistent inflammation. This study developed a machine learning-guided and chondrocyte membrane-camouflaged lipid nanoparticle carrying messenger RNA (CM-LNP@mRNA) platform for intra-articular SOX9 delivery. Random forest analysis identified the nitrogen-to-phosphorus and SM-102 ratios as primary determinants with feature importance values of 0.57 and 0.32 respectively. Following ML-guided formulation selection and experimental membrane-coating optimization, the final CM-LNP@mRNA formulation showed an encapsulation efficiency of 95.50% and a particle size of 133.70 nm. Compared with the conventional reference formulation prepared under the same final coating condition, encapsulation efficiency increased from 89.20% to 95.50% and particle size decreased from 145.40 nm to 133.70 nm. Membrane coating shifted the zeta potential from -25.57 mV to -35.07 mV. This transition provided biophysical evidence of successful surface modification. In interleukin-1β-stimulated chondrocytes, CM-LNP@mRNA increased the relative expression of Col2a1 and Acan from 0.20 to 0.33 and from 0.50 to 0.73, respectively, while reducing the relative expression of Mmp3 and Adamts5 from 10.50 to 7.80 and from 4.00 to 2.50, respectively. These alterations indicated a shift toward a matrix-preserving transcriptional state. Downstream matrix metalloproteinase 3 and prostaglandin E2 concentrations decreased from 37.10 ng/mL to 18.50 ng/mL and from 113.70 pg/mL to 76.50 pg/mL by day 7. This reduction demonstrated effective suppression of catabolic and inflammatory activity. In OA rats, CM-LNP@mRNA reduced the osteophyte volume from 4.00 mm3 to 2.00 mm3 and prolonged the thermal response latency from 7.50 s to 11.80 s. These improvements linked cellular metabolic regulation to functional joint recovery. These findings establish a strategy integrating formulation optimization with biomimetic membrane coating to modulate the OA microenvironment.

title: Machine learning-guided chondrocyte membrane-camouflaged lipid nanoparticles for intra-articular SOX9 mRNA therapy of osteoarthritis.

abstract: Targeted modulation of microglial activation with siRNA in neuroinflammatory diseases presents a compelling therapeutic strategy by enabling precise gene silencing while preserving beneficial immune responses. However, the immune-sensitive nature of microglia creates unique barriers to safe and efficient siRNA delivery. Dual pH- and redox-responsive polycationic nanogels with tunable molecular architectures are developed to overcome these barriers, enabling spatiotemporal delivery and intracellular degradation. Varying hydrophilic and hydrophobic monomer ratios tunes nanogel molecular architecture to control particle size, pH-responsive behavior, and therapeutic release. Disulfide crosslinkers enable selective degradation of polymer networks into fragments at intracellular glutathione levels, enabling controlled release and intracellular degradation. Increased hydrophobic composition yields smaller hydrodynamic size, optimal pH swelling profile for endosomal escape, and surface charge shifts that balance membrane disruption and biocompatibility. Degradation studies confirm redox-responsive crosslinks selective fragmentation at intracellular glutathione levels. Systematic siRNA loading studies demonstrate electrostatic interactions dominate, achieving high loading efficiency. Release studies mimicking intracellular environmental shifts confirm the spatiotemporal siRNA delivery from dual-responsive nanogels. Nanogels demonstrate first-pass cytocompatibility (MTS and LDH assays) with microglia at therapeutic concentrations. Both formulations achieve intracellular accumulation of carboxyfluorescein (FAM)-labelled siRNA in microglia, with higher efficacy for the more hydrophobic formulation. Future work will investigate the platform's innate immune response in microglia and functional knockdown of disease-relevant genes with target specific siRNA to modulate microglia's neuroinflammatory response. Collectively, these dual-responsive nanogels provide a foundational rational design framework for vectors that balance biosafety and delivery efficacy for siRNA therapies to microglia for targeting neuroinflammation.

title: Rational design of polycationic, biodegradable nanogels for intracellular siRNA delivery to microglia.

abstract: The ability of an organism to identify self and foreign RNA is central to eliciting an immune response in times of need while avoiding autoimmunity. As viral pathogens typically employ double-stranded RNA (dsRNA), host identification, modulation, and response to dsRNA is key. However, dsRNA is also abundant in host transcriptomes, raising the question of how these molecules can be differentiated. Two host pathways that regulate dsRNA are A-to-I RNA editing by adenosine deaminases (ADARs), and RNA interference (RNAi). Both mechanisms are important for normal organism development and function by regulating gene expression. Herein, we studied the structure and amount of siRNAs at editing sites and the ability of ADARs to prevent exogenous RNAi using the model organism, Caenorhabditis elegans. We found that the number of siRNAs targeting edited genes is significantly upregulated in ADAR mutant animals. We also found that despite an almost complete depletion of primary siRNAs generated from editing sites in wildtype animals, secondary siRNAs are generated from edited transcripts, suggesting ADARs antagonize only the first step of RNAi processing. We show that ADARs interfere with the efficacy of exogenous RNAi in vivo, probably to prevent trans-silencing, and have indications that ADR-2 binding to the dsRNA is needed for the efficient prevention of RNAi. This work sheds light on how the RNA editing process protects self-produced dsRNAs from aberrant recognition by the immune processes in the cell and from by-product degradation.

title: RNA binding by ADARs prevents RNA interference from attacking self-produced dsRNA.

abstract: Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD) is caused by mutations in the DMD gene, most of which are large exon deletions that result in loss of dystrophin protein. Adenine base editing (ABE) enables permanent gene correction by modifying splice sites to cause exon skipping and restoration of the DMD open reading frame. We previously demonstrated that adeno-associated virus 9-mediated (AAV9-mediated) delivery of adenine base editors allows efficient gene editing in mouse models of DMD. However, conventional AAV-based gene delivery approaches are complicated by their limited packaging capacity and high-dose-related toxicity. Here, we describe a single AAV vector encoding a compact adenine base editor, SlugABE8e, and a single-guide RNA, which enable efficient editing in a humanized DMD mouse model at a lower dose using the muscle-tropic MyoAAV4 capsid. Systemic MyoAAV4A delivery in juvenile DMD mice efficiently restored dystrophin expression in the heart and skeletal muscles. This molecular rescue was accompanied by reduced serum creatine kinase activity and diminished muscle pathology. A liver-detargeted MyoAAV4E-off capsid eliminated viral entry and editing in the liver. We also explored a high-fidelity base editor, SlugHF-ABE8e(V106W), which showed similar on-target and off-target editing to SlugABE8e. Together, these findings establish an all-in-one AAV strategy that efficiently mitigates DMD disease progression.

title: A single liver-sparing myotropic AAV ameliorates muscular dystrophy in humanized mice by base editing.

abstract: BackgroundJNJ-73763989 is a 2:1 combination of 2 N-acetylgalactosamine (GalNAc)-conjugated short interfering RNAs (siRNA) targeting the S (daplusiran) and X (tomligisiran) regions of the hepatitis B virus genome. In phase 2b studies, 48 weeks of JNJ-73763989-based combination treatments led to dose-dependent reductions in viral markers, including hepatitis B surface antigen. The objective of the INSIGHT study Panel 3 was to quantify intrahepatic concentrations of the siRNAs in human livers during and after treatment.MethodsIn the open-label, single-arm, single-center study, participants with chronic hepatitis B received 48 weeks of treatment with JNJ-73763989 200 mg every 4 weeks and nucleos(t)ide analog, with optional pegylated interferon α2a 180 µg weekly added after Treatment Week (TW) 40. Core liver biopsies were collected at TW12, TW40, and at Follow-up Week (FUW) 24.ResultsLiver biopsies were available from all 4 participants at TW12 and from 3 at TW40 and FUW24. Between TW12 and TW40, liver concentrations of daplusiran and tomligisiran increased 1.5- to 2.6-fold, consistent with intrahepatic accumulation. Twenty-eight weeks after the last injection of JNJ-73763989, the triggers were still measurable in 2 of 3 participants with 4.5- to 15-fold reduced concentrations from peak levels; the estimated liver half-life ranged from approximately 2.9 to 16.1 weeks.ConclusionsIn this first study to assess liver concentrations of GalNAc-siRNA in humans with sequential biopsies, long persistence of JNJ-73763989 triggers in human livers may partially explain the prolonged suppressive effect on viral parameters observed in phase 2 studies.

title: Liver concentrations of JNJ-73763989 siRNA triggers in patients with chronic hepatitis B (CHB): The INSIGHT study panel 3 results.

abstract: Adenosine deaminases acting on RNA (ADARs) convert adenosine positioned within double-stranded RNA (dsRNA) to inosine (A-to-I). This reaction can be redirected to a specific target transcript by exogenous guide RNAs (gRNAs) that recruit abundant endogenous ADARs without the need for exogenous protein delivery. Approximately 16,000 pathogenic G > A mutations are correctable by A-to-I conversion, thus representing a broad scope for therapeutic A-to-I editing. This review covers the key advances in gRNA engineering for endogenous ADAR-mediated RNA editing. We first discuss how ADAR biology informs rational gRNA design. We then survey gRNA design strategies that increase on-target editing efficiency and diminish bystander editing. Delivery modalities are then discussed for both unmodified and modified gRNAs as a strategy to minimize transcriptome-wide off-target editing. We conclude by outlining the outstanding challenges and future opportunities, including computational gRNA design, to guide the next generation of gRNAs towards the path of approved RNA editing medicines.

title: Advances in guide RNA engineering for endogenous ADAR-mediated therapeutic RNA editing.

abstract: Gene therapy has transformed modern biomedical research by enabling curative strategies that target the molecular basis of disease. Among genome-editing technologies, the CRISPR/Cas9 system has emerged as a versatile and efficient platform due to its programmability, simplicity, and precision. This review summarizes the evolution of gene therapy and highlights the therapeutic potential of CRISPR-based genome editing. CRISPR/Cas9 has demonstrated significant potential in correcting disease-causing mutations across multiple inherited disorders, including sickle cell disease, β- thalassemia, familial hypercholesterolemia, phenylketonuria, muscular dystrophies, and cystic fibrosis. Emerging technologies such as base editing and prime editing further improved editing precision and reduced unintended genomic alterations. However, challenges including off-target effects, DNA repair pathway bias, immune responses, and vector-associated toxicities remain major limitations. The review highlights the rapid progress of CRISPR-mediated therapeutics and emphasizes the importance of improving editing accuracy, delivery efficiency, and long-term safety. Advances in vector engineering and genome-editing platforms are expected to overcome current technical and ethical barriers, facilitating broader clinical applications. CRISPR/Cas9 and related genome- editing technologies represent promising disease-modifying and potentially curative therapeutic approaches. Continued optimization of precision, safety, and delivery systems will be essential for successful translation into routine clinical practice.

Participants from all the subprotocols have the option to continue treatment in a long-term extension study following their end of study visit.

abstract:
The goal of this pilot clinical trial is to learn if tirzepatide can treat active central centrifugal cicatricial alopecia (CCCA), a type of permanent scarring hair loss, in adults. The main questions it aims to answer are:

* Does tirzepatide improve the symptoms and signs of active CCCA?
* Does tirzepatide change the activity of genes in the scalp, especially genes related to scarring?
* Does tirzepatide promote hair regrowth?

Participants will:

* Inject tirzepatide once a week for 12 months.
* Visit the clinic for scalp examinations, photographs, and other health assessments.
* Have scalp biopsies at the beginning of the study and after 6 months of treatment.
* Have blood tests and other safety monitoring during the study.

There is no separate comparison group. Researchers will compare each participant's results during treatment with the participant's results at the beginning of the study.

abstract:
The goal of this clinical trial is to test the use of milk fat globule membrane (MFGM) in ready-to-use therapeutic food (RUTF) in children with severe acute malnutrition in Sierra Leone. The main questions it aims to answer are:

* Will the inclusion of MFGM in RUTF for 6-59-month-old Sierra Leonean children with severe acute malnutrition improve their neurodevelopment?
* Will the inclusion of MFGM in RUTF for 6-59-month-old Sierra Leonean children with severe acute malnutrition reduce its worst consequences: death, hospitalization, and remaining severely malnourished despite treatment?

Researchers will compare the MFGM-containing RUTF to standard RUTF, which contains skim milk powder.

Participants will:

* undergo measurement of length, weight, mid-upper arm circumference, and nutritional edema assessment every two weeks during severe malnutrition treatment
* be treated with either MFGM-RUTF or standard RUTF at a dose of 2 sachets per day for up to 12 weeks
* undergo neurodevelopmental testing using the Malawi Developmental Assessment Tool at the end of SAM treatment and 6 months later
* a subset of participants will undergo blood spot collection and stool sample collection

description:
Globally, approximately 15 million children are suffering from severe acute malnutrition (SAM) at any one time, a number that has not declined in recent decades despite significant technological advancements in agriculture and food science. SAM is a condition of total-body depletion of the nutrients required for health and development; without treatment, 50% of affected children will die. Whereas historically children with SAM were admitted to and treated within hospitals, the advent of ready-to-use therapeutic food (RUTF) and community-based management of acute malnutrition revolutionized SAM care by allowing it to occur safely and successfully by the child's caregiver in their own home.

RUTF was designed to provide the nutrients required for physical recovery in a safe, palatable format. It is equal parts peanut paste, sugar, vegetable oil, and skim milk powder, with added micronutrients and emulsifier. At inception, attention was not specifically paid to how RUTF's composition might impact neurodevelopmental recovery in children with SAM. Research over the past decade has revealed that even following successful treatment with RUTF, children diagnosed with SAM still score 1-3 standard deviations below age-based expectations on neurodevelopmental tests. This suggests that the nutrient profile of standard RUTF is not sufficient to recover the developmental damage incurred by SAM.

Recently, progress has been made toward improving the developmental trajectory of children with SAM by altering RUTF. A randomized, blinded trial in Malawi including 2,500 children with SAM showed that improving the polyunsaturated fatty acid (PUFA) profile of RUTF by reducing linoleic acid and adding docosahexaenoic acid (DHA) yields superior neurodevelopment 6 months after treatment, by 0.19 standard deviations on a standardized, culturally adapted neurodevelopmental test. This demonstrates that neurodevelopmental recovery in SAM is sensitive to the lipid profile of RUTF. Despite the benefits of improved PUFA RUTF, however, children with SAM remained 1 standard deviation below expectations in neurodevelopment.

The milk fat globule membrane (MFGM) in mammalian milk contains a host of nutrients and bioactive compounds supportive of physical health and brain development. Bovine MFGM added to infant formula has been tested in several clinical trials and has demonstrated a reduction in infectious episodes, such as diarrhea and ear infections, as well as improvement in cognitive development, compared with infant formula not containing MFGM. In these trials and others, MFGM has been shown to be safe and well-tolerated. Currently, RUTF contains skim milk powder as its high-quality protein source, and peanut and vegetable oils as the primary sources of fat. These vegetable fat sources are deficient in the lipids provided by MFGM: sphingolipids, cholesterol, and other phospholipids such as phosphatidylcholine and phosphatidylethanolamine, all of which play roles in brain development. It is possible that the lipids contained in MFGM may further support neurodevelopmental recovery in SAM children.

By acting as a natural emulsifier, MFGM also offers a food formulation advantage that is relevant to children with SAM. Animal model studies have demonstrated that emulsifiers can compromise the gut barrier. Children with SAM have damaged small intestinal barrier function, which can lead to translocation of gut bacteria and resulting systemic infection. As RUTF will compose nearly 100% of a child's intake for the duration of treatment - up to 3 months - it is possible that inclusion of emulsifier may impede gut healing and recovery. Considering this concern, the Manary lab ran a clinical trial in 2018-2019 testing a novel formulation of RUTF designed with oat in place of some skim milk powder and peanut, and without hydrogenated vegetable oil (standard emulsifier), because oat acts as a natural emulsifier. In this trial, children with SAM receiving the oat-RUTF had 10% absolute higher recovery and a 33% relative reduction in the worst SAM outcomes (death, hospitalization, or remaining severely malnourished). Like oat, MFGM in RUTF allows for omission of emulsifier and may yield similar benefits.

Given (1) the repeated finding that adding MFGM to infant formulas improves neurodevelopment, (2) the impaired neurodevelopment of children with SAM, (3) the current RUTF formulation lacking neuro-supportive fats provided by MFGM, (4) MFGM's natural activity as an emulsifier, and (5), the reality that RUTF provides the sole source of nutrition for children with SAM, it is plausible that adding this high-quality source of lipids and protein to RUTF may also benefit children with SAM in both immediate and long-term physical and cognitive recovery.

This will be an individually randomized, investigator/outcomes assessors-blinded, controlled clinical trial designed to determine if treatment of severely malnourished Sierra Leonean children 6-59-months of age with an RUTF made with MFGM-containing whey protein/fat concentrate will (1) improve neurodevelopment and (2) reduce a composite of poor SAM outcomes (death, hospitalization, remaining severely malnourished), compared with standard RUTF (S-RUTF). This trial will be conducted at 20 rural sites in Sierra Leone. 1600 children will be randomized 1:1 to receive 2 sachets per day of either MFGM-RUTF or S-RUTF. Children will receive their allocated RUTF and return to clinic fortnightly for repeat anthropometric measurements, illness questions, and to receive more RUTF until they achieve a clinical outcome or for a maximum of 12 weeks, at which point they will undergo Malawi Developmental Assessment Tool (MDAT) testing. Participants will be asked to return to clinic 6 (5-7) months later for MDAT testing, the global z-score from which will be the trial's co-primary outcome. A subset of participants will undergo blood spot and/or stool sample collection at the end of SAM treatment.

abstract: The "metal ion hypothesis" of Alzheimer's disease (AD) has gained widespread acceptance, but translating this understanding into effective therapies remains elusive. This likely stems from a simplistic understanding of metal homeostasis as merely a matter of "excess and deficiency." This article reviews the context-dependent roles of iron, copper, zinc, aluminum, and manganese in the pathogenesis of AD, with a particular focus on their bidirectional interactions with classic AD pathology (the ferroptosis hypothesis is relatively mature, while emerging hypotheses such as cuproptosis have not been fully elucidated). Metal homeostasis dysregulation can directly promote β-amyloid aggregation, tau hyperphosphorylation, oxidative stress, neuroinflammation, and regulated cell death. Conversely, these pathological processes can also alter the binding, storage, transport, and subcellular distribution of metal ions. Dysregulated metal ions function as "context-dependent" modulators of pathological processes. Their functional effects depend on metal species, concentration, binding state, subcellular compartment, and disease stage. Metal homeostasis dysregulation associated with AD may essentially reflect a redistribution between physiological and pathological pools. Ideal interventions should selectively neutralize pathological metal pools while preserving or restoring essential metal-dependent neuronal functions. By integrating the latest advances in the field of metal-targeted therapies (chelators, metabolic modulators, biomarkers, metal imaging, and gene editing), we emphasize that future treatments should shift from nonspecific metal clearance toward precise metal regulation and precision medicine.

title: Dysregulated Metal Homeostasis in Alzheimer's Disease: From Pathological Modulators to Therapeutic Targets.

abstract: Oxidized phospholipids (OxPLs) represent a class of molecules generated during evolution that shift from fundamental membrane building-blocks to key signaling mediators, linking lipid metabolism, cellular redox homeostasis and multi-faceted cell-fate control. Generated by both enzymatic and non-enzymatic peroxidation events, OxPLs engage in extensive signaling crosstalk with lyso-phospholipids and oxylipins. The FerroLipid framework describes iron-lipid peroxidation crosstalk to contextualize iron-dependent lipid signaling. OxPLs govern diverse regulated cell-death programs: they act as lipid death signals in apoptosis and ferroptosis, tune ferroptotic outputs through intrinsic antioxidant systems, and exert context-specific modulatory effects on pyroptosis and other cell-death modalities. Beyond cell-death execution, OxPLs signal through pattern-recognition, scavenger and nuclear receptors to orchestrate inflammation, membrane remodeling, phagocytic clearance, autophagy, mitophagy and protein homeostasis. Threshold-dependent accumulation of OxPLs drives pathological processes across neurodegenerative, metabolic, cardiovascular, neoplastic and infectious diseases; their disease-specific molecular signatures confer potential as both diagnostic biomarkers and therapeutic targets. Redox phospholipidomics coupled with mass-spectrometry imaging enables accurate, species-resolved profiling of distinct OxPL species. Multiple pharmacological approaches and gene-editing interventions have demonstrated tangible translational prospects for OxPL-oriented therapy. This review synthesizes existing knowledge of OxPL biology from evolutionary origins and signaling mechanisms to disease relevance, analytical tools and therapeutic opportunities. It highlights major unresolved research bottlenecks and provides a solid conceptual foundation for advancing lipid-targeted treatments for complex human disorders.

abstract:
BACKGROUND: Despite the fact that immunotherapy is reshaping the therapeutic landscape of bladder cancer, immune evasion remains a major obstacle to durable clinical benefit. Therefore, elucidating the mechanisms underlying immune resistance is essential for developing novel therapeutic strategies.
METHODS: In this study, we performed a genome-wide CRISPR-Cas9 screen in bladder cancer cells co-cultured with CD8+ T cells and identified the SLP adaptor and CSK-interacting membrane protein (SCIMP) as a key gene that enhances CD8+ T cell antitumor immunity.
RESULTS: SCIMP serves as a favorable prognostic biomarker in patients with bladder cancer treated with immunotherapy. Mechanistically, SCIMP restricts JAK1 phosphorylation in an adaptor-independent manner, suppressing the IFN-γ/JAK1/STAT5A/PD-L1 signaling axis. Meanwhile, YTHDF2 destabilizes the m6A-tagged SCIMP transcripts to reduce their expression. Remarkably, SCIMP synergizes with PD-1 blockade in suppressing tumor growth.
CONCLUSIONS: Collectively, these findings reveal a previously unexplored non-canonical role of SCIMP in preventing immune evasion and provide a potential therapeutic target for bladder cancer.

title: Non-canonical function of SCIMP restricts JAK1 activity to counteract immune evasion in bladder cancer.

abstract: Prostate cancers harboring CDK12 alterations exhibit aggressive clinical behavior and poor responses to current therapeutic strategies. Although CDK12 is categorized as a homologous recombination repair (HRR)-related gene, clinical evidence indicates limited benefit of poly (ADP-ribose) polymerase (PARP) inhibitor monotherapy in CDK12-defective tumors. To clarify the functional consequences of CDK12 loss and identify a mechanistically rational therapeutic approach, we generated CDK12-knockout (KO) prostate cancer cell lines using CRISPR/Cas9 and assessed cell-cycle regulation, DNA damage repair, and replication stress via flow cytometry, γH2AX immunofluorescence, and DNA fiber assays. CDK12 KO abrogated the G0-G1 checkpoint, permitting cell-cycle progression into the M-phase despite the persistence of unrepaired DNA double-strand breaks (DSB), and reduced ATM transcription, resulting in a DSB response phenotype resembling ATM deficiency. CDK12 loss also increased intrinsic replication stress and sensitized prostate cancer cells to ATR inhibition. In patient-derived xenograft models harboring CDK12 alterations, combined PARP and ATR inhibition led to enhanced DSB accumulation and selectively suppressed tumor growth in CDK12-defective models. These findings highlight the importance of interrogating individual genes within the HRR pathway to define distinct mechanistic vulnerabilities and provide a strong rationale for combined PARP and ATR inhibition as a novel therapeutic strategy for patients with CDK12-altered prostate cancer.

abstract: Mitochondria are essential structures that produce energy in cells through mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation and are one of the primary sources of reactive oxygen species (ROS). Mutations in mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) cause a wide range of hereditary illnesses with multisystem clinical symptoms, poor cellular bioenergetics, and decreased mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation. Effective treatment approaches have been hampered by the genetic complexity associated with mtDNA disorders, including heteroplasmy and tissue-specific diversity. The relationship between mutations in the mitochondrial DNA and oxidative stress is multidimensional and snowballing, with structural malfunction of the electron transport chain encouraging the development of ROS that causes further damage to mitochondrial DNA, lipids, and proteins. Under carefully regulated experimental conditions, cell-based disease models, in particular induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) and standard transmitochondrial cybrids, have become useful tools for studying disease mechanisms, simulating mutation-specific phenotypes, and assessing possible therapeutic interventions. This review provides the key roles of mutations and oxidative stress in the pathogenesis of the disease in the context of the primary role of the mitochondrial genome, its maternal inheritance, and the most common disorders, i.e., mitochondrial encephalomyopathy, lactic acidosis, and stroke-like episodes (MELAS) and myoclonic epilepsy with ragged red fibers (MERRF). We outline the use of cell-based models to study mitochondrial pathologies, including patient-derived primary cells and iPSCs, which could be differentiated into cell types of interest to the disease, and cybrid systems, which could isolate the contribution of single mutations in the mitochondrial DNA to an underlying background of controlled nuclear genetic backgrounds. Besides, the review focuses on innovative technologies to mend mutations in mitochondrial DNA, such as allotopic expression, mitoTALENs and mitoZFNs, and the new base-editing systems like DdCBEs. Included are the free cell-based therapies like mitochondrial transfer and nuclear transfer procedures. Finally, we discussed the measures to be taken to minimize oxidative stress, and these actions are standard: mitochondria- targeted antioxidants, mitophagy, and autophagy regulation. The study also looks at the present level of proof supporting these therapy techniques and discusses the advantages and disadvantages of existing experimental models. Although several gene editing and mitochondria replacement technologies have shown promising results in clinical and cellular research, their clinical translation is still restricted and needs more confirmation in terms of long-term therapeutic efficacy, safety, and delivery efficiency.

abstract: Investigators' recent findings from the pilot clinical trial in MCI individuals demonstrated EVOO improved vascular function and memory. Yet, up to date, whether EVOO protects against AD in individuals with a family history of AD is unknown. Thus, in this study, the investigators will recruit healthy individuals with a family history of AD for participation. From eligible participants, blood samples for ApoE genotyping will be collected, followed by metabolomics, lipidomics, and transcriptomics analyses at baseline. Participants will be randomized into 2 groups (n=20 each); one group will receive EVOO daily (\~2 tablespoons, 30 ml) for 6 months, and the second group will not receive olive oil. Both group participants will receive educational information on brain health and how environmental factors such as lifestyle, diet, and exercise could impact brain health. After 6 months, another blood sample will be collected from the participants to evaluate the effect of EVOO on metabolites, lipids, and genes, and thus physiological pathways. The investigators will perform non-targeted and comprehensive metabolomics, lipidomics, and transcriptomics analyses. Examples of metabolites to be analyzed are antioxidative and anti-inflammatory metabolites, neurotransmission, mitochondrial, tryptophan, and purine metabolisms. Examples of lipidomics include sphingomyelins (SMs), cholesterol esters (ChEs), phosphatidylcholines (PCs), phosphatidylethanolamines (PIs), phosphatidylinositols (PIs), and triglycerides (TGs). Transcriptomics will be used to identify changes in mRNAs involved in different pathways contributing to AD, such as genes involved in inflammation and oxidative stress, in both ApoE-dependent and independent fashion.
description: Several epidemiological and clinical studies proposed that adherence to the Mediterranean diet improves cognitive function and slows Alzheimer's disease (AD) progression. Extra virgin olive oil (EVOO) is one of the main elements of the Mediterranean diet. EVOO provides several health benefits, including strong anti-inflammatory and antioxidant effects. Findings from our preclinical published studies support the consumption of EVOO to protect the brain, prevent AD and delay disease progression. In addition, findings from the investigators' pilot clinical trial in mild cognitive impairment (MCI) individuals demonstrated EVOO improved cerebrovascular function and memory. However, the remaining question is whether EVOO could protect individuals from AD in individuals with a family history of AD, i.e., with a genetic predisposition. One of the major risk factors for AD is the genetic variation in apolipoprotein E (ApoE). ApoE is a major risk factor for developing late-onset AD, with ApoE4 being detrimental and ApoE2 protective. Compared to the most common ApoE3/3 genotype, each additional copy of the ApoE4 allele is associated with an increased risk of AD and a younger mean age at dementia onset, such that ApoE4 homozygotes are at the highest risk. Available reports have shown ApoE4 carriers have increased amyloid-β (Aβ) brain levels contributing to its accumulation and related pathology. Also, ApoE4 contributes to cerebrovascular dysfunction, increasing susceptibility to neurodegenerative insult. Besides, compared to ApoE3, ApoE4 carriers may not respond to some drugs suggesting the efficacy is ApoE genotype dependent. However, whether EVOO protective effect could extend to those with a family history of AD, i.e., with a genetic predisposition, specifically ApoE4, is unknown. Thus, the objectives of this study are: 1) To evaluate the effect of EVOO on molecular and biological pathways linked with AD by monitoring changes in blood metabolites (metabolomics), lipids (lipidomics), and genes (transcriptomics); and 2): To compare the effect of EVOO on analyzed pathways between individuals with ApoE3 and ApoE4. To accomplish both specific aims, the investigators will recruit healthy individuals with a family history of AD for participation. At baseline, blood samples will be collected from eligible participants for ApoE genotyping and metabolomics, lipidomics, and transcriptomics analyses. Participants will be randomized into 2 groups (n=20 each); one group will receive daily EVOO (\~2 tablespoons, 30 ml per day) for 6 months, and the second group will not receive olive oil. After 6 months, another blood sample will be collected from the participants to evaluate the effect of EVOO on metabolites, lipids, and genes.

abstract: Articular cartilage repair remains a major clinical challenge due to the limited regenerative capacity of the tissue and the poor therapeutic efficacy of current treatments. Although stem cell-based therapies hold promise, their clinical outcomes are often compromised by insufficient chondrogenic differentiation, phenotypic instability, and rapid cell loss in the dynamic joint environment. Herein, we report an ultrasound-responsive, bio-scaffold system (e-BMSCs/Gel) designed to enhance cartilage regeneration through coordinated biochemical and genetic regulation. In this system, bone marrow mesenchymal stem cells (BMSCs) are engineered by internalizing nanobubbles (NBs) loaded with TGF-β3 protein and CRISPR/Cas9 plasmids targeting the YAP (pCas9-YAP), termed T@NBspDNA. Additionally, to enhance cell retention and survival, engineered BMSCs (e-BMSCs) are encapsulated within a thermosensitive thiolated-chitosan/hydroxyapatite hydrogel that rapidly forms in situ. Under US stimulation, the synchronized activation of TGF-β3 release and YAP gene silencing significantly promoted the chondrogenic differentiation of e-BMSCs. Furthermore, in vivo evaluation in a rat articular cartilage defect model demonstrates that US-activated e-BMSCs/Gel effectively promotes hyaline-like cartilage regeneration and improves structural restoration of the defect site. Overall, this work presents a controllable bio-scaffold platform, offering a novel strategy for effective cartilage regeneration.

abstract:
BACKGROUND: Pathological cardiac hypertrophy is a major risk factor for heart failure. NIBP (NF-κB [nuclear factor kappa-B] inducing kinase- and inhibitor of NF-κB kinase subunit beta-binding protein) is a key regulator of cytokine-induced NF-κB signaling, but its role in cardiac hypertrophy remains unknown.
METHODS: We established transverse aortic constriction-induced cardiac hypertrophy in mice and phenylephrine-induced hypertrophy in neonatal rat ventricular myocytes. Genetic interventions included generation of whole-body Nibp knockout mice via CRISPR-Cas9; creation of cardiomyocyte-specific Nibp knockout mice using adeno-associated virus serotype 9-delivered Cre and single-guide RNAs in Rosa26-LSL-Cas9 mice; and cardiac-specific Nibp overexpression via adeno-associated virus serotype 9delivery. In neonatal rat ventricular myocytes, NIBP was knocked down or overexpressed using adenoviruses. Phenotypes were assessed by echocardiography, histology (wheat germ agglutinin, picrosirius redstaining), and molecular analyses. Mechanisms were investigated via RNA-sequencing, coimmunoprecipitation, and Western blotting for key signaling molecules.
RESULTS: NIBP protein was upregulated in hypertrophic hearts and cardiomyocytes. Both Nibp-knockout and cardiomyocyte-specific Nibp knockout attenuated transverse aortic constriction-induced cardiac dysfunction, hypertrophy, and fibrosis, whereas Nibp overexpression exacerbated these pathologies. Consistently, in neonatal rat ventricular myocytes, NIBP knockdown mitigated, while its overexpression aggravated, phenylephrine-induced cardiomyocyte hypertrophy and inflammatory responses. Mechanistically, NIBP directly interacted with IKKβ (inhibitor of NF-κB kinase subunit beta), enhanced its phosphorylation, and drove hyperactivation of the downstream NF-κB pathway. Overexpression of a kinase-dead IKKβ mutant reversed the hypertrophic effects of NIBP.
CONCLUSIONS: NIBP promotes pathological cardiac hypertrophy by activating the IKKβ/NF-κB axis, identifying it as a potential therapeutic target for cardiac remodeling and heart failure.

abstract:
Although immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) have substantially extended survival in many patients, most patients do not achieve durable responses on these treatments. There is a substantial unmet need for methods to sensitize more patients to ICIs. Studies have shown that personalized mRNA lipid nanoparticle vaccines enhance antitumor immunity in combination with PD1 inhibition, under the assumption that these vaccines generate T cells reactive against the targets encoded by the mRNA in the vaccines. However, it was recently found that mRNA vaccines targeting non-tumor antigens are also powerful adjuvants to immune checkpoint blockade.

Retrospective clinical data strongly suggests that receipt of COVID mRNA vaccines with ICIs is responsible for significant improvements in three-year overall survival in multiple large cohorts of patients with non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). Patients treated with these vaccines also have increased expression of programmed death ligand 1 (PD-L1) on their tumors.

This trial is designed to evaluate whether the Pfizer-BioNTech COVID mRNA vaccine improves responses to ICIs in patients with stage IV non-small cell lung cancer.

abstract:
IMPORTANCE: Angiotensinogen (AGT) is the precursor of angiotensin peptides and a key determinant of renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system activity. ART101 is an investigational N-acetylgalactosamine-conjugated small interfering RNA (GalNAc-siRNA) designed to durably suppress hepatic AGT synthesis.
OBJECTIVE: To evaluate the safety, tolerability, pharmacokinetics, and pharmacodynamics of single ascending doses of the AGT-targeting GalNAc-siRNA in healthy volunteers and to provide an initial exploratory assessment of blood pressure effects in patients with hypertension.
DESIGN, SETTING, AND PARTICIPANTS: This phase I study was conducted from January 2025 to April 2026 with 24-week follow-up. Part A was a double-blind, placebo-controlled, single ascending-dose trial; part B was an open-label, single-dose study. The study took place at Beijing Friendship Hospital, Capital Medical University, Beijing, China. Part A enrolled 40 healthy adults randomized 6:2 to receive the GalNAc-siRNA (25-600 mg) or placebo; 39 completed the study. Part B enrolled 8 patients with hypertension receiving the GalNAc-siRNA, 600 mg; all completed the study.
INTERVENTIONS: A single subcutaneous injection of the AGT-targeting GalNAc-siRNA (25, 75, 150, 300, or 600 mg) or placebo in part A; a single open-label subcutaneous injection of GalNAc-siRNA, 600 mg, in part B.
MAIN OUTCOMES AND MEASURES: The primary outcome was safety and tolerability; secondary outcomes included pharmacokinetics, pharmacodynamics, exploratory blood pressure assessments, and renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system biomarkers.
RESULTS: Among 40 healthy volunteers (27 [67.5%] male; mean [SD] age, 40.4 [7.8] years) and 8 patients (6 [75.0%] male; mean [SD] age, 47.3 [10.3] years) with hypertension, the AGT-targeting GalNAc-siRNA was well tolerated. In part A, treatment-emergent adverse events (TEAEs) occurred in 23 of 30 active-treatment participants (76.7%) vs 7 of 10 placebo recipients (70.0%); in part B, 6 of 8 patients (75.0%) had TEAEs. No serious adverse events, injection site reactions, or hyperkalemia were observed; all TEAEs were mild to moderate. Plasma exposure (maximum plasma concentration [Cmax] and area under the plasma concentration-time curve [AUC]) increased with dose over the wide dose range from 25 mg to 600 mg. Mean maximum serum AGT reductions of 93% (at 600 mg) in healthy volunteers and 90% (at 600 mg) in patients with hypertension were observed. At 24 weeks after a single 600-mg dose, the placebo-corrected 24-hour ambulatory systolic blood pressure decreased by 12.9 mm Hg in healthy participants.
CONCLUSION AND RELEVANCE: In this phase I study, no serious treatment-related safety signals were identified. Sustained, dose-dependent AGT reductions and exploratory blood pressure lowering were observed. These findings support further investigation of the AGT-targeting GalNAc-siRNA as a potential long-acting therapeutic for hypertension.
TRIAL REGISTRATION: China Drug Clinical Registry Identifiers: CTR20250041 (part A) and CTR20253973 (part B).

abstract: Background: Roughly one person in two carries Helicobacter pylori, a pathogen classified by the World Health Organization as a group I carcinogen, and the steady loss of antibiotic efficacy has made prophylaxis an urgent rather than an optional goal. No mRNA vaccine against this organism has yet been tested in the clinic, and CagW, a conserved inner-membrane subunit of the H. pylori type IV secretion system (T4SS), has never been evaluated as an mRNA-encoded antigen. Methods: A codon-optimised construct carrying a signal peptide, the CagW coding sequence and a human IgG Fc tag was synthesised, transcribed into mRNA, encapsulated in lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) and shown to direct antigen expression in HEK293T cells. C57BL/6 mice received three intramuscular doses of CagW-Fc mRNA-LNPs (5 ug mRNA each) at 14-day intervals; animals given alum alone, luciferase mRNA-LNPs or CagW protein adsorbed to alum served as comparators. Humoral readouts (IgG, IgG1, IgG2a, IgM, IgA and secretory IgA), lymphocyte proliferation, CD4+/CD8+ subsets, intracellular IFN-{gamma}, IL-4 and IL-17A and circulating cytokines were quantified before challenge, and protection was assessed after live challenge. Results: The formulation (93.2 nm; PDI 0.13; approximately 90% encapsulation) produced CagW-specific protein in vitro. Vaccination raised high-titre CagW-specific IgG (maximal on day 42), IgM and mucosal sIgA, and drove Th1/Th2-type cellular activation (IL-2, IL-4, IL-12, IFN-{gamma} and IL-17A). After challenge, immunised animals carried markedly fewer gastric bacteria and showed lower urease activity than controls. Conclusions: CagW-Fc mRNA-LNPs are therefore a credible mRNA vaccine platform for H. pylori and warrant further preclinical development.

The purpose of this study is to evaluate the safety of two doses (Dose 1 and Dose 2) of Chlamydia mRNA Vaccine candidate in adult participants aged 18 to 29 years (Chlamydia trachomatis seronegative) or 18 to 44 years (Chlamydia trachomatis seropositive). There will also be an assessment to potentially obtain an early immunogenicity signal of the Chlamydia mRNA vaccine candidate.

This study will consist of 2 Cohorts assessing the safety of the two different doses: Cohort A (Dose 1 or placebo) and Cohort B (Dose 2 or placebo).

All participants will be followed up to 12 months after the last study intervention administration. Thus, the expected duration of the participant's involvement will be 18 months.

abstract:
This is an open-label, first-in-human, dose escalation study of CV09070101 mRNA (CVHNLC) in patients with metastatic Squamous Non-Small-Cell Lung Cancer (sqNSCLC).

The study will evaluate the safety and tolerability of CVHNLC plus pembrolizumab in an Dose Escalation Part and, once the safety of this combination is established, CVHNLC plus prembrolizumab and chemotherapy (carboplatin and paclitaxel) will be evaluated in an Dose Expansion Part with the recommended dose selected from the Dose Escalation Part.
description:
Dose Escalation (Metastatic 1L Maintenance sqNSCLC) The Dose Escalation Part will be comprised of 3 dose cohorts with a starting dose of 100 μg (dose level 1). Once the starting dose is established as safe, further dose levels of 200 μg and 400 μg may be explored. Depending on safety assessment guided by a Bayesian Logistic Regression Model (BLRM) design intermediate dose levels may be explored. In case the HTD is exceeded at 100 μg, a lower dose level of 50 μg may be explored.

Approximately 3 to 6 patients will be enrolled per dose level/cohort. To better understand the safety and tolerability of CVHNLC, additional patients may be enrolled in enrichment cohorts at dose levels that have previously been determined to be safe in at least 3 patients. This may be before or while proceeding with the next higher dose. An enrichment cohort may have up to 10 patients enrolled.

Each dose level will start with the staggered enrollment of 3 patients. There will be a 2-week interval between the first CVHNLC administration of the first patient and the first CVHNLC administration of the second patient. The same approach will be used between the second and third patient. If the cohort is enriched with further patients, subsequent patients may be treated concurrently once the second patient has completed the 2 weeks after the first CVHNLC administration. The enrollment is followed by a safety data review by the Safety Review Team (SRT) after all patients in each cohort have completed their 4 weeks DLT evaluation period. Non-evaluable patients (patients that discontinue/withdraw during the DLT assessment period for a reason other than DLT) may be replaced.

Safety will be continuously monitored by the Sponsor's Safety Physician, Sponsor's Medical Responsible Person (MRP) and the medical monitor with a focus on DLTs, Grade ≥ 3 AEs occurring after the DLT period, SAEs, and AESIs. After completion of the DLT evaluation period in all patients enrolled in a dose cohort, the SRT will review the safety data from the respective and all previous dose cohorts together with the Coordinating Investigator and decide about the next steps e.g.:

* Escalation of the dose to the next level.
* Enrollment of additional patients at the same or lower dose level.
* Stop or pause enrollment in the Dose Escalation Part of the trial.

At the end of the Dose Escalation Part, an independent Data Safety Monitoring Board (DSMB) will recommend a dose for the Dose Expansion Part (RDE) based on review of the complete safety data from the Dose Escalation Part and the Sponsor will decide on the RDE.

Dose Expansion Part (Metastatic 1L sqNSCLC) The optional Dose Expansion Part will include patients with histologically confirmed metastatic sqNSCLC not amenable for surgical or locoregional therapy and eligible for 1L treatment with pembrolizumab and platinum-based chemotherapy (carboplatin/paclitaxel). Patients should not have received any prior systemic treatment for metastatic disease. Previous (neo-)adjuvant treatment is only permitted if there are at least 12 months between end of such treatment and development of metastatic disease. Patients will receive CVHNLC plus 4 cycles of carboplatin and paclitaxel and pembrolizumab (3-weekly) followed by pembrolizumab maintenance therapy. Patients who discontinue prematurely from chemotherapy due to toxicity may continue on CVHNLC plus pembrolizumab. The first dose of CVHNLC will be administered one week prior to chemotherapy to avoid the immune suppressive effect from concomitant administration of steroids as premedication/supportive medication to chemotherapy treatment. Once chemotherapy is completed, CVHNLC administration will be aligned with pembrolizumab treatment to reduce patient visit burden.

The Dose Expansion Part will start with a safety lead-in, where the first 6 patients will be evaluated with focus on treatment-related AEs, SAEs, and AESIs after having completed the Day 29 visit, before continuing the enrollment. The safety data will be reviewed by the SRT and in addition by the DSMB, which will give a recommendation on dosage for treatment continuation. Patients will receive CVHNLC plus pembrolizumab for up to 12 months or until disease progression or undue toxicity. Patients not progressing after this period may continue on pembrolizumab outside of the trial according to standard of care.

abstract: Skin fibrosis is driven in part by transforming growth factor-β (TGF-β) signaling and the matricellular protein connective tissue growth factor (CTGF). Elevated CTGF expression is a hallmark of fibrotic skin lesions and contributes to pathological extracellular matrix remodeling. In this project, an antisense oligonucleotide (AON) delivery system was developed for the treatment of skin fibrosis. In this respect, two antifibrotic agents, i) AON against CTGF and ii) antifibrotic polypeptide amphiphile, were self-assembled into nanofibers to enhance antifibrotic efficacy. The nanofibers were encapsulated in chitosan nanoparticles (CNPs) for protection and sustained release. Loaded CNPs were characterized by morphology, size, endosomal escape, and skin penetration using a transwell-based 3D skin model. The nanoparticles exhibited an average size of 220 nm. The encapsulation efficiency of CNPs was 52%, providing sustained nanofiber release over 7 days. With the use of nanoparticles, clear reduction trends were observed in CTGF, α-smooth muscle actin (αSMA), and collagen expression. CNPs penetrated the skin model gradually, revealing no cytotoxicity to skin cells. Overall, these results reveal the potential of the designed nanofibers as a therapeutic agent and the CNPs as the carrier of the nanofibers. The developed delivery system can be used as an alternative approach for the treatment of lesions in fibrotic skin.

abstract: Secreted frizzled-related protein 2 (SFRP2) is an important molecule that regulates cell growth and development and participates in hair follicle (HF) development and homeostasis. The present study seeks to determine whether SFRP2 directly targets dermal papilla cells (DPCs), the pivotal functional cell population within HF, and characterize the intracellular signaling regulatory network triggered downstream. In this study, a CRISPR/Cas9-mediated SFRP2 gene editing DPC model was established in vitro. Multi-omics analyses, including transcriptomics and metabolomics, were performed alongside functional assays to investigate the regulatory mechanisms of SFRP2 in DPCs. Among three designed single guide RNAs (sgRNAs), sgRNA3 showed the highest editing efficiency (67.0%) without off-target effects. Genetic editing of SFRP2 markedly increased the transcript levels of pivotal hair follicle‑development‑related genes (LEF1, CCND1 and Wnt2). Meanwhile, it suppressed TGF‑β1 transcription, which resulted in elevated proliferation capacity and diminished apoptotic activity within DPCs. Transcriptomic profiling identified 2288 differentially expressed genes (DEGs) enriched in PI3K-Akt, MAPK and TNF signaling pathways, while metabolomic analysis identified 185 differential metabolites (DMs) associated with apoptosis, ABC transporters, and PI3K-Akt signaling. Integrated multi-omics analysis confirmed PI3K-Akt signaling as a central regulatory axis. Western blot analysis revealed increased phosphorylation of PI3K and Akt following SFRP2 editing, indicating pathway activation. Treatment of SFRP2-edited DPCs with the PI3K inhibitor LY294002 reduced the elevated phosphorylation and reversed the functional phenotypes, confirming PI3K-Akt pathway involvement. Collectively, these findings indicate that SFRP2 mediates DPC biological activities by means of PI3K‑Akt‑driven transcriptional‑metabolic networks, yielding novel perspectives on the molecular regulatory machinery controlling HF physiology.

abstract: Staphylococcal bacteriophages with proven therapeutic efficacy in anti-staphylococcal therapy have large (~140 kb) genomes and belong to subfamily Twortvirinae. Representatives of four genera (Kayvirus, Silviavirus, Sepunavirus, and Twortvirus) are the most intensively studied and are advancing toward clinical applications. However, the functions of many of their genes remain unknown and cannot be predicted from sequence homology alone. The least explored and most diverse genomic regions are the long terminal repeats (LTRs), which comprise ~10% of the virion DNA. These regions were often omitted from early genome assemblies or misplaced in genomic maps. Only recent studies have shown that LTRs encode genes expressed immediately upon infection and involved in host takeover, genome establishment, and interactions with bacterial defense systems, highlighting their critical role in successful infection during phage therapy. This review synthesizes current knowledge on the genomic architecture, transcriptional organization, and molecular functions of LTR regions in Twortvirinae phages. By integrating comparative genomics with recent transcriptomic and phage-host interaction studies, we identify LTRs as key regulatory and evolutionary hubs in Twortvirinae biology and highlight major knowledge gaps concerning their roles in bacterial immunity and phage genome evolution. The enrichment of LTRs in targets of bacterial anti-phage defense systems, together with their dynamic evolution through gene gain, loss, and diversification, suggests a central role in phage adaptation to diverse hosts. Finally, our synthesis of available data allows us, for the first time, to infer which end of the phage genome enters the host cell first during infection.

abstract:
BACKGROUND: Seasonal influenza epidemics cause significant mortality, especially among the elderly. Influenza A virus triggers the host innate immune system through various mechanisms. Human enzymes belonging to the group of RNA-acting adenosine deaminases (ADARs) play a role in the innate antiviral immune response, partly by inducing mutations in viral RNA. The effect of this mechanismin influenza A virus infection remains unexplained in humans.
OBJECTIVE: The aim of this study was to assess the clinical impact of ADAR-induced mutations on influenza A virus in hospitalised patients.
METHODS: Full-genome deep sequencing of Influenza A virus was performed on respiratory samples from 75 hospitalised, Influenza A(H3N2) virus infected patients, aged 41 to 95 years. ADAR-associated mutations in minor viral subpopulations were analysed in relation to demographic and clinical factors.
RESULTS: ADAR-associated mutations showed a significant inverse correlation with viral load (p < 0.0001) and age (p = 0.0051), especially in patients older than 75 years. The association between ADAR-associated mutations and viral load was independent of age, inflammation, and disease severity (p < 0.001).
CONCLUSIONS: We found an association between ADAR-induced mutations and viral load, which may indicate an antiviral function of ADAR on influenza A virus. The lower mutation rate and associated higher viral load in the elderly suggest an age-dependent reduced ADAR activity, which may contribute to increased disease severity.

abstract: Chemical conjugation can modulate antisense oligonucleotide (ASO) pharmacology and improve organ-specific delivery, yet whole-tissue measurements provide limited information on cell-specific activity. Here, we used metastasis-associated lung adenocarcinoma transcript 1 (Malat1) knockdown as a pharmacodynamic readout to compare whole-tissue and cell-resolved activity of chemically conjugated ASOs in platelet-derived growth factor receptor alpha-enhanced green fluorescent protein (PDGFR-eGFP) mouse model to assess their in vivo uptake in PDGFR-expressing (GFP+) cells. This reporter mouse model uses PDGFR as an exemplar cellular marker and provides an accessible tool for evaluating ASO conjugate activity within mesenchymal stromal and progenitor populations, mainly tissue fibroblasts. Following subcutaneous administration, Malat1 was quantified in whole tissues and cell-sorted PDGFR+/GFP or PDGFR-/GFP- populations. ASO-mediated Malat1 reduction varied by tissue and conjugate chemistry, with palmitate conjugation producing the broadest extrahepatic activity and pronounced whole-tissue activity in heart and skeletal muscle. Cell-resolved analysis further revealed preferential palmitate-ASO activity within PDGFR skeletal-muscle populations. Preliminary safety assessment also showed conjugate-dependent differences, with body-weight loss and ALT elevation in tocopherol-ASO-treated male mice and spleen enlargement in both sexes. These findings present an in vivo modelling system for evaluating cell-specific ASO activity and demonstrate the advantages of cell-resolved assessment over whole-tissue measurements.

abstract: Extracellular vesicles (EVs) hold immense therapeutic potential, yet their clinical translation is hindered by nonspecific cellular uptake and the complexity and cost of surface engineering. Here, we present the EZON (Easy OligoNucleotide) EV modification platform, a cost-effective, post-isolation modification system that addresses both limitations simultaneously. The EZON platform employs unmodified DNA aptamers that bind directly to tetraspanin proteins on EV surfaces, eliminating the need for cholesterol conjugation, covalent chemistry, or genetic engineering of producer cells. EVs are thus easily and rapidly functionalized in a single incubation step at substantially reduced oligonucleotide cost. The EZON platform enables dual functionality: (1) the oligonucleotide anchor (ONA) sequence inhibits nonspecific cellular uptake, while (2) the display strand enables targeted delivery through ligand-mediated internalization. We demonstrate that our optimized ONA construct efficiently functionalizes EVs from multiple mammalian cell types. Cancer cells selectively internalized EZON-modified EVs functionalized with AS1411, an aptamer that targets nucleolin, whereas off-target internalization was suppressed. The platform's versatility extends to protein display via histidine-tag aptamers and therapeutic cargo delivery, as demonstrated by targeted doxorubicin delivery to head and neck squamous cell carcinoma cells. This rapid, modular approach transforms unmodified EVs into precision delivery vehicles within hours, offering a scalable solution for targeted therapeutics.

abstract: CIRV2 is a Phase IV randomized, open-label, trial of FDA-approved COVID-19 and/or influenza vaccines (no more than minimal risk) with longitudinal follow-up. In 2026 CIRV2 will compare immunogenicity and reactogenicity of the recombinant Novavax COVID-19 vaccine and the mRNA Pfizer-BioNTech COVID-19 vaccine.

outcomes.description: The primary endpoint is variant-specific immune response (magnitude and breadth) to licensed recombinant and mRNA COVID-19 products administered to adult MHS beneficiaries who are eligible for a fall COVID-19 vaccine and who are not severely immunocompromised. This will include quantifying the magnitude of binding and neutralizing antibodies to the vaccine variants and to the dominant variant present 30 days and 150 days post-vaccination. Specifically, we will test neutralizing titers (defined as the inverse serum dilution causing a 50% reduction in relative light units in a pseudovirus neutralization assay) and IgG binding antibody levels (measured in arbitrary units) against the following SARS-CoV-2 variants: XFG (vaccine strain), Wuhan-1 (ancestral strain), plus the dominant circulating variant(s) circulating during the fall of 2026 and winter of 2026-2027.
outcomes.measure: Variant-specific immune responses (Year 2 Only)
outcomes.time_frame: IgG binding antibody levels and neutralizing antibody titers will be assessed on serum samples obtained just prior to vaccination, 30 days (+/- 10 days), and 150 days (+/- 10 days) after vaccination.

outcomes.description: The primary endpoint is variant-specific immune response (magnitude and breadth) to licensed recombinant and mRNA COVID-19 products administered to healthy adult MHS beneficiaries. This will include quantifying the magnitude of binding and neutralizing antibodies to the vaccine variants and to the dominant variant present one month post-vaccination. Specifically, we will test neutralizing titers (defined as the inverse serum dilution causing a 50% reduction in relative light units in a pseudovirus neutralization assay) and IgG binding antibody levels (measured in arbitrary units) against the following SARS-CoV-2 variants: NB.1.8.1 and XFG (predominant circulating strains in fall 2025), JN.1 and LP.8.1 (vaccine strains), and Wuhan-1 (ancestral strain).
outcomes.measure: Variant-specific immune responses (Year 1 Only)
outcomes.time_frame: IgG binding antibody levels and neutralizing antibody titers will be assessed on serum samples obtained just prior to vaccination and 30 days (+/- 10 days after vaccination).

outcomes.description: Salivary and nasopharyngeal IgG and IgA antibody levels to vaccine SARS-CoV-2 strain and dominant SARS-CoV-2 circulating strain at 30 days and 5 months post vaccination will be compared between the study arms using GMT and GSD. T-tests will compare responses across two SARS-CoV-2 variants (i.e., the vaccine variant and the dominant circulating variant at the time of vaccination), stratified by vaccine type and adjusted for multiple comparisons (e.g., a Tukey's adjustment). A non-parametric comparison can be used if there is non-normally distributed data despite the use of GMT, these approaches also account for multiplicity (e.g., Kruskall-Wallis with a Dunn's adjustment for multiplicity adjustment).
