outcomes.description: Antigenic cartography and antibody landscapes may be performed by FDA collaborators to visualize antigenic drift from the vaccine with sequential variants, leveraging prior analysis approaches used by the study team. These analyses use relative differences in neutralizing antibody responses to generate two-dimensional maps (antigenic cartography) or three-dimensional landscapes that enable one to assess how antigenically similar different virus strains are to each other. Antibody landscapes are useful tools which can capture differential multiple serial antigenic exposures in comparisons of antibody titer and breadth between individuals assigned to receive the recombinant or mRNA vaccines (see examples from Wang et al., Cell Host Microbe, 2022).
outcomes.measure: Antigenic cartography and antibody landscapes
outcomes.time_frame: Antigenic cartography studies may be conducted using neutralizing antibody titers obtained just prior to vaccination and 30 days (+/- 10 days) after vaccination.

abstract: Phosphorothioate-modified antisense oligonucleotides (ASOs) enter cells, but their site of productive escape remains uncertain. We combined live-cell imaging and ratiometric pH measurements to follow a Malat1-targeting ASO internalized without a delivery vehicle. In U2OS cells, less than 4% of internalized ASO reached the nucleus under conditions that reduced Malat1 RNA by >90%. Most ASO accumulated in late endosomes, endolysosomes and lysosomes as foci and broadly distributed luminal signal. These compartments underwent neutralization without detectable membrane rupture or galectin-3 recruitment. ASO foci showed constrained motion, consistent with association with endolysosomal constituents. L-leucyl-L-leucine methyl ester-induced membrane damage or Calcium dependent lysosome exocytosis released dextran while retaining luminal ASO. Loss of the stress-granule scaffolding proteins G3BP1/2 modestly enhanced ASO activity without detectable endolysosomal damage. Tantalosin, a small molecule that perturbs endosomal recycling, redistributed the ESCRT-III protein IST1 to endosomes. It enhanced early escape of SYTOX Green and ASOs, detected by nuclear accumulation, and increased Malat1 knockdown, with cell-type-dependent responses. Tantalosin did not detectably increase nuclear ASO accumulation after sequestration in late compartments. These findings place productive ASO escape early in endocytic trafficking, most likely in early or recycling endosomes, before sequestration in largely nonproductive late compartments.

abstract: This is a prospective, multicenter, phase I/II, open-label, two-stage design of PD1+ TILs infusion in metastatic or advanced TNBC. TILS001 includes 3 parts. Previous to each phase inclusion, a specific ICF must be signed by the patient. Participants potentially eligible to participate in the clinical trial will be offered to sign a ICF three times prior to TILs treatment: 1) to allow for collection of archival FFPE tissue samples for determination PD1 by mRNA (Part #1), 2) prior to a fresh metastatic biopsy for selection, isolation and partial expansion of PD1+ TILs (Part #2) and 3) prior to allow for remaining study procedures and TILs therapy (Part #3, Main Consent).

description: This trial has been developed in TNBC, a breast cancer subtype with a particularly poor prognosis. The product used for treating participating patients will be selected PD1-positive TILs. Such TILs will be manufactured in Hospital Clinic under the name of NUMARZU-001. The procotol has been designed in three parts to better select participating patients. Molecular pre-screening has been established to select tumors with a higher probability of enrichment by PD1-positive TILs. The pre- screening consists of performing a tumor biopsy and selecting isolation and expansion of PD1- postive TILs to manufacture the final product NUMARZU-001. This part could last almost four weeks, as such patients will continue with the established treatment in the meanwhile. Finally, NUMARZU-001 will be administered if the patient is eligible for part three of the protocol.

abstract:
The Investigators have demonstrated in preclinical studies that RNA liposomes activate APCs, induce antigen-specific T cell immunity, and can supplant DCs in a cell therapy model for HGG and have shown feasibility and activity of this approach in preclinical models and in canine patients with a spontaneous malignant glioma. In one arm of this study, we will investigate the safety and immunologic activity of RNA-LP vaccines in pediatric patients with recurrent pHGG.

The investigators have also shown that intravenous administration of tumor mRNA loaded lipid particles (LPs) localizes primarily to lung, transfect antigen presenting cells (APCs) and lead to an activated T cell response for induction of anti-tumor immunity. In contrast to other formulations, RNA-LPs recruit multiple arms of the immune system (i.e. innate/adaptive), and remodel the systemic/intratumoral immune milieu, which remain potent barriers for vaccine, cellular, and checkpoint inhibiting immunotherapies. After only a single RNA-LP vaccine, the bulk of systemic and intratumoral dendritic cells (DCs) in mice display an activated phenotype; these activated DCs (harvested from tumors) expand antigen specific T cell immunity. In immunologically resistant pulmonary osteosacroma murine tumor models (i.e. K7M2), RNA-LPs induce robust anti-tumor efficacy in settings where immune checkpoint inhibitors (i.e. anti-PD-L1 therapy) do not confer therapeutic benefit. The investigators have already demonstrated safety of RNA-LPs in acute/chronic murine toxicity studies, and in client-owned canine trial.

In this study, we will investigate the manufacturing feasibility, safety and immunologic activity of RNA-LP vaccine in patients with recurrent pulmonary or unresectable osteosarcoma and recurrent pHGG.

description:
For recurrent pHGG there will be two non-randomized arms assigned at the discretion of the patient and treatment team:

* Arm 1-A single neoadjuvant pp65 RNA-LP (DP1) will be administered prior to surgical resection/biopsy, and then two adjuvant DP1.
* Arm 2-Surgical resection/biopsy will occur first and all three DP1 will be administered in the adjuvant setting

For recurrent OSA there will be three arms based on disease status on enrollment:

* Arm 1-Patients with unilateral pulmonary-only metastatic recurrent OSA
* Arm 2-Patients with bilateral pulmonary-only metastatic recurrent OSA
* Arm 3-Patients with unresectable OSA in any location.

The Phase I dose-escalation study for either recurrent/progressive pHGG or recurrent OSA cohort will be performed in 18 subjects using a 3+3 design. Both recurrent pHGG trial arms will be enrolled together as a single cohort for safety, and similarly all recurrent OSA trial arms will be enrolled together as a single cohort for safety during phase I.

abstract: Dentin is the primary mineralized tissue of the tooth, essential for pulp protection and enamel support. Its regenerative capacity is critical for dental health. This review summarizes recent progress in odontogenic regeneration, covering fundamental biological mechanisms and translational applications. A literature search of peer-reviewed studies on odontogenic regeneration, dental tissue engineering, and biomaterial-based strategies was conducted. Key advances include signaling pathway-guided stem cell differentiation into functional odontoblasts, which promotes reparative dentin matrix formation, and biomaterial innovations that provide optimized cellular microenvironments. Emerging clinical strategies, including 3D printing, growth factor delivery systems, and gene-editing approaches, are also discussed. Despite substantial progress, challenges remain in the precise control of stem cell fate specification, long-term biocompatibility of biomaterials, and high clinical costs. Future interdisciplinary integration holds promise for overcoming these hurdles, advancing personalized therapies, and expanding dental restoration and regenerative medicine. The evolving strategies offer meaningful potential for dentin-pulp complex regeneration, improved pulp preservation, personalized scaffold fabrication via 3D printing, and the eventual development of cost-effective, biocompatible clinical therapies.

abstract: Periodontitis is a common chronic inflammatory disease driven by pathogenic biofilms, leading to progressive periodontal tissue destruction and systemic health risks. Conventional therapies often fail to eradicate biofilms in deep periodontal pockets, promote antimicrobial resistance and offer limited regenerative potential. Although SDT has emerged as a promising alternative, its clinical efficacy is constrained by several material- and microenvironment-related barriers that have not been systematically addressed in previous reviews. Sonodynamic therapy (SDT) employs low-intensity ultrasound to activate sonosensitizers, generating reactive oxygen species (ROS) and inducing mechanical disruption of biofilms, with advantages of deep tissue penetration, broad-spectrum antimicrobial activity and low risk of resistance. Nevertheless, conventional sonosensitizers often exhibit poor water solubility, rapid clearance, limited specificity, and suboptimal ROS generation, while hypoxia, continuous fluid turnover, and mechanical disturbance within periodontal pockets further compromise local retention and therapeutic efficacy. Advances in biomaterials address these barriers by engineering high-performance sonosensitizers to enhance ROS efficiency, developing delivery systems to improve solubility and prolonged retention and integrating multimodal antibacterial and regenerative functions. This review summarizes the mechanistic basis of SDT with recent advances in sonosensitizer engineering, local delivery platforms, synergistic therapies, and multifunctional biomaterials, thereby linking antimicrobial performance to periodontal tissue regeneration. We further identify hypoxia, delivery efficiency, biosafety and the lack of standardized evaluation as key translational challenges, and propose future directions including AI-guided sonosensitizer design, precision delivery systems, and CRISPR-assisted antimicrobial combination strategies to accelerate the clinical translation of SDT for periodontitis management.

abstract: Autism spectrum disorder has been linked to disrupted RNA processing during corticogenesis, yet variant-specific mechanisms remain difficult to resolve. Isogenic cerebral organoids derived from a patient-derived induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC) line carrying the HNRNPH2-R114W variant and its CRISPR-corrected counterpart serve as a human developmental model to investigate variant-associated RNA dysregulation. Imaging quantification and exploratory bulk RNA sequencing, performed at a single developmental time point on a pooled organoid RNA from each genotype, identify coordinated remodeling of neuronal and metabolic programs, along with junction-centered splicing dysregulation involving 6,310 differentially used junctions. Computational structural docking situates HNRNPH2 RNA recognition motifs (RRMs) 1-3 within a spliceosomal context and locates residue R114 near a predicted RNA-contact interface, indicating that the R114W substitution may alter RNA engagement. Integration of differential expression with event- and isoform-level analyses identifies regulatory hubs enriched for axon guidance and synaptic signaling pathways. Single-cell-reference-based deconvolution suggests modest compositional shifts that are unlikely to account for the extent of transcriptional and splicing alterations observed. Collectively, these findings imply HNRNPH2-R114W in widespread RNA rewiring and define candidate isoform-level endpoints for mechanistic and therapeutic investigation in human cortical organoids. These molecular signatures open new avenues to examine how HNRNPH2-associated RNA dysregulation evolves across developmental time and recurs across independent biological contexts, providing a foundation for further mechanistic studies of this rare neurodevelopmental disorder.

abstract: Carbapenem-resistant Klebsiella pneumoniae (CRKP) poses a major public health threat due to high mortality and limited therapeutic options. Rapid and accurate detection of both species identity and resistance determinants is critical for clinical management. Here, we developed a dual-target recombinase polymerase amplification-CRISPR/Cas12a multiplex lateral flow assay (DRC-MLFA) for simultaneous detection of K. pneumoniae and blaKPC in a single reaction. This platform introduces a functionally differentiated dual-channel detection strategy, in which the K. pneumoniae signal is generated directly via RPA-lateral flow readout, while blaKPC detection is achieved through an additional CRISPR/Cas12a-mediated verification step. To enable one-pot integration, suboptimal protospacer adjacent motif (PAM) sequences were employed to delay Cas12a activation, thereby coordinating amplification and CRISPR detection within a single reaction system. Under optimized conditions, the assay achieved dual-target detection within 50 min at 37 °C, with a limit of detection of 101 CFU/μL and high specificity against non-target pathogens. Validation with 30 clinical samples showed strong concordance with quantitative PCR. This portable and low-cost biosensor provides a practical solution for point-of-care detection of CRKP and establishes a framework for integrating hierarchical specificity control into multiplex CRISPR diagnostics.

abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Tendon injuries heal through disorganized extracellular matrix (ECM) deposition rather than the restoration of native collagen architecture, thus resulting in suboptimal functional recovery. Although adipose-derived stem cells (ADSCs) are attractive for tendon regeneration because of their accessibility and expandability, their tenogenic differentiation efficiency is lower than that of tendon-derived stem cells (TDSCs). C1q/TNF-related protein 3 (CTRP3) is an adipokine implicated in ECM remodeling and fibrosis; however, its role in tendon lineage regulation is unknown.
OBJECTIVE: CTRP3 (C1q/TNF-related protein 3) contributes to extracellular-matrix remodeling and, in tendon, is associated with a pathological fibrotic matrix signature; we therefore reasoned that reducing CTRP3 would favor a more mature tendon-like matrix. Using a loss-of-function approach based on clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats (CRISPR)/CRISPR-associated protein 9 (Cas9), we investigated whether CTRP3 disruption alters tenogenic marker expression, at both the transcript and protein levels, and the tendon-associated ECM marker profile of canine ADSCs relative to wild-type ADSCs and native TDSCs.
METHODS: CRISPR/Cas9-mediated CTRP3-disrupted ADSCs were generated and validated using sequencing, quantitative polymerase chain reaction, and Western blotting. Wild-type ADSCs, CTRP3-disrupted ADSCs, and TDSCs were subjected to tenogenic induction for 0-3 weeks. Tenogenic transcriptional and ECM markers were analyzed at mRNA and protein levels.
RESULTS: CTRP3-disrupted ADSCs showed increased collagen type I and tenomodulin (TNMD) expression during tenogenic induction compared with wild-type ADSCs. COL III expression showed a transient increase followed by a decline, with lower expression in CTRP3-disrupted cADSCs than in WT cADSCs at week 2. CTRP3 disruption increased early Mkx and Scx expression at the earliest time points but did not consistently alter the early transcriptional program, which rose comparably across all groups. CTRP3-disrupted cADSCs showed partial, marker- and time-point-dependent overlap with native cTDSCs, mainly for selected late ECM markers rather than across the overall transcript and protein profiles.
CONCLUSION: CTRP3 disruption shifted the tendon-associated ECM marker profile during the tenogenic differentiation of ADSCs, with reduced COL III accumulation, rather than uniformly enhancing tenogenic differentiation. Although early transcriptional changes were observed, the more consistent differences were found in late tendon-associated ECM markers. The modulation of CTRP3 may represent a candidate strategy worth further investigation for stem cell-based tendon regeneration in veterinary medicine.

title: Abstract 13963: Endocardial-Specific and Sex-Dependent Role of RNA-Binding Protein DDX3X in Cardiac Development and Disease

abstract: Neurodegenerative diseases such as Parkinson's disease (PD), Alzheimer's disease (AD), Huntington's disease (HD), multiple sclerosis (MS), and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) place substantial burden on global public health. Mounting evidence identifies mitochondrial dysfunction as a central contributor to neuronal damage and progressive brain functional decline. As a narrative review, this work aims to dissect mitochondrial‑associated pathological features across these major neurodegenerative disorders, summarize under‑recognized emerging mechanisms, and highlight translational bottlenecks for mitochondrial‑targeted therapies. Mitochondria sustain neuronal survival by mediating oxidative‑phosphorylation‑driven energy production, biomolecule biosynthesis, calcium homeostasis, reactive oxygen species (ROS) metabolism, and apoptotic regulation. In PD, aggregated α‑synuclein (α‑syn) damages respiratory‑chain complex I, perturbs mitochondrial dynamics and blocks PINK1/Parkin‑dependent mitophagy. In AD, amyloid‑β together with hyper‑phosphorylated tau (p-Tau) impairs respiratory complex activity, axonal mitochondrial trafficking and mitophagic clearance. Mutant huntingtin induces multiple mitochondrial lesions in HD, while inflammation‑triggered oxidative stress secondarily compromises mitochondrial function in MS. Pathogenic mutations in ALS disrupt respiratory‑chain assembly, mitochondrial dynamics and mitophagy. Beyond classic mitochondrial defects including respiratory‑chain impairment, dynamic imbalance and defective mitophagy, emerging mechanisms such as mitocytosis, mitochondrial aminoacyl‑tRNA synthetase (mt‑aaRS) dysfunction and mitochondria‑associated membrane (MAM) disruption are discussed. Mitochondrial dysfunction drives neurodegeneration via energy exhaustion, aggravated oxidative stress, pathological protein aggregation and excessive neuronal apoptosis. We further recapitulate mitochondrial‑oriented therapeutic approaches including small‑molecule regulators, mitophagy activators, mitochondrial biogenesis promoters, gene‑editing strategies and mitochondrial transplantation. Notable translational obstacles remain, including limited blood‑brain‑barrier penetration of candidate drugs, narrow therapeutic time‑window post‑symptom onset, and prominent disease heterogeneity. By synthesizing basic experimental findings and pre‑clinical and clinical trial progress, this review provides updated insights into the pathogenesis of neurodegenerative diseases and facilitates the development of precise mitochondrial‑targeted therapeutic regimens.

title: The "Invisible Killer" of Neurodegeneration: Mitochondrial Dysfunction in Neurodegenerative Disorders, Mechanisms, Emerging Pathways and Therapeutic Strategies.

abstract: RNA 5-methylcytidine (m5C) modification plays an essential role in regulating RNA metabolism and functions in cellular processes. Tools to achieve temporal and transcript-specific m5C editing for functional studies are still limited. Furthermore, methods enabling m5C editing triggered by specific cellular signals to study m5C functions are currently lacking. Here, we present a temporally and conditionally controlled m5C writing platform engineered through integrating abscisic acid (ABA)-mediated chemically induced proximity with split-dCas13b-NSUN2/NSUN6 technology. This system enables the writing of m5C by reconstituting the split dCas13b-based m5C editing complex at the guide RNA (gRNA)-targeted RNA transcript sites under the control of the inducer ABA. The deposition of m5C is inducible, reversible and selective. The deposited m5C is biologically active and influences the stability of endogenous mRNA transcripts. Moreover, by incorporating ABA prodrugs, the m5C writing can be triggered by signals associated with distinct physiological or disease conditions (e.g., tumor microenvironment and senescence). This conditional m5C editing strategy provides a new programmable tool for studying m5C biology in a context-dependent manner and expands the repertoire of RNA modification editing technologies.

title: Impact of RNA modification and IL-12 boosts on mRNA-LNP vaccine-elicited CD8+ T cell responses

abstract: Transfer RNA-derived small RNAs (tDRs) are a class of functional small non-coding RNAs, many of which are induced by stress conditions and have been implicated in tissue injury and disease pathogenesis. However, their role in intestinal ischemia/reperfusion (I/R) injury remains unclear. Using tDR sequencing, we identified that tDR-Glu-TTC was significantly upregulated in intestinal tissues, plasma, epithelial cells, and human clinical samples; and its levels positively correlated with the severity of intestinal injury. Functionally, tDR-Glu-TTC exacerbates intestinal mucosal damage by activating TNF pathway-mediated necroptosis in intestinal epithelial cells. Mechanistically, tDR-Glu-TTC directly binds to and suppresses the RNA-editing enzyme ADAR1, impairing adenosine-to-inosine editing of autophagy-related transcripts (ATG18 and Lamp2). This inhibits autophagy, leading to the accumulation of damaged mitochondria, and the release of reactive oxygen species (ROS). The elevated ROS subsequently promotes TNF-α secretion, triggering TNF pathway-mediated necroptosis. Furthermore, increased ROS downregulates TRMT6/61A-dependent m¹A methylation of tRNA-Glu-TTC, increasing tDR-Glu-TTC biogenesis and forming a pathogenic positive feedback loop. Thus, therapeutic dual-target intervention using N-acetylcysteine combined with tDR-Glu-TTC-antagomir synergistically mitigated I/R-induced intestinal injury in vivo. In summary, our study unveiled a previously unrecognized mechanism by which tDR-Glu-TTC exacerbates intestinal I/R injury via the ADAR1/autophagy/ROS/necroptosis signaling axis, offering a promising therapeutic strategy for combating intestinal I/R injury.

title: 1048 Targeting the early ovarian cancer antigen ORF1p with an mRNA-LNP vaccine for cancer interception

abstract: SIRPA delivers an anti-phagocytic "don't-eat-me" signal through its expression on macrophage membrane surface and promotes tumor progression via membrane-independent mechanism. However, current CD47- and SIRPA-targeting agents only disrupt cell-surface inhibitory signaling, highlighting the therapeutic potential of degrading SIRPA. Here, we identified that E3 ubiquitin ligase TRIM2 interacted with SIRPA in vitro. Clinically, elevated TRIM2 expression is associated with prolonged overall and progression-free survival in renal-cell carcinoma (RCC) patients. Mechanistically, TRIM2 catalyzes K48-linked poly-ubiquitination of SIRPA, promoting its proteasomal degradation and reducing SIRPA protein levels. CRISPR/Cas9-mediated deletion of TRIM2 in macrophages upregulated SIRPA, significantly impairing phagocytosis of tumor cells. TRIM2 deficiency also promoted tumor growth by increasing intratumoral infiltration of M2-type macrophage, reducing accumulation of anti-tumor M1-like and antigen-presenting macrophages, and impairing effector CD8+ T-cell recruitment. Importantly, combined TRIM2 overexpression and PD-L1 blockade synergistically enhance anti-tumor immunity. Together, these results suggest that targeting TRIM2 may represent a novel therapeutic strategy against RCC by degrading SIRPA in macrophage and provide a roadmap for clinical application.

title: TRIM2 facilitates macrophage mediated anti-tumor immunity in renal cell carcinoma through enhancing SIRPA ubiquitination and degradation.

abstract: Cellular senescence is accompanied by profound lysosomal alterations, yet whether lysosome-associated factors actively drive aging remains unclear. Through a focused CRISPR/Cas9 screen in human mesenchymal progenitor cells (hMPCs), we identified N-acetylglucosamine-1-phosphotransferase subunits alpha and beta (GNPTAB), an enzyme responsible for lysosomal hydrolase targeting, as a positive regulator of cellular senescence. Genetic ablation of GNPTAB attenuated senescence, whereas its overexpression accelerated senescence. This pro-senescent function occurred independently of GNPTAB's canonical enzymatic role. Instead, GNPTAB binds to the innate immune adaptor stimulator of interferon genes (STING) through an interface involving the critical residue E1119, leading to activation of STING and its downstream TANK-binding kinase 1 (TBK1), as well as pro-inflammatory gene expression. A STING-binding-deficient GNPTAB mutant (E1119A) preserved canonical lysosomal functions but failed to induce senescence, while STING depletion abolished GNPTAB-driven senescence. Together, these findings uncover a new signaling pathway wherein GNPTAB engages STING to facilitate its activation, suggesting that the GNPTAB-STING interaction interface may serve as a potential therapeutic target for ameliorating age-related cellular dysfunction.

title: CRISPR screening identifies GNPTAB as a noncanonical STING activator driving cellular senescence.

abstract: Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) is a chronic, relapsing inflammatory disorder characterized by dysregulation of the intestinal immune system, in which functional abnormalities of phagocytes such as macrophages play a critical role in pathogenesis. Although conventional therapies such as anti-tumor necrosis factor-α (TNF-α) antibodies are widely used in clinical practice, they have limitations including low response rates and significant side effects, creating an urgent need for novel therapeutic strategies. In recent years, macrophage-directed immunotherapy has emerged as a cutting-edge approach for IBD treatment by reprogramming intestinal phagocytes to restore immune homeostasis. Unlike previous reviews that primarily focus on the M1/M2 polarization framework, this review integrates recent single-cell discoveries of novel macrophage subsets (e.g. SPP1+ and TREM2+ macrophages), systematically examines the crosstalk among signaling, epigenetic, and metabolic regulatory layers, and critically evaluates translational barriers from preclinical models to clinical application. By evaluating preclinical and clinical studies, we assess the potential and challenges of these strategies. Through in-depth analysis, this review aims to provide a theoretical basis for the development of more precise and effective immunotherapies for IBD and to point out future research directions. (Literature search: PubMed, Web of Science, and Embase; January 2000-December 2025.).

title: Macrophage-directed immunotherapy in Inflammatory bowel disease: advances in reprogramming intestinal phagocytes.

abstract: The rapidly global deployment of COVID-19 mRNA-LNP vaccines established the clinical feasibility of combining RNA medicine with LNP delivery systems, transforming a long-standing experimental concept into a scalable therapeutic modality, previously considered impossible. Currently, the value of mRNA-LNPs has been expanding from infectious disease vaccines to cancer immunotherapy, personalized neoantigen vaccination, in vivo immune-cell engineering, protein replacement therapy, mRNA-encoded biologics and genome editing, with particular relevance to hematology and oncology. However, in hematologic and oncologic settings, therapeutic success is constrained by biological barriers that less prominent in prophylactic vaccination. Systemically administered LNPs are strongly influenced by hepatic sequestration, protein corona formation and mononuclear-phagocyte clearance; solid tumors additionally present heterogeneous vasculature, variable enhanced permeability and retention, dense extracellular matrix, elevated interstitial pressure and limited intratumoral diffusion. Hematologic applications face a different set of constraints, including access to spleen and bone marrow, selective delivery to T cells, NK cells and hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells (HSPCs), and preservation of the normal marrow niche. In this Review, we therefore discuss the molecular and principles of formulation that underpin mRNA-LNP performance in hematology and oncology, including mRNA engineering, lipid nanoparticle architecture, intracellular trafficking and selective organ targeting(SORT) delivery strategies, oncology applications spanning neoantigen vaccines, tumor-microenvironment reprogramming, mRNA-encoded biologics, gene editing and combination therapy; and hematology applications including in vivo CAR-T, CAR-NK and HSPC engineering. We further consider how inefficient extrahepatic delivery, limited endosomal escape, context-dependent reactogenicity, repeat-dosing constraints and the manufacturing complexity of individualized products continue to limit broader clinical translation. Emerging strategies, including artificial-intelligence-guided RNA and lipid design, self-amplifying RNA, circular RNA and next-generation thermostable formulations, may help address these application limitations in the fields of hematology and oncology.

title: The advances and challenges of mRNA-LNP application in fields of hematology and oncology therapeutics.

abstract: mRNA-lipid nanoparticle (LNP) vaccines are detectable in human blood after vaccination, but platform-specific differences in systemic persistence and transcript integrity remain poorly defined. We analyzed serial blood samples from 73 participants receiving Moderna mRNA-1273 (three formulations), Pfizer/BioNTech BNT162b2, or an investigational receptor-binding domain (RBD) mRNA vaccine (three different doses). Using droplet digital polymerase chain reaction (ddPCR) assays, we quantified total and long-range linked ("intact") vaccine mRNA, and we measured vaccine-specific ionizable lipids by liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry (LC-MS). Across platforms, mRNA decay was fastest for mRNA-1273, intermediate for BNT162b2, and slowest for the RBD vaccine, with ionizable lipid decay following the same rank order. Notably, intact spike mRNA declined 2-fold faster after mRNA-1273 than BNT162b2 vaccination. Kinetics modeling revealed platform-dependent coupling of mRNA and lipid kinetics: intact mRNA tracked closely with SM-102 for mRNA-1273, whereas ALC-0315 persisted longer than intact mRNA for BNT162b2. A ten-fragment linkage ddPCR panel spanning the spike transcript showed lower linkage toward 3'-proximal regions that mirrored the administered mRNA-1273 formulation. Together, these data provide a quantitative framework for benchmarking mRNA-LNP platform kinetics and transcript integrity in humans.

title: In Vivo Blood Kinetics and Transcript Integrity of Three mRNA-Lipid Nanoparticle Vaccines in Humans.

abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Small interfering RNA (siRNA) has progressed from an experimental gene-silencing tool to an established therapeutic modality through advances in chemical modification and delivery. Lipid nanoparticles (LNP) and N-acetylgalactosamine (GalNAc)-siRNA conjugates have driven this clinical translation, particularly for liver-directed applications. Extending comparable delivery efficiency and selectivity to non-hepatocyte cell populations and extrahepatic tissues remains a major challenge.
AREAS COVERED: This review examines approved and late-stage siRNA therapeutics and the delivery principles underlying their clinical development. Relevant publications and clinical trial records from 1998 to 2026 were identified through PubMed and ClinicalTrials.gov, supplemented by regulatory agency reports. LNP-based delivery, GalNAc-mediated hepatocyte targeting, and emerging strategies for non-parenchymal liver cells and extrahepatic tissues are discussed, with emphasis on the factors governing cell-selective and productive delivery. Next-generation delivery technologies and the therapeutic distinctions between siRNA and antisense oligonucleotides are also considered.
EXPERT OPINION: The next phase of siRNA therapeutics will require a transition from organ-level accumulation toward functional cell-selective delivery. Improved receptor targeting, intracellular trafficking, and endosomal escape, together with rationally designed delivery systems, may extend RNA interference beyond hepatocytes and broaden its therapeutic applications in inflammatory, fibrotic, metabolic, and malignant diseases.

title: siRNA therapeutics: from hepatic delivery to extrahepatic targeting.

abstract: Adenosine-to-inosine RNA editing mediated by endogenous ADAR enzymes represents a promising therapeutic strategy because it can correct mutations at the transcript level without inducing permanent changes to the genome. However, existing systems face challenges, particularly the limited editing efficiency, which limits their practical applications. Here we introduce MARRS (multivalent ADAR1-recruiting RNA editing system)-an efficient and specific RNA editing platform that leverages engineered multivalent RNA aptamers to robustly recruit endogenous ADAR1 enzymes. By optimizing aptamers targeting the Zα domain of ADAR1 p150 and embedding them in a circular RNA scaffold, MARRS enables near-complete adenosine-to-inosine editing of RNA targets in cultured cells and mouse models, achieving efficiencies up to 100% in vitro and 84% in vivo. MARRS also exhibits remarkable versatility across a range of transcript targets while maintaining high specificity with minimal off-target effects. Operating without the need for exogenous enzymes, the MARRS system offers a safe, efficient and programmable platform.

title: Aptamer-mediated multivalent endogenous ADAR1 recruitment for highly efficient RNA editing.

abstract:
AIMS: Eplontersen is an antisense oligonucleotide that suppresses hepatic production of circulating transthyretin (TTR) by targeting TTR mRNA. We present baseline data from an ongoing trial, CARDIO-TTRansform, evaluating eplontersen in patients with TTR amyloid cardiomyopathy (ATTR-CM) and compare findings across previous ATTR-CM trials.
METHODS AND RESULTS: We evaluated 1432 patients enrolled in CARDIO-TTRansform from March 2020 to July 2023 who received ≥1 dose of study intervention (eplontersen or placebo) and had ≥1 post-baseline measurement. Mean (standard deviation) age was 76.4 (7.1) years; 9.4% were female; 88.8% were White. A total of 211 (14.7%) patients had hereditary/variant ATTR-CM (ATTRv-CM); Val122Ile (p.Val142Ile) was the most common genotype (n = 130). Patients spanned New York Heart Association functional classes I (n = 192), II (n = 997), and III (n = 243); 62.6% were National Amyloidosis Centre disease stage 1. Median (interquartile range) N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide was 2025 (1296-3465) pg/ml; n = 51 measured >8500 pg/ml. Median (interquartile range) high-sensitivity troponin T was 50 (35-69) pg/ml and mean left ventricular ejection fraction was 55.7% (9.7%). At baseline, 57.2% were on TTR stabilizer; 18.4% were on sodium-glucose co-transporter-2 inhibitors.
CONCLUSION: The baseline characteristics of CARDIO-TTRansform were consistent with previous ATTR-CM trials; however, CARDIO-TTRansform evaluated patients with a wide range of disease severity and receiving the contemporary standard of care for ATTR-CM. Overall, blinded baseline data suggest that CARDIO-TTRansform provides a unique opportunity to determine the clinical benefits of eplontersen in a contemporary setting and in clinically relevant subgroups of patients with ATTR-CM.

title: Baseline characteristics of patients with transthyretin amyloid cardiomyopathy in the CARDIO-TTRansform trial of eplontersen.

abstract: Premature ovarian insufficiency (POI) is a heterogeneous reproductive and endocrine disorder characterized by impaired ovarian function before the age of 40 years. Conventional management, particularly hormone therapy, addresses hypoestrogenic symptoms and long-term health risks but does not reliably restore endogenous ovarian activity or fertility. Stem cell-based strategies have therefore attracted considerable interest because of their potential paracrine, immunomodulatory, anti-apoptotic, angiogenic, and microenvironment-remodeling effects. This review summarizes current evidence on stem cell sources, therapeutic mechanisms, preclinical models, clinical studies, extracellular vesicle-based approaches, biomaterials, gene-editing strategies, and translational challenges in POI. Particular emphasis is placed on the distinction between mechanistic and animal evidence, uncontrolled or pilot human studies, and controlled clinical evidence. Across preclinical models, mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) frequently improve ovarian histology, hormone profiles, follicular parameters, and reproductive performance; however, these findings cannot be assumed to represent restoration of ovarian reserve or fertility in humans. Clinical evidence remains limited, heterogeneous, and predominantly derived from small non-randomized studies, with outcomes ranging from menstrual recovery and changes in AMH, FSH, estradiol, or antral follicle count to a small number of reported pregnancies. These surrogate changes should be distinguished from clinically meaningful endpoints such as ovulation, ongoing pregnancy, and live birth. Emerging approaches involving extracellular vesicles, biomaterials, and gene editing may improve cell retention or therapeutic potency, but most remain preclinical or early translational strategies. Overall, stem cell therapy should currently be regarded as an investigational approach for POI. Progress toward clinical translation will require standardized cell products, clearly defined dosing and administration routes, appropriate comparator groups, clinically meaningful reproductive endpoints, rigorous long-term safety surveillance, and adequately powered controlled trials.

abstract: Argonaute (Ago) proteins play pivotal roles in nucleic acid targeting across eukaryotes and prokaryotes. While eukaryotic Ago (eAgo) proteins utilize RNA guides to cleave complementary RNA, prokaryotic Ago (pAgo) proteins often employ DNA guides for DNA targeting. This study focuses on the short pAgo system from Pleomorphomonas koreensis (Pko-SPARDA), which consists of a DUF4365-APAZ protein (PkoRE) and an Ago protein (PkoAgo). Upon RNA-guided target DNA recognition, Pko-SPARDA exhibits nonspecific cleavage activity toward ssDNA, dsDNA, and RNA, demonstrating potential for nucleic acid detection. Biochemical characterization revealed that Pko-SPARDA prefers Mn2+ or Mg2+ as cofactors, operates optimally at 40-45 °C, and is sensitive to mismatches in the central and 3'-supplementary regions of the guide RNA. Notably, the system accommodates a range of guide lengths (14-40 nt) and shows higher activity with 5'-phosphorylated guides. Additionally, guide RNA 5'-phosphorylation universally enhances Pko-SPARDA trans-cleavage activity, and this principle extends to microRNA-guided activation, advancing the understanding of short pAgos and highlighting Pko-SPARDA's utility in molecular diagnostics by bridging a gap left by CRISPR systems due to its lack of sequence constraints like PAM motifs.

title: Multivalent ADAR1 recruitment for precise RNA editing.

abstract: Fhb7 is a gene derived from the homoeologous group-7 chromosomes of tall wheatgrass (Thinopyrum species), which confers resistance to Fusarium head blight (FHB) in wheat. Two resistance alleles at the Fhb7 locus (Fhb7Thp and Fhb7The2) were identified from Th. ponticum and Th. elongatum, respectively, and introgressed into the wheat genome by homoeologous recombination. Fhb7Thp was first cloned and reported to encode a glutathione S-transferase (GST), which detoxifies trichothecenes through de-epoxidation. However, a recent study has questioned the role of GST in Fhb7-mediated FHB resistance. To decipher the function of two GST-encoding alleles, Fhb7Thp and Fhb7The2, in FHB resistance, we generated haploid plants from three spring wheat lines (CS-Fhb7, WGC002, and FW23-009-80) carrying Fhb7Thp or Fhb7The2 through wide hybridizations with transgenic maize expressing Cas9 and guide RNA (gRNA) targeting GST. Of 57, 35, and 74 haploid plants derived from CS-Fhb7, WGC002, and FW23-009-80, respectively, 16, 5, and 9 had an insertion/deletion at the target sites of GST. Greenhouse evaluation of doubled haploid (DH) lines derived from the haploid plants for FHB resistance indicated that the GST-edited DH lines were significantly more susceptible and accumulated more deoxynivalenol (DON) than their corresponding wildtypes and non-edited DH lines, confirming GST as the causal gene for Fhb7-mediated FHB resistance. This study also demonstrated the power of wheat × maize hybridization coupled with genome editing in validating gene function in wheat.

title: CRISPR/Cas9-Mediated Mutagenesis of Two Alleles Encoding a Glutathione S-Transferase Confirms Their Identity as Fhb7 Conferring Fusarium Head Blight Resistance in Wheat.

abstract: Lung cancer is the leading cause of cancer-related deaths worldwide. Among them, non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) accounts for approximately 85% of all cases, while the mutation of KRAS oncogene plays a crucial role in its formation and metastasis. Here, we report a transcription activator-like effector (TALE) base editor that can accurately identify KRAS gene under the guide of TALE and sgRNA, convert C base to T base, thereby generating a stop codon and blocking the expression of KRAS. Besides, a targeted TALE base editing lipid nanoparticle (targeted TALE LNP) is developed by rationally designing with cancer-targeted EGFR peptide. The targeted TALE LNP exhibits a base editing effect, cancer targeting, and remarkable therapy efficacy in NSCLC cancer-bearing mice. In conclusion, the targeted TALE LNP has the potential to treat lung cancer with KRAS gene mutation through an approach of transcription activator-like effector base editing.

title: Transcription activator-like effector base editing delivered by a targeted lipid nanoparticle for therapy of lung cancer.

abstract: Lipid nanoparticle (LNP) formulations have enabled the in vivo delivery of messenger ribonucleic acid (mRNA) vaccines and therapeutics yet the delivery of RNA remains relatively inefficient. In order to improve LNP design there is a need to better understand how current mRNA-LNP formulations are trafficked and expressed in vivo. Importantly, no prior work has quantified mRNA-LNP transport through lymphatics. In the current study we profile the thoracic lymph uptake, plasma pharmacokinetics (PK), and tissue protein expression after intravenous (IV) and subcutaneous (SC) administration in rats of three common LNP formulations (ALC-0315, SM-102 and MC3 ionizable lipids) containing muGFP-P2A-nLuc reporter mRNA. After IV administration, the SM-102 and MC3 LNP formulations provided the most effective protection of mRNA in plasma. Despite this, tissue NanoLuc® Luciferase (nLuc) expression at 32 h post-dosing was relatively similar across formulations with highest expression seen in the liver and spleen. After SC injection, all formulations supported relatively low bioavailability of mRNA (0.42-0.87% dose) and slightly higher bioavailability of ionizable and PEG lipid (<5% dose) with PK profiles of the ionizable lipid and PEG lipid not completely matching the mRNA PK profiles. There was also greater lymphatic recovery of all ionizable lipids (3.1-4.3% dose) compared to mRNA (0.62-1.4% dose) and PEG lipid (1.9-2.0% dose). Together this data suggests that mRNA is lost prior to or during lymphatic transport. Importantly, concentrations of all mRNA-LNP components were 10-1000 fold higher in thoracic lymph compared to plasma after SC injection. At 32 h after SC injection, highest nLuc expression was seen in lymph nodes and tissues near the dosing site and in the liver and spleen. These findings demonstrating that mRNA-LNPs predominantly traffic from tissue injection sites via lymphatics, mRNA-LNP components may traffic separately from each other in both lymph and blood, and tissue protein expression reflects the PK of mRNA-LNPs at early timepoints.

title: Uncovering the lymphatic uptake, pharmacokinetics, and biodistribution of mRNA-lipid nanoparticles after intravenous and subcutaneous injection.

abstract: Vγ9Vδ2 T cells mediate HLA-independent targeting of tumor cells, offering unique opportunities for cancer immunotherapy, yet their therapeutic efficacy remains limited. Here, using a genome-wide CRISPR screen, we identify UDP-galactose 4-epimerase (GALE) as a tumor-intrinsic checkpoint that restricts Vγ9Vδ2 T cell-mediated killing. GALE is a key nucleotide-sugar metabolic enzyme that controls the interconversion of UDP-galactose and UDP-glucose, thereby supporting protein glycosylation and cell-surface glycan remodeling. Mechanistically, GALE promotes complex N-glycosylation of CD155 and CEACAM1, favoring their engagement with the inhibitory receptors TIGIT and TIM3, respectively, while limiting CD155 binding to the activating receptor CD226. GALE loss potentiates Vγ9Vδ2 T cell-mediated tumor killing in multiple mouse models and colorectal cancer patient-derived organoids. Together, these findings reveal how nucleotide-sugar metabolism shapes tumor-immune communication through complex N-glycan remodeling and identify GALE and its downstream receptor-ligand interactions as potential therapeutic targets for enhancing Vγ9Vδ2 T cell antitumor activity.

title: GALE is a tumor-intrinsic checkpoint of Vγ9Vδ2 T cell-mediated killing.

abstract: Experimental oncofertility remains fragmented across models of cancer biology, treatment-associated gonadotoxicity, fertility preservation, and reproductive recovery. We propose extending the Oncopig concept into a translational platform that reconnects these states within one genetically defined, cancer-bearing host. The Oncopig provides the oncologic backbone, combining programmable cancer in an immunocompetent large-animal host with clinically scaled intervention and longitudinal sampling. High-resolution porcine genomics, CRISPR-based genome engineering, somatic-cell nuclear transfer for line generation, comparative experimental pathology, and mature reproductive biotechnology extend this architecture toward reproductive endpoints. Here, programmability refers to deliberate specification of the cancer state-genotype, cell lineage or induction strategy, and timing-whereas the reproductive phenotype is measured longitudinally rather than programmed. Distant-cancer modules can test whether cancer status modifies gonadotoxicity, while reproductive-organ modules require disease-specific alleles, appropriate cell-of-origin targeting, and pathology-led validation. Because porcine and human reproduction align in several endocrine and gonadal processes but differ in cycle organization, implantation, placentation, and pregnancy, translation should emphasize process-level endpoints rather than numerical equivalence. The platform is particularly suited to unresolved questions involving targeted therapies and immunotherapies, preservation timing, and pediatric or prepubertal patients. Porcine reproductive biotechnology provides functional endpoints from gonadal tissue and gametes to embryos and offspring. Rather than replacing rodent or human-based models, the Oncopig framework adds an integrated translational layer for questions requiring clinically scaled intervention, longitudinal physiology, and functional reproductive recovery.

abstract: Chimeric antigen receptor T (CAR-T) cell therapy shows limited efficacy in solid tumors, partly owing to poorly defined tumor-intrinsic resistance mechanisms. Here we show that the epigenetic regulator BAZ2A drives resistance to CD70-targeted CAR-T therapy by reprogramming tumor lipid metabolism. Using an in vivo CRISPR screen in a mouse renal cell carcinoma model, we identify BAZ2A as a key mediator that promotes the production and accumulation of palmitic acid, a saturated fatty acid in the tumor microenvironment. Excess palmitic acid is taken up by CAR-T cells and impairs mitochondrial fitness by inhibiting PGC-1α activity, thereby enforcing a dysfunctional state. Pharmacologic inhibition of BAZ2A reduces lipid accumulation and restores CAR-T cell activity in vivo. These findings reveal an epigenetic-metabolic mechanism of immune resistance and suggest that targeting tumor lipid remodeling represents a therapeutic strategy to overcome CAR-T resistance in solid tumors.

title: BAZ2A-induced epigenetic states in cancer cells fuel palmitate accumulation in the tumor microenvironment driving CAR-T cell exhaustion.

abstract: The accelerating aging of the global population has made aging and its related diseases major public health challenges in the 21st century. Adipose tissue is not only an energy reservoir but also a crucial endocrine organ and metabolic regulator. Its dysfunction is closely linked to aging and the development of multiple diseases. This review outlines the key characteristics of adipocyte senescence and discusses its pathological contributions to obesity, type 2 diabetes, metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease, and cardiovascular diseases. It also summarizes current intervention strategies for adipocyte senescence, including senolytics, senomorphics, caloric restriction, physical exercise, and gene editing. We propose lipid prodrugs as promising adipose tissue delivery platforms that can be coupled with diverse therapeutic agents to increase the local concentration of drugs and minimize systemic toxicity. By utilizing the unique lipid metabolism of adipocytes, this strategy offers a new avenue for therapeutic intervention in adipocyte senescence and its associated metabolic disorders.

title: Intervening in Adipocyte Senescence: Lipid Prodrugs as an Emerging Strategy for Metabolic Disease Treatment.

abstract: Fowl adenovirus serotype 4 (FAdV-4) causes hepatitis-hydropericardium syndrome in poultry, yet viral subversion of host autophagy remains unclear. Here, we investigated the role of the viral structural protein Fiber-2 in modulating the host autophagy-lysosome pathway. Transcriptomic profiling of LMH cells expressing Fiber-2 revealed coordinated upregulation of autophagy-related genes, validated by quantitative PCR. Functional assays demonstrated that Fiber-2 expression leads to autophagosome accumulation and impaired autophagic flux, as shown by LC3-II/p62 analysis, tandem fluorescent LC3 reporter imaging, Bafilomycin A1 treatment, and transmission electron microscopy. Fiber-2 predominantly localizes to late endosomes and lysosomes, and GFP-Galectin-3 reporter assays indicate that it disrupts lysosomal membrane integrity rather than blocking autophagosome-lysosome fusion. Co-immunoprecipitation (Co-IP) and enrichment analyses identified BECN1, a key autophagy regulator, as a Fiber-2-interacting protein, and associated host proteins were enriched in autophagy-related pathways. Finally, CRISPR/Cas9-mediated deletion of Fiber-2 significantly reduced FAdV-4 replication at later stages of infection, consistent with a proviral role for Fiber-2. These findings indicate that Fiber-2 disrupts autophagic flux by inducing lysosomal dysfunction and membrane damage, thereby promoting FAdV-4 replication and uncovering a previously unrecognized mechanism of viral subversion of host degradative pathways.

title: Fiber-2 induces autolysosome dysfunction and impairs autophagic flux to promote FAdV-4 replication.

abstract: Alternative splicing (AS) generates distinct mRNA isoforms, and frequently distinct proteins, from single genes; its dysregulation is established in cancer, neurodegeneration, and immune disease. Sequencing now nominates candidate splice events at scale, but a nominated event does not become a usable measurement until an isoform-discriminating sequence has been converted into a physical signal. Existing AS reviews concentrate on sequencing workflows, computational event calling, or disease catalogs; the assay-engineering step that follows target nomination remains comparatively underserved, and it is where most translational failures occur. This review addresses that gap. We group postsequencing detection into five classes defined by the physical origin of the signal: (i) fixed-tissue in situ localization, (ii) live-cell RNA imaging, (iii) plasmonic and spectroscopic readouts, (iv) label-free nanophotonic biosensing combined with site-specific RNA processing, and (v) protein-level proteogenomic confirmation. These classes are compared on target definition, reported analytical performance, multiplexing, matrix compatibility, perturbation risk, and clinical readiness. The reported performance spans single-copy imaging of splice variants in living cells to label-free detection at 580 fM in under 30 min without cDNA synthesis or PCR. Three conclusions follow. First, assay selection should be governed by the class of claim being made rather than by platform novelty. Second, analytical sensitivity measured on synthetic targets systematically overstates readiness in clinical matrices; therefore, matrix-matched validation is not optional. Third, cross-laboratory comparison is currently obstructed by inconsistent reporting, which we address by proposing a minimum performance-reporting set and explicit platform-selection criteria. We close with emerging directions, including CRISPR-based isoform detection, biosensor integration with nanopore sequencing, AI-assisted probe design, and digital and microfluidic formats.

abstract: The 2nd Symposium on Pharmaceutical Bioengineering and Nanobiotechnology Applied to Advanced Therapies (SBINT 2025) was held in Goiânia, Brazil, under the theme "Challenges in preclinical evaluation: paving the way to translational relevance of advanced therapies." The meeting brought together approximately 150 participants from academia, industry, clinical institutions and regulatory agencies to discuss scientific, technological and regulatory barriers shaping advanced therapy medicinal products (ATMPs) in Brazil. Keynote lectures addressed human-relevant bioengineered platforms, organ-on-a-chip and microphysiological systems, regenerative biomaterials, extracellular vesicle-based therapies, nanobiotechnology-enabled nucleic acid delivery, clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats (CRISPR)-based genome and epigenome editing, and the Brazilian regulatory framework for ATMPs. The discussions highlighted the need for predictive preclinical models capable of capturing human-specific mechanisms, as conventional animal models may have limited translational value for personalized cell, gene and tissue-engineered products. Regulatory and roundtable sessions emphasized risk-based assessment, Good Manufacturing Practice-compatible infrastructure, product characterization, traceability, and the development of national biotechnological raw materials, analytical services and vector production capacity. Overall, SBINT 2025 underscored Brazil's scientific maturity and structural bottlenecks in regenerative medicine, highlighting the importance of coordinated action among academia, industry, clinical centers, regulators and funding agencies to support ATMP translation in Latin America.

abstract: Yeast platforms are rapidly transitioning from traditional eukaryotic model organisms to versatile, programmable chassis for next-generation human health applications. This review systematically examines the translational evolution of conventional and non-conventional yeasts including Saccharomyces cerevisiae, Komagataella phaffii, Saccharomyces boulardii, and Yarrowia lipolytica and redefines them as scalable biomanufacturing factories and advanced living therapeutics. We highlight milestone advancements in synthetic biology toolkits that lower technical barriers, such as CRISPR-mediated multiplex editing, modular cloning frameworks, and high-throughput secretion screening. We focus on sophisticated glycoengineering strategies for humanized N-glycosylation, alongside data-driven paradigms that leverage artificial intelligence to predict gene expression and streamline strain design. In clinical domains, we detail the established success of yeast in producing subunit or virus-like particle vaccines (e.g. HBV and HPV) and therapeutic enzymes (e.g. ecallantide), alongside its emerging role as gut-adapted live biotherapeutic products (LBPs) engineered for in situ delivery and biosensing. Finally, we explore specialized non-conventional platforms, focusing on lipid- and acetyl-CoA-rich hosts for lipophilic drug discovery, and stress-tolerant systems optimized for economical, feedstock-flexible bioprocesses. In summary, this review underscores the integrated value of yeast systems across disease modeling, industrial manufacturing, and clinical intervention, charting future directions to address global health challenges.

abstract: Psoriasis is a chronic inflammatory skin disease involving abnormal keratinocyte gene expression, yet the upstream epigenetic mechanisms driving these alterations remain unclear. Here we performed multiomics analyses (chromatin immunoprecipitation sequencing, CUT&Tag, ATAC-seq, and RNA sequencing) on psoriatic lesions, perilesional skin, healthy skin, and M5-stimulated HaCaT cells. Functional validation was performed using CRISPR-mediated superenhancer (SE) editing, epigenetic modulation, circular chromosome conformation capture sequencing, assay for chromatin-bound condensates by exploratory sequencing, coimmunoprecipitation, and fluorescence recovery after photobleaching. We found widespread activation of enhancers and SEs in lesions, including an interleukin 1 (IL-1)-SE regulating IL1A, IL1B, and IL36G transcription. BET inhibition reduced SE activity, repressed IL-1 cytokines, and relieved psoriasis-like inflammation in vivo. Fos-like antigen 1 (FOSL1) was identified as a key transcription factor enriched in active SEs and associated with condensate formation, contributing to the maintenance of EP300 occupancy and histone H3 lysine 27 acetylation deposition. Macrophage-derived IL-1 up-regulated FOSL1 through mitogen-activated protein kinase/ERK signaling, forming a positive feedback loop that amplified inflammation. This study revealed an FOSL1-SE-centered regulatory network driving keratinocyte inflammatory responses, providing previously unknown therapeutic targets for psoriasis.

abstract: Long non-coding RNAs are increasingly recognised as chromatin regulators, yet most remain functionally uncharacterised. DNAAF3-AS1, transcribed antisense to the ciliary dynein assembly factor gene DNAAF3, is almost exclusively associated with H3K36me3 in the HiMoRNA database. H3K36me3 ChIP-seq in human dermal fibroblasts following DNAAF3-AS1 knockdown with two independent antisense oligonucleotides revealed a marked reduction of gene-body H3K36me3, with residual signal shifted towards promoters. In FANTOM6 CAGE, DNAAF3-AS1 knockdown activated the p53 pathway and triggered differential promoter usage in genes enriched for p53 and apoptotic regulators. Consistently, genes that gained gene-body H3K36me3 upon knockdown were enriched for apoptosis-related pathways. In line with high expression of DNAAF3-AS1 in testis, analysis based on the adult human testis single-cell atlas suggests that DNAAF3-AS1 may contribute to promoter-level H3K36me3 regulation during late spermatogenesis. Together, these results identify DNAAF3-AS1 as a chromatin-associated lncRNA that links H3K36me3 maintenance to p53 signalling.

abstract: This phase III trial tests how well the addition of dinutuximab to Induction chemotherapy along with standard of care surgical resection of the primary tumor, radiation, stem cell transplantation, and immunotherapy works for treating children with newly diagnosed high-risk neuroblastoma. Dinutuximab is a monoclonal antibody that binds to a molecule called GD2, which is found on the surface of neuroblastoma cells, but is not present on many healthy or normal cells in the body. When dinutuximab binds to the neuroblastoma cells, it helps signal the immune system to kill the tumor cells. This helps the cells of the immune system kill the cancer cells, this is a type of immunotherapy. When chemotherapy and immunotherapy are given together, during the same treatment cycle, it is called chemoimmunotherapy. This clinical trial randomly assigns patients to receive either standard chemotherapy and surgery or chemoimmunotherapy (chemotherapy plus dinutuximab) and surgery during Induction therapy. Chemotherapy drugs administered during Induction include, cyclophosphamide, topotecan, cisplatin, etoposide, vincristine, and doxorubicin. These drugs work in different ways to stop the growth of cancer cells, either by killing the cells, by stopping them from dividing or by stopping them from spreading. Upon completion of 5 cycles of Induction therapy, a disease evaluation is completed to determine how well the treatment worked. If the tumor responds to therapy, patients receive a tandem transplantation with stem cell rescue. If the tumor has little improvement or worsens, patients receive chemoimmunotherapy on Extended Induction. During Extended Induction, dinutuximab is given with irinotecan, temozolomide. Patients with a good response to therapy move on to Consolidation therapy, when very high doses of chemotherapy are given at two separate points to kill any remaining cancer cells. Following, transplant, radiation therapy is given to the site where the cancer originated (primary site) and to any other areas that are still active at the end of Induction. The final stage of therapy is Post-Consolidation. During Post-Consolidation, dinutuximab is given with isotretinoin, with the goal of maintaining the response achieved with the previous therapy. Adding dinutuximab to Induction chemotherapy along with standard of care surgical resection of the primary tumor, radiation, stem cell transplantation, and immunotherapy may be better at treating children with newly diagnosed high-risk neuroblastoma.
description:
PRIMARY OBJECTIVE:

I. To determine if the event-free survival (EFS) of patients with newly diagnosed high-risk neuroblastoma assigned to early chemoimmunotherapy during Induction differs from that of patients who are not assigned to treatment that includes early chemoimmunotherapy.

SECONDARY OBJECTIVES:

I. To determine if early chemoimmunotherapy during Induction therapy improves end of Induction (EOI) response rates and overall survival (OS) for patients with newly diagnosed high-risk neuroblastoma.

II. To determine response rates, EFS, and OS following an Extended Induction regimen with chemoimmunotherapy in patients with progressive disease or a poor response to Induction therapy.

III. To compare the toxicities experienced by patients treated with chemoimmunotherapy during Induction versus those experienced by patients treated with standard Induction and to describe toxicities experienced during Extended Induction.

IV. To determine GD2 expression on tumor tissue and tumor cells in bone marrow and assess for associations with response and outcome.

EXPLORATORY OBJECTIVES:

I. To describe the association between tumor and host factors and outcomes in patients receiving protocol therapy.

II. To evaluate circulating biomarkers and markers of minimal residual disease at baseline and during therapy, and assess for associations with response and outcome.

III. To compare patterns of failure between patients treated with and without dinutuximab during induction.

IV. To determine the effect of telomere maintenance mechanisms on end of Induction response rates, EFS, and OS.

V. To explore the impact of high-risk neuroblastoma (HRNBL) and its therapy, including the addition of dinutuximab to Induction chemotherapy, on functional and quality of life outcomes in patients with HRNBL, as measured by caregiver (parent/legal guardian) and patient questionnaires.

VI. To describe the adequacy of diagnostic biopsy specimens, including those obtained by percutaneous core needle biopsy.

VII. To explore the associations between family-reported adverse social determinants of health and both clinical outcomes and biology.

VIII. To develop and validate deep learning predictors of Induction response based on diagnostic MIBG scans. (Imaging Objective) IX. To compare institutional versus central determination of overall response, individual response components (primary tumor, soft tissue and bone metastatic disease, and bone marrow metastatic disease), and poor end of induction response (PEIR) and good end of induction response (GEIR) determination. (Imaging Objective) X. To describe late toxicities (including impaired organ function, neuropsychiatric toxicity, and incidence of secondary malignancy) in patients treated with dinutuximab during Induction or Extended Induction to late toxicities in patients who have not received dinutuximab during these phases of therapy.

XI. To evaluate whether reduced dose radiotherapy to the primary site clinical target volume (CTV) in patients with complete response of the primary site at EOI results in comparable local control relative to historical cohorts.

XII. To compare post-transplant complications between treatment arms, and assess for associations with outcome.

XIII. To assess for associations between EOI response (including good end of Induction response \[GEIR\] and poor end of Induction response \[PEIR\]) and individual response components (primary tumor, soft tissue and bone metastatic disease, and bone marrow metastatic disease) with outcome (EFS and OS).

XIV. To describe and compare the changes in image-defined risk factors (IDRFs) between patients treated with and without dinutuximab during Induction and associate with surgical outcomes and local failure rates following primary tumor resection.

XV. To bank serial samples of blood, bone marrow, and tumor tissue for future research.

OUTLINE: Patients receive Induction cycle 1 and are then randomized to 1 of 2 treatment arms.

INDUCTION CYCLE 1: Patients receive cyclophosphamide intravenously (IV) over 30 minutes and topotecan IV over 30 minutes on days 1-5 in the absence of unacceptable toxicity.

ARM A:

INDUCTION CYCLES 2-5: Patients receive cyclophosphamide IV over 30 minutes and topotecan IV over 30 minutes on days 1-5 of cycle 2 in the absence of unacceptable toxicity. Patients then undergo stem cell harvest via apheresis. Patients then receive cisplatin IV over 4 hours and etoposide IV over 2 hours on days 1-3 of cycles 3 and 5, and vincristine IV on day 1, doxorubicin IV over 15 minutes, and cyclophosphamide IV over 1 hour on days 1-2 of cycle 4 in the absence of unacceptable toxicity. Patients undergo primary tumor resection after Induction cycle 4 or 5. Following Induction cycle 5, patients undergo testing to determine response to Induction therapy. Patients with a good tumor response proceed to Consolidation, while patients with a poor tumor response proceed to Extended Induction.

EXTENDED INDUCTION: Patients with a poor tumor response or progression during Induction receive temozolomide orally (PO), via nasogastric tube (NG), or via gastric tube (G-tube) on days 1-5, irinotecan IV over 90 minutes on days 1-5, and dinutuximab IV over 10 hours. Treatment repeats every 21 days for up to a maximum of 6 cycles in the absence of disease progression or unacceptable toxicity. If at any time during Extended Induction testing shows a good tumor response, patients proceed to Consolidation. If after 6 cycles of Extended Induction or if at any time progression is noted, patients are removed from the study.

CONSOLIDATION: Patients undergo two autologous hematopoietic stem cell transplantations (HSCTs) during Consolidation. Patients receive thiotepa IV over 2 hours on days -7 to -5 and cyclophosphamide IV over 1 hour on days -5 to -2 during HSCT 1. Patients then receive stem cell infusion IV on day 0. Between 6 and 10 weeks after stem cell infusion, patients receive melphalan IV over 30 minutes on days -7 to -5, etoposide IV over 24 hours on days -7 to -4, and carboplatin over 24 hours on days -7 to -4 during HSCT 2. Patients receive stem cell infusion IV on day 0. Between day +42 and day +80 after HSCT 2. Patients receive radiation daily for 12 treatments in the absence of disease progression or unacceptable toxicity.

POST CONSOLIDATION: Patients receive dinutuximab IV over 10 hours on days 4-7 and isotretinoin PO twice daily (BID) on days 11-24 of cycles 1-5. Treatment repeats every 28 days for up to 5 cycles in the absence of disease progression or unacceptable toxicity. Patients then receive isotretinoin PO BID on days 15-28 for 1 additional cycle, cycle 6.

Patients undergo blood and urine sample collection, echocardiogram (ECHO) or multigated acquisition scan (MUGA), bone marrow aspiration and/or biopsy, computed tomography (CT) scan, magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), iodine-123 meta-iodobenzylguanidine (I-MIBG) scan and possible fluorodeoxyglucose position emission tomography (FDG-PET) scan throughout the study.

ARM B:

INDUCTION CYCLES 2-5: Patients receive cyclophosphamide IV over 30 minutes, topotecan IV over 30 minutes on days 1-5, and dinutuximab IV over 10 hours on days 2-5 of cycle 2 in the absence of unacceptable toxicity. Patients then undergo stem cell harvest via apheresis. Patients receive cisplatin IV over 4 hours and etoposide IV over 2 hours on days 1-3 and dinutuximab IV over 10 hours on days 2-5 of cycles 3 and 5, and vincristine IV on day 1, doxorubicin IV over 15 minutes, and cyclophosphamide IV over 1 hour on days 1-2, and dinutuximab IV over 10 hours on days 2-5 of cycle 4 in the absence of unacceptable toxicity. Patients undergo primary tumor resection after Induction cycle 4 or 5. Following Induction cycle 5, patients undergo testing to determine response to Induction therapy. Patients with a good tumor response proceed to Consolidation, while patients with a poor tumor response proceed to Extended Induction.

EXTENDED INDUCTION: Patients with a poor tumor response or progression during Induction receive temozolomide PO, via NG tube, or via G-tube on days 1-5, irinotecan IV over 90 minutes on days 1-5, and dinutuximab IV over 10 hours. Treatment repeats every 21 days for up to a maximum of 6 cycles in the absence of disease progression or unacceptable toxicity. If at any time during Extended Induction testing shows a good tumor response, patients proceed to Consolidation. If after 6 cycles of Extended Induction or if at any time progression is noted, patients are removed from the study.

CONSOLIDATION: Patients undergo two autologous HSCTs during Consolidation. Patients receive thiotepa IV over 2 hours on days -7 to -5 and cyclophosphamide IV over 1 hour on days -5 to -2 during HSCT 1. Patients then receive stem cell infusion IV on day 0. Between 6 and 10 weeks after stem cell infusion patients receive melphalan IV over 30 minutes on days -7 to -5, etoposide IV over 24 hours on days -7 to -4, and carboplatin over 24 hours on days -7 to -4 during HSCT 2. Patients receive stem cell infusion IV on day 0. Between day +42 and day +80 after HSCT 2, patients receive radiation daily for 12 treatments in the absence of disease progression or unacceptable toxicity.

POST CONSOLIDATION: Patients receive dinutuximab IV over 10 hours on days 4-7 and isotretinoin PO BID on days 11-24 of cycles 1-5. Treatment repeats every 28 days for up to 5 cycles in the absence of disease progression or unacceptable toxicity. Patients then receive isotretinoin PO BID on days 15-28 for 1 additional cycle, cycle 6.

Patients undergo blood and urine sample collection, ECHO or MUGA, bone marrow aspiration and/or biopsy, CT scan, MRI, I-MIBG scan and possible FDG-PET scan throughout the study.

After completion of study treatment, patients are followed up at 3, 6, 9,12, 15, 18, 24, 30, 36, 42, 48, 54, and 60 months and then periodically for up to 10 years from enrollment.
