title: RNA base-modification and A-to-I editing landscapes of oxidatively stressed human retinal pigment epithelium under Quantum Molecular Resonance electrotherapy and blood-derived secretome.

abstract: Peripheral T-cell lymphomas (PTCL) comprise a biologically diverse and clinically aggressive family of mature T/NK-cell neoplasms, for which outcomes remain poor in the majority of patients treated with conventional anthracycline-based frontline regimens. Contemporary classifications (WHO-HAEM5 and ICC) increasingly incorporate immunophenotypic and molecular information, underscoring that "PTCL-NOS" is not a single disease but rather a diagnostic umbrella that includes biologically distinct entities and molecular subgroups. Among these are the TBX21- and GATA3-driven PTCL-NOS subsets, the latter associated with inferior survival and a distinctive cytokine/microenvironmental program. These advances, many of which were shaped by long-standing contributions from the Bologna group, support a rational shift from empiric chemotherapy toward mechanism-based and immune-based interventions. CAR-engineered cellular therapies have revolutionized the care of B-cell malignancies, yet translation to PTCL has been delayed by lineage-specific barriers: (i) fratricide during manufacturing when targeting shared T-cell antigens (e.g., CD5, CD7), (ii) the risk of profound and prolonged T-cell aplasia (a markedly less "replaceable" toxicity than B-cell aplasia), and (iii) product contamination by malignant T-cells in autologous platforms. Recent progress in genome editing (CRISPR/Cas9 and base editing), intracellular antigen "blocking" strategies, and alternative effectors (allogeneic "universal" CAR-T, CAR-NK, and iPSC-derived platforms) has begun to address these obstacles at the manufacturing level, while their downstream clinical consequences (e.g., prolonged cytopenias, infectious risk and delayed immune reconstitution) remain incompletely resolved. Early-phase clinical trials now demonstrate clinically meaningful responses for select targets, particularly CD7, CD5, TRBC1 and CD30, for the pan-T targets. However, the strongest efficacy data remain largely derived from T-cell lymphoblastic malignancies (T-ALL/T-LBL), whereas evidence in mature PTCL remains limited and at an earlier stage, with target-specific differences in safety, immune reconstitution and relapse patterns. This review synthesizes the biological rationale for antigen selection in PTCL, the emerging clinical evidence for leading CAR targets, and the engineering strategies most likely to improve the therapeutic index. It also proposes an integrated hematology perspective on how CAR-based therapies might be positioned relative to transplant and evolving targeted agents in relapsed/refractory PTCL.

title: Targeting Peripheral T-Cell Lymphomas with Chimeric Antigen Receptor Therapy: Mechanistic Challenges, Clinical Landscape and Future Engineering Perspectives.

abstract: Retinal degenerative diseases, including age-related macular degeneration (AMD), retinitis pigmentosa (RP), and Stargardt disease, represent leading causes of irreversible vision loss worldwide, collectively affecting hundreds of millions of people. Cell-based therapies, particularly those leveraging induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs), retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) transplantation, and CRISPR-Cas9 gene editing, have emerged as promising treatment modalities that may preserve, replace, or partially restore retinal function. However, these approaches face significant challenges in patient stratification, manufacturing consistency, surgical precision, and long-term outcome monitoring. Artificial intelligence (AI), encompassing machine learning (ML), deep learning (DL), and computer vision, is increasingly being integrated across the cell therapy pipeline to address these limitations. This review comprehensively explores the role of AI in enhancing cell-based retinal therapies, spanning disease diagnosis and patient selection, stem cell quality control and differentiation optimization, CRISPR off-target detection, retinal organoid characterization, scalable manufacturing, and post-transplantation monitoring through multimodal retinal imaging. Throughout, we distinguish direct retinal cell-therapy evidence from retinal-adjacent, cross-domain, and conceptual evidence. We also propose an AI-powered end-to-end pipeline that connects patient profiling through gene editing, cell production, and transplantation to longitudinal outcomes tracking (a forward-looking framework that needs to be clinically validated in future). While AI offers powerful tools to enhance efficacy, reproducibility, and personalization, it does not replace the clinical and biological foundations of cell therapy. Critical challenges remain, including data scarcity, algorithmic interpretability, regulatory compliance, and clinical validation. This review concludes that the strategic integration of AI has plausible potential to become supportive infrastructure for scalable and reproducible cell-based treatments for retinal diseases, although its necessity has not been demonstrated and prospective clinical validation is still required, and biological insight and rigorous empirical verification remain fundamental.

title: Artificial Intelligence as a Catalyst for Cell-Based Therapies in Retinal Disease.

abstract: Background: Allele-specific antisense oligonucleotides (ASOs) are increasingly used to selectively suppress transcripts containing pathogenic gain-of-function or dominant negative (GOF/DN) variants. However, most current approaches rely on patient-specific target selection of SNVs in cis with the disease-causing variant. This individualized approach may limit broader ASO applicability and could exacerbate inequities in access. Population-level selection of ASO-targetable SNVs is an alternative approach not previously explored at scale. Methods: For a curated set of >400 disease genes with putative toxic GOF/DN mechanisms, we applied a greedy algorithm to identify ASO-targetable SNVs that maximize population coverage in the 1000 Genomes Project dataset. Population coverage was evaluated across ''superpopulation'' ancestry groups and assessed in multiple diverse replication datasets. For each prioritized SNV we attempted to design allele-specific 15-mer and 20-mer ASOs meeting standard chemistry and sequence criteria. The presence of prioritized SNVs was assessed in two local cohorts with GOF/DN disorders: infants with epilepsy diagnosed by rapid short-read genome sequencing, and children with long-read genome sequencing data generated for bespoke ASO development. Results: We identified 7,927 SNVs (median 17.5 per gene) achieving a median cumulative heterozygous population coverage of 88.9% across 408 disease genes. More than two-thirds of genes (70.6%) reached [≥]80% coverage using a median of only four prioritized SNVs. Coverage was consistently high for all ''superpopulation'' ancestry groups, with median coverage proportions of [≥]85%. Prioritized SNVs generalized to independent ancestrally diverse replication datasets, achieving median coverage of 86.4% in the Human Genome Diversity Project and 90.3% in the All of Us Research Program. Many prioritized targets were compatible with established ASO design principles, enabling generation of candidate allele-specific 15-mer and 20-mer ASOs at scale for future experimental validation. The presence of prioritized targets in the rapid short-read sequencing cohort, and the overlap between prioritized targets and manually curated long-read genome sequencing targets, supports the clinical relevance of population-informed target selection. All SNV targets and candidate allele-specific ASO sequences are available at hawk-eye.research.sickkids.ca/knockdown. Conclusions: Prioritization of common SNV targets may facilitate the development of ASO therapies with broader population coverage, helping move the field beyond single-patient applications and toward more equitable opportunities for access.

title: Population-scale genome-wide prioritization of targets for allele-specific antisense oligonucleotide therapy design

abstract: Background/Objectives: Glioblastoma multiforme (GBM) remains the most aggressive and treatment-refractory primary brain tumor, with current therapeutic modalities providing minimal survival improvement. Chimeric antigen receptor (CAR)-based immunotherapies succeeded in hematologic malignancies but are constrained in solid tumors by tumor heterogeneity, immunosuppressive microenvironment, and delivery challenges. CD276 (B7-H3), a pan-cancer antigen overexpressed in gliomas and correlated with poor patient outcomes, represents a compelling immunotherapeutic target. Methods: Here, we developed a non-viral lipid nanoparticle (LNP)-based platform for transient CAR mRNA delivery to T cells and evaluated its application for generating CD276 (B7-H3)-targeted CAR-T cells against GBM. An in-house-assembled T-mixer incorporating polyether ether ketone (PEEK) tubing was integrated with a dual-syringe-pump system for controlled LNP production. Results: LNPs formulated with clinically relevant ionizable lipids, SM-102 and DLin-MC3-DMA, demonstrated high encapsulation efficiency and effective mRNA delivery. Cell-type-dependent expression kinetics were further characterized following LNP-mediated reporter mRNA delivery in K562, NK, NK92, and T cells, revealing differences in transgene expression across cell populations. LNP-mediated delivery of CD276 CAR mRNA enabled generation of CAR-expressing T cells that exhibited antigen-specific cytotoxicity against CD276-positive LN229 GBM cells in vitro. Conclusions: Collectively, this study demonstrates the feasibility of an adaptable LNP-based platform for non-viral CAR mRNA engineering of T cells and CD276-targeted cytotoxicity against GBM cells in vitro. The combination of transient CAR expression and LNP-mediated mRNA delivery provides a foundation for further optimization and evaluation in preclinical in vivo models.

abstract: SUGP1 (SURP and G-patch domain containing 1) participates in splice-site recognition through its interaction with SF3B1, and loss of this factor leads to aberrant splicing. While its role in pre-mRNA splicing is well-documented, its impact on small RNA pathways remains poorly understood. Here, we used CRISPR/Cas9-mediated SUGP1 editing in Bombyx mori BmE cell populations and RNAi to systemically knock down SUGP1 in Drosophila melanogaster. SUGP1 loss caused widespread splicing abnormalities in both species and reduced transposon-derived piRNA abundance as shown by small RNA-seq. Notably, the expression and splicing patterns of known piRNA pathway genes remained largely unchanged. Integrating silkworm transcriptomic data with the Flag-SUGP1 Co-IP/MS interactome revealed no direct association with the components of the piRNA biogenesis pathway, but identified a physical interaction with the Y-box protein (YBX), suggesting a potential link connecting splicing surveillance to RNA metabolism and proteostasis. Collectively, these correlative findings suggest that SUGP1 depletion perturbs global RNA processing, and piRNA reduction may represent a secondary outcome associated with cellular stress or dysregulated RNA metabolism within these two tested insect systems. These results suggest a potential indirect link between SUGP1-dependent splicing regulation and piRNA abundance in the tested insect models.

abstract: Background/Objectives: Plant mitochondrial genomes are structurally dynamic, and assembled paths may not reflect all molecular configurations. We characterized the mitochondrial genome of Rhododendron spinuliferum and evaluated repeat-associated structural heterogeneity and transcript support for mitochondrial RNA processing. Methods: Public PacBio HiFi reads were assembled and curated; Illumina reads from a second individual provided cross-individual sequence support. Candidate local connections were assessed by strict single-read two-junction phasing. Gene content, repeats, plastid-derived sequences, comparative genomics, phylogeny, predicted C-to-U RNA-editing sites, and mature exon junctions were also examined. Results: Three representative assembly paths totaled 786,593 bp and contained 32 protein-coding loci, three rRNA genes, and 19 tRNA types. A total of 226 HiFi reads supported four local configurations associated with two repeat pairs, and all four persisted across 24 filtering combinations. Nine mitochondrial plastid DNA transfer blocks covered 6.77 kb. Public RNA-seq data provided read-level support for 211 of 475 predicted editing sites and all 12 examined mature exon junctions of nad1, nad2, and nad5. Across six congeners, 99.7% of resolved homologous positions corresponding to RNA-supported sites retained genomic C. Conclusions: These results support repeat-associated local structural heterogeneity in the R. spinuliferum mitogenome and provide a curated DNA- and RNA-supported resource for comparative Rhododendron mitochondrial genomics.

abstract:
This is a first-in-human clinical study to evaluate the safety, tolerability and efficacy of RXRG001 administered in the ducts of the parotid glands in adult patients with radiation-induced xerostomia (dry mouth) and hyposalivation (reduced saliva production).

In Part 1 of the study (open-label, single-arm), patients will receive unilateral administrations of RXRG001 in 3 single ascending dose cohorts and in 3 multiple ascending dose cohorts.

Part 2 of the study has a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled design. Patients will receive bilateral administrations of RXRG001 in 3 multiple ascending dose cohorts.

abstract: Background: Infantile hemangioma (IH) is the most common benign vascular tumor of infancy, and propranolol, the current first-line treatment, requires prolonged twice-daily dosing and has adverse systemic effects. Methods: Using the public GSE127487 transcriptomic dataset together with weighted gene coexpression network analysis and protein-protein interaction network analysis, we identified JAG1, a principal endothelial Notch ligand, as the most connected node in the disease protein-protein interaction network, with elevated expression across all clinical stages of IH. To test its use as a drug target, we engineered a lipid nanoparticle (LNP) composed of SM-102/DSPC/cholesterol/DMG-PEG2000 that carried JAG1-specific siRNA. Results: At an N/P ratio of 8, the formulation efficiently encapsulated the siRNA, protected it from serum nucleases, and remained colloidally stable. LNP-mediated JAG1 knockdown reduced Matrigel network formation by hemangioma stem cells in vitro. In a hemangioma xenograft model, the intratumoral delivery of JAG1 siRNA reduced tumor volume by approximately 75%, tumor weight by approximately 80%, and microvessel density by more than half, without overt toxicity to the measures collected (body weight and clinical observation). Conclusions: In this preclinical model, JAG1 emerges as a credible therapeutic target, and LNP-delivered JAG1 siRNA is a promising gene-silencing strategy against IH angiogenesis.

abstract: Developing new cancer therapeutic strategies has become a central focus in precision oncology. However, a major challenge is the lack of robust models to accurately assess target vulnerability in patient-specific heterogeneous cancer cells, which limits the translation of research findings into effective clinical therapies. In this study, we developed an ex vivo blood-based model utilizing a versatile nano-delivery platform to evaluate the responsiveness of MDM2 knockout as a representative therapeutic approach in circulating malignant cells (CMCs) from patients stratified by their p53 status. In our genome editing plasmid delivery system (p@RPA), protamine sulfate was combined with a cell-penetrating peptide to condense the CRISPR-Cas9 plasmid into nano-cores. These nano-cores were then coated with chondroitin sulfate shells functionalized with the AS1411 aptamer, enabling the selective recognition of CD44 and/or nucleolin overexpressing malignant cells. Using the same vector, a molecular beacon delivery system (MBs@RPA) co-loaded with MBMDM2 for probing MDM2 mRNA, MBTP53 for probing TP53 mRNA and MBTP73 for probing TP73 mRNA was constructed for the in situ evaluation of biomarker changes induced by genome editing. p@RPA demonstrates satisfactory efficacy in mediating gene editing for MDM2 knockout in malignant cells. Notably, the knockout of MDM2 induces cell cycle arrest and leads to a marked upregulation of anti-tumor TAp73 irrespective of their p53 status. With efficient gene editing and mRNA probing achieved in patient-derived CMCs, we establish an ex vivo platform capable of in situ therapeutic efficacy assessment at single-cell resolution to explicitly reveal the underlying cellular heterogeneity across individual CMCs.

abstract: Colorectal cancer (CRC) is one of the most prevalent malignancies of the gastrointestinal tract worldwide. Notably, most patients with microsatellite-stable (MSS) tumors show primary resistance to immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs), creating an unmet clinical need. The mechanisms underlying immune evasion and strategies to overcome therapeutic resistance have therefore become important topics in CRC immunology research. Recent studies indicate that mitochondrial metabolic reprogramming contributes to immune evasion in CRC. Tumor cells display metabolic plasticity through dynamic shifts between glycolysis and oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS), which can intensify the depletion of critical nutrients, particularly glucose and glutamine, within the tumor microenvironment (TME). These metabolic changes can also promote the accumulation of immunosuppressive metabolites, including lactate, thereby impairing the function of effector cells such as CD8+ T cells and dendritic cells (DCs) and supporting the expansion of regulatory T cells (Tregs) and myeloid-derived suppressor cells (MDSCs). Lactate may further reshape the immune landscape through hydroxycarboxylic acid receptor 1 (HCAR1) signaling and histone lactylation. In parallel, mitochondrial quality control can regulate tumor immunogenicity by influencing mtDNA availability and cGAS-STING signaling. Therapeutic approaches targeting glycolysis, glutamine metabolism, fatty acid oxidation, lactate transport, and mitochondrial dynamics have shown immune-sensitizing activity in preclinical models. Nanodelivery systems and gene-editing technologies may improve the spatial and cellular specificity of these interventions. This review summarizes how mitochondrial metabolic reprogramming contributes to immune evasion in CRC and evaluates mitochondria-directed strategies for improving treatment responsiveness, particularly in MSS CRC.

abstract: There is growing interest in natural bioactive compounds as potentially safer and more sustainable sources of therapeutic agents. Terpenoids, one of the most structurally diverse and biologically active classes of natural products, are derived from repeating isoprene units and possess a broad range of pharmacological and industrial applications. This review provides a comprehensive overview of recent advances in terpenoid biosynthesis, structural classification, and therapeutic applications. It also discusses emerging approaches for enhancing large-scale production, improving functional efficacy, and overcoming pharmacokinetic limitations. Attention is given to terpenoids currently undergoing clinical evaluation, along with their progress toward commercial development. Despite substantial preclinical evidence supporting their therapeutic potential, the clinical translation of many terpenoids remains limited. Key challenges include poor aqueous solubility, low permeability, slow dissolution, and high lipophilicity, which can collectively restrict systemic bioavailability and therapeutic efficacy. Moreover, only a relatively small proportion of biologically active terpenoids have progressed to advanced stages of clinical development, highlighting a considerable gap between experimental findings and clinical application. This review integrates current knowledge of terpenoid biosynthesis, biological activities, production strategies, and translational development while highlighting sustainable and scientifically driven approaches that may facilitate their future therapeutic and commercial utilization.

abstract: Background/Objectives: Porcine reproductive and respiratory syndrome virus (PRRSV) remains a major threat to the global swine industry, while the emergence of variant pseudorabies virus (PRV) strains has further complicated disease control in China. This study aimed to develop a PRV-based viral vector platform for PRRSV antigen delivery and evaluate its safety, immunogenicity, and protective efficacy. Methods: A five-gene-deleted variant PRV strain, PRV-JM-DF, was used as the vector backbone. Candidate genomic insertion sites and endogenous late promoters were systematically screened, followed by construction of recombinant PRVs expressing PRRSV GP2, GP3, GP4, GP5, and M individually or as tandem antigen constructs. Recombinant viruses were characterized for antigen expression, replication, and genetic stability. Safety and immunogenicity were initially evaluated in female BALB/c mice, and the leading candidates were further assessed for safety, immunogenicity, and protective efficacy in 18 Landrace pigs of either sex following challenge with highly pathogenic PRRSV HuN4. Results: The TK locus supported efficient foreign-gene expression, and pUL39 exhibited the highest activity among the tested endogenous late promoters. The recombinant viruses retained replication competence and genetic stability. Among the candidates, rPRV-C-4T induced robust PRRSV- and PRV-specific neutralizing antibody responses and showed no obvious adverse effects during the experimental observation period in pigs. Following HP-PRRSV HuN4 challenge, all rPRV-C-4T-immunized pigs survived and exhibited reduced viremia, viral shedding and tissue viral loads, together with markedly alleviated pathological lesions. Conclusions: rPRV-C-4T provided protection against homologous HP-PRRSV HuN4 challenge while maintaining PRV-directed immune responses, supporting its potential as a PRV-vectored multivalent vaccine candidate.

abstract:
BACKGROUND: Chronic hepatitis B (CHB) remains a major global health problem. Functional cure is defined as sustained hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) seroclearance with undetectable HBV DNA 24 weeks after cessation of therapy. It has emerged as a clinically meaningful endpoint, associated with regression of liver fibrosis, reduced hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) risk, and a lower treatment burden. However, current CHB therapies, including nucleos(t)ide analogues (NUCs) and pegylated interferon-α (Peg-IFNα), rarely lead to functional cure despite adequate viral suppression, leading to a notable portion of patients remaining at risk for adverse liver-related outcomes, including hepatic decompensation and HCC. Hence, novel therapeutic agents are aimed at accelerating towards functional cure. They are categorized as virus-targeting and immunomodulatory therapies.
METHODS: This review summarizes the clinical evidence for emerging therapies aimed at acheiving functional cure, with a particular focus on RNA-targeting therapies. It also discusses practical considerations relevant to treatment selection.
RESULTS: Among these novel therapies, RNA-targeting therapies are currently the most promising, with bepirovirsen (an unconjugated antisense oligonucleotide) standing out as the only agent completed in Phase III study showing efficacious results. Combination regimens that use RNA-targeting therapies as backbone are increasingly pursued, leveraging potential synergistic effects to achieve higher rates of HBsAg seroclearance.
CONCLUSION: RNA-targetting therapies and combination regimens offer promising approaches in attaining functional cure in CHB. Further research should emphasize on the long-term efficacy and safety for these novel agents.

abstract: Chimeric antigen receptor-natural killer (CAR-NK) cells combine innate cytotoxicity with antigen-directed killing and promise as an immunotherapy with lower cytokine toxicity than CAR-T approaches. However, clinical translation is limited by challenges in transduction, persistence, tumor infiltration, and the immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment (TME). We performed a comprehensive literature review of recent preclinical and early-phase clinical studies, engineering strategies (CAR design, transduction technologies, gene-editing), manufacturing and expansion protocols, and trial outcomes in this review. We noted a reference to the advantages of CAR-NK, like multimodal killing (CAR-dependent and innate pathways), potential for allogeneic "off-the-shelf" use, and favorable early safety profiles. However, NK-specific obstacles persist: lower viral transduction efficiencies, short in vivo persistence, poor infiltration into solid tumors, and TME-mediated suppression (TGF-β, adenosine, metabolic stress). Engineering countermeasures such as IL-15 expression, checkpoint receptor knockout, chemokine receptor co-expression (e.g., CXCR1/4), DAP10/DAP12-based signaling domains, and non-viral delivery (transposons/CRISPR) have shown preclinical promise. CAR-NK therapy has developed from concept to a clinically actionable treatment line for hematologic malignancies and shows emerging potential in solid tumors when combined with TME-modulating strategies. This review provides robust evidence about CAR-NK therapies in hematological and solid tumors, with a great emphasis on the challenges they encounter, strategies, and innovative approaches to overcome these challenges, and forward-looking perspectives to improve future therapeutic CAR-NK designs and clinical outcomes.

title: CAR-NK cell immunotherapy: a comprehensive review of engineering platforms, clinical applications in hematological and solid tumors.

abstract: Efficient, biocompatible, and flexible application of CRISPR-Cas9 remains a major challenge in gene therapy. This study addresses a novel formulation method, focusing on organic solvent-free lipid nanoparticles for the efficient delivery of CRISPR-Cas9 components. Therefore, novel stealth lipids comprising the lipid anchor cholesterol hemisuccinate conjugated to poly(2-ethyl-2-oxazoline) (PEtOx) were synthesized and evaluated as a promising in vitro alternative to commercially available poly(ethylene glycol) (PEG)-based lipids. Our study identified PEtOx-lipids as markedly more biocompatible compared to PEG-based analogues (12-fold reduction in cytotoxicity; 99% reduced hemolytic effect) with high efficiency for mRNA gene delivery. We demonstrate successful CRISPR-Cas9 activity ex vivo and efficient uptake of PEtOx nanoparticles by macrophages in vivo (66.5% pos. F4/80+ macrophages). Our data demonstrate that PEtOx-based stealth lipids are a promising alternative to PEG. The resulting LNPs, optimized for fully aqueous manufacturing, address key limitations of current LNP systems, including immunogenicity and the reliance on ethanol-based production processes.

abstract: Lassa virus (LASV), the causative agent of the life-threatening febrile disease, Lassa fever, remains a major public health concern in West Africa, where hundreds of thousands of infections occur annually. However, no licensed vaccine is currently available, highlighting the urgent need for effective preventive measures. We previously demonstrated that an mRNA-lipid nanoparticle (LNP) vaccine expressing LASV glycoprotein precursor (GPC; LASgpc-mRNA-LNP) conferred protection against lethal infection with a recombinant lymphocytic choriomeningitis virus expressing LASV GPC in mice. In this study, we extended our previous work with the aim of evaluating the efficacy of an mRNA-LNP vaccine expressing LASV nucleoprotein (NP; LASnp-mRNA-LNP) and a bivalent vaccine combining LASgpc-mRNA-LNP and LASnp-mRNA-LNP. Using a lethal CBA/N mouse model of infection with ML29, an LASV live-attenuated vaccine candidate encoding LASV GPC and NP, we found that LASgpc-mRNA-LNP and LASnp-mRNA-LNP each conferred protection in the absence of detectable neutralizing antibody responses. We identified LASV GPC- and NP-derived CD4 and CD8 T-cell epitope peptides in CBA/N mice and demonstrated that vaccination induced robust antigen-specific T-cell responses. Importantly, the bivalent vaccine provided complete protection against lethal challenge with doses at which monovalent vaccines failed to protect all mice, suggesting a potential dose-sparing benefit of the bivalent formulation. Furthermore, the bivalent vaccine fully protected guinea pigs against lethal challenge with authentic LASV. Together, these findings establish LASV NP, in addition to GPC, as a protective antigen in the mRNA vaccine platform and provide a rationale for developing bivalent mRNA-LNP vaccines to improve protection against Lassa fever.

abstract: Spherical nucleic acids (SNAs) are a unique class of nucleic acid nanotherapeutics characterized by densely packed, radially arranged oligonucleotides surrounding a nanoparticle or molecular core, or core-free nanoscale structures. Compared with conventional linear nucleic acids, SNAs exhibit excellent cellular uptake, resistance to nuclease degradation, and efficient target recognition without the help of transfection agents. This review summarizes SNAs' structural diversity, design principles, and the multiscale delivery barriers they encounter. We mainly focus on liposomal SNAs (LSNAs) as programmable platforms for cancer immunotherapy. We emphasize how lipid chemistry, membrane architecture, and anchor stability control lymphoid distribution, immune-cell uptake, antigen presentation, and strong antitumor immunity, rather than seeing lipids as inert carriers. Furthermore, we also discuss current developments in gene silencing, CRISPR-based genome editing, and stimulus-responsive multimodal therapies, highlighting the significant therapeutic advancements of SNAs like clinical trial NU-0129 and LSNAs like cavrotolimod. Finally, we describe present translational obstacles and potential prospects by using SNAs as next-generation precision immunotherapeutics.

abstract: Huntington's disease (HD) is characterized by degeneration of striatal medium spiny neurons (MSNs), yet the human-specific regulatory mechanisms that contribute to neuronal vulnerability remain poorly understood. Here, we identify HD-LINC (LINC01139), a human-specific long intergenic noncoding RNA selectively induced in symptomatic HD patient-derived MSNs (HD-MSNs) and human HD caudate. Single-cell transcriptomic analysis in HD-MSNs revealed that HD-LINC was enriched in a symptomatic HD neuronal state associated with lipid metabolic and protein clearance regulation, while not observed in non-degenerative reprogrammed MSNs derived from pre-manifest HD individuals. Reducing HD-LINC attenuated mutant HTT aggregation, dystrophic neurites, DNA damage, and neuronal death, whereas HD-LINC overexpression exacerbated these phenotypes. Transcriptomic and lipidomic analyses further implicated HD-LINC in neuronal lipid regulation. We found that HD-MSNs exhibited aberrant accumulation of enlarged, low-mobility lipid droplets (LDs) within neurites, a previously unrecognized phenotype in patient-derived neurons. Critically, increased lipid peroxidation was observed within LD-enriched dystrophic neurites in HD-MSNs. HD-LINC knockdown cleared neuritic LD accumulation, restored soma-enriched LD distribution, and reduced lipid peroxidation. Finally, we developed antisense oligonucleotides that effectively reduced HD-LINC and reversed HD-LINC-associated phenotypes, nominating HD-LINC lowering as a potential therapeutic strategy in HD. These results identify HD-LINC as a human-specific regulator of neuronal LD spatial organization, lipid peroxidation, and neuronal degeneration in HD. They further reveal dysregulated neuritic LD accumulation driven by HD-LINC, and highlight lincRNA-mediated lipid dysregulation as a significant contributor to neuronal vulnerability to degeneration.

abstract:
BACKGROUND: Immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) have transformed the management of mismatch repair-deficient/microsatellite instability-high (dMMR/MSI-H) colorectal cancer (CRC), yet the ~95% of patients with mismatch repair-proficient/microsatellite-stable (pMMR/MSS) disease derive little benefit owing to an immunologically "cold" tumor microenvironment (TME), poor T-cell infiltration, myeloid dominance, TGF-β-enriched stroma, and the systemically immunosuppressive milieu imposed by hepatic metastases. Clinically tested combinations-multikinase inhibitor plus anti-PD-1, Fc-enhanced dual checkpoint blockade, chemotherapy- or antiangiogenic-ICI regimens-have so far produced modest, largely non-durable response rates that are further attenuated in liver-metastatic disease, motivating approaches that pharmacologically remodel the TME rather than only release checkpoint restraint.
OBJECTIVE: To provide an evidence-stratified synthesis of nanotechnology-enabled immunotherapy in CRC that explicitly separates (a) clinically established evidence, (b) strategies under early-phase clinical investigation, and (c) concepts that remain preclinical or are extrapolated from other tumor types, and to derive from this appraisal a biomarker-enriched translational research agenda.
METHODS: Narrative, integrative (non-systematic) review. PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, ClinicalTrials.gov, and ASCO/ESMO/AACR proceedings were searched from January 2010 through April 2026. Each strategy was appraised according to the highest available level of evidence, the tumor type and model system in which the evidence was generated, and its demonstrated CRC specificity.
RESULTS: In current clinical practice, nanomedicine in CRC is essentially limited to nanoparticle-formulated cytotoxics exploited for pharmacokinetic advantage (e.g. liposomal irinotecan), whereas nano-enabled immunotherapy is confined to a small number of early-phase trials-most notably lipid nanoparticle (LNP)-formulated individualized neoantigen mRNA vaccines in ctDNA-positive resected CRC and hafnium-oxide nanoparticle radioenhancers-none of which has yet demonstrated a progression-free or overall survival benefit in MSS CRC. Against this background we critically appraise six classes of strategy: (i) LNP-based mRNA neoantigen vaccines; (ii) polymeric and inorganic nanocarriers for STING and TLR agonists; (iii) tumor-associated macrophage-repolarizing nanoparticles; (iv) nano-radiosensitizers and photothermal/photodynamic platforms priming immunogenic cell death; (v) nano-formulated checkpoint inhibitor delivery; and (vi) locoregional nano-strategies directed at hepatic metastasis-specific immunosuppression. For categories (ii)-(vi) the supporting evidence is predominantly murine (largely subcutaneous CT26/MC38 models) or extrapolated from immunologically "hot" tumors such as melanoma and non-small-cell lung cancer, in which both the underlying biology and the checkpoint backbone differ materially from MSS CRC. Recurrent translational barriers include low, highly heterogeneous nanoparticle accumulation in human tumors, dense TGF-β-rich stroma and elevated interstitial pressure, mononuclear phagocyte system clearance, liver-metastasis-specific tolerance that subcutaneous models do not reproduce, unresolved manufacturing/CMC and regulatory pathways, and the absence of validated pharmacodynamic biomarkers of intratumoral immune conversion.
CONCLUSION: Nanotechnology offers a mechanistically coherent and experimentally testable-but at present clinically unproven-set of strategies for converting "cold" MSS CRC into immune-responsive disease. We therefore position nano-enabled immunotherapy as a research priority rather than an imminent standard of care, and argue that its clinical value can only be established through biomarker-enriched, paired-biopsy early-phase trials with pharmacodynamic endpoints of immune conversion and prospective stratification by metastatic site (particularly hepatic involvement) and consensus molecular subtype.
LIMITATIONS: This is a narrative rather than systematic review; it is therefore subject to selection and publication bias, and much of the evidence synthesized is preclinical and of limited direct translational certainty.

abstract: Short RNA oligonucleotides directed at the 3' splice site region of EGFR exon 3 reduced the proliferation of A172 glioblastoma cells, while the same oligonucleotides had no detectable effect on A549 lung adenocarcinoma cells. Glioblastoma carries EGFR amplification in roughly a third of IDH-wildtype cases, and the A172 line harbours a tandem duplication in the EGFR tyrosine kinase domain. Because exon definition in human genes depends on RNA-binding proteins that engage exonic sequence near splice sites, we used the SpliceAid database to identify candidate RNA-binding proteins at EGFR exons 2 and 3. Y-box binding protein 1 (YB-1, encoded by YBX1), reported to drive glioblastoma growth through its RNA-binding function, scored highly immediately adjacent to the exon 3 3' splice site. We designed four 2'-modified RNA oligonucleotides carrying a nuclear localisation signal: two antisense oligonucleotides against the exon 3 region (asRNA1, spanning the splice site; asRNA2, downstream of it), a decoy complementary to the asRNA2 target (dRNA2), and a decoy carrying the YB-1 consensus binding sequence (dYB-1). In A172 cells, all four reduced EGFR protein in a single Western blot experiment, and asRNA1, asRNA2 and dRNA2 reduced proliferation relative to scrambled RNA at days 1 to 3; dYB-1 produced a comparable reduction at day 3. None of these effects was seen in A549 cells. YB-1 protein level and subcellular distribution were unchanged by the oligonucleotides, arguing against an indirect route through altered YB-1 abundance. These observations are preliminary. Every experiment reported here was performed once: the proliferation data come from single plates with three wells per group, analysed by Dunnett's test against the scrambled-RNA control, and the Western blot, RT-PCR and immunocytochemistry panels are single runs presented as representative observations. Direct binding of YB-1 to the targeted EGFR sequence has not been demonstrated. We post this work as a preprint so that the design strategy and the initial observations are available while these questions remain open.

abstract:
Background:

Warts, hypogammaglobulinemia, infections and myelokathexis syndrome (WHIMs) is a rare disorder that affects the immune system. People with WHIMs can have severe infections all over their body. WHIMs is caused by a mutation in the CXCR4 gene. Treatment with drugs can help control the infections but does not cure the disorder. Researchers want to try a treatment where they collect stem cells from a person with WHIMS, use base-editing to replace the bad gene with a healthy version, and return the new cells to the person. This could cure WHIMs.

Objective:

To test a treatment using base-edited stem cells in people with WHIMs.

Eligibility:

People aged 3 years and older with WHIMs.

Design:

The study has 4 stages.

Stage 1: Screening. Participants will be screened at 1 or more visits. They will have a physical exam with blood tests. A sample of tissue and fluid (biopsy) will be taken from the bone marrow in the hip.

Stage 2: Apheresis. Blood will be taken from the body through a needle; the blood will pass through a machine that separates out the stem cells. The remaining blood will be returned to the body through a different needle. The collected stem cells will undergo gene editing.

Stage 3: Treatment. Participants will stay in the hospital for about 4 weeks. They will receive 3 drugs to prepare their body for the procedure. Then the edited stem cells will be returned to their bloodstream. They will stay in the hospital until they recover.

Stage 4: Follow-up. Participants will have 8 follow-up visits over 5 years. Long-term visits will continue for 15 years.

description:
Study Description:

This is a phase 1/2, non-randomized study of a single infusion of autologous hematopoietic stem/progenitor cells (HSPC) base-edited to repair CXCR4 mutations in 10 participants with (Warts, Hypogammaglobulinemia, Infections, and Myelokathexis) WHIM syndrome.

Primary Objective: Evaluate safety of treatment with BE-HSPC CXCR4 in participants with WHIM syndrome.

Secondary Objectives:

Evaluate:

* Efficacy.
* Genetic correction.
* Immune reconstitution.
* Clinical efficacy.

Exploratory Objective:

Evaluate off-target (OT) editing activity.

Primary Endpoint:

Safety assessed by:

* Incidence of adverse events (AEs) for each participant.
* Evaluate overall incidence of AEs for the study.
* Incidence of serious adverse events (SAEs).

Secondary Endpoints (24 months post-study agent infusion):

* Efficacy: \>= 5% gene edited circulating myeloid cells by 12 months after BE HSPC infusion.
* Gene correction:

  --Frequency of corrected alleles in peripheral blood cells (such as myeloid, T, B, and natural killer \[NK\] cells).

  --\>200/microL edited neutrophils by 12 months post receipt of the BE HSPC infusion.
* Immune reconstitution:

  * T, B, and NK cell number improvement from baseline.
  * B-cell function: immunoglobulin (Ig) production.
* Clinical efficacy: Improvement from baseline problems such as recurrent infection, wart burden, gastrointestinal complaints, or immune dysregulation.

Exploratory Endpoint:

Evaluate for frequency of OTs by high-throughput sequencing (HTS) of the target mutation at the genomic locus 2 years post-infusion.

abstract: Mitochondrial RNA editing events were previously reported in only three unrelated species within the phylum Heterolobosea (Discoba): Naegleria gruberi and Acrasis kona (which performs C-to-U substitutions) and Pharyngomonadida sp. BB2 (which inserts single nucleotides by a yet unknown mechanism). We present novel high-quality genome assemblies obtained via a combination of whole-genome and targeted sequencing approaches and predicted proteomes for two species, Paravahlkampfia ustiana and Heteramoeba clara, representing an understudied clade of the phylum. Surprisingly, we discovered RNA editing events of C-to-U substitutions and mononucleotide insertions co-existing in the mitochondria of P. ustiana, while the two systems were both absent in H. clara. In addition, P. ustiana also exhibits A-to-I editing sites in rRNA transcripts encoded in multicopy circular rDNA plasmids. RNA editing events in P. ustiana were verified by proteomics, Illumina short RNA reads, ONT long cDNA and direct RNA reads. We elaborate on the potential mechanisms of mitochondrial insertional editing by investigating several aspects of the RNA transcription machinery and base modifications in template DNA and mRNA products. We report additional cases of C-to-U RNA editing in other species of Heterolobosea and explore the distribution of various putative components of the C-to-U editosome, including the DYW domain-containing pentatricopeptide repeat (PPR) proteins, across the phylum expanding the understanding of the evolutionary dynamics underlying this phenomenon, which remains understudied outside land plants. The comparative analysis of available sequence data from Heterolobosea revealed that C-to-U RNA editing was acquired relatively deep in the evolution of Heterolobosea and subsequently underwent repeated losses.

abstract: Women at risk for development of breast cancer and experiencing vasomotor menopausal symptoms (hot flashes) will be randomized to bazedoxifene (BZA) plus conjugated estrogens (CE) for 6 months versus a wait list control. Two risk factors for development of breast cancer will be studied pre-study and after 6 months: fibroglandular volume (FGV) on mammogram as assessed by Volpara software and proliferation by Ki-67 immunocytochemistry in benign breast tissue acquired by random periareolar fine needle aspiration (RPFNA). Change in biomarkers will be compared between groups.

institutions.label: National Cancer Institute (NCI)

description: Phase IIB trial of 6 months of BZA 20 mg +CE 0.45 mg (subsequently designated as BZA+CE) vs a waitlist control. Trial is informed by prior results of a single arm trial that used Duavee® (combination of BZA+CE that is FDA-approved for relief of hot flashes). Since Duavee® is currently not available commercially, the two separate components are used instead. Breast imaging, benign breast tissue by RPFNA, and blood for biomarkers will be obtained at baseline and at 6 months using similar assessment techniques. The primary endpoint is the difference between the BZA+CE and control groups for absolute change from baseline to 6 months in the risk biomarker fibroglandular volume (FGV). Volpara® fully automated assessments overcome the interpretive variance inherent in subjective assessments. Additional endpoints include changes in benign breast epithelial immunolabeling for Ki-67, estrogen receptor alpha (ERα), progesterone receptor (PR), and anterior gradient-2 protein (AGR2); and systemic levels of bioavailable hormones, IGF-1, IGFBP3, and measures of insulin sensitivity. The modifying effects of baseline BMI, visceral adipose, and plasma BZA concentrations on markers will be studied.

BACKGROUND/AIM: Current clinicopathological factors inadequately capture the biological heterogeneity of non-muscle-invasive bladder cancer (NMIBC). This study investigated the prognostic significance of ubiquitin-like protein 3 (UBL3), a molecule involved in extracellular vesicle sorting and immune regulation, in NMIBC.
MATERIALS AND METHODS: Following an exploratory analysis of public RNA-sequencing databases, we evaluated tissue samples from patients who underwent transurethral resection for primary NMIBC. A discovery cohort (n=37) was assessed for UBL3 mRNA via qRT-PCR and protein expression via immunohistochemistry (IHC) quantified using digital H-scores (QuPath). A separate internal validation cohort (n=192) was subsequently evaluated by IHC. The primary endpoint was recurrence-free survival (RFS).
RESULTS: The database analysis indicated that high UBL3 expression was associated with longer RFS in early-stage bladder cancer. In the discovery cohort, higher UBL3 mRNA levels were associated with prolonged RFS [hazard ratio (HR)=0.33, p=0.004]. mRNA levels also were associated with digital H-scores (ρ=0.39, p=0.018). In the separate internal validation cohort, elevated UBL3 protein expression was associated with a reduced risk of recurrence. A multivariable Cox regression confirmed that a higher UBL3 H-score (HR=0.95 per 10-point increase, p=0.023), alongside a negative preoperative urine cytology and immediate intravesical chemotherapy, remained independently associated with RFS.
CONCLUSION: Elevated UBL3 expression was associated with prolonged RFS in patients with NMIBC following transurethral resection of bladder tumor. While UBL3 has potential as a prognostic biomarker, establishing its definitive clinical utility will require mechanistic investigations and validation across independent, multicenter cohorts.

abstract: APOE4 is the strongest genetic risk factor for late-onset Alzheimer's disease, yet the cellular mechanisms linking APOE variants to disease risk remain unclear. We previously found that APOE4 expression causes lipid droplet accumulation in oligodendrocytes, reducing myelination, but the underlying mechanisms were unknown. Using a genome-wide CRISPR screen and assay for transposase-accessible chromatin (ATAC) sequencing in human-induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-derived oligodendrocytes, we identified decreased Wnt signaling and overactive glycogen synthase kinase-3 beta (GSK3B) as key regulators of lipid-droplet accumulation. Genetic and pharmacological inhibition of GSK3B reduced lipid droplets in APOE4 oligodendrocytes and increased myelination in three-dimensional iPSC-derived brain organoids. Pharmacological GSK3B inhibition also reduced lipid droplets and improved myelination in APOE4;PS19 tau transgenic mice. Together, these findings establish a mechanistic framework linking Wnt/GSK3B signaling to APOE4-driven disruptions in oligodendrocyte lipid metabolism and myelination, pointing to GSK3B as a potential therapeutic target for APOE4-associated Alzheimer's disease.

abstract:
The purpose of this study is to compare the impact of high-intensity interval training (HIIT) versus moderate-intensity continuous training (MICT) on human health outcomes in healthy sedentary subjects, over 12 weeks of exercise training.

The investigators will compare several health parameters, such as changes in multiomics profile, cardiorespiratory fitness, muscle strength, and body composition, before and after 12-week interventions of either HIIT or MICT.

abstract:
The aim is to study whether a multiallergen oral immunotherapy (OIT) strategy with slow up-dosing and low treatment dose against food allergy in young children (0.5-3 years) is safe and effective, a method to cure food allergy and to prevent the development of new food allergies.

Clinical randomized controlled (1:1) blinded interventional trial (RCT) with 2 intervention arms (group A and B).

Among 80 children reacting at the multiallergen food challenge, 40 children will be randomized to receive OIT (oral immunotherapy) with multiallergen powder with a final dose of approximately 200 mg protein of each included food (egg, milk, soy, wheat, walnut, peanut, hazelnut, cashew, almond, lentils)(group A) or to receive placebo powder (gluten-free oatmeal) (group B).

A sub-analysis will be performed of the children not reacting to the baseline challenge, who will be randomized to eat a low dose of the multiallergen powder (group C) or placebo powder (gluten-free oatmeal) (group D) and no specific advice.
description:
Today, there is no established curative treatment for food allergies, and those affected must avoid the food that triggers symptoms. The most studied method is oral immunotherapy (OIT) which have mainly been carried out on children \>4 years of age. The OIT method implies that the allergic individual eats initially very low doses and gradually increasing amounts of the allergen until a maintenance dose is reached. The treatment aims to induce desensitization or tolerance to the allergen.

Intervention: The intervention substance is a powder containing a prespecified amount of 10 allergens (egg, milk, wheat, lentils, soy, walnut, peanut, hazelnut, cashew, almond), which are the most triggering allergens in children. The product is developed in cooperation with Research Institute of Sweden (RISE).

Clinical randomized controlled (1:1) blinded interventional trial (RCT) with 2 interventions arms (group A and B). A sub-analysis will be performed of the children not reacting to the baseline challenge (group C and D).

Group A: Children with food allergy (sensitization and positive baseline challenge), receiving multiallergen powder OIT, slow up-dosing until 3 teaspoons of the multiallergen powder is reached daily. Food challenge will be performed after 1 and 2 years. 2 years treatment.

Group B: Children with food allergy (sensitization and positive baseline challenge), receiving OIT with placebo (gluten-free oatmeal) followed by maintenance, in total 2 years. Food challenge will be performed after 1 and 2 years.

After the first 20 participants in groups A and B have completed the one-year challenge, tolerance will be evaluated. If children in group A have a statistically significant (p \< 0.05) higher tolerated cumulative dose at the one-year challenge than group B the multiallergen powder is considered more effective than placebo and all children in group B will be offered a cross-over following the one-year challenge.

Group C and D: sensitized children with a negative baseline challenge will be randomized 1:1 for treatment with multiallergen powder or placebo powder in a lower amount, 1 teaspoon daily and can introduce food in accordance with Swedish guidelines. After one year a food challenge will be performed.

Selection for group A to D: All children 0.5-3 years of age in Stockholm County who had a positive blood test for suspected food allergy to one or more of the 10 included allergens with specific immunoglobulin E (IgE) \>0.1 kUA/L, are eligible as possible study participants. The data is obtained from the Karolinska University Laboratory's test results register. Information letters will be sent to families with IgE-sensitized children.

Inclusion groups A to D: Children 0.5-3 years old at inclusion with positive IgE \>0.1 kUA/L against at least one of the 10 above mentioned allergens. Eighty children, group A (n=40) and group B (n=40) also need a positive baseline food challenge.

Children with a negative food challenge (group C and D) (number is not determined) do not react at the baseline challenge.

Primary outcome: Tolerance to 900 mg protein, cumulative dose, of each of the 10 included allergens, at the food challenge after two years OIT treatment or placebo (group A and B).

Secondary outcomes: Tolerance to cumulative dose of 900 mg protein of each food, evaluated with a food challenge after one years in all children (group A-D). Changes in immunological markers, eczema and asthma status and changes in quality of life in relation to interventions.

outcomes.description:
To study different immunological biomarkers (e.g. T-helper cell population and polarization and IgE-levels) before, during and after OIT treatment and compare this to the placebo group. Immunological marker in mononuclear cells in peripheral blood will be analyzed ex vivo with flowcytometri and RNA-sequencing platforms. Circulating immunological factors, e.g. cytokines and chemokines will be analyzed in plasma with ELISA-based methods. Mononuclear cellpopulations in peripheral blood will be exposed to different stimuli (such as sensitizing allergen, anti-C D3/ C D28) in vitro, type and level of reaction in the different cellpopulations will be monitored at mRNA- and protein-level.

Blood sampling will be collected in connection with the visit for the baseline challenge, at the challenge at 1 years (group A-D) and 2 years (A-B).

outcomes.description: Clinical examination including eczema grading will be performed at the food challenges and basic clinical examination at each study-visit. Eczema grading will be evaluated using Eczema area and severity index (EASI), score between 0-72.

outcomes.description: Clinical examination including evaluation asthma status will be performed at the food challenges and basic clinical examination at each study-visit. Asthma status will be evaluated with a clinical examination, use of asthma medication, number of wheezing episodes as well as hospitalization prior to the study visit.
outcomes.measure: Changes in asthma status in relation to interventions

outcomes.description: To evaluate changes in quality of life before and after multiallergen OIT using the "Food allergy quality of life questionnaire-parental form" (FAQLQ-PF) validated and translated into Swedish. Comparisons will be made between the OIT group and the placebo group. FAQLQ-PF is a multidimensional parent report measure to assess children between 0-12 years. There are 14 items for children below 4 years old which are scored on a 7 point scale from 0 (no impact of HRQL) to 6 (extreme impact of HRQL). FAQLQ-PF include questions for food-allergy specific QoL with general emotional impact, food anxiety, social and dietary limitations. Overall and domain specific HRQL scores will be calculated. Higher score mean worse outcome and a score of ≥ ±0.5 will be considered clinically relevant.
outcomes.measure: Changes in quality of life in relation to interventions

abstract:
This randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial aims to investigate whether n-3 polyunsaturated fatty acid (PUFA) supplementation attenuates abdominal visceral fat accumulation induced by experimental sleep restriction.

Forty healthy adults aged 18-50 years will be randomly assigned to receive n-3 PUFA supplementation (approximately 1.1 g/day of EPA and DHA) or a matching placebo. The intervention will last approximately 75 days, including a 19-day residential sleep protocol consisting of 3 adaptation days, 14 days of sleep restriction (4 hours per night), and 2 recovery days.

The primary outcome is the change in abdominal visceral adipose tissue area measured by CT. Additional assessments include body composition, metabolic and inflammatory markers, gut microbiota, microbial metabolites, and adipose tissue molecular profiles.
description:
Experimental sleep restriction provides a controlled model for investigating the metabolic consequences of insufficient sleep. This study will examine whether n-3 PUFA supplementation modifies visceral fat accumulation and related biological responses during sleep restriction.

Participants will undergo a standardized residential sleep protocol with continuous polysomnographic monitoring. Abdominal CT will be performed on Days 3 and 17 to assess changes in visceral and subcutaneous adipose tissue. Additional measurements will include dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry, ambulatory blood pressure monitoring, cognitive assessments, biological sample collection, and exploratory molecular analyses.

The study will also explore potential mechanisms involving gut microbiota, microbial metabolism, inflammation, and adipose tissue responses.

abstract:
Adipose tissue is with endocrine properties and secretes many cytokines. Some of these cytokines are concerned with ischemic heart disease. I hypothesized that significant surgical reduction in adipose tissue mass leads to decrease in its cell population which may pose significantly reduced production of adipokines ( Leptin and Angiotensin) associated with ischemic heart disease in obese people.

Study objectives are analysis of Leptin, Angiotensin-II, mRNA expression analysis of leptin, leptin receptor and Angiotensin-II. investigation of genetic variations in the Leptin, Leptin receptors, Angiotensin-I and Angiotensin-II receptors, confirm SNPs of selected sample. Ddetermination of the association of genetic variation in Leptin receptor, angiotensin-I and Angiotensin-II receptors with Leptin and Angiotensin-II levels and determination of effect of genetic variation on the transcriptional regulation.

Case control study having 212 patients (106 patients in each group) with type I Obese adults, both males and pre-menopausal females belonging to ASA 1 and 2 requiring stagged liposuction will be included. Exclusion of subjects with Diabetes mellitus, Metabolic syndrome, Endocrine disorders, on statin drugs, not willing to participate.

After informed consent, blood samples will be taken to quantify plasma levels of Leptin and Angiotensin II pre-operatively by ELISA.

DNA will also be extracted from blood and SNPs will be analysed. The selected SNPs will be amplified by PCR and product will be purified and analysed by agarose gel electrophoresis.

Patients will undergo liposuction and RNA will be isolated from subcutaneous adipose tissue for reverse transcription.

After 3 months, patients will be called back for second session of liposuction and plasma level of Leptin and Angiotensin II will be quantified again. Similarly, expression profile of transcription factors will also be analysed again. Paired t-test will be used to compare clinical parameters like serum adipokines levels and adipokines expression levels and p value \<0.05 will be taken as statistically significant. The results will be utilized to determine impact of surgical reduction on plasma level and expression of the adipokines in minimizing cardiovascular risk factors.
description:
INTRODUCTION:

Overweight and obesity belong to the main public healthcare problems in many developed countries. Causes of obesity are considered to be the combination of genetic, epigenetic and environmental factors. In case of morbid obesity, the human organism suffers from an excess of subcutaneous and visceral adipose tissue.1 Adipose tissue plays a principal role in overall metabolic homeostasis, and its dysfunction can lead to metabolic disorders, most notably type 2 diabetes and cardiovascular disease.2 Mature adipocytes express all components of the renin- angiotensin system (RAS) including angiotensin Il (Ang II), and also express the type 1 (AT1) and type 2 (AT 2) angiotensin receptor subtypes.3 For cardiovascular disease, perivascular adipose tissue (PVAT) is a specific adipose tissue and now recognized to be an endocrine organ with important physiological and pathological effects on vascular homeostasis and vascular diseases.(4) PVAT dysfunction may induce several pathophysiological states such as obesity, atherosclerosis or hypertension.4-6 There are essentially two major types of adipose tissue with different functions: brown adipose tissue (BAT) containing multiple lipid droplets and densely packed mitochondria, and white adipose tissue (WAT) with large lipid droplets and relatively low expression levels of UCP-1(mitochondrial uncoupling protein-1).4 Ang II is produced from angiotensin I (Ang I as a result of the catalytic action of angiotensin-converting enzyme I (ACE-1). Ang Il plays an important role in the regulation of blood volume, blood pressure, cardiac function, and electrolyte balance.7 On the other hand, Leptin is a protein classified within the adipokine family and is currently recognized as a hormone consisting of 167 amino acids with a molecular weight of 16 kD. It is predominantly synthesized in adipocytes, and its production is contingent upon the volume of fat deposits in the body. It is known that leptin inhibits the orexigenic pathway and stimulates the anorexigenic pathway, underscoring its pivotal role in body weight regulation.8 The relationship between leptin and the RAAS is bi-directional. Leptin not only stimulates sympathetic nervous system activation and angiotensin-dependent mechanisms, but it also seems to be a major driver in the aldosterone production in obese patients.9 Moreover, leptin appears to play a role in heart protection. The increased blood volume in obese patients increases cardiac output and stimulates biomechanical stress and structural remodeling that may result in cardiac hypertrophy. A correlation between plasma leptin levels and cardiac hypertrophy has been clinically demonstrated.10 There is evidence for both angiotensin and leptin receptors in several brain regions involved in regulation of sympathetic nerve activity. Ang II may modulate the action of leptin and adiponectin in obesity. Blocking of RAS increases plasma adiponectin suggesting a role of Ang II in decreased levels of adiponectin. Supporting this, Ang I1 infusion decreased plasma adiponectin and adiponectin mRNA in adipose tissue. Ang II also interacts with adiponectin in their target cells.11 Considering the role of Ang II and Leptin in the regulation of obesity, I hypothesized that significant surgical reduction in adipose tissue mass leads to decrease in its cell population which may pose significantly reduced production of adipokines associated with ischemic heart disease in obese people.

OBJECTIVES:

Analysis of adipokine levels (Leptin, Angiotensin-II) in patients with type I obesity (Quazi Experimental).

mRNA expression analysis of leptin, leptin receptor and Angiotensin-II (Quazi Experimental).

Investigation of genetic variations in the Leptin, Leptin receptors, Angiotensin-I and Angiotensin-II receptors (Case Control).

Confirm SNPs of selected sample. Determine the association of genetic variation in Leptin receptor, Angiotensin-I and Angiotensin-II receptors with Leptin and Angiotensin-II levels.

Determine effect of genetic variation on the transcriptional regulation.

OPERATIONAL DEFINITION:

Significant Fat Reduction A removal of 1 liter or more lipoaspirate through liposuction will be considered as significant.

Tumescence Injection of fluid in the fat removal area containing Ringer Lactate each litter with 40ml 2% xylocaine and 1ml of 1:1000 Epinephrine till the area is blanched and showing fountain sign.

Polymorphism Defined a discontinuous genetic variation resulting in the occurrence of several different forms or types of individuals among the members of a single species. A discontinuous genetic variation divides the individuals of a population into two or more sharply distinct forms.

HYPOTHESIS:

Significant surgical reduction of adipose tissue reduces the level of adipokines (Leptin and Angiotensin) associated with cardiac risk in plasma and their expression in adipose tissue.

MATERIAL AND METHODS:

Study design Case control study. Setting The study will be conducted at Advanced Research Centre for Biomedical Sciences (ARCBS), KEMU and Jinnah Burn and Reconstructive Surgery Center / AIMC, Lahore.

Duration The study will be expected to complete within two years after the approval of synopsis.

Sample size Sample size of 212 patients (106 patients in each group) is estimated by using 95% confidence level and 10% absolute precision with expected percentage LEPrs7799039 as in FEN as 19.1% and healthy control as 14.1%.(12) n = Z 1-α/2 \[P1 (1- P1) +P2 (1- P2)\] d2 Z 1-α/2 = confidence level 95 % = 1.96 P1 = population proportion I = 19.1% P2 = population proportion II = 14% d2 = absolute precision 10% SNP analysis will be done in all the 212 subjects with 106 taken as cases (Obese type 1) and 106 as controls (Normal BMI).

Out of 106 cases, liposuction will be performed in selected subjects. Similarly, sequencing will be done in selected subjects. Sampling technique Non Probability Consecutive Sampling.

SAMPLE SELECTION:

Inclusion Criteria: Type I Obese adults, both males and pre-menopausal females, Patients requiring stagged liposuction, American Society of Anesthesiology (ASA) class 1 and 2 (as determined by consultant anesthesiologist) Exclusion Criteria: Patients who are with Diabetes mellitus, Metabolic syndrome, Endocrine disorders, on statin drugs, not willing to participate.

DATA COLLECTION PROCEDURE:

Informed consent will be obtained from the study subjects for donation of blood and adipose tissue samples in the proposed study, which will be conducted under a protocol approved by the Institutional Review Board of King Edward Medical University (Appendix I). The information of the study subjects will be kept confidential, and the subjects will be recruited against lab record number or archive number.

Sample Collection: Patients will undergo lipo-aspiration under tumescence by Colman's technique. Each unit of tumescent fluid will include xylocaine 40ml, Hartmann's solution 1000ml and 1ml adrenaline. A multi hole 5mm liposuction cannula attached with suction machine will be inserted through the incisions using controlled back and forth motion. All the patients will be followed fortnightly. Analysis of pre and post procedure blood and adipose tissue samples will be done. For DNA extraction, 5ml blood will be collected.

Quantification of Serum Adipokines levels by ELISA: Serum will be separated after clotting through centrifugation at 3000 rpm and stored at -70°C. ELIS A will be performed on samples by standard protocol for the quantification of adipokines (Leptin, Angiotensin I1) pre-operatively and three months post operatively DNA Extraction: 5ml blood will be collected in EDTA-coated tubes. Genomic DNA will be extracted from whole blood by using commercially available kits.

Restriction Fragment Length Polymorphism Analysis of SNPs: The selected SNPs will be amplified by polymerase chain reaction (PCR) by using the primers given in Table 1. Amplicons will be detected on 2.5% agarose gel and stained with DNA gel stain. DNA bands will be detected by gel documentation instrument under UV light. PCR product will be purified by using commercially available kit and digested with restriction enzymes. The restriction product will be analyzed by agarose gel electrophoresis.

Sequencing of SNPs: Sequencing of SNPs will be done using specific primers by Sanger Sequence using ABI 3500, Genetic Analyzer (Applied Biosystems, Thermo Fisher Scientific, USA) and the sequences will be analyzed using the BLAST program at National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI). Amino acid sequences will be predicted by the standard code and will be aligned using the ExPASY online tool for translation. Sequencing will be done on study subjects and compared with same number of healthy persons for comparison.

RNA Isolation and cDNA Synthesis: RNA will be isolated from subcutaneous adipose tissue by using commercially available kits. 1ug RNA will be reverse transcribed using commercially available Transcription First Strand cDNA kit and oligo (dT) primers.

Real-time PCR Analysis for Gene Expression Analysis: Quantitative real-time PCR analysis will be carried out by using SYBR Green real-time PCR Master Mix and an ARIAmix, real-time PCR system (Agilent Technologies). Cycling conditions for real-time PCR will be 3 min at 95°C, followed by 40 cycles of 30 S at 95°C, 30 S at 60°C and 30 S at 72°C. Results will be analysed using the ΔΔCt method and will be presented as fold difference in mRNA level relative to GAPDH. The expression profile of transcription factors will be analyzed.

DATA ANALYSIS PRODECURE:

Data will be entered and analyzed using statistical Package for Social Sciences (SPSS-26). Quantitative variables like age, BMI, lipid profile and adipokine levels will be presented as mean ± SD. Qualitative variables like family history of obesity, family history of heart diseases and gender will be presented frequency and percentages. Paired t-test will be used to compare clinical parameters like serum adipokines levels and adipokines expression levels. Odds ratio and 95% CI will be used for SNP analysis. Whereas p value \<0.05 will be taken as statistically significant. Pearson equation will be used to determine association of adipokines levels with clinical parameters and expression levels.

OUTCOME \& UTILIZATION:

The results will be utilized to determine impact of surgical reduction on plasma level and expression of the adipokines in minimizing cardiovascular risk factors.

abstract:
BMD006 is an off-the-shelf antitumor mRNA vaccine targeting lung cancer and lung metastatic solid tumors.

This is a single-center, open-label, dose-escalation clinical trial. The study aims to evaluate the safety, tolerability, preliminary efficacy, pharmacokinetic (PK), and pharmacodynamic (PD) profiles of BMD006 in patients with advanced lung cancer or advanced solid tumors with lung metastasis who have progressed on or are ineligible for standard therapeutic options. This trial also further explores the clinical efficacy of BMD006 in combination with Immuno-Oncology (IO) therapy.

In addition, this study aims to explore the clinical efficacy of BMC001 in combination with Immuno-Oncology (IO) therapy.

The trial comprises three study arms: BMD006 monotherapy dose escalation, BMD006 plus IO therapy dose escalation, and BMD006 plus IO therapy dose expansion.

abstract: An Exploratory Study on the Use of mRNA Tumor Vaccines in the Treatment of Refractory Rhabdomyosarcoma
description: The purpose of this study is to evaluate the efficacy and safety of an personalized neoantigen mRNA vaccine in combination withthe anti-PD-1 antibody toripalimab and the CpG-1018 adjuvant in the treatment of patients with refractory rhabdomyosarcoma. The vaccine will be designed based on the specific tumor characteristics of each patient, providing a tailored therapeutic regimen with the aim of prolonging overall survival in patients with refractory rhabdomyosarcoma

abstract: We report the preclinical and early clinical evaluation of in vivo genome editing for Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD), delivered via a single AAV9 vector. In humanized DMD mice, systemic administration achieved targeted genome editing, partial dystrophin restoration, and improved muscle function. In non-human primates, efficient on-target editing was achieved with no dose-limiting toxicity identified under the conditions tested. In an open-label, dose-escalation, first-in-human clinical trial (NCT06594094), post-treatment muscle biopsies provided early molecular evidence of hfCas12Max-mediated genome editing and detectable dystrophin expression in participants with DMD. However, at the higher dose level (1.0 × 1014 vg/kg), one participant experienced a treatment-related fatal serious adverse event, characterized by marked complement activation and systemic cytokine response shortly after dosing. This work provides initial human proof-of-concept for muscle genome editing while crucially highlighting the critical role of immunologic risks and the narrow therapeutic window of systemic adeno-associated virus (AAV)-CRISPR therapies, underscoring the need to develop safer dosing and immunomodulation strategies.

abstract: Klebsiella pneumoniae (KP) poses a significant threat to global public health, and effective preventive measures are urgently needed. The widespread antibiotic resistance of KP underscores the critical need for vaccine-based strategies. Although numerous vaccine candidates against KP have been investigated, none has yet been licensed. mRNA-LNP vaccines against KP have only recently begun to be explored, and their ability to deliver conserved outer membrane protein antigens remains largely untested. In this study, we constructed an mRNA vaccine encoding the highly conserved outer membrane protein X (OmpX) of KP-the first mRNA-LNP vaccine targeting this antigen-and evaluated its immunogenicity and protective efficacy in mice. Immunoinformatics analyses predicted concordance between the in silico and in vivo outcomes: bioinformatics tools were used to evaluate the antigenicity, immunogenicity, physicochemical parameters, and secondary and tertiary structures of OmpX, and the C-ImmSim server was used to simulate the vaccine-elicited immune responses. We then performed mouse immunization and challenge experiments to characterize the humoral and cellular immune responses induced by the OmpX vaccine. The mRNA vaccine was immunogenic in mice, eliciting high titers of OmpX-specific antibodies. OmpX-Fc mRNA-LNPs also induced robust cell-mediated immunity, with significantly elevated IFN-{gamma} and IL-4 levels indicative of combined Th1/Th2 cellular responses. Serum from OmpX-immunized mice promoted significantly greater complement-mediated KP cell lysis than serum from the alum or luciferase mRNA-LNP control groups. Notably, OmpX-Fc mRNA-LNP immunization conferred complete protection against lethal KP challenge, with 100% survival and a significant reduction in visceral bacterial burden. These data establish a promising mRNA vaccine strategy for inducing broad immune responses and promoting serotype-independent immunity against KP.

abstract: Irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) is a common, often disabling disorder of gut-brain interaction whose molecular basis remains incompletely defined, leaving diagnosis largely symptom-based and treatment largely non-mechanistic. We argue that the serotonin (5-hydroxytryptamine; hereafter 5-HT, the primary term used throughout, with "serotonin" retained in less technical contexts) signalling axis-positioned at the interface of the gut microbiota, enterochromaffin (EC) cells, enteric neurons, and the mucosal immune system-is a central, unifying integrator of IBS pathophysiology, and that reframing IBS around this axis offers a route toward mechanism-based subtyping and therapy. We first synthesise how microbiota-driven tryptophan metabolism, short-chain fatty acid and secondary bile acid signalling, and epigenetic regulation of tryptophan hydroxylase 1 (TPH1) shape EC-cell serotonin output, before examining the neuroimmune consequences of dysregulated serotonin secretion-mast cell activation, macrophage polarisation, neurogenic inflammation-and the microbiota-serotonin-gut-brain connectome linking vagal afferent signalling, blood-brain barrier permeability, and central neurotransmitter networks. We then discuss molecular stratification of IBS subtypes through serotonergic endotyping-incorporating SLC6A4 and TPH1 polymorphisms, single-cell transcriptomics, and spatial metabolomics-and critically evaluate next-generation therapeutic strategies, including engineered probiotic chassis, CRISPR-mediated microbial editing, and AI-guided nanomedicine, distinguishing proof-of-concept findings from clinically validated approaches. We conclude that reconceptualising IBS as a disorder of disrupted microbial serotonergic ecosystems, rather than a purely symptom-defined syndrome, offers a coherent and testable framework for biomarker discovery and precision, mechanism-directed therapy, while highlighting the causal-directionality and clinical-translation gaps that must be closed before this framework can be applied at the bedside.

abstract: Probe-based PCR assays are commonly used to evaluate gene expression in antisense oligonucleotide (ASO)-treated samples, but assay design and postextraction processing may introduce substantial measurement bias. We investigated workflow-dependent differences in measured knockdown across PCR-based and RNA-sequencing assays using an allele-specific gapmer ASO, targeting a linked single nucleotide polymorphism of a dominant-negative SPTAN1 variant. Exogenous ribonuclease H (RNase H) activity during reverse transcription or ribosomal RNA (rRNA)-depletion inflated apparent knockdown and reduced RNA-sequencing coverage at the ASO-binding site. In droplet digital PCR (ddPCR), allele-specific detection probes overlapping the ASO-binding site produced substantially greater apparent knockdown than nonoverlapping probes, particularly following workflows with active RNase H. Spike-in experiments showed that this bias was not reproduced by adding ASO to purified RNA before complementary DNA (cDNA) synthesis or to cDNA before ddPCR, but emerged when ASO was present during rRNA depletion. Together, these findings show that exogenous RNase H activity during RNA processing and ASO-probe overlap can distort measurements of gapmer-mediated transcript reduction. Poly(A)-based RNA sequencing, reverse transcriptase with reduced RNase H activity, and nonoverlapping PCR detection probes can minimize measurement bias when evaluating gapmer ASO-mediated knockdown.
