description: In observational studies, small daily doses of lithium have been associated with a 77% reduced risk of developing Parkinson's disease (PD). In addition, lithium therapy has been effective in preventing neuronal death and behavioral symptoms in several PD animal models. Recently, our group has shown 24-weeks of low-dose lithium therapy in PD to improve both MRI and blood-based biomarkers implying that lithium may be slowing the progression of the disease. However, these findings stem from only three of four patients receiving MRIs. A larger study will be required to determine if these promising results can be replicated. The proposed study will enroll 20 additional PD patients who will be randomly assigned to receive either lithium 20mg/day or identically-appearing placebo capsules for 24 weeks. This will be a double-blind study meaning that neither the patients nor the study team will know to which therapy patients have been assigned. Positive results from this study will support further research on lithium that could eventually support lithium as a disease-modifying therapy for PD that could improve patients' long-term prognoses.

description: In observational studies, small daily doses of lithium from smoking cigarettes have been associated with a 77% reduced risk of developing Parkinson's disease (PD). In addition, lithium therapy has been effective in preventing neuronal death and behavioral symptoms in several PD animal models. Recently, our group has shown 24-weeks of low-dose lithium therapy in PD to be associated with improvements in both MRI and blood-based biomarkers implying that lithium may be slowing the progression of the disease. However, these findings stemmed from only three of four patients receiving MRIs. Our group is now conducting two larger studies enrolling a total of 35 PD patients who are being treated with either 45mg/day or 20mg/day of lithium or placebo therapy for 24 weeks. Because our earlier study showed maximum improvements in PD biomarkers in patients with serum lithium levels of 0.25-0.50mmol/L and there are large interpatient variations in serum lithium levels achieved from the same lithium dosage, this present study will adjust lithium dosing in each patient to achieve this target serum lithium level for an additional 24 weeks. MRI and blood-based biomarker changes from Baseline will be compared in patients with serum lithium levels ≥ 0.25mmol/L and \<0.25mmol/L from one of the 24-week studies and within individual patients. Results from this study may identify a target serum lithium level range associated with maximum improvements in PD biomarkers that can be used in the design of future, larger lithium PD lithium trials, which may eventually support lithium as a disease-modifying therapy for PD that could improve patients' long-term prognoses.

abstract: Trastuzumab deruxtecan (T-DXd) has demonstrated clinical efficacy in advanced HER2-low to -ultralow breast cancer. We employed a mouse model of triple-negative breast cancer in the difficult-to-treat brain metastasis setting to determine T-DXd efficacy and investigate mechanism(s). T-DXd (10 and 3 mg/kg) was compared to an identical ADC except HER2-nonbinding (control) in a hematogenous model of HER2-ultralow brain-tropic triple-negative breast cancer, MDA-MB-231-BR7 (231-BR). The roles of HER2 and the neonatal Fc receptor (FcRn) were determined by CRISPR-Cas9 deletion and shRNA knockdown, respectively. 231-BR cells exhibited HER2 0+ staining, with occasional membrane expression. T-DXd at 10 mg/kg reduced 231-BR brain metastases by 49% (P=0.002), while a dose reduction showed a 30% (ns) metastasis reduction, each compared to the control-ADC. HER2-specific and -nonspecific ADC uptake into metastases was accompanied by a 23-47% tumor cell Ki-67 decline, and 5-fold increase in tumor apoptosis. A HER2 CRISPR-Cas9 knockout 231-BR formed multiple brain metastases but was insensitive to T-DXd in vivo. 231-BR tumor cells expressed FcRn, potentially enabling nonspecific ADC uptake. Analysis of human tumors showed TNBC tumors expressed FcRn mRNA. T-DXd failed to inhibit brain metastases in two 231-BR FcRn knockdown clones compared to a 231-BR clone transduced with a scrambled shRNA where T-DXd inhibited brain metastases (67% reduction, P=0.01). Despite ultralow HER2 expression, the HER2 binding capacity of T-DXd is a significant contributor to its efficacy. Breast cancers variably express FcRn, suggesting that nonspecific tumor cell uptake of T-DXd via FcRn is also a potential mechanism of T-DXd action.

abstract: Psoriasis is a chronic immune-mediated skin disorder characterized by persistent inflammation, epidermal hyperproliferation, and complex interactions among immune cells, keratinocytes, cytokines, and genetic factors. Although conventional topical agents, systemic small molecules, and biologics have improved disease management, their clinical utility is often limited by insufficient efficacy, adverse effects, treatment resistance, and poor patient adherence. Recent advances in molecular biology have identified numerous pathogenic genes, signaling pathways, and regulatory RNAs involved in psoriasis, providing opportunities for the development of gene-based therapeutics, including antisense oligonucleotides, plasmid DNAs, small interfering RNAs, messenger RNAs, microRNAs, aptamers, and CRISPR/Cas9 systems. These therapeutics enable precise modulation of disease-associated targets at the genomic and transcriptional levels, offering advantages over conventional pharmacological approaches. However, their topical administration is hindered by the formidable cutaneous barrier, limited skin penetration, poor cellular uptake, and susceptibility to enzymatic degradation. This review summarizes the cellular, molecular, and genetic mechanisms underlying psoriasis pathogenesis and discusses the therapeutic potential of diverse gene-based approaches. Particular emphasis is placed on topical delivery platforms designed to overcome cutaneous barriers, including permeation enhancers, nanocarrier-based systems, and physical enhancement technologies. Recent advances in the integration of these delivery strategies with gene therapeutics for targeted psoriasis treatment are highlighted. Finally, current challenges related to delivery efficiency, long-term safety, manufacturing scalability, and regulatory approval are discussed, together with future perspectives for the clinical translation of topical gene-based therapeutics toward precision psoriasis management.

abstract: Marburg virus disease (MVD), a deadly zoonotic illness in humans, is caused by the Marburg virus (MARV), a single-stranded RNA virus belonging to the Orthomarburgvirus genus of the Filoviridae family. There are currently no approved vaccines or efficient antiviral therapies for MARV, despite high morbidity and fatality rates of the virus, particularly in Africa. Recognizing its epidemic potential and its inclusion on the WHO list of blueprint priority pathogens, an immunoinformatics approach was used to design novel multi-epitope saRNA vaccine candidates (MB-saVaxI and MB-saVaxII) targeting the viral GP, NP, VP40, and VP35 via CD8 + , CD4 + , and B cell epitopes. These epitopes were derived from target protein sequences and incorporated into MB-saVaxI and MB-saVaxII after validation for antigenicity, non-allergenicity, non-toxicity, and conservation. Additionally, the selected epitopes were conjugated to suitable adjuvants via various linkers, thereby enabling the design of a potentially stable vaccine. Additionally, the designed MB-saVaxI and MB-saVaxII were incorporated into the standard saRNA model, in which ORF-2 encodes the target vaccine peptide. Moreover, biophysical analyses unveiled that the developed vaccines are basic (pI < 7), soluble (GRAVY < 0), and stable (aliphatic index < 80). Subsequently, docking of MB-saVaxI to TLR2 (-938.3) and TLR4 (-902.4), and MB-saVaxII to TLR3 (-1485.4) and TLR7 (-1543.6) demonstrated significant affinity, with detailed hydrogen-bond interactions validated by MM-GBSA and molecular dynamics simulations. Furthermore, MB-saVaxI and MB-saVaxII were effectively cloned in-silico into Escherichia coli, and immune simulations indicated that the vaccines triggered robust innate and adaptive immunity, with a sustained memory response and TH cell activation, as evidenced by IFN-γ and IL-2 production. Additionally, the mRNA structure of MB-saVaxI and MB-saVaxII remained stable throughout the expression pathway in the host. However, extensive in-vitro and in-vivo studies are needed to establish the safety and efficacy of this vaccine candidate conclusively.

abstract: Cancer remains a formidable challenge in global oncology, with conventional treatments often failing to achieve durable responses in advanced stages. Adoptive cell therapy (ACT), despite its revolutionary success in hematological malignancies, faces critical bottlenecks in solid tumors, including a hostile immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment (TME), restricted cellular trafficking, and the rapid onset of T-cell exhaustion. This review systematically explores the evolution of ACT platforms, ranging from foundational tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes (TILs) to precision-engineered chimeric antigen receptor (CAR)-T and T-cell receptor (TCR)-T therapies. We highlight how innovative engineering strategies such as the integration of "armored" CARs, synthetic gene circuits, and CRISPR/Cas9-mediated gene editing have been employed to enhance the persistence and polyfunctionality of effector cells. Beyond T-cell-centric approaches, we examine the emerging landscape of diverse immune effector cells, including CAR-natural killer (NK) cells, and CAR-macrophages (CAR-M), which offer unique advantages in antigen recognition and safety profiles. Furthermore, we detail the synergistic potential of multimodal combination regimens, where ACT is paired with immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs), localized radiotherapy, or nanotechnology-based delivery systems to dismantle TME barriers and achieve systemic anti-tumor immunity. By tracing the journey of therapeutic cells from ex vivo expansion to intratumoral infiltration and cytotoxicity, this review illuminates the molecular mechanisms governing therapeutic efficacy. Finally, we discuss the current clinical trial landscape, manufacturing hurdles, and the regulatory pathways essential for transitioning these sophisticated cellular products from bench to bedside.

title: Innovations and emerging trends in adoptive cell therapies for solid tumors: engineering strategies and clinical translation.

abstract: Liver fibrosis is a severe complication of diverse chronic liver diseases characterized by a dysregulated hepatic microenvironment, and effective clinical therapeutic strategies for this condition remain lacking to date. Chimeric antigen receptor macrophages (CAR-Ms) hold considerable therapeutic potential for liver fibrosis via antigen-specific recognition and efferocytotic activity, yet their clinical translation is largely hindered by the sophisticated ex vivo preparation procedures. Herein, we report an in situ CAR-M engineering strategy that uses a phosphatidylserine (PS)-incorporated, macrophage-targeted lipid nanoparticle (LNP) for the codelivery of CAR messenger RNA (mRNA) and Cas9 mRNA in vivo. Our findings demonstrate that this engineered LNP achieves efficient targeting of liver-resident macrophages. Transfection with fibroblast activation protein α (FAPα)-CAR mRNA equips macrophages with the capacity to specifically target activated hepatic stellate cells (aHSCs), whereas Cas9-mediated follistatin-like protein 1 (FSTL-1) gene editing enhances the efferocytotic function of macrophages in liver tissues. Consequently, functional CAR-Ms are generated in situ, which elicits robust antifibrotic effects, including reduced collagen deposition, restored sinusoidal architecture and enhanced immune-mediated antifibrotic activity. Collectively, our customized LNP-mediated in situ engineering of liver macrophages into CAR-Ms enables precise antifibrotic intervention for liver fibrosis and circumvents the cumbersome ex vivo CAR-M preparation process.

title: In situ CAR-M engineered by liposomal mRNA nanomedicine remodels fibrotic microenvironment for ameliorating liver fibrosis.

abstract: The generation of memory B cells following influenza virus vaccination and their rapid recruitment into the virus-specific immune response following infection is an essential component of vaccine-induced protection. We have previously reported the capacity of an influenza hemagglutinin (HA) expressing mRNA-LNP vaccine administered to newborn African green monkeys (AGM) to elicit both HA head- and stem-specific antibodies that exhibit a wide array of effector functions. Vaccine-induced responses culminated in enhanced protection compared to non-vaccinated newborn AGM. These results were noteworthy given the lack of an approved influenza vaccine for this age group. Here, we evaluated early antibody and cellular responses following respiratory infection of vaccinated versus naïve animals to gain insights into the events that may be associated with the improved protection in vaccinated newborns. Seven days following challenge, we find an increase in the number of class-switched, affinity matured antibody secreting cells in the lung draining lymph nodes of vaccinated newborns, consistent with recall of memory B cells and rapid differentiation into antibody secreting cells (ASCs). Our data are consistent with a vaccine-mediated affinity advantage in the ASC population. While this benefit extended to HA head-specific germinal center B cells, it was not the case for cells binding HA stem. This was the result of unexpectedly higher apparent affinity of these cells in naïve animals. These data extend our understanding of how vaccination and infection shape activation and differentiation of the head- and stem-specific responses in infants following influenza virus infection.

title: Distinct regulation of influenza HA head- versus stem-specific B cell responses in HA mRNA-LNP vaccinated and naïve infant African green monkeys.

abstract: Takotsubo Syndrome (TTS) is an acute, potentially life-threatening condition often complicated by ventricular dysfunction and arrhythmias. Atrial fibrillation (AF) is common in TTS patients and associated with increased mortality. However, the arrhythmic mechanisms, genetic variability underlying TTS, and personalised therapy remain unclear. We generated induced pluripotent stem cell-derived atrial and ventricular cardiomyocytes (iPSC-CMs) from TTS patients and provoked TTS-like events by isoprenaline (Iso) stimulation. Compared with controls, atrial TTS iPSC-CMs exhibited enhanced diastolic sarcoplasmic reticulum (SR) Ca²⁺ leak and increased arrhythmogenic potential following Iso exposure. Iso-induced stress further increased systolic Ca²⁺ transient amplitude and reduced phosphodiesterase 4 (PDE4) activity in TTS iPSC-CMs. Under baseline conditions, atrial TTS iPSC-CMs demonstrated unchanged Ca2+ transient amplitude, reduced diastolic Ca2+, elevated SERCA2 activity with faster Ca²⁺ decay compared to controls, which could be explained by increased phosphorylation of PKA-specific phospholamban S16. In contrast, ventricular TTS-iPSC-CM showed increased L-Type Ca2+ current density, but reduced Ca2+ transient amplitude with increased resting Ca2+ leak and reduced PDE4 activity post-Iso-exposure. In atrial TTS iPSC-CMs, the PDE4 activator MR-L2 restored PDE4 activity, normalised several defects in Ca²⁺ handling and prevented arrhythmias more efficiently than the β-blocker metoprolol. Genetic analyses identified variants in the Ca²⁺ handling genes AHNAK and CASQ2 in TTS. Using CRISPR/Cas9, we generated isogenic rescue and mutation-insertion lines, confirming a causal role of p.P5390T in catecholamine-induced arrhythmogenic phenotypes in atrial TTS iPSC-CMs. Our findings support a mechanistic link between genetic predisposition to an excessive catecholaminergic stress response, dysregulated PDE/cAMP signalling, and atrial arrhythmogenesis in TTS-CMs, identifying PDE4 as a potential therapeutic target in this critical condition.

abstract:
BACKGROUND: Invasive fungal infections caused by Aspergillus fumigatus and other pathogenic fungi represent a major global health threat, with treatment increasingly complicated by the emergence of antifungal drug resistance. Azole antifungals serve as the first-line therapy for aspergillosis, but resistance rates vary substantially across geographical regions. This study aimed to characterize the antifungal resistance landscape among clinical fungal isolates from Hangzhou and Yiwu cities in Zhejiang Province, Eastern China, and to elucidate the molecular mechanisms underlying azole resistance in Aspergillus fumigatus.
RESULTS: We analyzed 110 Aspergillus clinical isolates for antifungal susceptibility. Among A. fumigatus strains, 8.6% exhibited azole resistance, with half of these harboring the tandem repeat mutation TR34/L98H in the cyp51A gene. One resistant strain carried the TR46/Y121F/T289A mutation combination. Minimum inhibitory concentration testing revealed that 8.6% of A. fumigatus isolates were resistant to amphotericin B We identified one resistant isolate without known resistance mutations and characterized it through whole-genome sequencing and transcriptomic analysis. Novel mutations S437F in cyp51A and P298T in hmg1 were discovered; however, functional validation using CRISPR-Cas9 demonstrated these mutations do not directly confer resistance. Instead, transcriptomic profiling revealed significant upregulation of ergosterol biosynthesis pathway genes and efflux transporter genes, suggesting alternative resistance mechanisms. Among non-A. fumigatus species, all A. niger isolates displayed resistance to itraconazole and posaconazole.
CONCLUSIONS: This comprehensive regional surveillance reveals concerning patterns of antifungal resistance among major human pathogenic fungi in Zhejiang Province, China. The identification of both classical resistance mutations and novel transcription-mediated resistance mechanisms highlights the complex and evolving nature of antifungal resistance. These findings emphasize the critical need for continued surveillance programs and rapid resistance detection methods to inform clinical treatment strategies and improve patient outcomes.

abstract: On 16 November 2023, the United Kingdom Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency approved Casgevy (exagamglogene autotemcel), the first CRISPR-based gene therapy for a genetic disease, offering patients with transfusion-dependent beta-thalassemia (TDT) freedom from lifelong monthly transfusions. Yet in China, which carries the world's largest TDT patient population, no patient has received the therapy through the public health system, and the access gap is not explained by price or manufacturing economics alone. This paper argues that prevention-era institutional architecture constrains cure-era access through three lock-in mechanisms: cognitive (the direction of genetic information flow), infrastructural (the spatial distribution of treatment capacity), and fiscal (the structure of payment responsibility). Drawing on a structured comparison of four countries selected to represent distinct institutional pathway types (Cyprus, ecclesiastical-public certification; China, administrative filing; Thailand, public health universal coverage; India, federal fragmentation), the analysis proposes a typology of barrier configurations and illustrates them through four exploratory cases. The administrative-filing pathway is associated with high barriers across information, geographic, and economic dimensions; trust-intention is not assessable on current evidence. The ecclesiastical-public pathway is associated with medium information and low geographic barriers with medium fiscal and low-confidence trust barriers; the universal-coverage pathway provides a balanced platform that remains under-activated for gene therapy; and the federal-fragmented pathway fails the precondition of patient identification. No pathway simultaneously optimizes all four readiness dimensions. Presented as a hypothesis-generating typology rather than a tested diagnostic model, the framework relates pathway type to barrier configuration and offers testable hypotheses for pathway-specific intervention design and for extension to sickle cell disease, hemophilia, and other genetic conditions entering the curative era.

abstract: Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) is a prevalent disorder characterized by excessive hepatic lipid accumulation, frequently progressing to steatohepatitis, fibrosis, and cirrhosis. Transcription factor EB (TFEB) coordinates lysosomal biogenesis, autophagy, and lipid catabolism, and therefore represents a potential therapeutic target; however, safe and direct strategies for selectively enhancing hepatic TFEB activity remain limited. Here, liver-targeted lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) were developed to deliver mRNAs encoding wild-type TFEB or the constitutively active TFEB S211A mutant, and their efficacy was evaluated in cellular and choline-deficient, L-amino acid-defined high-fat diet (CDAHFD)-induced mouse models of MASLD. LNP-mediated delivery increased hepatic TFEB expression, enhanced autophagic flux, and reprogrammed metabolic pathways toward fatty acid oxidation (e.g., CPT1A and ACOX1) while suppressing the expression of lipogenic genes (e.g., FASN, ACC, and SREBP1). Consequently, targeted TFEB mRNA therapy significantly reduced hepatic triglyceride content, attenuated steatosis, lowered MASLD activity scores, and decreased fibrotic remodeling. Mechanistically, transcriptomic profiling, ChIP-qPCR, promoter-reporter assays, and targeted knockdown models indicated that TFEB exerts its protective effects against lipid accumulation at least partly by transcriptionally activating the fibroblast growth factor 21 (FGF21) signaling pathway. Collectively, these findings establish LNP-mediated TFEB mRNA delivery as a useful preclinical approach for investigating hepatic biology and provide a targeted, transient, and non-integrating genetic strategy with potential for the treatment of MASLD.

title: Lipid nanoparticle-mediated transcription factor EB mRNA delivery for the treatment of metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease.

abstract: Background: Parkinson's disease is defined by progressive dopaminergic neurodegeneration and -synuclein pathology. Endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress and clathrin-mediated endocytosis dysfunction are implicated in disease pathogenesis, but the molecular mechanisms connecting these processes remain poorly understood. Here, we investigate a miR-103a-3p/AGFG1 axis as a regulator link between endocytic trafficking and ER stress in Parkinson's disease. Methods: MiR-103a-3p and AGFG1 were examined in plasma and postmortem substantia nigra from patients with Parkinson's disease and controls. Gain- and loss-of-function studies, target validation and live-cell imaging were used to define the role of the miR-103a-3p/AGFG1 axis in ER stress and endocytic trafficking. The pathway was further investigated in SNCA A53T and LRRK2 G2019S hiPSC-derived neurons. Therapeutic targeting of AGFG1 was evaluated using antisense oligonucleotides (ASOs) in vitro and in a 6-hydroxydopamine mouse model. Results: MiR-103a-3p was significantly reduced in Parkinson's disease plasma and substantia nigra, whereas AGFG1 was increased in nigral tissue. MiR-103a-3p directly repressed AGFG1 and attenuated thapsigargin-induced ER stress, while miR-103a-3p inhibition or AGFG1 overexpression exacerbated stress signalling. AGFG1 knockdown reversed the effects of miR-103a-3p inhibition, establishing AGFG1 as a functional downstream effector. Mechanistically, AGFG1 associated and co-trafficked with clathrin-positive vesicles, whereas ER stress progressively disrupted AGFG1-clathrin vesicle dynamics, revealing an association between endocytic trafficking and stress signalling. In genetic Parkinson's disease models, SNCA A53T and LRRK2 G2019S neurons showed mutation-dependent differences in AGFG1 expression and stress regulation. eIF2 phosphorylation increased in both SNCA A53T and LRRK2 G2019S neurons, whereas AGFG1 and GADD34 upregulation was selective to SNCA A53T neurons. Importantly, ASO-mediated AGFG1 suppression attenuated ER stress in vitro and preserved nigral dopaminergic neurons with improved motor performance in vivo. Conclusion: Our findings identify the miR-103a-3p/AGFG1 axis as a previously unrecognised molecular link between endocytic trafficking dysfunction and ER stress in Parkinson's disease, and support AGFG1 as a mechanistically potential therapeutic target.

title: Dysregulation of miR-103a-3p/AGFG1 axis links endocytic trafficking dysfunction to ER stress in Parkinson's disease

abstract: Colorectal cancer liver metastasis (CRLM) remains a major cause of cancer mortality, yet the metabolic mechanisms that remodel metastatic RNA-splicing programs are poorly defined. Here, integrated quantitative proteomics and lysine 2-hydroxyisobutyrylation (Khib) proteomics of patient-matched normal mucosa, primary CRCs, and liver metastases revealed a progressive increase in global Khib, with enrichment on RNA-splicing proteins. Serine/arginine-rich splicing factor 9 (SRSF9) emerged as a Khib-modified splicing factor whose expression and K155 Khib levels increased from normal tissue to primary tumors and liver metastases. Gain and loss of function studies in CRC cell lines, patient-derived organoids, subcutaneous xenografts, and splenic injection liver metastasis models showed that SRSF9 promotes proliferation, invasion, tumor growth, and liver colonization. Mechanistically, K155 Khib stabilized SRSF9 protein; the K155R mutation accelerated degradation and abolished SRSF9-driven malignant phenotypes. KAT7 and SIRT6 act as regulators of Khib modification, which positively and negatively modulate the K155 Khib modification of SRSF9, respectively. SRSF9 bound CD44 pre-mRNA through its RRM1 domain and promoted alternative splicing toward the oncogenic CD44V8-10 isoform, which was elevated in patient tumors and metastases and rescued the impaired proliferation and metastatic capacity caused by SRSF9 loss. Finally, a CD44V8-10-targeting antisense oligonucleotide suppressed CRC growth and liver metastasis in preclinical models. These findings define a KAT7/SIRT6-regulated Khib-SRSF9-CD44V8-10 axis that couples metabolic acylation to metastatic splicing and nominate CD44V8-10 as a therapeutic vulnerability in CRC liver metastasis.

title: 2-Hydroxyisobutyrylation of SRSF9 Regulates CD44 Alternative Splicing to Promote Colorectal Cancer Liver Metastasis.

abstract: Inherited platelet disorders (IPDs) comprise a heterogeneous group of rare genetic diseases affecting platelet production and/or function, with clinical manifestations ranging from mild mucocutaneous bleeding to severe hemorrhage, multisystem disease, and predisposition to hematologic malignancy. Treatment remains predominantly supportive, and curative options are limited. Future translation will require disease-specific selection of gene addition, allele-specific approaches, or precise genome editing, together with safer conditioning, efficient lineage-restricted correction, and rigorous long-term assessment of genotoxicity and clonal evolution. A shared hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells platform combined with disease-specific genetic engineering may ultimately enable curative treatment of selected severe IPDs.

title: Gene Therapy for Inherited Platelet Disorders: From Proof of Concept to Clinical Translation.

abstract: Antisense oligonucleotides (ASO) are nucleotide polymers that hybridize to sense strands and have been successful in treating a variety of diseases. A wide range of strategies have been investigated to optimize and develop ASO for clinical studies. A key objective for this study was to provide an overview of the range of detailed data that can be obtained and provide an updated method review on how to design surface plasmon resonance (SPR) kinetic experiments for DNA oligonucleotide hybridization studies that can also be applied to other ASO including peptide nucleic acids (PNA). We describe many lessons learned from published literature and provide a state-of-the-art strategy and methods for generating not only kinetic but also thermodynamic characterizations of oligonucleotide hybridization. In this study we have performed an SPR kinetic and thermodynamic analysis for the hybridization of HIF1 antisense DNA strands to its immobilized Intron2-Exon3 splice site sense DNA strand to provide insight, in general, on the optimal length and insight into optimal design of DNA ASOs. We provide a process on how to design experiments to: 1.) obtain oligonucleotide-length dependent kinetics, 2.) analyze reactions to obtain association and dissociation rate kinetics (ka, kd), assess if hybridization follows a 2-state model and to obtain kinetic dissociation constants (Kd), 3.) perform temperature-dependent hybridization kinetics to obtain thermodynamic values ({Delta}H{degrees}, {Delta}S{degrees} and {Delta}G{degrees}) that can give insight into the molecular interactions driving hybridization, 4.) compare experimental thermodynamic values to values derived from nearest-neighbor prediction models to identify atypical reactions and importantly 5.) enable calculations to predict oligomer hybridization affinity at the physiological 37 {degrees}C temperature to assess if the design of the oligomer will have the required cellular activity for a therapeutic effect. The strategy and results presented throughout the paper are compared to previous SPR reports and suggestions made to optimize kinetic studies.

title: Fundamentals on the Kinetic and Thermodynamic Analysis of Oligonucleotide DNA Hybridization by Surface Plasmon Resonance: A Guide for HIF1α Antisense Design.

abstract: Explore the potential function of Carbonic Anhydrase 2 (CA2) in the pathophysiology of preeclampsia. Peripheral blood and placental samples were collected from healthy pregnant women and patients with preeclampsia. Placental CA2 expression was validated in independent clinical cohorts and experimental mouse models. HTR-8/SVneo cells were cultured and transfected with a CA2 overexpression plasmid to evaluate trophoblast dysfunction. Bulk RNA sequencing was performed to identify downstream genes associated with CA2 overexpression, followed by VEGFA rescue experiments. Hypoxia-related regulation of CA2 was investigated. Lipid nanoparticle (LNP)-encapsulated siRNA against CA2 was constructed in an L-NAME-induced PE model to evaluate therapeutic effects. CA2 expression was significantly increased in placental tissues and maternal serum from women with PE and was also elevated in experimental PE mouse models. CA2 predominantly localized in trophoblast cells, and correlated positively with serum creatinine and urea and correlated negatively with fetal birth weight. CA2 overexpression markedly suppressed trophoblast proliferation, migration, and invasion, without affecting apoptosis. Transcriptomic analysis suggested that vascular endothelial growth factor A (VEGFA) acted as a downstream mediator of CA2, and VEGFA overexpression partially rescued CA2-induced trophoblast dysfunction. CA2 expression was upregulated under hypoxic conditions and regulated by hypoxia-inducible factor-1α (HIF-1α). LNP-mediated CA2 silencing partially improved placental structure and fetal outcomes in vivo. CA2 is upregulated in the preeclamptic placenta and is associated with placental dysfunction and adverse fetal outcomes. Mechanistically, CA2 may act downstream of HIF-1α and contribute to trophoblast dysfunction partly through modulation of VEGFA signaling, and CA2 silencing partially improved maternal and fetal outcomes, highlighting CA2 as a potential therapeutic target for preeclampsia.

title: Hypoxia-Driven CA2 Promotes Trophoblast Dysfunction in Preeclampsia.

abstract: Owing to the intrinsic instability of mRNA, its routes of administration are limited, and to date, only injectable delivery has been clinically applied. In contrast, oral administration exposes mRNA to a variety of substances in the gastrointestinal (GI) tract. Despite these challenges, oral delivery remains the most familiar and convenient route for patients, making the development of orally administrable mRNA-encapsulated lipid nanoparticles (mRNA-LNPs) highly desirable. However, no studies have directly examined how mRNA-LNPs are affected within the GI environment. In the present study, we investigated the effects of representative GI components on mRNA-LNPs. Among several digestive enzymes, pepsin markedly reduced the protein-expression efficiency of the particles, whereas amylase had no effect. Pepsin-treated particles exhibited increased size, suggesting that structural alterations contributed to the observed functional loss. Lipase at high concentrations impaired nanoparticle function. Because lipase hydrolyzes ester bonds in lipids, we examined LNPs incorporating C12-200, an ionizable lipid lacking ester bonds, instead of SM-102. The C12-200 formulation showed reduced susceptibility to lipase-induced functional loss, indicating that enzymatic lipid degradation underlay the observed effects. Simulated gastric fluid also significantly diminished particle functionality. A detailed analysis of the relationship between functionality and pH revealed that impairment primarily occurred at approximately pH 1 but not at pH ≥ 3. Collectively, these findings identify the key GI factors that compromise mRNA-LNP integrity and provide important insights into the rational design of orally administrable mRNA-LNP formulations.

title: Comprehensive Evaluation of Gastrointestinal Factors Influencing the Stability and Function of mRNA-Encapsulated Lipid Nanoparticles.

abstract: Rare disease is a condition that affects a small fraction of the population. In most cases, it has a known genetic cause but could also be associated with other contributing factors. As the affected individuals may exhibit diverse symptoms due to the genetic and phenotypic heterogeneity, non- or misdiagnosis of rare diseases is common. Their low incidence and prevalence present an obstacle to developing new therapies despite a major unmet need with only a few treatment options available. This is particularly relevant to rare neurological disorders as there are major difficulties in studying the mechanisms of initiation and progression of the central nervous system (CNS) disorders. Recent advances in biotechnology, specifically the use of human induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) for modeling diseases, have been instrumental in providing a flexible platform that not only reflects the effects of genetic disturbances on the development of CNS disorders but also is capable of providing insights into complex multifactorial disorders. Whether the human iPSCs are harvested from the affected individuals or using the gene-editing tools on cells from healthy individuals, valuable models can now be made available for studying these orphan conditions. In this narrative review, we explore the benefits of using human iPSC models over the existing platforms of other primary cell lines and animal models for the disease modeling and drug discovery and discuss the limitations and future aspects of the iPSC use in the investigation of rare neurological disorders.

abstract: This Phase 1 study will evaluate the safety, tolerability, and immune responses of investigational CH505 HIV vaccine regimens in adults in overall good health without HIV. Participants will receive CH505 protein nanoparticle vaccines (DV901-NP) formulated with the investigational adjuvant ACU-026-001-1, followed by either CH505 protein nanoparticle (DV902-NP) or CH505 mRNA vaccine boosters. The study will assess the ability of these regimens to induce HIV-specific immune responses, including B-cell responses associated with the development of broadly neutralizing antibodies. An immunology cohort will also evaluate how the location of booster vaccination affects immune responses.

abstract: CAI-Vax (Cancer Antigen Individualized Vaccine Design) arranges selected antigens and generates synonymous coding sequences for personalized mRNA vaccine constructs. We evaluated 357 vaccine-candidate peptides from 31 patients across four published cohorts. At the primary cumulative MHCflurry percentile-rank threshold of [≤]2%, HLA-aware search reduced predicted junction-spanning peptide-allele binder occurrences by 3.49 per junction relative to amino-acid-pattern optimization (paired Hodges-Lehmann estimate; nominal 95% interval 2.75-4.48; Holm-adjusted P = 7.45 x 10-). All 31 primary paired differences and the estimated effects in all 16 threshold-by-normalization settings favored HLA-aware search within the MHCflurry model used for optimization. Among 25 patients with an exact solution for the additive search objective, single-start greedy search found the minimum in 5 patients and the best individual heuristic in 16. Selecting each patients best result across all tested heuristics increased this to 19. MHCflurry and NetMHCpan EL identified identical tied best-plan sets in 6 of 31 patients after rescoring six frozen plans per patient. In a retrospective internal analysis, repeat-aware synonymous encoding reduced maximum 10-mer multiplicity in every patient, with mean codon-use-preference losses of 0.0041-0.0055 across cohorts; however, it performed worse than matched random encoding for 6-mers. These findings demonstrate that HLA-guided construct optimization can reduce predicted junctional binding within the optimization model, although the preferred antigen arrangement depends on the prediction model used. Experimental studies are needed to determine the biological and manufacturing relevance of these computational differences.

abstract: Next-generation sequencing has radically transformed the diagnostic capability of rare neurodevelopmental disorders (RNDDs), yet translating these molecular insights into viable therapeutics remains a hurdle. While gene-directed modalities, specifically viral-mediated supplementation, antisense oligonucleotides (ASOs), and CRISPR-based activation or precision editing, offer a means to rescue loss-of-function phenotypes, successful clinical implementation requires moving past the reductive framework of merely increasing the expression of the target gene towards approaches that account for spatial, developmental, and therapeutic windows. This review uses HNRNPU-related rare neurodevelopmental disorder (HNRNPU-RNDD), a condition marked with global developmental delay and refractory epilepsy, as an exemplar to discuss these translational hurdles. We discuss the homeostatic boundaries of this scaffold attachment factor, where unregulated overexpression risks localised cytotoxicity, and altered chromatin dynamics compromise editing safety. Furthermore, we assess how cell-type sensitivity and narrow developmental windows may dictate clinical efficacy. By using HNRNPU-RNDD to critically analyse the challenges of using each therapeutic platform, we hope to inform the creation of gene-directed therapies that aim to treat disorders resulting from structural pleiotropic dosage-sensitive proteins.

title: Challenges in Gene-Directed Therapies for Rare Neurodevelopmental Disorders Using HNRNPU as an Exemplar.

abstract: Nonsense mutations account for approximately 20% of pathogenic variants in inherited retinal diseases (IRDs). With advances in gene therapy, nucleic acid-based nonsense suppression strategies, including suppressor tRNAs, RNA pseudouridylation, and adenosine-to-inosine RNA editing, have demonstrated therapeutic potential in preclinical studies. These next-generation approaches offer substantial opportunities for engineering and optimization, with the potential to enable precise and efficient restoration of full-length functional proteins. In this review, we propose that IRDs represent an attractive group of diseases for the clinical translation of these next-generation therapies owing to their high burden of nonsense mutations and the unique advantages of ocular gene therapy. We further outline key strategies to accelerate clinical translation, spanning therapeutic engineering, preclinical validation, and mutation-guided clinical trial design.

title: Rethinking nonsense suppression therapies in inherited retinal diseases.

abstract: Spinocerebellar Ataxia 27B (SCA27B) is a late-onset neurodegenerative disorder caused by a heterozygous pathogenic GAA•TTC repeat expansion in intron 1 of FGF14. Despite being a common genetic cause of adult-onset cerebellar ataxia, the underlying molecular mechanisms remain unclear. Here, we performed simultaneous reprogramming and CRISPR-Cas9 genome editing to generate four induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC) lines and their respective isogenic gene-corrected controls. All lines exhibited normal karyotypes, pluripotency, and trilineage differentiation capacity. These paired iPSC lines provide a valuable platform for investigating the pathomechanism(s) of SCA27B and can be used for screening of potential therapeutic treatments.

abstract: Lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) are the leading platform for RNA delivery, enabling applications ranging from mRNA vaccines to CRISPR therapeutics. Ionizable lipids, such as DLin-MC3-DMA (MC3), play a central role in nucleic acid encapsulation and intracellular delivery, yet the molecular mechanisms governing LNP structure and function remain incompletely understood. The internal organization of LNP cores is highly sensitive to pH and has been described by inverse hexagonal, cubic, and lamellar phases that influence delivery performance. Here, we investigate the pH-dependent structure and dynamics of MC3-containing LNPs using two-dimensional infrared (2D IR) spectroscopy and molecular dynamics (MD) simulations. Both experiments and simulations reveal pronounced pH-dependent changes in the local environment surrounding the lipid ester linkage. At pH 4, strong electrostatic interactions between RNA and protonated MC3 produce broader spectral features consistent with increased interfacial heterogeneity and hydration. In addition, the frequency fluctuation dynamics exhibit a 46% slowdown in RNA-loaded LNPs relative to empty LNPs. In contrast, increasing the pH from 4 to 8 narrows the ester carbonyl band by ∼10 cm-1 and yields nearly identical dynamics for loaded and empty LNPs, indicating a more homogeneous and less hydrated lipid interface. MD simulations further demonstrate that MC3 protonation modulates RNA binding, interfacial hydration, and lipid packing. Together, these results highlight RNA-lipid electrostatic interactions as an important factor influencing the local environment within LNPs and potentially their pH-dependent behavior, providing molecular-level insights into the rational design of next-generation RNA delivery systems.

title: RNA-Lipid Interactions Control Structure and Dynamics of Lipid Nanoparticles.

abstract: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) is characterized by a dense desmoplastic stroma and early metastatic dissemination, both of which contribute to its poor prognosis. While forkhead box protein 3 (FOXP3) is best known as a lineage-defining transcription factor in regulatory T cells (Tregs), its aberrant expression in cancer cell-specific FOXP3 (c-FOXP3) may also support tumor-cell-intrinsic progression. Our findings suggest that high c-FOXP3 expression is closely linked to aggressive disease behavior and metastatic progression in PDAC. c-FOXP3 enhanced migration, invasion within three-dimensional collagen-rich matrices, and dissemination in orthotopic models. Integrated transcriptomic analysis, chromatin immunoprecipitation, and wild-type versus binding-site-mutant promoter assays identified matrix metalloproteinase 19 (MMP19) as a direct transcriptional target of c-FOXP3. MMP19 silencing significantly attenuated c-FOXP3-driven migration, matrix invasion, and metastasis. Single-cell sequencing further showed that MMP19 is abundant in cancer-associated fibroblasts but also defines a distinct epithelial pool that is reduced after epithelial Foxp3 deletion. Pharmacological profiling did not identify a validated MMP19-selective inhibitor, whereas the FOXP3-targeting antisense oligonucleotide AZD8701 reduced FOXP3 together with MMP19 mRNA and was accompanied by lower PDAC-cell migration and invasion in vitro. Together, these findings extend the known functions of FOXP3 beyond its classical role in immune tolerance and define a tumor-cell-intrinsic c-FOXP3-MMP19 program that supports matrix-invasive behavior in PDAC and provide preliminary evidence that c-FOXP3 is pharmacologically accessible.

title: Cancer cell-specific FOXP3 licenses MMP19-dependent matrix remodeling and metastatic dissemination in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma.

abstract: Somatosensation is mediated by dorsal root ganglion (DRG) neurons, which convert physical and chemical stimuli into electrical signals. However, the full repertoire of molecular components underlying somatosensation remains incompletely identified. Here we developed an efficient postnatal CRISPR-Cas9 knockout platform for interrogating DRG-expressed genes (such as Piezo2, Trpv1 and Scn9a) in mice using AAV9-mediated single-guide RNA delivery. Combining this approach with somatosensory behavioral assays, we performed a targeted screen of 20 genes and identified Creld1 as a cross-model regulator of somatosensation. Either single-guide RNA-mediated postnatal knockout or tamoxifen-induced Cre-mediated deletion of Creld1 in DRG neurons resulted in profound behavioral deficits in touch, temperature, pain and itch, whereas its overexpression enhanced touch and thermal responses. Mechanistically, CRELD1 functions as an auxiliary regulator of voltage-gated sodium channels (Nav) for controlling DRG neuron excitability. Together, this work establishes a robust postnatal screening platform for behavioral genomics and identifies Creld1 as a master regulator of somatosensory function.

abstract: Most existing CRISPR/Cas12a methods for small molecules detection employ DNA aptamers as an intermediary, while RNA aptamers remain underexplored. The conventional CRISPR/Cas12 system offers limited programmability due to its partially conserved crRNA sequence. In this study, we developed an aptamer-regulated CRISPR/Cas12a system based on split crRNA. We divided the full crRNA into a crRNA handle segment (RH) and a crRNA spacer segment that is identical to the RNA aptamer sequence of target (RS-Apt). RS-Apt was endowed with dual functions: activating the activity of Cas12a and binding to target small molecules, ingeniously linking non-nucleic acid targets with the CRISPR system. The strong affinity between the target and RS-Apt reduces the amount of RS-Apt available to participate in the CRISPR system, resulting in a decrease in the fluorescence signal of the system. Within 1.5 h, the system for theophylline (TP) exhibited a linear range from 50 nM to 200 µM and a detection limit (LOD) of 2 nM, while the system for tobramycin (TOB) showed a linear range of 200 nM to 100 µM with an LOD of 63 nM. Notably, visual semi-quantitative detection of TP and TOB was achieved via lateral flow strips. Moreover, the system achieved satisfactory recovery and visual detection of TP using lateral flow strips in TP-spiked serum samples. This system can detect different targets simply by changing the sequence of the RS-Apt and activator, without the need for complex sequence design of the chains or large-scale instruments, providing a new strategy for CRISPR/Cas12a in the detection of small molecules.

abstract:
This is an open-label, window of opportunity platform study for subjects with muscle-invasive bladder cancer (MIBC) who are deemed ineligible or refuse cisplatin-based neoadjuvant chemotherapy and are scheduled to undergo definitive surgery (radical cystectomy), or are planning to undergo trimodality therapy (maximal transurethral resection of the bladder tumor followed by concurrent chemoradiation).

The primary objective of this study is to assess changes to immunogenomic markers after treatment with pembrolizumab alone and in combination with the selective class I histone deacetylase (HDAC) inhibitor (entinostat).

institutions.label: Merck Sharp & Dohme LLC
Syndax Pharmaceuticals

description:
The study will enroll 20 subjects with a confirmed diagnosis of MIBC (cT2-T4aN0M0) who are planned for definitive therapy with either radical cystectomy without cisplatin-based neoadjuvant chemotherapy or trimodality therapy.

Prior to study entry, subjects must consent to having tissue collected for research purposes during the scheduled cystectomy or maximal TURBT. After screening and enrollment, baseline blood and archived transurethral resection of the bladder tumor (TURBT) tumor tissue will be collected from each subject for baseline analyses. Subjects will then start on clinical trial treatment followed by either radical cystectomy or maximal TURBT followed by chemoradiation.

Blood and tumor will be collected from each subject at the time of cystectomy or maximal TURBT. The investigators do not anticipate delays in surgery due to the planned schedule of the preoperative treatment administration for the purposes of this study and based on previous reported results of the trial which includes pembrolizumab and entinostat treatment in melanoma reported an acceptable safety profile. Phase I data identified grade 1/2 fatigue as the most common entinostat-related toxicity, with neutropenia and anemia only occurring at doses exceeding those proposed for this study. Safety stopping rules for drug-related toxicity will dictate whether the trial should be halted if subjects are experiencing drug-related toxicity that delays or interferes with the standard of care procedures.

outcomes.description: Gene expression levels with the CD8 T cell gene signature were measured using RNA sequencing. The expression level of each gene in the signature were log2 transformed and the mean of the signature genes was calculated in each sample. Then the mean expression of signature in each sample was compared to the average expression and variability across other sample to center the expression values (mean = 0) and scale them by standard deviation and generate a Z-score. Change in z-score was then calculated between pre- and post-treatments for each individual patient and then changes in z-score were compared between treatment arms. An increase in Z-score with treatment denotes an increase in expression of the immune gene signature (IGS).

abstract:
The goal of this clinical trial is to first define the Safety and Optimal Biological Dose (OBD) of study drug TGX-007 and to then further investigate the safety and efficacy in patients with newly diagnosed or recurrent Glioblastoma.

TGX-007 is a gene therapy drug delivered by a harmless adeno-associated virus (AAV) vector which delivers two combined therapeutic payloads to enable killing of proliferative cells and activation of an anti-tumour immune response. One is herpes simplex virus thymidine kinase (HSV-tk), which converts the pro-drug valaciclovir into an active drug that can kill tumour cells and the other is interleukin 12 (IL-12), which activates the body's immune system to recognise and fight the tumour.

Patients newly diagnosed with glioblastoma suitable for standard of care surgery and chemoradiotherapy or patients with recurrent glioblastoma suitable for further surgery may be eligible for the study. Patients will receive TGX-007 by a direct intratumoural injection and will then take the pro-drug valacyclovir orally for up to 21 days before proceeding to standard of care surgery.

The study is split into two phases. Phase I will treat patients at different dose levels of TGX-007 to identify the Optimal Biological Dose that will be used to further expand the study into Phase II. Phase II will expand the number of patients treated at the selected OBD to investigate how effective TGX-007 is at treating newly diagnosed and recurrent GBM.

Approximately 68 people aged 18-70 will take part in the study.

abstract:
This Phase 2, multi-center, single-arm study evaluates the safety, tolerability, and activity of neoadjuvant PRTX007 in combination with pembrolizumab in participants with resectable Stage III melanoma. Neoadjuvant immunotherapy has demonstrated improved clinical outcomes compared with adjuvant-only approaches, but there remains a need to enhance pathologic response rates without significant added toxicity.

Participants will receive oral PRTX007, a Toll-like receptor 7 (TLR7) agonist prodrug, administered in combination with intravenous pembrolizumab prior to surgical resection. The primary objective is to determine the major pathologic response (MPR) rate following neoadjuvant therapy. Secondary objectives include evaluation of safety, pathologic complete response, event-free survival, overall survival, pharmacokinetics, and immune-related biomarkers.

This study aims to determine whether the addition of PRTX007 to pembrolizumab improves antitumor immune responses and clinical outcomes in patients with Stage III melanoma.
description:
This study investigates whether combining the TLR7 agonist PRTX007 with pembrolizumab enhances immune-mediated tumor response in the neoadjuvant setting for Stage III melanoma, with the goal of improving pathologic response rates and clinical outcomes while maintaining an acceptable safety profile.

Design This is a Phase 2, multi-center, open-label, single-arm study conducted in Australia. The study will enroll approximately 48 participants with resectable Stage III melanoma.

The study consists of two parts:

* Part A: 24 participants will be enrolled, including an initial dose-escalation safety run-in using a 3+3 design to evaluate tolerability and dose-limiting toxicities.
* Part B: An additional 24 participants will be enrolled if sufficient activity is observed in Part A.

Treatment Plan

Participants will receive neoadjuvant therapy consisting of:

* PRTX007: Oral administration for 3 days on and 4 days off per week for 9 cycles (7-day cycles)
* Pembrolizumab: 200 mg intravenous infusion every 3 weeks for 3 cycles Following completion of neoadjuvant therapy, participants will undergo definitive surgical resection.

Post-surgical treatment will be response-adapted:

* Participants achieving MPR may receive observation or pembrolizumab alone
* Participants without MPR will receive adjuvant PRTX007 in combination with pembrolizumab

VT-20101 is an Open-label, Phase 1b, Single-ascending dose study that will evaluate the safety of VERVE-201 administered to patients with Refractory Hyperlipidemia.

abstract: Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) is a prevalent chronic liver disorder, with its progressive form, metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH), characterized by steatosis, inflammation, hepatocyte injury, and fibrosis. However, the underlying mechanism remains incompletely understood. Here, we performed an in vivo CRISPR screen in Cas9 mice fed a methionine- and choline-deficient (MCD) diet to identify epigenetic regulators of MASH. SETDB1 emerged as a key modulator: hepatocyte-specific loss of Setdb1 exacerbated steatosis, inflammation, ductular reaction, and fibrosis, whereas Setdb1 overexpression markedly alleviated these pathological features. Notably, human liver samples showed decreased SETDB1 expression with advancing MASLD. Furthermore, SETDB1 deficiency increased hepatic ferroptosis by upregulating ACSL4, aggravating MASH pathology, whereas ACSL4 knockout reduced liver injury in the absence of SETDB1. SETDB1 overexpression protected against liver damage by repressing ACSL4. Therefore, the SETDB1-ACSL4-ferroptosis axis regulates MASH progression and represents a potential therapeutic target.

abstract: Ehrlich carcinoma (EC) and its ascitic form, Ehrlich ascites carcinoma (EAC), are among the oldest and most widely used experimental tumor models in cancer research. Although they have traditionally been used for anticancer drug screening, their potential to address broader aspects of aggressive tumor biology has received comparatively less attention. EC/EAC exhibits several characteristics associated with advanced malignancy, including rapid tumor growth, angiogenesis, immune dysregulation, metabolic changes, therapeutic resistance, and complex interactions between the tumor and host. These features make EC/EAC a useful complementary model for studying different aspects of tumor progression. However, research using these models has largely focused on transcriptional changes and individual signalling pathways, while post-transcriptional regulatory mechanisms remain less explored. In particular, the role of the RNA-induced silencing complex (RISC), a major component of microRNA-mediated gene regulation, is still poorly understood in EC/EAC. In this review, we discuss the major limitations of current EC/EAC research, including the limited use of multi-omics approaches, single-cell and spatial analyses, functional genomics, immune checkpoint profiling, and integrated systems-level studies. We further discuss how incorporating RISC-centered regulatory networks with emerging approaches such as CRISPR-based studies, spatial transcriptomics, and metabolic profiling could provide deeper mechanistic insights and improve the translational value of these models. Bringing together the strengths of this established tumor model with contemporary approaches in cancer biology could help reposition EC/EAC as a relevant and versatile platform for studying tumor progression and therapeutic responses.

abstract: Tools for manipulating RNA that rely on nonhuman proteins, such as ISC-based and Cas-based scaffolds, can lead to unintended and little-understood effects on human cells and present challenges in therapeutic translation. Replacing them with human proteins engineered for expanded, programmable functions could bypass the limitations of these foreign proteins. Here we demonstrate that human Argonaute 2 (AGO2) can be repurposed as a modular RNA targeting domain. AGO2 fused to a C-to-U deaminase enables AGO-led targeted editing of RNA (ALTER). Using guide RNAs that remodel target RNA structure for selective editing and reduced nuclease activity, we show that ALTER achieves, on average, 1.9-fold higher C-to-U editing on mRNA targets in HEK293T cells compared with Cas13 editors CURE and RESCUE. Transcriptome-wide RNA-seq revealed similar or lower levels of off-target editing compared to the same Cas13-based editors. Machine learning models predict that far fewer immunogenic peptides will result from ALTER and we show that ALTER is amenable to a validated workflow for artificial intelligence-directed deimmunization.

abstract: T cell receptor-engineered T (TCR-T) cell therapy has emerged as a promising adoptive cellular therapy for solid tumors by enabling recognition of intracellular antigens presented via human leukocyte antigen (HLA) molecules. Unlike chimeric antigen receptor T cell therapy, TCR-T cell therapy targets a broader antigen repertoire, including cancer-testis antigens, neoantigens, and viral antigens. Recent clinical advances, highlighted by the approval of afamitresgene autoleucel in synovial sarcoma, demonstrate meaningful antitumor activity. However, several limitations remain, including HLA restriction, antigen heterogeneity, toxicity related to on-target/off-tumor effects, and mechanisms of resistance such as antigen loss and T cell exhaustion. Advances in antigen selection, gene editing, and synthetic biology are improving both safety and efficacy. Combination strategies and next-generation engineered constructs are expected to overcome current barriers. This review summarizes the biological rationale, clinical evidence, safety considerations, and resistance mechanisms of TCR-T cell therapy in solid tumors and discusses future directions to optimize their therapeutic potential.

abstract: Buffaloes are important contributors to agricultural production in many developing countries, yet poor semen cryosurvival remains a major challenge for efficient artificial insemination and genetic improvement. In recent years, small extracellular vesicles (sEVs) have emerged as important mediators of intercellular communication and reproductive function; however, their potential as supplements for improving buffalo semen cryosurvival remains poorly understood. Therefore, this study evaluated the influence of adding a seminal plasma-derived small extracellular vesicle-enriched preparation to a Tris extender using post-thaw sperm traits, oxidative status, DNA integrity, HSP70 and PRM1 transcript abundance, and fertility of Kundhi buffalo bull semen. Seminal plasma-derived particles were isolated and characterized by nanoparticle tracking analysis, showing a mean diameter of 117.8 ± 2.47 nm, modal diameter of 89.4 ± 1.41 nm, and concentration of (3.21 ± 0.05) × 1011 particles/mL. Thirty-two ejaculates from four Kundhi buffalo bulls were pooled and extended with a Tris extender supplemented with 0, 25, 50, 100, or 200 μg/mL sEV-enriched preparation before cryopreservation. Post-thaw sperm quality, early apoptosis, DNA fragmentation, lipid peroxidation, antioxidant enzymes, and relative mRNA abundance of HSP70 and PRM1 were assessed. All evaluated post-thaw variables differed (P < 0.05) after supplementation, whereas 50 μg/mL revealed the strongest response. The EV-50 group showed higher total motility, progressive motility, viability, and HOST-positive spermatozoa, however reduced early apoptotic sperm, DNA fragmentation, and MDA concentration than the control group. EV-50 also enhanced SOD, catalase, total glutathione, HSP70 and PRM1 expression (1.91 ± 0.07-fold and 1.69 ± 0.05-fold, respectively). In fertility validation, pregnancy rate increased from 41.7% in the control group to 56.7% in the EV-50-treated semen group, with higher odds of pregnancy (OR = 1.83; P = 0.028). In conclusion, supplementation with 50 μg/mL of the sEV-enriched preparation improved post-thaw sperm quality, redox homeostasis, DNA integrity, HSP70 and PRM1 transcript abundance, and field fertility, supporting its potential as a cryopreservation supplement for enhancing the reproductive performance of Kundhi buffalo semen.

abstract: Tropical theileriosis, caused by Theileria annulata, continues to be the most significant tick-borne disease affecting cattle, particularly in endemic regions where it leads to significant production losses. Prompt and reliable diagnosis is critically important for timely treatment and disease control; however, conventional diagnostic methods have important limitations. Microscopic examination lacks sensitivity, particularly in carrier animals, while PCR requires specialized laboratory infrastructure. To overcome these limitations, a fluorescence-based RPA-CRISPR/Cas12a assay targeting the multicopy mitochondrial cytb gene was developed for rapid detection of T. annulata. Five RPA primer pairs were designed and evaluated, and primer set-5, generating a 324-bp amplicon, exhibited the best amplification performance. A CRISPR RNA (crRNA) was designed within the selected amplicon to enable specific Cas12a-mediated target recognition. The assay was completed within 50 min and demonstrated no cross-reactivity with DNA from Theileria orientalis, Babesia bigemina, Babesia bovis, Anaplasma marginale, and bovine host DNA, confirming excellent analytical specificity. Sensitivity analysis using recombinant plasmid DNA demonstrated a detection limit of approximately ten copies per reaction. The field evaluation of the assay was done by testing 206 bovine field samples. showed that the developed assay identified 163 positive samples, exceeding the detection rates obtained by PCR (151 positives) and microscopy (116 positives). On comparison with PCR, the assay achieved 100% diagnostic sensitivity, 78.18% specificity, 92.64% positive predictive value, 100% negative predictive value, with an overall agreement of 94.17%. These findings indicate that the RPA-CRISPR/Cas12a platform is a rapid, sensitive, and accurate molecular diagnostic approach with strong potential for field application and point-of-care diagnosis of bovine tropical theileriosis, particularly in resource-constrained settings.

abstract: Huntington's disease (HD) is caused by a CAG repeat expansion in the huntingtin (HTT) gene, encoding an elongated polyglutamine stretch in the corresponding mutant HTT (mHTT) protein. HD pathogenesis is driven by multiple neurotoxic mHTT protein species, including HTT1a and repeat-associated non-AUG translation (RAN) proteins, which increase in expression as mutant CAG repeats lengthen due to somatic expansion. VO659 is an investigational CAG repeat-targeting antisense oligonucleotide (ASO) that lowers mHTT protein levels by blocking translation. Here, we show that VO659 allele-preferentially lowers levels of multiple neurotoxic mHTT protein species in a CAG repeat length-dependent manner, relatively sparing wild-type HTT, while becoming more efficacious as somatic expansion occurs. VO659 reduced HTT1a mRNA levels in HD fibroblasts with an ultra-long CAG repeat, blocked the translation of HTT1a and polyalanine-containing RAN proteins derived from HTT exon 1 overexpression constructs, and displayed a long tissue half-life in mouse brain, supporting an infrequent dosing regimen. A first-in-human, open-label phase 1/2a clinical trial (NCT05822908) is currently ongoing in HD patients. VO659's unique CAG repeat-dependent and allele-preferential mechanism of action holds promise for its therapeutic effect in HD patients by targeting multiple core neurotoxic proteins derived from (somatically) expanded mHTT CAG repeats, while sparing wild-type HTT expression.

abstract: Large insert gene editing in ex vivo, primary human T cells represents an important approach for engineering next-generation cellular immunotherapies. While CRISPR-based editing is well-established for small genetic modifications, large insert knock-in remains a technical bottleneck. This review examines current strategies for achieving efficient, precise and safe integration of large genetic elements. We compare delivery methods for CRISPR components, highlighting electroporation of Cas9 ribonucleoproteins as the most efficient but often cytotoxic approach; emerging alternatives such as cell-penetrating peptides and lipid nanoparticles offer improved cell viability at the expense of editing efficiency. The influence of genomic locus selection, guide RNA design and chromatin context on editing outcomes, as well as the role of homology-directed repair (HDR) template design is evaluated. Various template formats-including linear double- and single-stranded DNA, plasmids, circular single-stranded (css) DNA and recombinant adeno-associated virus (rAAV)-are assessed for their efficiency, toxicity and risk of off-target integration. Where possible, cross-study normalisation is used to enable meaningful comparisons. rAAV templates consistently achieve the highest insertion rates but come with concerns regarding cost, size limitations and insertional mutagenesis, whereas non-viral approaches such as cssDNA templates show promise. Additionally, we review the use of small-molecule modulators to enhance HDR efficiency, noting trade-offs between improved insertion rates and potential genomic instability. Overall, successful large insert editing requires balancing of editing efficiency, cell viability and genomic safety considerations. Continued optimisation of delivery systems, template design and repair pathway modulation will be critical for advancing scalable and clinically viable T-cell therapies.

abstract: Bacterial infection is a major cause of delayed wound healing, while overuse of antibiotics has accelerated the emergence of antimicrobial resistance. Developing multifunctional antibacterial biomaterials that eradicate bacteria without relying on conventional antibiotics is therefore highly desirable. Herein, we report an injectable polyethylene glycol (PEG)-based hydrogel incorporating gold nanorods (ARs) and a DNA nanostructure-mediated silver and antisense oligonucleotide delivery system (A-C@Ag) to achieve synergistic antibacterial therapy and enhanced skin regeneration. The hydrogel is formed by rapid thiol-maleimide crosslinking of PEG precursors containing AR@A-C@Ag, providing excellent injectability, biocompatibility, and mechanical stability. Upon near-infrared irradiation, the AR generates mild photothermal heating to directly damage bacteria and simultaneously promotes the on-demand release of Ag+ and antisense oligonucleotides from the DNA nanostructure, resulting in markedly enhanced antibacterial activity against both Staphylococcus aureus and Escherichia coli by facilitating bacterial membrane disruption. In a S. aureus-infected full-thickness wound model, AR@A-C@Ag/Gel under NIR irradiation significantly accelerated wound closure by efficiently eliminating bacteria, suppressing inflammation, promoting angiogenesis and collagen deposition, and facilitating the regeneration of skin appendages. This work demonstrates that integrating DNA nanostructure-enabled drug delivery with mild photothermal therapy represents an effective strategy for constructing antibiotic-free antibacterial hydrogels for infected wound repair.

abstract: Necroptosis is a critical response to secondary brain injury following intracerebral hemorrhage (ICH). Z-DNA Binding Protein 1 (ZBP1) binds to dsRNA and promotes the activation of Receptor-Interacting Protein Kinase 3 (RIPK3). This study investigated whether Adenosine Deaminase Acting on RNA 1 (ADAR1) inhibits neuronal necroptosis after ICH. ADAR1-knockdown mice and ZBP1flox/flox/Thy1-Cre+/- mice were subjected to collagenase VII-induced ICH. Brain edema and neurobehavioral deficits were assessed. The expressions of ADAR1 and ZBP1 were investigated by qPCR, western blot, immunofluorescence, and ELISA. Protein interactions were performed using co-immunoprecipitation. ADAR1p150 was reduced in both ICH patients and mice. ZBP1 and ADAR1 both bound to dsRNA. ADAR1p150 suppressed ZBP1 activation, potentially through functional antagonism and dsRNA editing, although causality remains to be established. Knockout of ZBP1 resulted in increased ADAR1p150 expression and reduced brain edema. Etanercept and shRNA-mediated ADAR1 knockdown promoted ZBP1 expression. Complementation of the ADAR1 Zα truncation did not reduce ZBP1 in ADAR1-knockdown cells. The inhibitory effect of ADAR1 on ZBP1 was attenuated in ADAR1Zα-/- cells. These data show that the Zα domain is required for ADAR1 to suppress ZBP1, but they do not establish whether this suppression depends on RNA editing or on dsRNA binding alone.

title: ADAR1 Inhibits ZBP1-Driven Neuronal Necroptosis After Intracerebral Hemorrhage.

abstract: Most RNA-cleaving DNAzymes are limited to cleaving between combinations of the four canonical ribonucleotides. Through in vitro selection, we isolated ICD11-1T, a DNAzyme that selectively cleaves at inosine, a non-canonical RNA modification generated by adenosine deamination. ICD11-1T cleaves inosine-containing substrates with a rate constant of 0.1 min-1 and achieves >103-fold selectivity over adenosine, discriminating between nucleosides that differ at the C6 and N1 positions of the purine ring. Molecular dynamics simulations revealed that the inosine positions the cleavage site near the catalytic core, whereas the adenosine complex sequesters it away, accounting for the stringent specificity. Using ICD11-1T, we constructed a fluorescent biosensor that enabled imaging of endogenous ADAR (adenosine deaminase acting on RNA) editing activity in fixed and permeabilized cells. This work provides a proof-of-concept tool for studying adenosine-to-inosine (A-to-I) RNA editing and establishes a strategy for expanding the functionality of DNAzymes.

title: Exploiting inosine as a distinctive cleavage site for deriving a highly specific RNA-cleaving DNAzyme.

abstract: Preeclampsia originates in placental dysfunction yet it is detected only after maternal hypertension and proteinuria or other organ damage emerge, by which point disease-modifying interventions are not available, and delivery of the baby and placenta remains the only cure. Nanotechnology offers a route to reduce this diagnostic-therapeutic latency. Nanostructured biosensors and liquid biopsy platforms detect placental proteins, cell-free RNA/DNA, and extracellular vesicles at femtomolar concentrations and in a multiplex manner, enabling earlier risk stratification when integrated with machine-learning models. In parallel, placenta-targeted lipid-, peptide-, polymeric-, dendrimeric-, and small extracellular vesicle-based nanocarriers deliver angiogenic mRNA, antiangiogenic siRNA, antioxidants, and immunomodulators selectively to the trophoblast cells while limiting fetal exposure. Placenta-on-a-chip platforms and ex vivo placental perfusion models provide human-relevant test beds for these systems. We critically appraise these advances, examine the safety-by-design, manufacturing bottlenecks, and regulatory constraints unique to obstetric nanomedicine, and outline the convergence of theranostics and digital health that could move preeclampsia care from reactive symptom management toward proactive, placenta-targeted monitoring and therapy.

title: Nanotechnology-Driven Precision Diagnostics and Therapeutics for Preeclampsia.

abstract: CRISPR-Cas9 relies on a dual CRISPR RNA (crRNA)-trans-activating crRNA (tracrRNA) guide, yet whether RNA-based anti-CRISPRs exist for this system has remained unknown. Here, we identify a phage-encoded small non-coding RNA, rAcrIIA1, that adopts an unexpected chimeric crRNA-tracrRNA architecture, faithfully recapitulating the entire single-guide RNA (sgRNA) of Cas9. Cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) structures of the Cas9-rAcrIIA1 binary complex and the Cas9-rAcrIIA1-DNA ternary complex reveal that rAcrIIA1 engages Cas9 nearly identically to the native sgRNA, competitively blocking crRNA and tracrRNA loading and thereby abolishing DNA interference. Strikingly, beyond its natural inhibitory function, rAcrIIA1 is fully reprogrammable: with variable guide sequences, it directs Cas9 for sequence-specific DNA cleavage with efficiency comparable to the canonical sgRNA, and it activates trans-cleavage more potently. Thus, rAcrIIA1 provides an experimentally validated, mechanistically resolved RNA-based inhibitor of CRISPR-Cas9, reveals a distinct anti-CRISPR mechanism through complete sgRNA mimicry, and serves as a versatile bifunctional scaffold for genome editing and diagnostics.

abstract: The major goal of this study is to evaluate a new type of cell transplantation therapy for individuals with hereditary PAP, study a new treatment that may be useful for treatment of other diseases, and research mechanisms that drive the development and function of lung macrophages.

description:
Hereditary pulmonary alveolar proteinosis (hPAP) is a rare lung disease characterized by the progressive accumulation of pulmonary surfactant in alveoli resulting in progressive hypoxemic respiratory failure, and in some patients, secondary infections and/or pulmonary fibrosis. While hPAP affects men, women, and children, most patients present as children. The lung structure appears well-preserved in many cases with pathogenesis being driven by the consequences of the filling of alveoli with surfactant sediment; however, some patients develop respiratory failure caused by pulmonary fibrosis requiring therapeutic lung transplantation.

Hereditary PAP is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutations in the genes (CSF2RA or CSF2RB) encoding the GM-CSF receptor alpha or beta chains, respectively. Mutations in these genes disrupt GM-CSF receptor function, blocking GM-CSF signaling and impairing the removal of excess surfactant from alveoli by alveolar macrophages (AMs).

This study is an open-label, non-randomized, single center clinical treatment study to evaluate the feasibility of manufacturing CSF2RA gene-corrected macrophages, as well as the safety, tolerability, efficacy, and durability of CSF2RA gene correction/pulmonary macrophage transplantation (PMT) therapy in three patients with hPAP caused by recessive homozygous or compound heterozygous CSF2RA mutations. In addition to safety and tolerability, the clinical trial will evaluate outcome measures related to clinical efficacy and biologic signature of CSF2RA gene-correction/PMT therapy, as well as pharmacokinetics, pharmacodynamics, and the mechanism of action.

The clinical trial design includes a 2-month observation period, a Baseline visit, 5-month treatment period, and Short-, Medium-, and Long-Term follow-up periods of 1, 4, and 10 years, respectively. Each patient will serve as their own self-control and receive a split-dose comprising three administrations of autologous, bone marrow cluster of differentiation 34+ (CD34+) cell-derived, lentiviral CSF2RA gene-corrected macrophages at a minimum of 2-month intervals, delivered by direct bronchoscopic instillation of cells into individual lung segments (5.8x105 cells/segment); an increasing number of cells at each administration will be achieved by sequentially increasing the number of segments treated. Current standard medical care (whole lung lavage and supplemental oxygen) will be continuously available to all enrolled patients.

Assessments will include safety (adverse events and serious adverse events), tolerability (short-term, treatment-emergent pulmonary symptoms), efficacy (beneficial effects on clinical, physiological, and radiological manifestations of hPAP), durability (persistence of beneficial effects), and mechanism of action (persistence, CSF2RA-expression, and function of alveolar macrophages (AMs)).

Expected results will inform the feasibility, safety, tolerability, efficacy, durability, and mechanism of action of gene transfer/PMT as therapy of hPAP. These results will impact the field because it departs markedly from the current inefficient, highly invasive method of physically removing surfactant by whole lung lavage (WLL) and instead uses a novel approach to restore AM function. This study is expected to establish the feasibility of a novel, specific therapy for children with hPAP and a new type of cell transplantation therapy (PMT) that may be useful for other diseases.
