outcomes.description:
Patient global impression of severity (PGIS) and patient global impression of change (PGIC) will be assessed in relation to the patient's overall impression of disease severity and change from baseline. PGIS will assess the current breathing problems and the impact on daily physical activity. The current severity of hPAP (PGIS) will be assessed on a five-point scale ranging from none, mild, moderate, severe, to very severe.

PGIC will assess the change from baseline in breathing problems and impact of breathing problems on daily physical activity. The change from baseline in hPAP severity (PGIC) will be assessed on a five-point scale ranging from much improved, somewhat improved, no change, somewhat worse, to much worse.

The PGIS and PGIC parameters will be evaluated just prior to PMT, immediately upon completion of PMT, and daily for 5 days following PMT.

outcomes.description:
Change in lowest peripheral blood oxygen saturation value measured by the STandardized Exercise Protocol testing (STEP Test) performed weekly before and after initiation of PMT Therapy.

Standardized exercise oximetry to measure blood oxygen saturation will be performed at home weekly during the study. Briefly, a pulse-oximeter will be placed on the finger with the participant at rest sitting in a chair. Three baseline (resting) readings will be taken over a 3 minute period. Then the participant will step on and off a standard step for a period of 5 minutes followed by a 3 minute seated recovery. The pulse oximeter will record oxygen saturations every minute of the test. Data will be transmitted to the site via the mobile health platform. The lowest peripheral blood oxygen saturation will be determined from the collected data.

The SF-36 Questionnaire is a 36-item, patient-reported survey of patient health. The questionnaire consists of eight scaled scores (each 0-100), which are the weighted sums of the questions in their section, with each question carrying equal weight. The lower the score the more disability. The eight sections are 1) vitality, 2) physical functioning, 3) bodily pain, 4) general health perceptions, 5) physical role functioning, 6) emotional role functioning, 7) social role functioning and 8) mental health.

abstract:
This exploratory trial will have three parts. Part A is a dose escalation part, Part B is an expanded safety and dose evaluation part, and Part C is a safety and immunogenicity evaluation part in individuals with recurrent HSV-2 genital herpes.

Part A will focus on the safety evaluations, and in addition, vaccine-induced immune responses (specifically neutralizing antibodies) will also be analyzed to assess if there is a dose-response.

Part B of the trial will expand the safety characterization for two dose levels of BNT163 selected based on Part A data and will also enable a more comprehensive assessment of the impact of pre-existing immunity to HSV-1 and -2 on the safety and immune responses to BNT163.

Part C will evaluate safety and immunogenicity of BNT163 compared to a placebo in a three-dose regimen in participants with a history of HSV-2 recurrent genital herpes.
description:
In Part A, participants will be randomized 5:1 to BNT163:placebo. In Part B, participants will be randomized 1:1 to either of the two selected dose levels based on data from Part A. In Part C, participants will be randomized 1:1 to BNT163:placebo.

In Part A \& B, participants will receive three intramuscular doses of a fixed dose level of the BNT163 vaccine (Part A and B) or placebo (Part A only).

In Part C, participants will receive three intramuscular doses of one fixed dose level of the BNT163 vaccine or placebo. In this part, continuous suppressive antiviral therapy is given over the entire vaccine dosing period (during and between vaccine doses) to prevent administration of the vaccine concomitantly to viral replication and active genital herpes.

abstract: We aimed to study the stability of a Beta (β)-SARS-CoV-2 virus-like particle (VLP) vaccine in a series of preliminary experiments using selective stabilizing excipients. β-SARS-CoV-2 VLPs were produced and purified using established methodologies. The thermostability of VLPs was tested at 4°C and -30°C in the presence or absence of stabilizers polysorbate 80, sorbitol, or L-histidine in the presence of a physiological NaCl concentration of 137 mM. The integrity of VLPs was assessed using ELISA, Western immunoblot, and dynamic light scatter (DLS). β-SARS-CoV-2 VLPs were stable at 4°C for 14 days, and the addition of stabilizing excipients improved stability compared to VLPs in PBS alone. Storage of VLPs at -80°C maintained particle integrity by DLS analysis for up to 2 years. Excipients helped to maintain the antigenicity of the VLPs by ELISA and Western immunoblot, and DLS analysis revealed that VLPs retained their particulate structure.IMPORTANCESARS-CoV-2 continues to circulate globally and cause significant illness. The problem of waning immunity to mRNA/LNPs has necessitated frequent boosters to keep pace with emerging variants. The development of alternative vaccines, therefore, remains a priority. Protein- based vaccines, like VLPs, offer a safe alternative able to produce longer-lasting immune responses. In this preliminary stability analysis, the β-SARS-CoV-2 VLPs were found to be stable at 4°C, and the addition of excipients improved VLP stability. Storage of VLPs at -30°C and -80°C also showed that the VLPs are stable for extended periods. Our findings will be of importance for the ongoing development of a SARS-CoV-2 VLP-based vaccine.

abstract: Expanded CAG/CTG repeats cause more than 15 different diseases that all remain without a disease-modifying treatment. Because repeat length accounts for most of the variation in disease severity, contracting CAG/CTG repeats presents an attractive therapeutic avenue. Here, we show that the CRISPR-Cas9 nickase targeted to CAG/CTG repeats leads to efficient repeat contractions in Huntington's disease (HD) patient-derived neurons and astrocytes and in myotonic dystrophy type 1 patient-derived neurons. The approach was allele selective and free of detectable off-target mutations. Injection of the Cas9 nickase into the striatum of the R6/1 mouse model of HD using adeno-associated viral vectors led to repeat contractions in more than half of striatal neurons. Upon injection, we observed a reduction in the number of inclusion bodies, an improved gene expression profile, and amelioration of locomotion deficits in the open field test. The effects were greater than expected from the contractions induced, suggesting that non-cell autonomous mechanisms may be involved. Our results provide the proof of concept that correction of CAG/CTG repeats can improve HD phenotypes in a mouse disease model.

abstract: Lipid nanoparticles (LNP) are widely used for nucleic acid delivery, with current optimization efforts mainly focusing on refining formulation features, enabling extrahepatic targeting, and improving therapeutic efficacy. Particle shape and internal architecture are variables often overlooked in LNP design, although they critically influence particle stability, biodistribution, cellular uptake, and transfection. Here, we investigate how formulation and process parameters impact LNP shape, morphology, and internal structure, and how these structural features, in turn, influence mRNA loading, cell uptake, and expression. We demonstrate that modulation of lipid composition by increasing DSPC content drives a transition from compact spherical to vesicular non-spherical morphologies, with altered RNA loading at the single-particle level. While non-spherical LNP exhibited higher cellular uptake than spherical LNP, it was identified that this increase was relatively modest compared with the substantially higher and sustained protein expression for non-spherical structures. This suggests that increased uptake alone cannot explain the enhanced transfection performance. The trend was conserved across LNP formulations comprising clinically relevant ionizable lipids SM-102, ALC-0315 and DLin-MC3-DMA. Taken together, these findings establish LNP shape and internal morphology as functionally relevant design variables that should be considered in the design of next-generation LNP with improved mRNA delivery and expression.

abstract:
This study tests whether certain medicines and a skin treatment can slow down or partly reverse the body's aging process.

As people age, the activity of their genes changes in predictable ways. Researchers can now measure a person's "biological age" from these gene-activity patterns in skin and blood. This study uses that measurement to see whether treatment can lower a person's biological age compared with their own starting point.

Adults in the study take geroprotective ("age-protecting") agents by mouth or by injection. A separate skin serum containing small anti-aging peptides is applied to certain areas of skin, and those treated areas are compared with untreated areas on the same person.

Skin and blood samples are taken at set times to measure biological age and markers of cell aging before, during, and after treatment. The main goal is to find out whether treatment lowers measured biological age in skin and blood. The study also looks at whether the treatments are safe and well tolerated.

description:
This is a prospective, single-group interventional study with two treatment components, systemic and topical. Each participant contributes paired treated and untreated samples and serves as their own internal control, reducing inter-individual variability in clock measurements.

Systemic component: participants receive geroprotective agents administered orally or subcutaneously. Candidate agents include metformin, low-dose chloroquine, ivermectin, and a defined nutritional supplement (collagen lysate; black seed oil or its active constituent thymoquinone; urolithin; and controlled pH modulation with citric, acetic, or glycolic acid), used alone or in combination per protocol.

Topical component: an aqueous serum of small, water-soluble anti-aging peptides below the \~500-Dalton stratum corneum penetration cutoff - GHK-Cu (\~404 Da), AHK-Cu (\~418 Da), Epitalon (\~390 Da), PGP/Pro-Gly-Pro (\~269 Da), and CLV/Cys-Leu-Val (\~333 Da) - is applied at approximately 1-3 mg/mL to defined skin sites. Treated sites are compared with matched untreated contralateral, adjacent, or distant sites on the same participant.

Blood, skin biopsies, exfoliated skin cells, plucked hair follicles, and saliva are used to assess treatment effect locally and systemically.

Objectives Primary: determine whether treatment produces a statistically significant reduction in START/REST-derived transcriptomic biological age in skin, hair, saliva, and peripheral blood, relative to each participant's baseline and untreated reference tissue.

Secondary: characterize changes in molecular markers of cellular senescence, inflammaging/SASP, transcriptional fitness, and metabolic cofactors; assess concordance between systemic and local rejuvenation signals; evaluate safety and tolerability of each agent across the treatment period.

Procedures and Sampling Skin biopsies, exfoliated keratinocytes, plucked follicles, saliva, and blood are collected at scheduled baseline, on-treatment, and post-treatment timepoints for transcriptomic profiling and senescence-marker analysis.

Outcome Definition Age-reversal is defined prospectively as a statistically significant decrease in clock-derived biological age in treated tissue relative to both baseline and untreated reference tissue.

Significance The study aims to provide the first transcriptional clock-anchored human evidence that combined systemic and topical geroprotection can drive coordinated rejuvenation across tissues.

abstract: Differences in individual radiosensitivity are not currently reflected in radiotherapy treatment planning, and identifying genetic drivers of this variation is a key step in personalising future treatments. While the role of DNA double-strand break (DSB) repair in radiosensitivity is well-studied, the impacts of single-strand break (SSB) repair defects are relatively unexplored. Through targeted SSB repair gene knockout, we show that disrupted SSB repair increases radiosensitivity, with stronger effects for high Linear Energy Transfer (LET) radiation. Mechanistic studies identified both an increase in DSB production at low LETs, due to delayed SSB repair, and higher levels of unrepaired complex damage at high LETs. This altered sensitivity is also reflected by differences in disease-specific survival for patients with SSB repair gene alterations in a retrospective pan-cancer clinical analysis. SSB repair pathway disruption may therefore be clinically relevant and important to consider for radiotherapy personalisation, particularly for high-LET radiation treatments.

abstract: Retinoic acid-inducible gene-I (RIG-I) plays a pivotal role in recognizing and combating RNA viruses in humans, and it has become a drug target of significant interest. RIG-I agonists composed of dsRNA represent antiviral and antitumor therapies, however the development of small-molecule RIG-I agonists, with their potential for improved pharmacokinetics, remains an unmet need. Here, we report small-molecule RIG-I agonists that directly activate the RIG-I receptor protein. These agonists stimulate the first step in RIG-I signaling by triggering release of the signaling domains (CARDs) from an autorepressed form of the protein. This was achieved by developing a sensitive high-throughput screening (HTS) assay that directly monitors CARD expulsion through optical methods. The resulting screen hits were refined and optimized, leading to a specific RIG-I agonist that induces a robust interferon response. This study establishes a pharmacophore and assay for development of small molecules that precisely modulate RIG-I signaling.

abstract:
OBJECTIVE: To determine if common genetic variants at the chromosome 1p13 locus which predisposes to Paget's Disease of Bone (PDB) regulate Macrophage Colony stimulating factor (M-CSF) expression in bone cells and to determine if there is dysregulation of M-CSF in patients with PDB.
METHODS: The regions surrounding single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNP) previously associated with PDB at a genome wide significant level were deleted in clones of MG63 osteoblast-like cells using CRISPR/Cas and levels of M-CSF mRNA and protein were evaluated in cells with and without deletions. Serum M-CSF was measured by ELISA in PDB and controls and values in patients were related to clinical features of PDB and biochemical markers of bone remodelling.
RESULTS: Deletion of the region surrounding rs484959 increased expression of M-CSF mRNA by 1.31 fold [95%,1.04-1.58], p = 0.026 and M-CSF protein by 1.91 fold [1.25-2.57], p = 0.013, compared with control cells. Serum M-CSF was significantly elevated in PDB versus controls (mean ± SD = 781.7 ± 678 vs. 541 ± 491 pg/mL, p < 0.001). Furthermore, M-CSF levels were associated with number of affected bones (p = 0.029), bodily pain assessed by SF-36 (p = 0.026) and biochemical markers of bone turnover.
CONCLUSION: The rs484959 SNP is a regulatory variant which modulates M-CSF mRNA and protein expression in osteoblasts. Serum M-CSF is increased in PDB, is associated with pain, disease extent and biochemical markers of bone remodelling. This suggest that there is dysregulation of M-CSF in PDB and that this cytokine may play a role in pathogenesis of the disease.

abstract: Methamphetamine use disorder (MUD) poses a significant global health challenge, lacking FDA-approved pharmacotherapies. Despite extensive exploration of therapeutic targets and interventions, effective treatment remains scarce due to challenges in delivering therapeutic agents to relevant brain regions at effective concentrations. Nanoparticle-mediated delivery offers a promising approach for transporting various therapeutic cargos to the central nervous system, including small molecules, nucleic acids, peptides, proteins, and gene-editing systems. However, the application of nanomedicine strategies in addressing the unique pathophysiological characteristics of MUD has not been systematically assessed. This review presents a problem-focused analysis of how lipid-based, polymeric, inorganic, biological, and hybrid nanocarriers tackle successive delivery obstacles such as systemic stability, blood-brain barrier (BBB) penetration, brain region-specific distribution, and controlled release of intracellular cargo. We compare preclinical nanotherapeutic approaches encompassing small-molecule neuroprotective agents, anti-METH vaccines, gene-silencing RNAs, neurotrophic proteins, and emerging gene-editing methods, outlining their respective benefits, limitations, and design considerations. Additionally, we explore key factors influencing nanomedicine performance in MUD, including protein corona formation, the impact of METH-related BBB dysfunction and neuroinflammation on nanoparticle distribution, and the disparity between acute animal models and chronic human MUD with relapse tendencies. In conclusion, we present a systematic framework for aligning nanocarrier characteristics with distinct delivery obstacles and therapeutic needs. We also emphasize forthcoming avenues such as disease-triggered nanocarriers, targeted delivery to specific regions, combined nanomedical approaches, theranostic strategies, and standardized assessments of biodistribution, effectiveness, safety, and translational potential.

abstract:
BACKGROUND: Cystine/glutamate antiporter (xCT) imports extracellular cystine in exchange for intracellular glutamate. Although it plays an essential role in diabetes-associated processes such as impaired wound healing, its contribution to diabetic encephalopathy (DE) remains unclear.
METHODS: Wild-type and xCT-deficient (xCT-/-) mice were subjected to type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) induction using a highfat diet combined with streptozotocin. xCT expression and activity in the brain were evaluated through quantitative polymerase chain reaction, Western blotting, immunofluorescence, chloride-dependent [14C]-L-cystine uptake, and measurements of extracellular glutamate. An adeno-associated virus (AAV)-mediated Clustered Regularly Interspaced Short Palindromic Repeats (CRISPR)/Cas9 approach was employed to generate region-specific, cell type-restricted xCT knockout animals. Neuronal injury and cognitive function were evaluated via in vivo propidium iodide (PI) and neuronal nuclei antigen (NeuN) double staining, the Y-maze spontaneous alternation test, the Morris water maze test, and the object location test.
RESULTS: xCT deficiency protected mice from T2DM-induced DE. Mechanistically, hyperglycemia upregulated xCT expression via activating transcription factor 4 (ATF4), thereby enhancing xCT function in hippocampal astrocytes. This maladaptive increase promoted excessive extracellular glutamate, neuronal loss, and cognitive impairment. Both astrocyte-specific deletion of xCT and pharmacological inhibition of xCT ameliorated these deficits.
CONCLUSION: These findings identify astrocytic xCT as a key driver of diabetes-induced glutamate excitotoxicity and DE progression, underscoring its potential as a therapeutic target.

title: Astrocytic Cystine/Glutamate Antiporters Promote Diabetic Encephalopathy via the Induction of Glutamate Excitotoxicity.

abstract: Impaired protein folding in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) causes ER stress and activates the unfolded protein response (UPR), which can induce apoptosis during prolonged ER stress. ER stress is therapeutically targeted in plasma cell malignancies, such as multiple myeloma (MM), but these treatments remain noncurative, and UPR signaling in B-cell malignancies is incompletely understood. A targeted CRISPR-Cas9 screen in RPMI-8226 cells exposed to thapsigargin identified known ER stress regulators (XBP1, IRE1, and calreticulin) and the translation factor eIF5A (eukaryotic translation initiation factor 5A), whose role in ER stress remains unclear. Competition assays showed that eIF5A depletion is detrimental under basal conditions but confers a proliferation advantage during thapsigargin treatment. Inducible EIF5A knockouts confirmed reduced sensitivity specifically to thapsigargin, loss of eIF5A had no or sensitizing effects on cell death induced by other ER stress drugs. Polysome profiling revealed that not general translation, but the translation of specific mRNA transcripts coding for UPR components and apoptotic proteins was affected by eIF5A depletion. Correspondingly, EIF5A KO cells showed reduced thapsigargin-induced UPR activation. In conclusion, these findings indicate that loss of eIF5A alters the stress response in MM cells.

title: A role for eIF5A in translational control of stress-inducible proteins in multiple myeloma cell lines.

abstract: Astrocytes have emerged as central regulators of neuroinflammation, extending far beyond their traditional roles as structural and metabolic support cells. In neurological disorders, astrocytes undergo reactive remodeling that encompasses morphological, transcriptional, metabolic, and functional changes. Rather than fitting into a fixed A1/A2 dichotomy, reactive astrocytes exist along a disease-, region-, and stage-dependent continuum shaped by local pathology and intercellular crosstalk. This review summarizes how astrocytes contribute to neuroinflammatory processes in Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, Huntington's disease, central nervous system injury, infection, multiple sclerosis, epilepsy, and autism spectrum disorder. We highlight convergent mechanisms, including cytokine and chemokine release, complement activation, glutamate and ion homeostasis disruption, oxidative stress, metabolic reprogramming, and blood-brain barrier regulation, while emphasizing disease-specific astrocytic programs. We further discuss astrocyte interactions with microglia, neurons, oligodendrocytes, endothelial cells, and peripheral immune cells, as well as key regulatory pathways, epigenetic remodeling, and lipid-dependent metabolic signaling. Finally, we evaluate current and emerging astrocyte-targeted therapeutic strategies, including metabolic modulation, receptor targeting, gene editing, nanodelivery, and gut-brain axis interventions. Defining functionally validated astrocyte states and developing biomarker-guided, stage-adaptive therapies may enable more precise intervention in neuroinflammatory and neurodegenerative diseases.

title: The Role of Astrocytes in the Inflammatory Response in Neurodiseases.

abstract: Type 1 diabetes (T1D) is characterized by autoimmune-mediated destruction of pancreatic β-cells, resulting in lifelong insulin dependence and disease burden. Stem cell-derived islet (SCI) replacement therapies have emerged as a promising strategy to restore endogenous insulin production; however, immune rejection, inflammatory stress, and intrinsic β-cell vulnerability remain major barriers to durable graft survival. Recent advances in gene editing and stem cell engineering have accelerated the development of next-generation SCIs designed to evade immune recognition while enhancing resistance to diabetogenic stress pathways. In this review, we examine genetic engineering strategies aimed at improving β-cell protection through modulation of antigen presentation, immune checkpoint signaling, cytokine responsiveness, and cellular stress adaptation. We discuss established immune-evasive targets including beta-2-microglobulin (B2M), class II major histocompatibility complex transactivator (CIITA), cluster of differentiation 47 (CD47), programmed death-ligand 1 (PD-L1), and cytotoxic T-lymphocyte-associated protein 4-immunoglobulin (CTLA4-Ig), alongside emerging stress-resilience pathways involving renalase (RNLS), thioredoxin-interacting protein (TXNIP), and unfolded protein response regulators. We further highlight how β-cell stress can amplify immune recognition and graft dysfunction. Collectively, these approaches support multifunctional engineered SCIs designed to overcome immune-mediated and intrinsic stress-related barriers to durable β-cell replacement. Literature was identified through PubMed and Google Scholar searches conducted from February through September 2026.

abstract:
Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) is a major cause of acute respiratory infections (ARIs), which occur in seasonal outbreaks. Among the adult population, immunocompromised individuals, particularly lung transplant recipients and recipients of allogeneic haematopoietic stem cell transplants (HSCTs), are at the highest risk of severe ARI. RSV can also cause prolonged inflammation of the airways, leading to persistent deterioration in lung function. Thus, in lung transplant recipients, RSV is a major cause of chronic lung allograft dysfunction (CLAD), the leading cause of lung transplant failure and mortality beyond the first post-transplant year. In recipients of ACSH, RSV infection is associated with the onset and/or worsening of bronchiolitis obliterans syndrome, which leads to increased mortality. Preventing RSV-associated lower respiratory tract disease (LRTD) and its short- and long-term consequences in these populations is therefore a key priority.

Three inactivated RSV vaccines, targeting the RSV fusion glycoprotein in its pre-fusion conformation (RSVpreF), have recently been approved for use in adults. These comprise two recombinant protein vaccines - one with an adjuvant (RSVpreF3-AS01, Arexvy®, GSK) and one without (RSVpreF, Abrysvo®, Pfizer) - and one mRNA vaccine. Although these vaccines have demonstrated their safety, immunogenicity and efficacy (reducing the risk of RSV-related IMRI by approximately 80-85 per cent) in adults aged 60 and over, the pivotal trials excluded immunocompromised patients.

To date, there is limited data on the efficacy, immunogenicity and tolerability of these vaccines in high-risk immunocompromised populations, such as recipients of bone marrow transplants and allogeneic stem cell transplants. Real-world studies suggest that RSV vaccines may reduce the risk of RSV-associated acute respiratory infection and hospitalisations in elderly immunocompromised adults. With regard to immunogenicity, the available cohort studies, conducted on small sample sizes, indicate that the vaccine response is heterogeneous and, overall, lower than that observed in immunocompetent older people. Preliminary data suggest that booster vaccination regimens may be necessary to optimise the immune response in these populations.

Given the significant morbidity associated with RSV in recipients of bone marrow transplants and allogeneic stem cell transplants, it is a priority to assess the immunogenicity and safety profile of RSV vaccines, and to determine the optimal vaccination schedule for these high-risk, immunocompromised populations.

The investigators hypothesise that the immune response to RSV vaccines in severely immunocompromised TP and ACSH recipients is weaker than in immunocompetent older adults, and that enhanced vaccination strategies may be required. In this study, two vaccination strategies will be evaluated in these populations:

* a single dose of the adjuvanted RSVpreF3-AS01 vaccine (Arexvy®),
* or a booster regimen comprising two doses of the non-adjuvanted RSVpreF vaccine (Abrysvo®), administered one month apart.

abstract: Diacylglycerol O-acyltransferase 2 (DGAT2), a key enzyme in hepatic triglyceride (TG) synthesis, is considered a promising therapeutic target for metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH). Small interfering RNAs (siRNAs) targeting conserved regions of human and mouse DGAT2 mRNA were designed, synthesized, and screened in vitro, leading to the identification of a GalNAc-conjugated siRNA, VX093L, which mediates potent DGAT2 mRNA knockdown in both human and mouse hepatocytes and exhibits sustained hepatic DGAT2 silencing in healthy mice. In a high-fat diet (HFD)-induced MASH mouse model, the effects of VX093L (1 or 3 mg/kg, biweekly) were evaluated in comparison with the approved drug resmetirom (10 mg/kg, daily). Eight-week treatment with VX093L potently silenced hepatic DGAT2 (>80%, p < 0.0001), thereby inhibiting hepatic TG synthesis, resulting in significantly ameliorating hepatic steatosis. Notably, the improvement in steatosis translated into effective attenuation of fibrosis, with 1 mg/kg VX093L exhibiting better anti-fibrotic efficacy compared to resmetirom, and this benefit was not accompanied by increased inflammation. In conclusion, VX093L represents a promising siRNA-based therapeutic for the treatment of MASH.

abstract:
The purpose of this study is to evaluate the safety, tolerability, biological activity, and initial efficacy of PM647a, an investigational Prime Editing therapy, in adults and adolescents with Alpha-1 Antitrypsin Deficiency (AATD).

AATD is caused by a mutation (change) in a gene called SERPINA1 that prevents the cells in your liver from producing a functional protein (alpha-1 anti-trypsin; AAT) that helps protect your lung tissue. PM647a is designed to precisely correct the prevalent disease-causing mutation (SERPINA1 Pi\*Z (E342K)) with the goal of restoring functional AAT. This is the first study of PM647a in humans. Participants will receive a single intravenous (IV) infusion of PM647a and will be monitored closely to evaluate safety, how the body responds to treatment, changes in AAT protein levels, and whether treatment may improve signs and symptoms of AATD.
description:
This is a Phase 1/2 open label study evaluating PM647a in adults and adolescents with Alpha-1 Antitrypsin Deficiency (AATD) who are homozygous for the SERPINA1 p.E342K pathogenic variant, also known as the PiZ allele (PiZZ genotype). Enrollment and treatment will begin with Group A, which includes participants with lung manifestations only. Group B will open subsequently and will include participants with both lung and liver manifestations or liver manifestations only. Additionally, a set of 3 to 6 participants with AATD penetrant lung disease (with or without liver disease), will be enrolled to further understand the effects of PM647a on local pharmacodynamic effects through BAL (BAL cohort).

The study will evaluate the safety of PM647a, determine an appropriate dose for future studies, and assess whether treatment restores normal synthesis and secretion of functional AAT and improves clinical measures of AATD. Participants will receive a single IV infusion of PM647a and will undergo regular safety evaluations, laboratory testing, imaging, and clinical assessments for approximately 48 weeks after treatment. Participants will then be asked to enroll in a separate long-term follow-up study to continue monitoring safety and treatment effects for an additional 14 years.

abstract: The purpose of this double-masked, randomized, placebo-controlled, paired-eye study is to evaluate the efficacy, safety and tolerability of Sepofarsen in subjects with Leber Congenital Amaurosis (LCA) due to the c.2991+1655A\>G (p.Cys998X) mutation in the CEP290.

institutions.label: Sepul Bio

description:
This is a double-masked, randomized, placebo-controlled, paired-eye study in which one eye of each subject will serve as a control.

At the start of the study the two eyes of each subject will be randomized such that one eye receives sepofarsen and the other eye receives placebo for the first year. In the second year, for all subjects, the eye that was randomized to receive sepofarsen will continue to receive sepofarsen. For the eye that was randomized to placebo in the first year, treatment in the second year will be allocated, as follows: 50% of the eyes will continue to receive placebo, and 50% of the eyes will receive sepofarsen.

Sepofarsen and placebo will be administered via intravitreal injection every 6 months.

abstract:
This pilot study will assess the safety and feasibility of using an implantable microdevice to measure local intratumor response to chemotherapy and other clinically relevant drugs in malignant brain tumors.

* The device involved in this study is called a microdevice.
* The drugs used in this study will only include drugs already used systemically for the treatment of gliomas.
description:
This research study is a Pilot Study, which is the first time investigators are examining this study device in brain tumors.

The FDA (the U.S. Food and Drug Administration) has not approved the microdevice as a treatment for any disease.

Investigators are studying the safety of the microdevice and the effects of different drugs for each specific tumor. Brain tumors are known to be very different from each other and respond differently to different drugs. It would be very helpful to find out what drugs have the best chance of working in each specific tumor.

This research study involves drugs that are released by a small device, as small as the tip of a needle, that is inserted into the tumor at the time of surgery and is removed at the end of the surgery. The goal of this research study is to prove that microdevices can be used to find out which drugs have better effects on treating malignant brain tumors.

Participants will be in this research study for up to 30 days.

Expected enrollment is about 30 people.

abstract: As a powerful gene-editing tool, the clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats (CRISPR)/CRISPR-associated (Cas) system features simple construction, precise targeting, and higher editing efficiency, bringing prospects of radical cures for numerous critical illnesses at the genomic level. To date, ex vivo CRISPR/Cas-based gene therapies represented by Casgevy have achieved significant clinical advances. Nevertheless, cumbersome operational workflows and prohibitive treatment costs severely hinder their widespread clinical accessibility. In contrast, in vivo CRISPR/Cas-based gene therapies stand out with convenient administration procedures and reduced overall costs, endowing them with enormous translational potential. Although it holds great promise, the clinical translation of in vivo CRISPR/Cas-based gene therapies remains hampered by a number of factors. Among those multiple obstacles restricting the clinical translation of in vivo CRISPR/Cas-based gene therapies, delivery systems constitute the core bottleneck dominating in vivo editing efficiency and therapeutic potency. Centered on delivery platforms for in vivo CRISPR/Cas-based gene therapies, this review systematically summarizes prevailing in vivo CRISPR/Cas nano delivery systems, recapitulates relevant preclinical and clinical outcomes, discusses translational hurdles, and prospects the evolution of next-generation delivery systems, aiming to facilitate further development of in vivo CRISPR/Cas-based gene therapies.

abstract: Unconjugated antisense oligonucleotides (ASOs) and GalNAc-conjugated small interfering RNAs (siRNAs) have emerged as transformative therapeutic modalities, but their translation remains hindered by complex pharmacokinetics characterized by rapid plasma clearance, heterogeneous tissue uptake, and prolonged intracellular retention. Physiologically based pharmacokinetic (PBPK) modeling offers a mechanistic framework to integrate these processes across species, yet applications to oligonucleotides remain limited, and existing efforts are typically restricted to specific chemistries or routes of administration. This study aimed to develop a cross-species PBPK platform to characterize the plasma and tissue disposition of unconjugated ASOs and GalNAc-siRNAs in preclinical species and humans, and to evaluate the consistency of estimated drug-specific parameters with pre-specified allometric scaling relationships within the domain of compounds and routes considered. Published datasets spanning mice, rats, non-human primates, and humans were integrated for representative unconjugated ASOs (Malat-1, GluR1, p-tau, tominersen) and GalNAc-siRNAs (ALN-AT3, givosiran, fitusiran). The PBPK model incorporated 11 tissue compartments, cerebrospinal fluid substructures, tissue substructures, endosomal trafficking, non-specific binding in kidney and liver, and ASGPR-mediated internalization for GalNAc-siRNAs. Parameters for endocytosis, exocytosis, and degradation were estimated, and estimated values were compared with pre-specified allometric exponents to assess physiological plausibility (i.e., as a consistency check rather than independent inference of scaling laws). The model captured plasma, liver, kidney, and CNS profiles across species, reproducing rapid systemic clearance with prolonged tissue half-lives. Estimated parameter values for endocytosis, exocytosis, and non-specific kidney binding were consistent with pre-specified allometric exponents (b = -0.25 and -0.2, respectively), supporting the physiological plausibility of the estimates. Sensitivity analyses identified endocytosis and rate of degradation as dominant determinants of systemic and tissue disposition. This work establishes a translational PBPK platform for unconjugated ASOs and GalNAc-conjugated siRNAs, enabling quantitative interspecies extrapolation within the domain of the compounds, routes, and species studied. The framework provides a mechanistic basis to support dose selection, safety assessment, and clinical translation for these subclasses; extrapolation to other oligonucleotide subclasses (e.g., GalNAc-ASOs, unconjugated siRNAs, LNP-formulated oligonucleotides) will require additional datasets and dedicated validation.

abstract: Current variant classifications do not capture clinical severity relative to other pathogenic variants in the same gene. We propose phenotype-exceeding-(mono)allelic-knockout (PEAK) as a term for variants associated with a more severe clinical phenotype than that of heterozygous null alleles. This mechanism-independent designation may facilitate genotype-phenotype interpretation and identify candidates for allele-selective therapeutic development.

abstract:
UNLABELLED: Intermittent fasting (IF) improves metabolic health, yet whether hepatic ketogenesis is required for mediating its effects remains unclear. Here, we investigated how ketogenesis contributes to the systemic and liver-specific metabolic effects of IF in male and female mice. Fasting increased circulating ketone bodies in both sexes, with females showing a greater increase, indicating intrinsic sex differences in ketone metabolism. IF reduced body weight gain and adiposity in both sexes, and these benefits persisted when Hmgcs2 expression was knocked down in adult mice, using an antisense oligonucleotide approach to inhibit ketogenesis. In contrast, hepatic benefits were sex- and ketogenesis-dependent. IF markedly reduced steatosis and fibrosis in male mice, but these improvements were attenuated when Hmgcs2 expression was suppressed. In contrast, female mice showed minimal hepatic benefit from IF and had heightened susceptibility to steatosis, fibrosis, and inflammatory activation upon Hmgcs2 knockdown. Single-cell transcriptomic analyses identified neutrophils and myofibroblasts as key responders to hepatocyte-derived ketone bodies. IF suppressed neutrophil-driven inflammatory signaling in an Hmgcs2-dependent manner, and ketone bodies attenuated low-grade inflammation in cultured neutrophil-like cells. This ketogenesis-inflammation-fibrosis axis was further supported by human Genotype-Tissue Expression liver coexpression analyses. Together, these findings demonstrate that although body weight and antiobesity actions of IF are largely ketogenesis-independent in both sexes of mice, its hepatic antisteatotic and antifibrotic effects are sexually dimorphic and ketogenesis-dependent in male mice.
ARTICLE HIGHLIGHTS: We investigated whether ketogenesis is required for the metabolic benefits of intermittent fasting (IF) and whether these effects differ between sexes. We specifically asked whether ketogenesis drives IF-mediated protection against obesity and fatty liver disease in male and female mice. We found that IF reduced adiposity independently of ketogenesis in both sexes, but its antisteatotic and antifibrotic effects were ketogenesis-dependent in male mice and minimal in female mice. These findings reveal a sex-dependent ketogenesis-inflammation-fibrosis axis and highlight the need to consider sex and ketone metabolism when designing dietary or therapeutic interventions.

abstract: Gene therapy offers a fundamental approach to treating genetic disorders, malignant tumors, and refractory chronic diseases by directly modifying or replacing defective genes at the molecular level. Driven by policy support, increased investment, and technological innovation, China has achieved remarkable progress in adenoviral and adeno-associated virus (AAV) vectors, gene editing, genetically engineered immune cells, oncolytic microorganisms, and small nucleic acid drugs. This review provides a comprehensive narrative overview of the technical principles, product pipelines, and clinical advances in these fields. Notable achievements include the approval of AAV-based gene therapy products in China, the entry of multiple in vivo and ex vivo gene editing therapies into clinical trials, a leading number of CAR-T trials worldwide with expansion into solid tumors and autoimmune diseases, encouraging efficacy of oncolytic virotherapy in liver cancer and melanoma, and positive clinical data of small interfering RNA/antisense oligonucleotide drugs for chronic hepatitis B and hypercholesterolemia. However, challenges remain including suboptimal tissue specificity, off-target risks, limited cargo capacity, high production costs, and poor accessibility. Future directions should focus on tissue-selective vectors, precise editing tools, off-the-shelf cell products, scalable manufacturing, and improved regulatory frameworks. With abundant clinical resources and strong manufacturing capabilities, China is poised to play a significant role in the global gene therapy landscape.

abstract: Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) remains a major cause of severe lower respiratory tract disease in infants, older adults, and immunocompromised individuals, underscoring the need for vaccine strategies that balance systemic protection with frontline respiratory immunity. Although adenoviral and RNA-based RSV are both promising platforms, how the platform itself shapes systemic versus respiratory mucosal immunity under the same antigenic context remains insufficiently defined. We conducted a head-to-head comparison of an LNP-delivered saRNA vaccine (LNP-RSV-preF saRNA) and a recombinant Ad5-vectored vaccine (Ad5-RSV-preF) in mice using intramuscular prime-boost immunization. The two platforms drove distinct immune architectures rather than just differences in response magnitude. LNP-RSV-preF saRNA preferentially promoted respiratory mucosal immunity, including elevated BALF IgG, pulmonary antibody-secreting cells, CD69+ T cells, and lung-resident memory T (TRM) cells, as well as cycling and memory-associated CD8+ T-cell states and durable lung IgA memory. In contrast, Ad5-RSV-preF induced stronger systemic immunity, featured by higher early serum IgG, splenic polyfunctional effector T cells, enhanced germinal center/TFH responses, and effector-polarized CD8 + T cells, with sustained systemic humoral memory. Ad5-vectored and LNP-saRNA vaccine platforms induce distinct compartmentalized immune responses to the same RSV preF antigen. This study establishes a framework for rational platform selection in RSV vaccine design, enabling tailored strategies to balance systemic immunity and respiratory mucosal memory.

abstract:
CAD is driven by atherosclerosis in the coronary arteries and is a major cause of myocardial infarction, heart failure, arrhythmias, and premature death. Despite contemporary secondary prevention including lipid lowering, revascularization when indicated, and antiplatelet therapy, participants with established CAD, particularly those post-ACS, remain at clinically meaningful residual risk of recurrent atherothrombotic events.

Intensifying antithrombotic therapy can reduce ischemic events but typically increases bleeding, as exemplified by the addition of low dose rivaroxaban to aspirin in stable atherosclerotic disease. This persistent efficacy-safety trade-off supports development of antithrombotic approaches that reduce pathological thrombosis while preserving hemostasis.

RBD1119 is a GalNAc-conjugated siRNA that targets factor XI mRNA in hepatocytes. The GalNAc moiety binds the asialoglycoprotein receptor on hepatocyte surfaces, enabling receptor mediated endocytosis and preferential hepatic uptake. Once internalized, RBD1119 mediates cleavage of factor XI mRNA via the RNA interference pathway, reducing hepatic factor XI expression and lowering circulating factor XI levels.

This multicenter, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, phase II trial will evaluate the PD, safety, and PK of subcutaneously administered RBD1119 in participants with stable coronary artery disease (CAD).

description:
CAD is caused by atherosclerosis in the coronary arteries and remains a leading cause of MI, heart failure, arrhythmias, and premature death, with substantial residual risk of recurrent atherothrombotic events even after standard secondary prevention. More intensive antithrombotic therapy can lower ischemic events, but this benefit is often offset by increased bleeding, highlighting the need for treatments that better separate antithrombotic efficacy from bleeding risk. Factor XI, part of the intrinsic coagulation pathway, has emerged as a promising target because its inhibition reduces thrombin amplification and prolongs aPTT without affecting prothrombin time, suggesting potential for safer anticoagulation with less disruption of normal hemostasis.

The trial comprises screening, treatment, and long-term safety follow-up periods. Participants will be allocated to one of three different dose levels of RBD1119 or placebo: low-dose (n=40), medium-dose (n=60), high-dose (n=60) or placebo (n=40). Approximately 200 participants will be randomized.

Randomization to the RBD1119 low-dose dose group and corresponding placebo proceeds without dose-specific staggering. Randomization to the medium-dose group is initially limited to 10 participants, comprising 8 participants assigned to RBD1119 medium-dose and 2 assigned to placebo. Further randomization is paused until participants have received Dose X on Day Y and completed safety follow-up through Day 43. Randomization resumes only after IDMC review, a recommendation to continue, and Sponsor authorization. Initiation of the high-dose group requires prior IDMC review of the initial medium-dose cohort and Sponsor authorization. The same initial cohort, safety follow-up, IDMC review, and authorization process is then applied to the high-dose group. A planned IDMC review will not be delayed solely because fewer than all 10 participants in an initial dose cohort have received the second dose or completed follow-up through Day 43.

abstract: Cowpea Chlorotic Mottle Virus (CCMV) is an icosahedral plant virus composed of 180 monomeric units of the capsid protein. Virions encapsulate the viral RNA genome, which can be removed from the virion by changing pH conditions, after which the capsid proteins can be reversibly assembled to form empty CCMV virus-like particles (VLPs), or VLPs that have encapsulated either heterologous DNA or RNA. Earlier research has shown that CCMV VLPs are suitable as delivery vehicles for heterologous DNA/RNA molecules into mammalian cells, leading to subsequent expression of their encoded genes. In this study, we evaluated the potential of CCMV VLPs to encapsulate nucleic acids and transfer them to fish cells in vitro, and to zebrafish larvae and juveniles in vivo. VLPs containing pVax-GFP plasmid (3690 bp) were stable for up to 5 weeks in buffer at pH 7.2 and pH 5, whereas VLPs containing GFP-mRNA (1168 nt) were stable for up to 3 weeks, but only when stored in a buffer at pH 4.5. When administered directly to the culture medium, VLPs were readily taken up by fish as well as mammalian cell lines but could not unpack and transfer nucleic acids to the cells. VLPs delivered by transfection however, could transfer nucleic acids to the cells, leading to reporter gene expression. When VLPs were administered directly to the culture medium along with the cell-penetrating peptide dfTAT, only VLPs containing pVax-GFP in pH 7.2 buffer were able to transfer DNA to mammalian but not fish cells. In vivo however, upon intramuscular injection, the same VLPs were able to transfer plasmid DNA to myocytes of zebrafish larvae and juveniles as efficiently as when injecting naked plasmid DNA. Altogether, these findings provide the foundation for future studies on the use of CCMV VLPs as delivery vehicles for DNA or RNA to fish cells.

abstract: RNA-based genetic cargos have emerged as versatile tools in both fundamental research and translational medicine, with growing applications in regenerative medicine, gene therapy, cell therapy, and vaccination. As the field advances beyond single-RNA delivery, coordinated engineering of multiple RNA species is enabling increasingly sophisticated and combinatorial biological functions. However, this shift raises a fundamental challenge: what combination and stoichiometry of RNA species should be delivered together to achieve a desired cellular function? As the number of RNA components increases, the design space expands combinatorially, making conventional optimization strategies labor-intensive and poorly scalable. Here, we introduce StoichRNA, a framework for scalable exploration of multi-RNA stoichiometry in a single experiment. Individual RNA species are delivered independently, each coupled to a distinct fluorescent marker that reports its intracellular abundance. Because uptake is stochastic, each cell acquires a unique combination and copy number of RNA components. Across a sufficiently large population, cells collectively sample a broad stoichiometric landscape, allowing single-cell readouts such as flow cytometry to quantitatively map system output as a function of intracellular RNA composition. We first establish the conceptual validity of this approach by showing that StoichRNA-derived single-cell data can recover and predict the behavior of fixed-ratio RNA formulations. We then apply this framework to representative RNA circuits, demonstrating that StoichRNA can reveal design principles and identify improved stoichiometries that would be difficult to uncover through conventional workflows. Finally, we extend StoichRNA optimization to translationally relevant settings, including control of cell-state engineering in human induced pluripotent stem cells and tuning of RNA-based logic circuits for precision medicine applications. Together, these results establish StoichRNA as a generalizable strategy for engineering combinatorial RNA systems and provide a scalable solution to a central bottleneck in RNA circuit design.

abstract: The goal of this clinical trial is to look at the effect of SGLT2 (Sodium glucose transporter 2) inhibition in patients receiving a kidney-transplant 6 weeks earlier at Oslo University hospital. Rikshospitalet. Investigators will search for answers along three pathways: Can SGLT2 inhibitor 1) preserve glomerular filtration rate (GFR), 2) reduce interstitial fibrosis in the kidney, and 3) favorably improve metabolic risk factors for graft failure such as visceral obesity, glucose intolerance and high blood pressure? The participants (N=330) will be randomized to either dapagliflozin 10 mg or placebo o.d. in a blinded fashion. Researchers will than use kidney transplant biopsies, measured GFR, blood pressure sampling, glucose tolerance test (OGTT), dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DXA scan) and estimated GFR from the two groups in comparison, to evaluate the effect treatment. The participants will be followed for a total of 3 years.

description:
This is a randomized, placebo-controlled trial with dapagliflozin 10 mg vs. placebo o.d. in kidney transplant patients. The patients are randomized 1:1 to active: placebo treatment 6 weeks after transplantation and followed for a total of 150 weeks (156 weeks post-transplant).

Before treatment initiation (6 weeks after transplantation) the following investigations will be performed;

1. Estimated GFR: Assessed using the Modification of Diet in Renal Disease 4 (MDRD-4) formula and is presented as mL/min/1.73 m2. Plasma creatinine concentrations are to be analyzed at the Department of Medical Biochemistry where the patient is followed and is presented as mmol/L. (Estimated GFR will be calculated from at least 4 plasma creatinine measurements per year).
2. Blood sample: Measured variables include plasma creatinine, hemoglobin, hematocrit, sodium, potassium, magnesium and uric acid.
3. Kidney tissue analyses: a.) Light microscopical evaluation in formalin-fixed and paraffin-embedded (FFPE) kidney graft biopsies: Semi-quantitative estimation of percent graft fibrosis in the renal cortex according to the Banff classification, percent interstitial fibrosis and percent inflammation outside fibrotic scars. b.) Immunohistochemistry: Graft samples will be deparaffinized and boiled in antigen retrieval solution and then exposed to primary antibodies against collagen and extracellular matrix markers, e.g. periostin, tenascin and picrosirius red. In addition, p16INKa, a marker of premature aging, and endothelial markers to evaluate capillary density will be used.

   c.) Samples will be digitally scanned to perform digital morphometric evaluation using the softwares 3D Histech, Analysis Pro and QuPath. Areas not of interest (renal medulla, scar tissue, capsule or subscapular areas), poor quality scans and artefacts will be excluded. Digital software will also be used to estimate glomerular volume and mesangial volume fraction using QuPath. All evaluations will be performed by investigators blinded for the study participants' identity and clinical data. This is an explorative study, and no power estimate is available.

   d.) The investigators will also perform molecular analyses, mRNA and proteomics in a subsample (n=25 in intervention, n=25 in control group, matched for age, gender and eGFR as appropriate) at the same two time-points as described above (altogether n=100 biopsies processed for RNA sequencing and proteomics), using standard bulk mRNA/miRNA sequencing and proteomics of whole sections from 'RNA later' kidney graft biopsies (Genomics and Proteomics Core Facilities, UiO). The investigators will also perform bioinformatic analyses focusing on fibrosis.
4. Oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT): Will be performed in persons not on glucose-lowering treatment by ingestion of 75 g glucose dissolved in water (or 1 g/kg if body weight is \<75 kg). Blood samples for measurements of glucose, insulin and C-peptide are collected at 0, 30 and 120 min, respectively. Glucose tolerance is assessed by the 2-h glucose value, while first phase insulin release is primarily reflected by the 30 min insulin value which is included in the Stumvoll equation which measures both first and second phase insulin release. Insulin sensitivity will be assessed by the Matsuda equation.
5. Protein/creatinine ratio: Will be assessed at the Department of Medical Biochemistry where the patient is followed. Open urinary stix is not considered appropriate, partly due to the risk of unblinding in case of glucosuria detection by a combined stix. (Protein/ creatinine ratio will be collected from at least 4 urine sample measurements per year)
6. Blood Pressure: Will be assessed as both systolic and diastolic measure, and measurements are performed according to standard procedures (measured in mmHg ). The same standard will be followed for blood pressure measurements at the local hospitals.
7. Metabolomics: Urine and serum will be sent on dry ice in larger batches. LC-MS methodology will be used for the analysis, using a commercial kit (Biocrates). ELISA methodology will in addition be used in case verification analyses are necessary. This exploratory analysis will focus on markers for fibrosis, inflammation and secretion function in the kidney tubuli.

   After 2 weeks the patients will go through repeated blood sampling and blood pressure measurements, followed by the following procedures;
8. Measured GFR: Assessed at the Laboratory for Renal Physiology, by the iohexol serum clearance method utilizing the Bayesian estimate 4-point method. Serum samples are to be obtained 10 min, 30 min, 2 h and 5 h after administration of 5 mL Omnipaque (300 mg I/mL). measured GFR (Iohexol serum clearance) and DXA assessed body composition (subcutaneous and visceral fat percentage of total fat mass) is assessed, after 72 weeks of treatment all investigations/biobanking performed before and after 2 weeks are repeated. Then, after 150 weeks, the final visit is performed, including blood pressure measurements and the urinary protein/creatinine ratio and clinical chemistry determinations.
9. DXA scan: Total body composition will be determined by a narrow fan-beam Lunar Prodigy Densitometer (GE Healthcare) and all the scans will be analysed using enCORER software version 14.10 (GE Medical Systems, Lunar Corp., Madison, WI). The automated software is capable of discriminating subcutaneus adipose tissue (SAT) and visceral adipose tissue (VAT) within android region of interest (ROI). In vivo, short-term coefficients of variation for total body tissue and lean and fat mass are 0.1%, 0.8%, and 2.5%. The VAT short-term repeat measurement error coefficient of variation is 9.8% DXA-derived VAT was previously validated against CT, the standard method for the quantitative assessment of intra abdominal adipose tissue.

At week 78 patients will go through repeated analyses of the tests listed above. They will also go through 24 hour blood pressure tests 8 weeks, 72 weeks and 150 weeks after randomization.

Throughout the study all plasma creatinine and urinary protein/creatinine ratios will be included in the study clinical research form (CRF). Safety measures will also be included. Measured GFR will measure the chronic GFR slope, while estimated GFR will assess the total GFR slope (both the early dip and the chronic slope of GFR). Furthermore, after the final study visit, which represents150 weeks of blinded treatment, all patients will be allowed further open treatment with SGLT2-inhibitors to the discretion of the treating physician and the patient. Furthermore, eGFR slope, graft loss and cardiovascular events will be followed based on annual data from the Norwegian Renal Registry for up to 10 years after transplantation.

For a more detailed description of primary and secondary objectives and endpoints see bellow.

abstract: Crustacean aquaculture, particularly shrimp, crab, and lobster production, contributes around US$10 billion annually to the global food supply but remains highly vulnerable to viral and bacterial diseases. Pathogens such as White Spot Syndrome Virus (WSSV), Yellow Head Virus (YHV), Taura Syndrome Virus (TSV), and Vibrio species continue to cause substantial economic losses, and conventional management based on visual inspection, histopathology, and antimicrobial treatment is often slow and insensitive. This review examines how nucleic acid technologies are reshaping diagnostics, therapeutics, and surveillance in crustacean health management. Molecular diagnostic platforms including PCR, quantitative PCR, reverse transcription PCR, loop mediated isothermal amplification, recombinase polymerase amplification, and multiplex assays allow rapid, sensitive, and specific detection of pathogens, often before clinical signs appear. RNA interference shows strong therapeutic promise against viral pathogens, with experimental studies reporting 40 to 80% reductions in cumulative mortality, although stability, dosing, delivery, and production cost continue to limit commercial use. CRISPR (Clustered Regularly Interspaced Short Palindromic Repeats) and Cas (CRISPR-associated) has emerged as a powerful platform for functional genomics, immune gene characterisation, and the future development of disease resistant strains, though application in crustaceans remains largely proof of concept. Environmental DNA and molecular biosurveillance enable early pathogen detection through water and sediment sampling, supporting proactive biosecurity and precision aquaculture. Persistent barriers include scalability, infrastructure gaps in producing regions, regulatory uncertainty, and public acceptance. Future progress will rely on improved delivery systems, expanded crustacean genomic resources, and integration of molecular tools with digital farm management to deliver sustainable disease control.

abstract: Lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) have transformed RNA therapeutics through their high delivery efficiency, scalable manufacturing, and favorable safety profiles, as demonstrated by COVID-19 mRNA vaccines and clinically approved small interfering RNA (siRNA) therapeutics. However, extending RNA delivery beyond the liver to extrahepatic tissues, including the spleen, lungs, lymph nodes, brain, and tumors, remains challenging because of the intrinsic hepatotropism of conventional LNPs and their limited cell-type specificity. Recent advances in lipid chemistry, particle engineering, surface functionalization, protein corona modulation, and route-specific administration have enabled new strategies to redirect LNPs toward specific tissues and cell populations. This review systematically examines these approaches and highlights key determinants of LNP tropism, including formulation composition, surface properties, endogenous protein adsorption, and administration route. We further discuss the clinical translation of extrahepatic LNP delivery, covering clinically validated products, emerging therapeutic candidates, and gaps between preclinical models and human applications. Major challenges include cell-resolved biodistribution, long-term safety, repeated-dose immunogenicity, cross-study comparability, and standardized quantitative assessment. Finally, we explore how high-throughput screening, machine learning, and data-driven design can accelerate the rational optimization of next-generation LNPs. These advances may facilitate precise tissue- and cell-selective RNA delivery, expanding the therapeutic potential of RNA medicines beyond the liver.

abstract: Introduction In February 2025, a single infant with carbamoyl phosphate synthetase 1 deficiency received a customized base-editing therapy, and individualized gene editing has since been discussed as an emerging category of care. No one has yet counted whether this category exists in the registered study record. Methods We conducted a cross-sectional census of interventional studies of human gene-editing agents registered on ClinicalTrials.gov. Records were retrieved through the ClinicalTrials.gov application programming interface, version 2, with a verbatim, intervention-scoped query and a fixed census date of 17 September 2026. Eligibility was verified from each record's own fields, and every exclusion is supported by the field value that justifies it. Two independent screening passes classified each eligible record as single-participant or n-of-1, multi-variant umbrella or platform-designated, or conventional cohort. Agreement was quantified with Cohen's kappa and a 95% confidence interval (CI). Records in the individualized and platform classes were re-verified against their complete registry entries and version histories. We also searched public US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) records for the regulatory route of each census record. Reporting follows the Strengthening the Reporting of Observational Studies in Epidemiology (STROBE) statement. Results Of 212 retrieved records, 64 were excluded, and 148 were eligible. Four eligible records were single-participant or n-of-1 designs, and three were multi-variant umbrella or platform-designated designs, giving a census of seven studies. Of the remainder, 140 were conventional cohorts, and one was an editing arm inside a non-editing platform trial. Version histories confirmed the four single-participant designs; one of them reached an enrolment of one through a revision made before enrolment began. The same histories showed that three other records had an enrolment of one or two only because of termination or under-enrolment. Only two of the 148 eligible records describe a construct designed for the individual participant. No publicly verifiable platform technology designation was located for any census record, and the census query returned no expanded-access record. Of 23 studies completed more than 12 months before the census, five had posted results (21.7%, Wilson 95% CI: 9.7%-41.9%); because this interval is wide, the figure is reported as context only. Agreement on design class was moderate (kappa, 0.540; 95% CI, 0.264-0.815). Conclusions Nineteen months after the first individualized CRISPR treatment, the registry contains seven individualized or platform-designated gene-editing studies, and only two records describe an individualized construct. The regulatory pathway used by the index case was not retrievable from the registry, and no regulatory route could be verified from public records; this is an absence of public evidence, not evidence that no route existed. These counts describe the ClinicalTrials.gov record, not the prevalence of individualized gene editing, and the design-class counts are provisional given moderate agreement.

abstract: Infant neuroblastoma (NB), defined by diagnosis during the first year of life, represents a clinically heterogeneous disease spectrum ranging from localized tumours with favourable outcomes and a capacity for spontaneous regression, to high-risk metastatic disease requiring intensive multimodal therapy. In infants, treatment intensity is determined by disease stage, tumor biology, MYCN status, risk classification, symptoms, response to therapy, and metastatic involvement, particularly relevant to high-risk disease, consequently the potential toxicity of intensive treatment is specific to high-risk disease, as compared to favorable risk tumors which can be managed with surgery, reduced frequency techniques, or observations. Important determinations of neuroblastoma biology and prognosis are genetic alterations involving MYCN and ALK, but the predominately investigated field with therapeutic feasibility of targeting these changes with CRISPR/Cas9 is in preclinical neuroblastoma models rather than in infants. An investigational hypothesis is accordingly considered by their potential relevance to infant neuroblastoma rather than an established clinical application. The safe and efficient in vivo delivery of CRISPR/Cas9 components remains a major challenge, owing to cargo size, immunogenicity, and degradation, particularly within the delicate physiological environment of infants. This review emphasises the need for advanced delivery systems, focusing on the potential of nanoparticle-mediated approaches. Emerging preclinical findings support the feasibility of nanoparticle-mediated CRISPR/Cas9 delivery, although direct evidence in infant neuroblastoma remains limited. Importantly, the evidence for nanoparticle-mediated CRISPR/Cas9 therapy remains largely preclinical. Studies performed in general neuroblastoma models, non-cancer models, or adult cancers should not be interpreted as direct evidence of efficacy in infant neuroblastoma.

title: Precision gene editing in infant neuroblastoma: a review of nanoparticle: enabled CRISPR/Cas9 therapies.

abstract: Fluorogenic RNA aptamers have emerged as powerful molecular tools for cancer imaging, biosensing, and biomarker detection due to their high specificity, low background fluorescence, and genetic encodability. These short RNA molecules activate fluorescence upon binding specific fluorogens, enabling real-time visualization of intracellular targets and dynamic molecular processes in living systems. Recent advances in RNA structural engineering, fluorophore optimization, and biosensor integration have significantly expanded the translational applications of fluorogenic aptamers in oncology. This mini-review summarizes the structural principles, fluorescence activation mechanisms, and cancer-related applications of fluorogenic RNA aptamers and related nucleic acid biosensors. Foundational studies describing the architecture of fluorogenic aptamer families, including Spinach, Broccoli, Mango, Pepper, Squash, and Beetroot, are discussed with emphasis on G-quadruplex-mediated fluorogen stabilization and fluorescence enhancement. Furthermore, recent developments in CRISPR/Cas-assisted fluorogenic biosensors, dual-color RNA imaging systems, fluorogenic DNAzymes, and amplification-driven aptamer platforms are highlighted. Direct applications across multiple malignancies, including brain, breast, colorectal, liver, lung, prostate, and skin cancers, demonstrate the growing utility of these technologies for tumor-associated RNA detection, epigenetic biomarker analysis, molecular imaging, and therapeutic monitoring. In addition, advances in fluorescence brightness, structural stability, and multiplex imaging strategies have improved the sensitivity and adaptability of fluorogenic RNA systems for complex biological environments. Despite current limitations related to RNA stability, intracellular delivery, and tissue penetration, fluorogenic RNA aptamers represent highly promising tools for next-generation precision oncology. Continued integration with nanotechnology, live-cell imaging, artificial intelligence, and molecular diagnostics is expected to enhance further their clinical and translational potential in cancer research and personalized medicine.

title: Fluorogenic RNA aptamers in cancer: emerging platforms for molecular imaging, biosensing, and precision oncology.

abstract: Nanomedicine has become an important translational platform in oncology by enabling altered pharmacokinetics, controlled exposure, reduced systemic toxicity, intracellular delivery of nucleic acids, and improved handling of complex therapeutic payloads. Early cancer nanomedicines, including pegylated liposomal cytotoxics and albumin-bound drug products, demonstrated that nanoscale formulation design could improve the clinical utility of established anticancer agents. More recently, lipid nanoparticles, RNA therapeutics, individualized neoantigen vaccines, gene-regulatory approaches, and immune-modulating delivery systems have expanded the role of nanoparticles from passive drug carriers to programmable oncology platforms. This narrative review examines the developmental evolution of cancer-focused pharmaceutical nanoparticles, with emphasis on liposomes, lipid nanoparticles (LNPs), albumin-bound systems, polymeric particles, polymeric micelles, nanocrystals, nanoemulsions, solid lipid nanoparticles, inorganic particles, extracellular vesicles, and hybrid delivery technologies. Each platform class is treated systematically, covering representative approved products, formulation characteristics, route of administration, clinical evidence, and the specific development risks that limit it. There view connects platform design with oncology-specific barriers, including tumor heterogeneity, variable enhanced permeability and retention (EPR) effects, dense extracellular matrix, abnormal tumor vasculature, mononuclear phagocyte clearance, protein-corona formation, endosomal escape, immune activation, and the difficulty of translating animal tumor models into clinical benefit. These barriers are organized as a sequential delivery cascade, and the behavior of each platform class is compared step by step rather than described as a set of universal phenomena. Nanoparticle candidates that accumulated well in preclinical tumors but failed in clinical trials are examined alongside approved products, because the contrast between the two is where most of the transferable lessons sit. A product-development perspective is used to discuss critical quality attributes (CQAs), manufacturing scalability, potency testing, sterility strategy, stability, release methods, regulatory expectations, commercial feasibility, and clinical differentiation. A development-to-translation framework is proposed for comparing cancer nanomedicine platforms across formulation maturity, analytical maturity, manufacturing maturity, biological rationale, clinical evidence, regulatory readiness, and commercial feasibility; regulatory and commercial maturity are scored separately, the criteria behind each level are defined explicitly, and the resulting rankings are presented as a heuristic aid to discussion rather than a validated quantitative metric. Future progress in oncology nanomedicine will depend not only on novel materials or targeting claims, but also on disciplined product design, biologically meaningful potency assays, scalable manufacturing, patient-selection strategies, and clear integration with precision oncology.

abstract: This is an open-label, dose escalation study in patients with relapsed and refractory autoimmune diseases. Study drug, TI-0032-III injection, is composed of lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) targeting T cells that encapsulate circular RNA encoding the CD19 chimeric antigen receptor (CAR), which is a therapeutic biological product. It is clinically intended for the treatment of various relapsed and refractory B cell-related autoimmune diseases, such as systemic lupus erythematosus, sjögren's syndrome, systemic sclerosis, idiopathic inflammatory myositis, and antiphospholipid syndrome.

abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) in Staphylococcus aureus (S. aureus) poses a serious global health threat, undermining treatment outcomes and necessitating the development of innovative therapeutic strategies. Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) is a major contributor to this burden, with increasing prevalence in hospitals, contaminated food, and environmental sources. The coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) pandemic further intensified S. aureus resistance due to widespread antibiotic misuse. Biofilm formation, which facilitates the horizontal transfer of resistance genes such as mecA (methicillin resistance gene A), plays a central role in the development of resistance. To counteract antibiotic-resistant S. aureus, alternative approaches have emerged, including antimicrobial peptides (AMPs), photodynamic therapy (PDT), and drug repurposing guided by artificial intelligence (AI). Cutting-edge technologies such as clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats (CRISPR)-CRISPR-associated protein 13a (Cas13a)-based gene editing and engineered bacteriophages offer promising avenues for targeting resistant strains. Natural compounds such as thymol and chlorogenic acid (CGA) have also shown potential in reducing resistance and inhibiting biofilm formation. Effective management of AMR requires strengthened antibiotic stewardship programs (ASPs), robust surveillance systems, and public health measures such as proper hand hygiene and environmental sanitation. Combining antibiotic adjuvants (AAs) with existing antibiotics and leveraging bioactive peptides (BAPs) can enhance antibiotic efficacy against multidrug-resistant (MDR), extensively drug-resistant (XDR), and pan-drug-resistant (PDR) S. aureus. This review investigates the prevalence and resistance mechanisms of S. aureus in clinical, food, and environmental contexts, explores promising alternative therapies, and emphasizes the urgent need for global antimicrobial stewardship (AMS) and sustainable intervention strategies.

abstract: Obesity leads to metabolic dysregulation and thus drives complications including type 2 diabetes, cardiovascular disease, steatotic liver disease and some cancers. Obesity is primarily driven by lifestyle factors, which impacts individuals differently depending on their genetic susceptibility. Studies on this genetic risk have provided major insights into gene networks that modulate obesity development, including incretins and their regulatory circuits. Indeed, incretin-based therapeutics (i.e. GLP1 RA) have proven to be enormously successful in promoting weight loss, but do so with several ongoing challenges including significant weight rebound upon cessation, loss of lean mass, and side effects that reduce therapeutic longevity. Thus, ongoing research is necessary to identify additional interventions that overcome or minimise these concerns. To this end, in our previous work we have identified a novel lipid regulatory protein with potential to influence lipid storage. In the current study, we use antisense oligonucleotides (ASO) to silence this protein in mouse models of diet induced obesity, and demonstrate that once weekly IP injections of ASO prevents the development of obesity, and defends against the progression of existing obesity. This is shown to be effective in multiple mouse strains fed different diets over various time frames, with gene targeting ASOs leading to reductions in fat mass, no change in lean mass, along with improvements in whole body glucose tolerance and steatotic liver disease. Additional studies demonstrate that this phenotype is likely driven by effects in adipose tissue, but not liver, and is not linked to activation of the Type 1 Interferon response, a previously implicated off target effect of ASO administration. Thus, these studies demonstrate that our injectable ASO approach in mice can successfully treat obesity in the absence of major change in lean mass, thus positioning this intervention as a therapeutic program that works alternatively to, or in conjunction with current weight loss medicines.
